Operators at the same level associate left-to-right. Thus x | y & z means x | (y & z), while x ~ y & z means (x ~ y) & z. Parenthesise policy expressions even when precedence is known:

jj file list -- 'root:"src" ~ root-glob:"**/*.generated.*"'
jj diff -- '(glob:"**/*.rs" | glob:"**/*.toml") ~ glob:"target/**"'
jj split -- 'tests & ~glob:"**/fixtures/**"'

The function inventory is intentionally small in the target release: all() selects every path and none() selects no paths. Most practical composition is written with patterns and operators. Fileset aliases can add domain vocabulary:

[fileset-aliases]
LOCK = '**/Cargo.lock | **/package-lock.json | **/uv.lock'
SOURCE = 'root-prefix-glob:"src/**" | root-prefix-glob:"include/**"'
'not:x' = '~x'

An alias can be a symbol, a function, or a pattern alias. Alias functions can be overloaded by parameter count, but a user alias with a builtin name shadows the builtin. Description tables with definition and doc make aliases visible to completion.

Quoting: three concrete failures

CommandWhat happensCorrect form
jj diff ~Cargo.lockThe shell may interpret ~ as a home-directory expansion or pass an unintended token.jj diff '~Cargo.lock'
jj diff '~"Foo Bar"'The inner quotes are fileset-language quotes because ~ is an operator. The outer quotes are shell quotes that preserve the whole expression.For a simple path, either jj diff 'Foo Bar' or jj diff Foo\ Bar is sufficient; with the operator, use jj diff '~"Foo Bar"'.
jj diff "Foo(1)"The shell removes its double quotes, so jj receives Foo(1) and may parse the parentheses as fileset syntax.jj diff -- 'file:"Foo(1)"': outer quotes are for Bash; inner quotes are for jj's fileset parser.
jj diff ~glob:**/*.rsShell metacharacters and jj operators are exposed simultaneously.jj diff '~glob:"**/*.rs"'

There are two different quoting layers. In jj diff -- 'file:"Foo(1)"', the outer single quotes are removed by Bash and preserve the complete fileset argument; the inner double quotes reach jj and tell its fileset parser that Foo(1) is a literal path, not an expression containing parentheses. For a simple path containing spaces, the fileset parser does not require inner quotes: the shell can either quote the argument, as in jj diff 'Foo Bar', or escape the space, as in jj diff Foo\ Bar. Once the fileset contains an operator or function call, use inner fileset quotes for the literal path, as in jj diff '~"Foo Bar"'. Do not confuse shell escaping with fileset escaping: a backslash inside an outer single-quoted fileset is passed to jj rather than removed by Bash. The safest durable rule is to quote the complete fileset and quote inner literal strings when the fileset parser needs to distinguish a path from an operator.

Evaluate before rewriting

There is no separate fileset evaluator command, so use a read-only consumer. jj file list displays matching paths in a tree; jj diff --name-only shows changed paths; and jj file search --name-only tests a content-related path restriction.

jj file list -r @ -- 'root-prefix-glob:"src/**"'
jj diff -r @ --name-only -- 'root:"src" ~ root-glob:"**/*.rs"'
jj file list -r main@origin -- LOCK

When evaluating a fileset for a rewrite, first establish the selected tree and then the selected change. A fileset cannot select a path that is absent from the source tree. The separate question of which paths are materialised in the current workspace is covered with workspace management in Part XII.

Consumer contracts

ConsumerFileset roleImportant interaction
diffRestricts displayed paths.Does not change commit range; use -r/--from/--to separately.
restoreRestricts copied/undone content.Commit options choose source/destination; fileset is not a commit selector.
squashRestricts diff ownership movement.Partial squash can leave a non-empty source and rewrite descendants.
splitSelects content for one side.Unselected paths remain in the other resulting change; inspect both.
fixRestricts fixer paths.Commit domain is selected by -s; fixer configuration also filters files.
commitSelects paths included before child creation.Unselected working-copy edits remain in the new child.
file list/show/searchTree/search path selection.Commit option controls the tree; file search pattern controls content.
resolveRestricts conflicted paths.Use resolve --list to discover valid paths first.

The fileset language selects paths for a command; it does not decide the general materialisation policy of a workspace. That second concern is intentionally deferred to Part XII.

Fileset review checklist

  1. Which coordinate system does the expression use: cwd or root?
  2. Is the intent exact file, prefix, non-recursive glob, recursive glob, or prefix-glob?
  3. Did the shell preserve the expression?
  4. What does the expression select in jj file list?
  5. Is the consumer selecting output, file contents, diff ownership, or workspace materialisation?
  6. Does a partial operation leave a source remainder or rewrite descendants?
  7. Would a fileset alias shadow a builtin or depend on a repository-specific config layer?

The 0.45.1 grammar, patterns, precedence, aliases, and functions in this chapter follow jj help -k filesets. Appendix D repeats them as a compact reference; the chapter supplies the reasoning and command interactions.

Fileset laboratory: evaluate paths against a real tree

A fileset is evaluated against a tree, not against a commit graph. Begin with a repository tree like this:

.
|-- Cargo.toml
|-- src/
|   |-- main.rs
|   |-- parser.rs
|   \-- parser/
|       |-- lexer.rs
|       \-- tests.rs
|-- tests/
|   |-- cli.rs
|   \-- fixtures/
|       |-- basic.txt
|       \-- malformed.txt
|-- docs/
|   |-- design.md
|   \-- api/
|       \-- parser.md
\-- .github/workflows/check.yml

The same path can be selected in several ways, with different scope. A literal file names one path. A glob pattern is interpreted according to the fileset grammar and its matching scope. A root-qualified expression makes the repository root explicit; a cwd-qualified expression makes the command’s current directory explicit. This distinction matters when a command is run from src/parser or from a script whose working directory is not stable.

jj file list 'file:src/parser.rs'
jj file list 'root-file:src/parser.rs'
jj file list 'glob:src/**/*.rs'
jj file list 'root-glob:src/**/*.rs'
jj file list 'cwd-file:parser.rs'
jj file list 'cwd-glob:**/*.rs'

Run these from the repository root and from src/parser to see why explicit root forms are safer in documentation and automation. A shell glob such as src/**/*.rs can be expanded by the shell before jj sees it, depending on shell options. Quote the entire fileset. The glob: prefix is part of jj’s language and is not a request for the shell to expand anything.

Set algebra over paths

Fileset union, intersection, and difference operate over the set of paths matched in the selected tree. A typical review selection can be expressed as:

'glob:src/**/*.rs | glob:tests/**/*.rs'
'glob:**/*.rs ~ glob:**/tests.rs'
'glob:src/**/*.rs & glob:**/parser/**'

Read these left to right only after applying the documented precedence. Parenthesise mixed expressions. The first selects Rust source and Rust tests. The second removes files named tests.rs from an otherwise recursive Rust selection. The third selects parser paths that are also Rust paths. all() and none() are useful as identity and empty values in aliases, but an unconstrained all() passed to a rewriting command is a powerful operation: inspect it first.

[fileset-aliases]
rust = 'glob:**/*.rs'
parser-code = 'glob:src/parser/**/*.rs | root-file:src/parser.rs'
non-tests = 'rust ~ glob:**/tests.rs'

Keep fileset aliases semantically narrow. An alias named source should document whether it includes generated code, tests, examples, and hidden directories. Aliases are configuration, so a repository-local alias can alter the meaning of a command copied from another repository. When portability matters, expand the alias in a review script or print the active config with jj config list.

Filesets and commit selection are orthogonal

Many commands accept both a commit selection and a fileset. The commit answers “which tree or diff is being operated on?”; the fileset answers “which paths within that tree or diff?”. Confusing these layers is a common source of destructive surprises.

Command familyCommit roleFileset role
diffCompare a commit or range of trees.Limit displayed paths.
restoreChoose source and destination commits.Copy only selected paths from source to destination.
squashChoose source and destination changes.Move selected diff paths into the destination.
splitChoose the commit to divide.First commit owns selected paths; remainder stays in the other commit.
fixChoose commits whose files are passed through fixers.Some fixers or command forms restrict paths.
file list/show/searchChoose the tree or commit to inspect.Filter the displayed or searched paths.

For a partial squash, inspect both the source and destination before and after:

jj diff --from C --to C- 'glob:src/**/*.rs'
jj squash --from C --into B 'glob:src/parser/**/*.rs'
jj show C
jj show B

The exact option spellings and whether a command accepts a positional fileset or an option are version-sensitive; use the 0.45.1 entries in Part XV. The semantic test remains stable: a partial operation should leave an inspectable residual diff or a changed destination, not an unexplained disappearance.

Quoting and pattern failures

There are three different failure classes. First, the shell expands an unquoted wildcard and jj receives several path arguments or none. Second, jj parses a valid fileset but its scope is relative to a different working directory than intended. Third, the fileset is valid but selects an empty set because glob syntax was mistaken for regular-expression syntax. Diagnose in that order:

# Show what the shell would pass without running jj.
printf '%s\n' 'glob:src/**/*.rs'

# Ask jj to enumerate the selection.
jj file list 'root-glob:src/**/*.rs'

# Compare a literal and a glob.
jj file list 'root-file:src/parser.rs'
jj file list 'root-glob:src/**/parser.rs'

Do not use a regex mental model for glob wildcards. A glob’s *, **, directory separators, and prefix rules have language-specific semantics. Case-insensitive forms are explicit; they should not be assumed from the filesystem’s case behaviour. A path containing spaces or brackets must be quoted for both the shell and, where applicable, the fileset parser.

Filesets in patch-stack surgery

Filesets are most valuable when a change is conceptually mixed. Suppose B contains an API implementation and an unrelated documentation edit, while C contains tests for both. Rather than splitting by individual diff hunk interactively without a stated invariant, select the path family first:

B: src/parser.rs + docs/api/parser.md
C: tests/cli.rs + tests/fixtures/*

intent:
  move only docs/api/parser.md from B into a documentation change
  keep src/parser.rs in B
  preserve all C tests

Use diff to confirm the diff ownership, then squash or split with an explicit fileset. If a descendant’s tests become conflicted after the parent’s tree changes, that is evidence that the test diff depended on the old context; it is not evidence that the fileset was ignored. Inspect the evolved descendant and resolve or adjust it.

With restore, the direction matters. --from selects the source tree and --into selects the destination commit. A fileset limits copied content; it does not select which commit is edited. This makes a useful “take one generated file from a known commit” operation, but it is not a branch reset and should not be described as one.

Filesets as an API boundary

For shell automation, accept a fileset expression as one argument and pass it as one argument. Avoid concatenating user text into a larger unquoted revset/fileset. Print selected paths before mutation, and use a temporary operation bookmark if the operation is broad. A robust pattern is:

set -eu
paths='root-glob:src/**/*.rs ~ root-glob:src/**/generated/**'
jj file list "$paths"
jj diff -r @ "$paths"
# Only after review:
jj fix -s 'mutable() & ::@' -- "$paths"

If a command does not consume a fileset in the installed release, do not emulate it by passing paths after a revset. Some commands treat extra arguments as commits, options, or errors. The reference entry should be consulted for the command’s grammar, while this chapter supplies the language model needed to reason about selections.

Fileset semantics laboratory: path sets, not path strings

A fileset evaluates against a repository tree and returns a set of paths. The returned set has no commit identity and no template type. This separation is more than terminology: a command can select one commit and a fileset can select many paths within that commit's tree. If a command accepts both, the two selectors are evaluated independently and combined at the command's semantic boundary.

shell token                  jj parser                  consumer
"src ~ glob:\"**/*.gen\"" →  path-set expression     →  {src/**} minus generated files
                              operators/functions        applied to a tree or diff

There are three parsers to keep apart. The shell performs quote removal and, unless prevented, pathname expansion. jj then parses the remaining argument as a fileset. Finally the command decides whether the set applies to a tree, a diff, a snapshot policy, or a file metadata operation. A correct fileset can still produce an unexpected result if it is passed to a command whose default commit is not the one the reader had in mind.

Pattern families

In 0.45.1, an unqualified path is a cwd-relative prefix-glob. It matches the named file and paths below a named directory. The explicit forms make the intended scope reviewable:

FormMeaningExample and consequence
cwd:"path"Cwd-relative path prefix.cwd:src means src below the invocation directory.
file:"path"One exact cwd-relative file.Does not recursively include siblings.
glob:"*.rs"Cwd-relative Unix glob.Matches Rust files at that directory level, not below every subdirectory.
prefix-glob:"*.rs"Glob plus matching descendants of a matched prefix.Equivalent in shape to glob:"*.rs" | glob:"*.rs/**".
root:"docs"Workspace-root-relative prefix.Stable when a script changes cwd.
root-file:"LICENSE"One exact root-relative file.Useful for a root policy file without matching a directory.
root-glob:"docs/**/*.md"Root-relative recursive glob.Matches Markdown files below docs.
root-prefix-glob:"src"Root-relative prefix glob.Includes the src directory and its descendants.
glob-i:"*.TXT"Case-insensitive glob.Explicitly controls case; do not infer it from the filesystem.

“Recursive” belongs to the pattern form. glob:"*.c" is not the same as a shell command that expands **/*.c, and a plain src is not the same as file:"src". When reproducibility matters, prefer an explicit root-prefixed pattern and state whether it is exact, glob, or prefix-glob.

Fileset consumer precedence and operators

The fileset operators are set algebra over paths. Function calls and pattern aliases bind most tightly. Prefix complement ~x selects every path except x; intersection x & y selects paths in both; difference x ~ y selects x minus y; union x | y selects paths in either. In the target grammar, intersection and difference bind more strongly than union, and equal-strength infix operations associate from the left.

src | docs & ~glob:"**/*.generated"
(src | docs) & ~glob:"**/*.generated"
root-prefix-glob:"src" ~ root-glob:"src/**/generated/**"
all() ~ root-file:"Cargo.lock"

The first expression means src | (docs & ~generated), not “everything under src or docs, then remove generated files”. The second expresses the latter. A path expression that looks obvious in prose should be parenthesised when it combines a positive union with an exclusion. This also makes diffs and review scripts resilient if another person later adds a third path family.

Fileset complement is bounded by the relevant tree. It does not select a path that is not present in the tree merely because that path would exist in the filesystem. Fileset evaluation for a historical tree is consequently independent of whether that path happens to be present in the current working directory.

Quoting and shell failure modes

Quoting has two jobs: protect the argument from the shell, and, when required, quote a path literal inside the fileset grammar. A bare simple path can omit the inner quotes, but whitespace, parentheses, operators, and punctuation require them. Glob characters do not necessarily require inner quotes for jj, but shell quotes are still needed to stop the shell expanding them.

CommandWhat the shell may doRobust spelling
jj diff src/*.rsExpands files before jj sees one fileset; result depends on cwd contents.jj diff 'glob:src/*.rs'
jj diff ~fooUnquoted operator can be interpreted or split by shell policy.jj diff '~"foo"'
jj diff "Foo Bar"Shell protects whitespace; jj can parse a literal path.jj diff '"Foo Bar"' when combining with operators.
jj diff src | docsThe shell creates a pipeline.jj diff 'src | docs'
jj diff 'glob:**/*.rs'Safe shell token, recursive jj glob.Same; document the recursive intent explicitly.

In a shell function, do not place untrusted path text inside a larger unquoted revset/fileset. Pass paths as separate arguments when the command supports literal file arguments, or construct one carefully quoted fileset with a language-aware interface. A path beginning with a dash belongs after -- where the consumer supports it.

Evaluate a real tree

Use this tree for experiments:

Cargo.toml
Cargo.lock
src/main.rs
src/generated/schema.rs
src/parser/mod.rs
src/parser/tests.rs
tests/cli/basic.rs
tests/fixtures/input.json
docs/guide.md
docs/generated/api.md
scripts/check.sh

Evaluate each expression with jj file list before passing it to a rewrite:

jj file list -- 'root-prefix-glob:src'
jj file list -- 'root-glob:src/**/*.rs'
jj file list -- 'root-glob:src/**/*.rs ~ root-glob:src/**/generated/**'
jj file list -- 'root-prefix-glob:src | root-prefix-glob:tests'
jj file list -- 'root-prefix-glob:docs & ~root-glob:docs/generated/**'
jj file list -- 'root-file:"Cargo.toml" | root-file:"Cargo.lock"'

The expected selected sets are, respectively, all src paths; all Rust files below src; all non-generated Rust files below src; src and tests; non-generated docs; and the two root lock/manifest files. Record actual output in a fixture rather than embedding guessed order in a policy script: path ordering is a presentation concern unless the command defines it as a contract.

To test cwd semantics, run once from the repository root and once from src/. A plain parser means different things in those locations because it is cwd-relative. The root-prefixed spelling means the same repository path in both locations. This is one of the most useful reasons to write aliases in root coordinates.

Consumer contracts

The same fileset language is consumed by commands with different effects:

ConsumerCommit sideFileset effectRisk boundary
diffEndpoint or selected commit.Narrows rendered diff paths.It does not narrow the commit set itself.
restoreSource and destination/change.Copies or reverses selected paths.Wrong direction can overwrite intended content.
squashSource/current and destination parent.Moves selected diff hunks/files into another change.Descendants may be rebased and conflict.
splitOne change, usually current.Separates selected paths or diff hunks into a new change.Unselected content remains at the original boundary.
fixConfigured commit set.Restricts fixer input and changed files.Formatter output can rewrite many changes.
file list/show/searchSelected tree/commit.Lists or reads matching entries.Inspection does not mean filesystem materialisation.
file track/untrackWorking-copy snapshot policy.Changes what future snapshots consider.It is not deletion or publication.

For a diff operation, first inspect the source diff and destination tree. Then use the command's documented read-only form—jj diff for content inspection or --dry-run on a command that provides it—save the operation ID, and only then apply the fileset. The path selector answers “which paths”; it does not answer “which side wins”, “which change owns the result”, or “whether a descendant should be restored”. Those are command semantics.

Fileset aliases

Fileset aliases provide names for path policy. They live under [fileset-aliases] and may be a symbol, a parameterised function, or a table with definition and completion documentation:

[fileset-aliases]
source = 'root-prefix-glob:"src" | root-prefix-glob:"include"'
generated = 'root-glob:"**/generated/**" | root-glob:"**/*.lock"'
reviewable(x) = 'x ~ generated'

docs.definition = 'root-prefix-glob:"docs"'
docs.doc = 'Documentation files'

Use a descriptive alias only when its coordinate and exclusions are stable. An alias named source should not silently include generated code one day and exclude it the next. Parameterised aliases are language expressions, not shell interpolation; callers pass a fileset expression as one argument:

jj diff -- 'reviewable(source)'
jj file list -- 'docs ~ root-glob:"docs/generated/**"'

Test aliases from the repository root and a subdirectory, against complete repository trees, and against a tree with spaces or punctuation in a path. Keep fileset aliases separate from revset aliases with similar names; a command will not convert one language into the other.

Case study: split a mixed change without changing its review story

Suppose the current change contains a parser implementation, generated schema output, and a documentation example. The intended review story is “implementation first, generated output and docs second”. A fileset can make that ownership explicit, but it cannot decide whether generated output should be regenerated or copied.

before:
  A--B(@)
     B = src/parser/mod.rs
         src/generated/schema.rs
         docs/guide.md

desired:
  A--B--C(@)
     B = src/parser/mod.rs
     C = src/generated/schema.rs + docs/guide.md
jj diff -r @ -- 'root-file:"src/parser/mod.rs"'
jj diff -r @ -- 'root-glob:"src/generated/**" | root-file:"docs/guide.md"'
jj split -- 'root-glob:"src/generated/**" | root-file:"docs/guide.md"'
jj log -r '::@'
jj diff -r @-
jj diff -r @

The exact interactive result depends on the split mode and fileset supplied, so verify the resulting parent edge and diff ownership rather than inferring it from success. If a descendant existed, it would be automatically rebased over the new boundary and could receive a new commit ID or a stored conflict. Path selection controls content ownership; the DAG records the consequences.

Fileset review checklist

  1. Which parser sees the token first: shell, jj fileset, or the consumer?
  2. Is the path coordinate cwd-relative or workspace-root-relative?
  3. Does the pattern match one file, a directory prefix, a glob, or a recursive glob?
  4. Are operators parenthesised so exclusion applies to the intended union?
  5. Does the target command use the fileset for a diff, a tree copy, a snapshot policy, or metadata?
  6. What is the exact commit set on which the fileset is being applied?
  7. Could the selected path be absent from the current filesystem even though it exists in the repository tree?
  8. What commit, descendant, bookmark, and operation changes will follow?
  9. Has the selection been printed with jj file list or a read-only diff?

The reference card in Appendix D is intentionally dense, but this reasoning process prevents an apparently harmless path argument from becoming a broad rewrite.

Part VI — Bookmarks and publication refs

A bookmark is a name attached to a commit. It is a publication handle, not the unit of local work. A local bookmark can be created, moved, deleted, forgotten, renamed, listed, tracked, or untracked. The 0.45.1 command family is: jj bookmark advance, create, delete, forget, list, move, rename, set, track, and untrack.

jj bookmark create review -r @
jj bookmark set review -r @
jj bookmark move review --to @
jj bookmark track review --remote origin
jj bookmark untrack review --remote origin
jj bookmark forget review
jj bookmark delete review

set chooses or creates a local name at a commit; move changes an existing name; delete asks the remote publication machinery to delete when pushed; forget removes local knowledge of the bookmark without necessarily expressing a remote deletion. Inspect help for exact confirmation and force flags in your release.

Tracking is a relationship

local bookmark review  <-------- tracking relationship -------->  review@origin
        points to @                                                 points to server tip

@ can move without moving review.
review can be moved without changing @.
Tracking does not mean “follow the working copy”.

Remote bookmarks are imported names such as main@origin. If two remotes have a bookmark named main, the remote qualifies it: main@origin and main@gerrit. A local bookmark may track one corresponding remote bookmark; tracking controls expected push/pull relationship and safety checks, not automatic movement.

Tags are separate immutable-ish names supplied by Git-compatible repositories. Use jj tag list, set, delete, track, and untrack as the installed command permits; do not use tags as a substitute for a moving review bookmark.

Bookmark and tag state laboratory

A bookmark has a local target, optional remote targets, and possibly a tracking relationship. Treat those as fields in a state record:

local ref record:
  name = review
  local target = C
  tracked remote = review@origin
  observed remote target = B
  status = ahead by one / unsynchronised

remote ref record:
  name = review
  remote = origin
  target = B
  tracking local = review

The local bookmark does not “point to the working copy” unless its target happens to equal @. Moving @ by new, edit, or ordinary snapshotting does not move review. Moving review does not change the tree of C. A push turns the local ref record into a server request; a fetch turns a server ref into a remote-bookmark observation.

Create, set, move, advance

jj bookmark create review -r @
jj bookmark set review -r @
jj bookmark move review --to @
jj bookmark advance review --to @

Create requires that the name not already exist. Set is a convenient create-or-update operation and can allow a backwards/sideways move with --allow-backwards. Move targets existing names and can select names by their current commits. Advance is intended to move forward to a descendant or a configured target; it is a useful batch operation when several publication refs should follow a known graph boundary.

OperationChangesDoes not change
createadds a local name at a targetworking copy, commit trees, remote server
setmoves/creates names at a targetcommit graph; remote until push
movemoves existing namescontent and change identities
advancemoves eligible names forwardunrelated refs and commit content

Delete versus forget

Delete expresses that a local bookmark should cease to exist and, when tracked and pushed, can express remote deletion. Forget removes local knowledge. These are intentionally different because a user may have merged a GitHub PR and want to remove the local name without deleting a server branch, or may want to delete a stale server branch.

# local cleanup, preserve server state
jj bookmark forget review
jj bookmark forget --include-remotes review

# request server deletion
jj bookmark delete review
jj git push --remote origin --deleted

--include-remotes forgets remote observations too; a future fetch recreates a remote bookmark that still exists at the server. It is not a server deletion. Keep the distinction in cleanup scripts.

Tracking is a relationship, not movement

jj bookmark track review --remote origin
jj bookmark untrack review --remote origin
jj bookmark track review@origin

Tracking associates a local bookmark with a corresponding remote bookmark. It makes ahead/behind/synced state meaningful and gives push safety a known expected remote target. It does not move the local bookmark when @ moves, does not rebase a stack, and does not pull changes automatically.

With two remotes, the relationship is three-dimensional:

review (local) --tracks-- review@github
       |
       \--------------- review@gerrit is a different remote bookmark

main@github and main@gerrit can point to different commits.

Use --remote or an exact name@remote to avoid tracking the wrong remote. A bookmark may be tracked to one or more corresponding remote states according to the backend's model; the command's list output is authoritative for the actual repository.

Normal, deleted, and conflicted remote state

Fetching a remote that deleted or moved a ref changes the imported remote-bookmark state. A local bookmark can be ahead, behind, diverged, or absent. A conflicted bookmark/tag has multiple added or removed targets rather than one normal target. Before pushing a conflicted ref, inspect all targets and resolve the naming/ref policy; do not assume the last fetched value is the desired one.

jj bookmark list --all-remotes
jj bookmark list --remote origin --tracked
jj log -r 'remote_bookmarks("review", "origin")'
jj log -r 'bookmarks("review")'

The exact string-pattern arguments to revset ref functions are release-sensitive; use the local help form when filtering names. The conceptual distinction remains stable: a local name is an explicit local ref, a remote name is an observation, and tracking is metadata linking them.

Tags and release policy

Tags are useful at release points because their meaning should not change as a mutable change stack evolves. A local tag can be set to @, listed, tracked to a remote tag, and pushed. Moving an existing tag needs --allow-move in the target CLI and should require a release-policy review.

jj tag set v2.4.0 -r @
jj tag list --all-remotes
jj tag track v2.4.0@origin
jj git push --remote origin --tag v2.4.0

Do not use a tag as a review branch just because both are names. A moving review boundary wants a bookmark; a release identity wants a tag. jj 0.45.1 provides tracked/untracked remote-tag predicates; build release queries from the supported tag and ref functions documented in Appendix C.

Publication invariant

Before publishing, be able to answer four questions:

  1. Which exact local bookmark is being pushed?
  2. Which remote and URL will receive it?
  3. Which remote bookmark was fetched as the expected old target?
  4. Which commit/change is the intended tip, and is it conflicted, empty, divergent, or immutable?
jj git remote list
jj bookmark list --remote origin --all-remotes
jj log -r 'review | review@origin'
jj diff --from review@origin --to review
jj git push --dry-run --remote origin --bookmark review

If any answer is unclear, stop at inspection. A publication ref is a small interface with potentially large external consequences; the local graph-first workflow does not remove that boundary.

Git backend: two object worlds and an import/export boundary

In a Git-backed repository, jj and Git share enough storage to interoperate, but they do not share the same semantic model. Git stores commit objects, trees, blobs, and refs. jj stores change metadata, operation history, workspace state, conflict values, and its view of bookmarks/tags. Some jj state is represented in Git-compatible objects; not all of it is meaningful to Git.

jj commit/change/operation/workspace model
        |
        |- exportable commit/tree/blob → Git object database
        |- local bookmark/tag → Git ref when exported
        \- change evolution/op/workspace/conflict metadata → jj semantics

Git refs/objects ← fetch/import → jj remote-bookmark/ref view

Colocated repository discipline

Colocation is valuable when GitHub/Gerrit tooling, hooks, Git inspection, and jj need one working directory. It also creates two writers and two sets of expectations. A Git command can update refs without jj seeing them until import. A Git command that updates the worktree can race with jj's snapshot. A jj rewrite can make Git's current branch/ref appear surprising until export.

jj git colocation status
jj git export
git -C "$(jj root)" show-ref
git -C "$(jj root)" log --all --oneline
git -C "$(jj root)" fetch origin
jj git import
jj bookmark list --all-remotes

Use one writer for the working directory. Git inspection commands that do not touch the worktree are usually safe; Git checkout/reset/restore commands require a snapshot boundary and explicit coordination. After Git-side ref changes, import before interpreting jj's remote state. After jj bookmark changes, export before asking a Git-native tool to inspect refs.

Clone and init choices

ChoiceWhere metadata livesUse when
jj git clone (0.45.1 default)jj plus a top-level Git checkout, unless git.colocate=falseNormal choice when Git/gh/Gerrit tools are part of daily work.
jj git clone --no-colocatejj repository with its backing Git data hidden under .jjUse when jj should own the workspace and Git is primarily transport.
jj git clone --colocateExplicitly request the normal colocated layoutUseful as documentary/script intent even though it is normally the default.
jj git init (0.45.1 default)Initialise a colocated Git-backed jj repository unless git.colocate=falseStart a repository that ordinary Git tools can also open.
jj git init --no-colocateInitialise with the backing Git repository hidden below .jjExplicit non-colocated layout.
jj git init --git-repo PATHUse an existing Git repository as the backing repository; mutually exclusive with --colocateIf PATH is the destination itself and contains .git, jj creates a colocated workspace. If PATH names a different Git directory, jj uses a non-colocated layout.

After a clone, identify the trunk bookmark and remote name. The default remote is often origin, but a GitHub fork/upstream or Gerrit repository may use different names. Do not write scripts that assume the remote URL from a directory name.

Fetch, import, export, push

jj git fetch --remote origin
jj git import
# graph work happens here
jj git export
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark review

Fetch is network object/ref transfer plus local remote-bookmark update. Import is local Git-ref observation. Export is local jj-to-Git-ref update. Push is network publication. A normal jj command can perform some import/snapshot work at its boundary, but explicit commands make automation and diagnosis clearer.

OperationNetwork?Primary directionChanges local commit DAG?
fetchyesremote Git → local objects/remote refsusually no mutable rewrite
importnolocal Git refs → jj viewno, but ref state changes
exportnojj bookmarks/tags → Git refsno
pushyeslocal Git refs/objects → remoteno, but remote state changes

Native Git commands that are safe, conditional, or hazardous

Command classAssessmentRequired boundary
git show, git log, git cat-fileUseful inspection of Git objects.Remember Git cannot show jj change/evolution semantics.
git show-ref, git for-each-refUseful ref inspection.Import after ref changes.
git fetchCan update Git refs.Run jj git import before relying on them.
git pushExternal publication.Explicit ref/remote; jj will not make a pushed mistake local-undoable.
git checkout, git reset, git restoreWorktree/ref writers.Do not race jj snapshot; import refs afterward.
gh pr checkoutGit-oriented hosting workflow.Inspect worktree and import refs before jj work.

Credentials, SSH, and signing

jj's Git transport commonly uses Git's URL, credential helper, SSH agent, and known-host configuration. Gerrit and GitHub may have different hosts, keys, or permissions. Keep transport authentication separate from commit signing: an SSH key used to connect to a remote is not automatically a commit-signing key, and a good local signature does not grant push permission.

jj git remote list
ssh-add -l
git config --get-regexp 'credential|url|core.ssh'
jj sign -r @
jj log -r @ -T 'if(signature, signature.status(), "unsigned") ++ "\n"'

Do not put secrets in jj aliases or repository config. Test authentication with a harmless fetch, inspect the destination URL, and use a controlled key/agent environment in CI. Signing a stack rewrites IDs; publish the resulting bookmark only after checking the entire descendant chain.

Private commits and Git compatibility

Some jj/Git policies allow commits to be marked private so they are not pushed by ordinary publication. Private is a publication policy, not a different change identity or a hidden filesystem state. The exact private-commit configuration and push flags are release-sensitive; inspect the 0.45.1 help/schema before depending on them.

jj log -r 'mutable() ~ ::remote_bookmarks()'
jj git push --remote origin --tracked
jj git push --remote origin --all

Use explicit bookmark selection for review work. Broad --all is appropriate only when all local names/tags are intended for that remote. A private mutable change can still be a descendant of a public bookmark and can still affect a pushed descendant if the graph boundary is not selected carefully.

Part VII — Git backend and interoperability

With the Git backend, jj stores its own metadata under .jj and uses Git objects/refs for interoperability. A colocated repository has both .git and jj metadata at one worktree; a non-colocated repository keeps jj's view separate. Colocation is convenient for an advanced Git user because Git-native tools, gh, hooks, and editors can inspect the same object database. It also means two programs can race to update refs or the worktree.

jj git init --colocate
jj git clone https://example.test/project.git project
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj git import
jj git export
jj git push --bookmark review --remote origin
jj git remote list
jj git root

jj notices Git-side ref changes during import/snapshot boundaries; after running native Git, use jj git import or a normal jj command that imports refs. Native Git does not understand change IDs, operation history, conflicts as jj values, or workspace pointers. It can inspect and transport Git objects, but its rewrites may make jj bookmarks/remote state stale until imported.

For colocated scripts, GIT_DIR=$(jj git root)/.git is sometimes useful, but prefer git -C "$(jj root)" ... and let jj report its root. Never use Git to reset the worktree while a jj process is snapshotting it. Git credentials, SSH agents, and signing configuration are generally consumed through the Git transport or configured jj signing/authentication facilities; test the exact credential helper in the target environment.

Push safety

Push bookmarks, not arbitrary working-copy commits, unless you deliberately use jj 0.45.1's change-based push mode and understand the bookmark it creates. A tracked bookmark gives jj a lease-like expectation about the remote value. An exceptional host-side force update is safe only when the changed remote tip is the one you intended to replace; review jj bookmark list, jj log -r 'review|review@origin', and jj's --dry-run preview first.

Git interoperability laboratory

The Git backend has two related but distinct storage views. jj stores its commit and operation metadata in the repository’s jj backend; the Git backend can also read and write Git objects and refs. A colocated repository adds a Git view to an existing checkout so that native Git commands and jj commands operate on nearby data. Colocation is convenient precisely because it removes a transport boundary; it is also risky because two tools can mutate related state without sharing jj’s operation semantics.

working tree
    |
    |-- jj view: commit DAG, change IDs, operation DAG, workspace
    |
    \-- Git view: commits/trees/blobs, refs, index, remote-tracking refs

A Git commit object is still a Git object, but jj gives it additional meaning. In the jj 0.45.1 Git backend, jj-created commits can contain a non-standard change-id commit header when git.write-change-id-header is enabled. The value is a reverse-hex encoding of jj’s change identity, as described in the Git compatibility documentation. This header is object data, not a standard Git identity field: ordinary git log and git show do not normally print it, git cat-file -p can, and native Git operations are not required to preserve it. Independently, .jj records the change’s evolution, operations, and workspace view. Thus “the change ID is in the jj view” is the semantic statement; “the Git backend serialises a change-id header” is the 0.45.1 storage detail.

Laboratory: jj @, Git HEAD, and object reachability

0.45.1 verified boundary. Run this experiment in a disposable colocated repository. It is intentionally about pointers and reachability, not about converting a jj commit into Git at publication time.

Start with one ordinary Git commit, then let jj snapshot an edit without creating or moving a publication bookmark:

git -c init.defaultBranch=main init demo
cd demo
git config user.name "Example User"
git config user.email user@example.invalid
printf '%s\n' base > note
git add note && git commit -m base
jj git init --colocate
printf '%s\n' jj-snapshot >> note
jj status

Now ask both tools what they consider current. Use the full ID printed by the first command in the later commands:

jj log --no-graph -r @ -T 'commit_id ++ "\n"'
git status --short
git symbolic-ref HEAD
git log --oneline --decorate -3
git log --all --oneline --decorate -6
git show-ref
git cat-file -t JJ_COMMIT_ID
git cat-file -p JJ_COMMIT_ID | sed -n '1,14p'

In a colocated repository, jj log reports a new working-copy commit and git cat-file -t reports commit. The object was created locally when jj made the snapshot; jj git push is not the conversion step. At the same time, git symbolic-ref HEAD may remain refs/heads/main, with that ref still pointing at the earlier Git commit. Therefore git log, whose default starting point is Git’s HEAD, need not show the jj working-copy commit. git log --all may show more because it walks every ordinary and implementation ref that Git considers reachable, including a temporary refs/jj/keep/* retention ref in this release; do not treat that implementation ref as a publication interface. git show-ref makes the distinction visible. An object can exist in the object database without being reachable from HEAD, a local branch, or any other ref that a particular Git command walks.

The two status commands answer different questions. jj status describes the filesystem relative to jj’s working-copy commit and snapshots the filesystem at the command boundary. Git status compares the filesystem with the Git index and HEAD. In a colocated repository, a jj snapshot can therefore include note in the jj commit while Git still reports the path as modified relative to its index. The Git index is not jj’s staging area, and a Git status letter is not evidence that jj failed to record the edit.

Finally create an explicit publication boundary:

jj bookmark create review -r @
jj git export
git show-ref refs/heads/review
git symbolic-ref HEAD

The local review ref now reaches the same commit object, while Git HEAD can still name refs/heads/main. In a colocated workspace, creating or moving a bookmark may export its ref as part of the normal jj operation, so the explicit jj git export is a useful idempotent boundary for scripts. If the bookmark named by HEAD is deliberately moved or checked out through a coordinated Git operation, the target of HEAD can change; that is a different event from jj advancing its workspace-local @. A push sends the selected exported ref and reachable objects to a remote; it does not promise to move local HEAD.

Eventjj stateGit stateWhat may move
Filesystem editWorking tree differs from the recorded snapshot.Index/worktree comparison changes.No object or ref need exist yet.
jj snapshot or rewrite@, commit DAG, operation view, and possibly descendants change.Git-backend commit/tree/blob objects are created; implementation retention refs may appear.Not necessarily HEAD or refs/heads/*.
Bookmark create/set and exportA named jj bookmark points at a selected commit.Its corresponding local Git ref is updated by export/normal colocated synchronisation.The bookmark ref; HEAD only if it names that ref and it is moved.
jj git fetch then importRemote-bookmark observations enter jj’s view.Objects and remote-tracking refs are fetched, then read by jj.Remote-tracking refs; not local @ by itself.
jj git pushLocal graph is selected through a bookmark/tag/ref.Remote Git ref and reachable remote objects are updated.Remote state only, apart from local transport bookkeeping.
Native Git checkout/reset/commitMay leave jj’s view stale until import/snapshot.Git HEAD, refs, index, worktree, or objects can change.Whatever that Git command explicitly writes.

This model also explains the directory boundary. In a colocated repository, top-level .git remains the Git object database, refs, remotes, and native-tool layer; .jj remains the jj view, operation log, workspace metadata, and jj backend state. In a non-colocated repository, the backing Git repository is hidden below .jj; ordinary Git commands run in the worktree do not find a top-level .git. Use jj git root and explicit Git directory arguments only when you have deliberately chosen that integration.

Classify native Git commands before using them in a colocated workflow:

ClassExamplesBoundary
Read-only inspectiongit log, git show, git cat-file, git show-refSafe for state, but Git cannot display jj evolution or workspace semantics.
Git-ref mutationgit update-ref, git branch -f, git fetchImport before relying on the new ref view; record the exact ref.
Worktree/index mutationgit checkout, git reset, git restore, git add, git commitSerialise with jj; snapshot or import before interpreting the result. Git’s index is separate.
Network publicationgit push, gh pr createExplicitly select remote and ref; local jj operation recovery cannot undo server state.

Reference: colocated versus non-colocated layout

QuestionColocatedNon-colocated
Native Git commands in the project directory?Yes, subject to safe coordination.Use a separate Git checkout or explicit Git directory.
Git refs visible to jj?Imported/exported through the colocated backend.Managed through jj’s Git backend and transport.
Index meaningGit tools may update it; jj snapshots filesystem state, not Git staging intent.There is no native Git index in the normal working directory.
Concurrent writers?More ways to race; serialise Git/jj mutations.Still serialise jj operations, but fewer accidental ref mutations.
Best useGitHub/Gerrit tooling, hooks, IDEs, gradual adoption.Clean jj-only automation and isolated experiments.

In a colocated repository, a native git switch or git reset changes Git’s checkout/index/ref state. jj may not immediately incorporate all such changes into its integrated view. Run the appropriate jj Git import command or a normal jj command that refreshes the Git view before relying on a Git-side ref movement. Conversely, a jj bookmark push/export can update Git refs that a native Git process sees later. Treat the directory as a shared mutable resource.

Clone, init, fetch, import, export

jj git clone https://example.org/project.git project
jj git init --colocate
jj git remote list
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj git import
jj git export
jj git root

jj git clone creates a jj repository backed by Git objects and configures a remote; in 0.45.1 it is colocated by default unless git.colocate=false or --no-colocate is used. jj git init has the same default, while --no-colocate explicitly hides the backing Git repository below .jj. --colocate is worth spelling in scripts when the layout is a deliberate precondition. fetch transfers remote objects and updates remote-bookmark observations; import refreshes jj’s view from Git refs where needed; export writes jj bookmark state into Git refs. The distinction between fetch and import matters when native Git has changed refs or when a script needs to separate network activity from local ref reconciliation.

Use jj git root to obtain the Git root when a tool expects GIT_DIR or a repository path:

GIT_DIR=$(jj git root) git -C "$(jj root)" show HEAD
git --git-dir="$(jj git root)" for-each-ref

Check the command’s output shape before embedding it in a path. A root command returns a directory; it is not automatically the value of GIT_DIR in every layout. Prefer git -C when operating on the working tree, and use --git-dir only when the command’s path semantics require it.

Fetch and remote bookmarks

Fetch updates the local observation of remote refs. It does not move the workspace’s @ and does not rebase local work automatically merely because the remote trunk advanced. After fetching, inspect:

jj git fetch --remote origin
jj log -r 'main@origin'
jj log -r 'main@origin..@'
jj log -r 'remote_bookmarks()'

A remote bookmark is not a local bookmark with a decorative suffix. It is a name imported from a remote namespace. A local bookmark can track it, which gives jj a relationship for ahead/behind and push safety. Tracking does not make the local bookmark follow a working-copy commit; the local target still moves only through an explicit bookmark operation or a graph rewrite that preserves its target relationship.

Push safety and ref publication

Push sends selected local bookmarks or tags to a remote. In jj 0.45.1, the safest scripted form names the remote and bookmark and performs the available --dry-run preview before the real push:

jj log -r 'bookmarks(exact:"pr/parser")' -T 'commit_id ++ "\n"'
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark pr/parser --dry-run
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark pr/parser

A non-fast-forward update is not automatically evidence that force is required. Compare the local bookmark target with the remote bookmark target and determine whether the local target descends from the remote target, whether another actor moved the remote, and whether server policy permits replacement. The tracking relationship supplies safety context; it is not a lease substitute for all server-side races. In jj 0.45.1, jj git push has no --force, --force-with-lease, or generic allow-rewrite option: its own safety check accepts a backwards update only when the remote still matches the state jj last fetched. Treat an exceptional host-side replacement as a separate, explicitly audited native-Git or hosting operation.

--tracked, --all, --deleted, and tag options widen the publication set. They are convenient interactively and dangerous in generic scripts. A script that publishes every tracked bookmark can unexpectedly update a second review or a stale local publication name. Prefer one explicit bookmark per publication action.

Credentials, SSH, and signing

jj Git transport normally uses Git’s configured remote URLs and credential mechanisms. SSH keys, agents, known-host verification, credential helpers, and HTTPS tokens remain deployment concerns; do not put secrets in jj config committed to a repository. Test authentication with a read-only fetch before a push. A remote URL can be inspected with jj git remote list or native Git configuration, but redact credentials from logs.

Signing is a property of commits or transport policy, not a synonym for a jj change ID. jj 0.45.1 provides jj sign and jj unsign; configure the signing key and inspect the resulting signature fields through templates or Git verification. A rewrite after signing produces a new commit and generally requires signing the successor again. Gerrit and GitHub may apply additional server-side verification; local signing does not guarantee acceptance.

Native Git tooling: a safe contract

Use Git for tools that have no jj equivalent—gh, hooks, server-specific commands, object inspection, and specialised diff tools—but establish a boundary:

  1. Before a Git-side mutation, inspect jj’s current operation and workspace state.
  2. Make one class of mutation at a time: files, Git refs, or jj graph.
  3. After changing refs with Git, run the jj import/refresh path and inspect remote/local bookmarks.
  4. After changing graph state with jj, export/import as required and check what Git sees.
  5. Do not run two writers against the same working directory concurrently.

For GitHub, gh pr view and gh pr merge operate on server state and may fetch or inspect refs; they do not understand jj’s operation DAG. For Gerrit, server review commands and refs/for/... transport semantics are likewise outside jj’s local graph model. Keep the local bookmark that a host consumes explicit and verify it after every host-side action.

Part VIII — GitHub workflows

Branchless feature and pull request

main@origin
     |
     A
     |
     B
     |
     C
     |
     @

Fetch main, create or edit a child, and work without a local publication bookmark. Your stack is visible by graph and revset. When the change is ready, create a bookmark only for publication:

jj git fetch --remote origin
jj new main@origin
# edit files; let jj snapshot
jj describe -m 'Add bounded cache'
jj bookmark create cache-pr --revision @
jj git push --bookmark cache-pr --remote origin

GitHub sees a branch ref because Git transport requires one; locally, the ref is disposable. After the pull request merges, fetch, move/edit onto updated main as appropriate, and jj bookmark forget cache-pr or delete it after confirming the server state.

Stacks and review

For one PR use one change. For stacked PRs, publish one bookmark per review boundary, each pointing at a stack tip:

jj bookmark create pr-base -r A
jj bookmark create pr-feature -r B
jj git push --bookmark pr-base --bookmark pr-feature --remote origin
jj rebase -b @ -o main@origin

Rewriting A automatically rebases B and its descendants. Move the publication bookmarks after the rewrite and push through jj's fetched-state safety check; jj 0.45.1 has no force flag on jj git push. An exceptional host-side replacement is a separate, explicitly reviewed operation. GitHub's UI merge operation is a server-side ref/graph action; jj learns its result on fetch.

gh pr create --head cache-pr, gh pr view, and gh pr checkout can coexist with jj. Treat gh pr checkout as a Git-oriented worktree/ref operation and inspect the result with jj status and jj git import. Fork remotes need explicit names: origin may be your fork while upstream is the source; qualify remote bookmarks in revsets.

GitHub PR lifecycle: local graph versus publication ref

GitHub consumes Git refs. jj lets the developer organise mutable work without local bookmarks and creates a bookmark only when a server-facing boundary is needed. The lifecycle has two independent timelines:

local jj timeline:  edit → rewrite → rebase → inspect → rewrite
GitHub timeline:              publish ref → review → update ref → merge

A local rewrite can happen many times between two GitHub ref updates.
The remote bookmark is an interface snapshot, not the local working state.

Single-change PR

main@origin -- base -- @
                         unnamed mutable change

publish:
main@origin -- base -- P
                         ▲
                       pr/cache
                       pr/cache@origin
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj new main@origin -m 'Cache: bound memory use'
# edit files
jj status
jj diff
jj bookmark create pr/cache -r @
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark pr/cache
gh pr create --head pr/cache --title 'Bound cache memory'

The local bookmark is now a publication name. The working-copy commit can still be amended with jj describe, jj squash, or ordinary filesystem edits. After the next snapshot, the bookmark still points at the old commit until it is moved:

jj describe -m 'Cache: bound memory use and expose metrics'
jj bookmark set pr/cache -r @
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark pr/cache

Whether the push is a fast-forward depends on the server's previous ref and the rewrite. jj's push safety checks and remote tracking expose the expected old target; do not solve a rejection with an unreviewed native-Git replacement. In jj 0.45.1, jj git push has no force flag. Inspect:

jj bookmark list --remote origin --tracked
jj log -r 'pr/cache | pr/cache@origin'
jj diff --from 'pr/cache@origin' --to pr/cache

Stacked PRs

main@origin -- A -- B -- C
                   ▲    ▲
                 pr/api pr/metrics

Use one publication bookmark per server review boundary. The base PR's bookmark points to B and the dependent PR's bookmark points to C; the dependent PR should be created with the base PR as its target branch according to GitHub's UI policy.

jj bookmark create pr/api -r B
jj bookmark create pr/metrics -r C
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark 'pr/*'
gh pr create --head pr/api --base main
gh pr create --head pr/metrics --base pr/api

When A or B is rewritten, descendants are rebased locally and both bookmark targets may receive new commit IDs. Update bookmarks deliberately, then push both. A common mistake is moving only the top bookmark, leaving the base PR pointing to a predecessor that no longer represents the intended boundary.

jj edit B
# modify the early API change
jj describe -m 'API: correct quota invariant'
jj log -r 'pr/api | pr/metrics | ::@'
jj bookmark set pr/api -r B
jj bookmark set pr/metrics -r C
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark pr/api --bookmark pr/metrics

Main moves during review

GitHub's main branch can move while local PR refs are under review. Fetch first, then rebase the mutable stack onto the new remote bookmark. In a stack, select the stack roots or use the branch selection that matches the actual graph:

jj git fetch --remote origin
jj log -r 'main@origin'
jj rebase -b 'roots(main@origin..pr/metrics)' -o main@origin
jj log -r 'pr/metrics:: & mutable() & conflicts()'
jj resolve
jj bookmark set pr/api -r 'subject(exact:"API: correct quota")'
jj bookmark set pr/metrics -r @
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark 'pr/*'

The exact stack-root expression should be verified in the repository; the important sequence is fetch, inspect, select, rebase, resolve, move publication refs, push. Do not rebase a remote bookmark itself. Remote bookmarks are observations of server refs and are normally immutable boundaries for local mutable work.

Merge, closure, replacement, and cleanup

After GitHub merges, the local repository does not learn the server graph until fetch. Fetch the updated main and decide whether local changes are now ancestors of it:

jj git fetch --remote origin
jj log -r 'main@origin | pr/cache | ::pr/cache'
jj log -r 'pr/cache ~ ::main@origin'
jj bookmark forget pr/cache
jj bookmark forget --include-remotes 'pr/cache'

Use forget when the local publication name should disappear without asking GitHub to delete the branch. Use bookmark delete followed by an explicit push when the server branch should be removed. If a PR is closed and replaced, keep the old bookmark long enough to compare/refute server state, then forget it and create a new publication name or move the existing one intentionally.

Workflow: fork/upstream topology

jj git remote add github git@github.com:me/project.git
jj git remote add upstream git@github.com:org/project.git
jj git fetch --remote upstream
jj new main@upstream
jj bookmark create me/cache -r @
jj git push --remote github --bookmark me/cache

Here main@upstream is the imported source boundary and the local bookmark is pushed to the fork. A local origin default can be unsafe if it changes meaning between clones. Use explicit remote arguments in aliases and qualify both remote bookmarks in revsets.

Native gh/Git interaction

gh pr view and gh pr create can operate against a colocated repository. Commands such as gh pr checkout are Git-oriented and may create/move refs or alter the worktree in ways jj must import. After any command that changes Git refs:

jj git import
jj status
jj bookmark list --all-remotes

Do not allow gh, Git, and jj to write the same worktree concurrently. The host/UI can merge or close a PR without local filesystem changes; fetch is the observation boundary.

Push rejection decision tree

  1. Fetch the named remote and inspect local/remote bookmark targets.
  2. Determine whether the server changed independently or the local bookmark was rewritten.
  3. Compare the intended tree and ancestry with jj diff and jj log.
  4. If the ref should advance normally, rebase or move it to the expected descendant.
  5. If replacement is intentional, use the hosting system's documented replacement mechanism and record why; jj git push itself has no force flag in jj 0.45.1.
  6. If the wrong ref was pushed, repair the server ref separately; jj undo only repairs local operation state.

GitHub field laboratory: one local graph, several PR views

A pull request is a server-side interpretation of a Git ref. jj has no obligation to organise local work around that ref. The local graph can therefore be optimised for editing while a publication bookmark exists only at the boundary GitHub needs to see. The cost is that the bookmark is an interface object whose target must be maintained explicitly.

A single PR over time

time 0:       main@origin--A--B(@)       no local bookmark
publish:      main@origin--A--B
                              ▲
                            pr/cache
                            pr/cache@origin
after review: main@origin--A--B'(@)
                              ▲
                            pr/cache      (old until moved)
                            pr/cache@origin (server's last copy)

The distinction between pr/cache and pr/cache@origin is the useful state. The local bookmark can move to B' before the push; the remote bookmark remains the last fetched observation. A log that prints only the local bookmark hides work waiting to be published, while one that prints only the remote bookmark hides the server's lag.

jj git fetch --remote origin
jj new main@origin -m 'Cache: bound memory use'
# edit, test, and inspect the working-copy commit
jj diff -r @
jj bookmark create pr/cache -r @
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark pr/cache

GitHub-specific commands can now create the pull request. The server may choose a merge base, report checks, and expose a review URL; those are server facts, not jj graph facts. The local invariant is that the bookmark named in the Git push points to the tree and ancestry intended for review.

When review requests a change, edit the logical change rather than creating a fixup branch:

jj edit 'change_id(PR_CHANGE)'
# edit files
jj status
jj diff
jj describe -m 'Cache: bound memory use and expose metrics'
jj bookmark set pr/cache -r @
jj diff --from pr/cache@origin --to pr/cache
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark pr/cache

A non-fast-forward refusal is a safety signal. It can mean that the remote advanced, the tracking observation is stale, the local target is not a descendant, or server policy/authentication failed. Fetch and compare before considering any replacement. In jj 0.45.1 there is no force option on jj git push; if a host permits an exceptional replacement through another interface, treat that as a separate publication-policy decision, not a repair for an unclear graph.

Stacked PRs and review boundaries

main@origin--A--B--C--D(@)
               ▲     ▲
             pr/api  pr/metrics

One bookmark at D can publish one PR containing the stack. Two bookmarks can publish dependent review boundaries: the base bookmark at B and the dependent bookmark at D. The dependent PR's base is a GitHub setting; jj's responsibility is to publish the two intended refs and preserve their ancestry.

IntentLocal publicationServer boundary
One review containing a stackOne bookmark at the tip; push the range it makes reachable.How GitHub displays individual commits and chooses its merge base.
Two dependent reviewsOne bookmark per boundary; update both after rewrites.Set the dependent PR's base to the first PR.
Independent reviewsSeparate roots or bookmarks from one base.Each PR targets trunk rather than another review ref.

When an early member changes, descendants may receive new commit IDs because their parent IDs changed. Their jj change IDs ordinarily remain stable because they are successors, not duplicates. Move every affected publication bookmark deliberately:

jj edit 'change_id(API_CHANGE)'
# repair the early change
jj describe -m 'API: reject negative quota'
jj log -G -r 'roots(main@origin..@)::'
jj diff --from pr/api@origin --to pr/api
jj diff --from pr/metrics@origin --to pr/metrics
jj bookmark set pr/api -r 'change_id(API_CHANGE)'
jj bookmark set pr/metrics -r 'change_id(METRICS_CHANGE)'
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark pr/api --bookmark pr/metrics

Do not select a current review target by an old commit ID after a rewrite. Use the current bookmark or change ID when the intention is to follow the logical change, and use evolog to confirm the successor.

Trunk movement, rejection, and cleanup

Upstream main can advance while a PR is under review. A safe update is fetch, inspect, rebase only local mutable roots, resolve stored conflicts, move publication boundaries, and push:

jj git fetch --remote origin
jj log -G -r 'main@origin | pr/api | pr/metrics | ::pr/metrics'
jj rebase -b 'roots(main@origin..pr/metrics)' -o main@origin
jj log -r 'conflicts() & ::pr/metrics'
# resolve, then update each boundary and publish
jj bookmark set pr/api -r 'change_id(API_CHANGE)'
jj bookmark set pr/metrics -r 'change_id(METRICS_CHANGE)'
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark pr/api --bookmark pr/metrics

If another machine published a successor of the same logical change, fetching may expose divergence rather than a simple rejection. Compare the evolutions before choosing a successor, creating a new bookmark, or using the 0.45.1 converge command. A host-side or native-Git force update that merely suppresses the warning discards evidence and possibly another contributor's review.

Forks, gh, and the Git boundary

jj git remote add github git@github.com:me/project.git
jj git remote add upstream git@github.com:org/project.git
jj git fetch --remote upstream
jj new main@upstream -m 'Fix parser'
jj bookmark create me/fix -r @
jj git push --remote github --bookmark me/fix

Here the fork is the publication destination and upstream is the source boundary. Qualify remote bookmarks and use explicit --remote in aliases. gh pr view, gh pr create, and gh pr merge operate on server state. gh pr checkout is designed around Git refs and worktrees; after any Git-side ref operation, serialise writers, run jj git import if necessary, and inspect status/bookmarks. Do not let gh and jj mutate one worktree concurrently.

GitHub lifecycle checklist

  1. Fetch the intended source remote.
  2. Develop unnamed mutable work until a review boundary exists.
  3. Use change IDs for local continuity and bookmarks for server interfaces.
  4. Print local and remote bookmark targets before every update.
  5. Update every stack boundary after an early rewrite.
  6. Fetch and compare before force-updating a rejected ref.
  7. After merge or closure, fetch, compare, and clean names deliberately.

Part IX — Gerrit

Gerrit reviews commits as patch sets and uses a message footer such as Change-Id: I... to associate new commit IDs with an existing review. A jj change ID is different: it identifies a jj evolution and is not a Gerrit Change-Id. Preserve Gerrit's footer in descriptions when the server/plugin requires it, and do not infer review identity from the jj change ID.

jj 0.45.1 includes the gerrit command family and jj gerrit upload. Gerrit upload support is specialised and should be checked against the installed help and server setup. Git transport still matters: a traditional upload ref is commonly refs/for/main, with topics and push options supplied according to Gerrit policy. The server-specific protocol and UI depend on the Gerrit installation; local jj testing can establish only the client-side transport and selection behaviour.

Realistic mutable-stack workflow

jj git clone ssh://gerrit.example/project repo
cd repo
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj new main@origin -m 'API: introduce quota'
# edit; snapshot
jj new -m 'API: wire quota'
# edit; snapshot
jj log -r '::@ & mutable()'
jj gerrit upload --remote origin --remote-branch main

In jj 0.45.1, the Gerrit command accepts the options shown in this chapter; server-side acceptance remains a Gerrit policy question. The example expresses the workflow, not a universal server configuration. If using Git push directly, the equivalent transport is typically:

git push origin HEAD:refs/for/main

When review requests changes to the first change, jj edit A, edit or jj squash, then allow automatic descendant rebasing to update B. Re-upload the series. Gerrit associates each patch set by its Change-Id footer, while jj retains change IDs through rewrites. When a review lands, fetch and rebase the remaining mutable stack onto main@origin; abandon obsolete local changes only after inspecting the operation log.

GitHub and Gerrit in one repository

jj git remote add github git@github.com:me/project.git
jj git remote add gerrit ssh://gerrit.example/project
jj git fetch --remote github
jj git fetch --remote gerrit
jj log -r 'main@github | main@gerrit'

Use separate publication bookmarks such as github/topic and gerrit/topic where your naming policy permits, or at least use clear prefixes. Conditional configuration can select different push defaults by repository path. Never assume a remote named origin is safe: inspect the full remote URL before pushing.

Gerrit patch-stack lifecycle

Gerrit reviews a sequence of Git commits as patch sets. A new Git commit ID can still update an existing Gerrit review when its message contains the same Gerrit Change-Id footer and the server accepts it. jj's change ID is generated and stored by jj for local evolution; it is not the Gerrit footer, is not a server lookup key, and must not be substituted for one.

jj identity:       change qqq... → qqq... → qqq...
Git identity:      commit 111... → 222... → 333...
Gerrit identity:   Change-Id Iabc... (same review, new patch sets)

A stack:
main@origin -- A -- B -- C
               |    |    |
             I-A  I-B  I-C

Prepare descriptions

Use descriptions that retain Gerrit trailers. A jj description is a complete commit message and may contain multiple trailers. Do not assume jj change_id output is a trailer. If a Gerrit hook or upload command adds a footer, capture and inspect the resulting description before building a stack policy.

jj new main@origin
jj describe -m 'API: introduce quota

The first change establishes the invariant.

Change-Id: I1111111111111111111111111111111111111111'
jj new -m 'API: wire quota

Change-Id: I2222222222222222222222222222222222222222'
jj new -m 'API: expose metrics

Change-Id: I3333333333333333333333333333333333333333'
jj log -r '::@' -T 'change_id.short() ++ " " ++ description ++ "\n"'

The footer values above are examples. A real server may reject malformed, duplicated, or policy-forbidden trailers. Whether jj itself inserts a footer, and how it interacts with a Gerrit plugin, must be checked against the installed gerrit upload help and server configuration.

Upload the stack

jj git fetch --remote gerrit
jj log -r 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main --revision 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'

The exact commit expression should select the intended stack and no unrelated mutable work. Use --dry-run first. In 0.45.1, important upload dimensions include remote, remote branch, commit, reviewers, CC, labels, topic, hashtags, message, WIP/ready/private state, notifications, validation, merged state, attention set, deadline, custom options, and repeated --option. Treat options that alter review metadata as server-facing side effects, not ordinary local graph operations.

A direct Git transport alternative is commonly git push gerrit HEAD:refs/for/main, with server-specific push options in the ref suffix or options. That form bypasses jj's Gerrit-aware selection and should be used only when the repository's Gerrit policy is understood.

Review changes an early change

uploaded:
main -- A_1(I-A) -- B_1(I-B) -- C_1(I-C)

edit A locally:
main -- A_2(I-A) -- B_2(I-B) -- C_2(I-C)
       new Git IDs; same jj changes and Gerrit footers

jj edit 'subject(exact:"API: introduce quota")'
# edit files
jj describe -m 'API: introduce quota

Correct the invariant for zero-budget callers.

Change-Id: I1111111111111111111111111111111111111111'
jj log -r '::@'
jj log -r '::@ & conflicts()'
jj gerrit upload --dry-run --remote gerrit --remote-branch main
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main --revision 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'

The local descendants are automatically rebased over the new A. Their Git commit IDs change because their parent changed, even if their diffs are unchanged. Gerrit can recognise each new commit as a new patch set only if the footer/server rules match. jj's change ID is useful for selecting and following the local change; Gerrit's footer is the review association.

Rebase after trunk movement

jj git fetch --remote gerrit
jj log -r 'main@gerrit'
jj rebase -b 'roots(main@gerrit..@)' -o main@gerrit
jj log -r '::@ & conflicts()'
jj resolve --list
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main --revision 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'

If a change has already landed, the fetched trunk may make one stack member an ancestor of main@gerrit. Remove that landed change from the mutable stack by rebasing the remaining descendants onto the new trunk, not by blindly uploading the old series again. Inspect the graph and review IDs first.

Partial landing and remaining stack

before server submit:  main -- A -- B -- C
after A lands/fetch:   main′-- A(remote)
                                  \
                                   B′ -- C′

The precise local shape depends on the server's submitted commit and fetch mapping. The invariant is that the remaining changes must be rebased onto the fetched trunk that contains the landed work. Their jj change IDs may persist through the local rebase; their Git commit IDs will change; Gerrit Change-Ids remain the server association if preserved.

Conflict in a reviewed stack

A trunk rebase can produce a stored conflict in B′ while C′ remains a descendant. Resolve the conflict in the local change, inspect every descendant, and re-upload the series. If the server rejects a patch set, separate the local graph repair from Gerrit-side review cleanup; changing a local description cannot delete a server review.

jj log -r '::@ & conflicts()'
jj resolve --tool meld
jj diff -r 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'
jj gerrit upload --dry-run --remote gerrit --remote-branch main
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main

Topics, reviewers, and options

Review metadata can be attached on upload with reviewer, CC, label, topic, hashtag, WIP/ready, notification, and custom option flags in the target CLI. Make these choices explicit in a publication alias or command; do not assume a topic is encoded by a local bookmark name. A local bookmark is optional for jj's stack, while Gerrit upload needs a selected commit set and remote branch.

Gerrit and GitHub from one repository

jj git remote add github git@github.com:me/project.git
jj git remote add gerrit ssh://gerrit.example/project
jj git fetch --remote github
jj git fetch --remote gerrit
jj log -r 'main@github | main@gerrit'
jj bookmark create github/pr-cache -r @
jj git push --remote github --bookmark github/pr-cache
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main --revision 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'

The same local mutable stack can be published through two distinct mechanisms, but publication boundaries should be explicit. A bookmark intended for GitHub does not control Gerrit upload, and a Gerrit Change-Id footer does not make a GitHub branch a review. Use remote-qualified revsets and explicit remote options.

Local and server boundaries

BehaviourWhere it is determined
jj change IDs survive ordinary local rewritesjj's local evolution model.
Commit IDs change when parents, content, or metadata changeGit object identity and jj's rewrite operation.
Git remote/ref fetch and push mechanicsjj's Git backend and the Git server.
Gerrit footer remains in a rewritten description if the user preserves itLocal commit-message content; footer acceptance is server policy.
Gerrit review association, patch-set UI, permissions, submit, and topicsThe target Gerrit installation and its project policy.

This boundary matters: a bare Git remote can transport commits and refs, but it does not implement Gerrit's review database.

Gerrit protocol map: local commits and review refs

Gerrit workflows combine three identities: the Git commit ID uploaded over Git transport, jj’s change ID used for local evolution, and Gerrit’s Change-Id footer used by the server to associate patch sets. A fourth name may be involved: the local bookmark or remote bookmark used to reach the commit. Keep all four visible when diagnosing a review.

IdentityWhere it livesWhat survives a normal rewrite?What it is for
Commit IDGit object graph and server patch setNo; new tree/parent/metadata gives a new ID.Exact object, build, fetch, server evidence.
jj change IDjj change evolution metadata/renderingNormally yes, as a successor relation.Local logical change across amendments.
Gerrit Change-IdCommit message footerYes if description is preserved.Server review identity and patch-set association.
Bookmark/refLocal/remote Git ref namespacesOnly if explicitly moved/exported.Reachability and publication.

A review command should print all relevant fields before upload:

jj log -r '@:: & mutable()' -T '
change_id.short() ++ "\t" ++ commit_id ++ "\t" ++
description.first_line() ++ "\n"
'
git log -n 1 --format='%H%n%B'  # inspect Gerrit footer through Git when needed

Use the native Git command only as a cross-check of the exported commit object. The jj description is the source of the commit message in the jj model; a colocated Git view may lag until export/import or normal backend synchronisation occurs.

Upload a stack deliberately

A stack upload should define its base and its upper boundary. The explicit query @:: & mutable() selects the mutable descendant closure of the current workspace commit, but can include a temporary child or omit a sibling review. For a repeatable review, select the exact stack by bookmark, remote trunk, or a named revset alias and print the result.

jj log -r 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::' --no-graph \
  -T 'commit_id.short() ++ " " ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'
jj gerrit upload --dry-run --remote gerrit \
  --remote-branch main -r 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'

Do not assume that a range’s root is the review base in a graph containing merges. If the stack forks, take the roots and heads explicitly and decide whether Gerrit should receive one linear series or several independent changes. Gerrit’s server interpretation of multiple commits and dependencies is authoritative; jj can prepare the graph but cannot change server review policy.

Review feedback on an ancestor

When an early change is amended, all descendants are candidates for automatic rebasing. This is precisely the operation that makes mutable stacks attractive, but it also means every later review commit may receive a new Git ID. Preserve each descendant’s description and Gerrit footer, inspect conflicts, run tests on the final head, and re-upload the series. If only one review is intended to change, do not accidentally upload an unrelated sibling.

jj edit 'change_id(qxy...)'
# edit and test
jj describe -m 'Core: reject invalid limits

Change-Id: I1234567890abcdef'
jj log -r 'change_id(qxy...)::'
jj log -r 'change_id(qxy...):: & conflicts()'
