jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main -r 'change_id(qxy...)::'

If a descendant conflict is not yet understood, stop before upload. The conflict is stored and inspectable, but server-side review cannot generally represent an unresolved jj conflict as a meaningful diff. Resolve at the lowest commit that establishes the intended API, then retest descendants.

Topics, options, and server state

Gerrit topics and upload options are server metadata. A topic can group a series without changing jj graph topology. Reviewers, CCs, labels, hashtags, notification policy, WIP/ready/private state, and custom push options should be treated as part of the upload request, not as commit identity. Record them in a script or checked-in review note if the review must be reproducible.

In 0.45.1, gerrit.default-remote, gerrit.default-remote-branch, and gerrit.review-url can provide repository-specific defaults. The portable form passes remote and branch explicitly. This book does not claim that a particular Gerrit server enables every upload option; server plugins, permissions, and version determine acceptance.

After a change lands

Landing changes on Gerrit changes the remote branch, not the local operation DAG. Fetch, inspect the new remote bookmark, identify the corresponding local logical change, and rebase remaining changes. If the landed commit is not equivalent to the local one—for example, the server applied a submit strategy that changed the resulting commit—use diff/content and message evidence rather than assuming commit IDs match.

jj git fetch --remote gerrit
jj log -r 'main@gerrit'
jj log -r 'remote_bookmarks() & description(substring:"Core")'
jj rebase -s 'roots(remaining_stack)' -d main@gerrit

Once a review is abandoned or replaced, keep a temporary bookmark until the replacement is verified. Then delete local publication names that no longer represent active server refs and use jj git push --deleted only when the deletion is intentional and permitted.

Gerrit stack lifecycle: three identities and two review iterations

Gerrit is unusually well matched to jj's mutable history, but only if the identities are kept separate. A local change ID says which jj evolution is being edited. A commit ID says which exact tree, parents, and metadata are being uploaded. A Gerrit Change-Id: I... footer says which server review should receive a new patch set. The local bookmark or remote bookmark answers how the object is reached. None of these four identifiers is a substitute for another.

jj graph                 exported commit             Gerrit review
A (base)                 1a2...                      -
B (API)                  2b3... + Change-Id: Iapi    API, patch set 1
C (tests)                3c4... + Change-Id: Itest   tests, patch set 1
D (metrics)              4d5... + Change-Id: Imet     metrics, patch set 1

jj change IDs remain stable through ordinary rewrites;
commit IDs change; Gerrit associates the new object by footer.

An existing Change-Id footer remains the server-facing review identity: upload uses it to update the corresponding Gerrit change with a new patch set. If the selected commit has no footer, jj 0.45.1 generates one from the jj change ID for the commit object it uploads. That generated trailer is added to the uploaded object only; it is not added to the local commit in the working repository. The uploaded commit ID can therefore differ from the local commit ID, and fetching the result can expose divergence. If you want the footer and resulting commit ID to exist locally before upload, configure templates.commit_trailers with format_gerrit_change_id_trailer(self). This still does not make a jj change ID equal to a Gerrit review identity: it derives a footer for transport. Server association, permissions, and patch-set policy remain Gerrit-dependent.

Create and prepare the stack

jj git fetch --remote gerrit
jj new main@gerrit -m 'API: introduce quota'
# edit implementation
jj new -m 'API: validate quota'
# edit tests
jj new -m 'Metrics: expose quota counters'
# edit metrics
jj log -G -r 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'
jj diff -r 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'

The current working-copy commit is an ordinary mutable stack tip. There need not be a local bookmark. An existing Gerrit footer is preserved and associates the uploaded object with the existing review. When a footer is absent, jj gerrit upload in 0.45.1 derives one from the jj change ID and adds it to the uploaded commit only. This is convenient, but it means the uploaded commit ID may not match the local commit ID. If local and uploaded IDs should match, configure templates.commit_trailers so the footer is generated during local snapshotting; otherwise record the upload-time object and expect a possible divergence after fetch. The following is illustrative message content when choosing to keep the footer locally:

[templates]
commit_trailers = '''
if(
  !trailers.contains_key("Change-Id"),
  format_gerrit_change_id_trailer(self)
)
'''
API: introduce quota

Change-Id: I0000000000000000000000000000000000000001

Use jj describe or an editor while editing one change at a time. Keep the footer in the body rather than trying to encode it in a bookmark. Confirm every selected commit:

jj log -r 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::' -T '
change_id.short() ++ " " ++ commit_id ++ "\n" ++
description ++ "\n"

A stack may be uploaded through the specialised command:

jj gerrit upload --dry-run --remote gerrit \
  --remote-branch main --revision 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit \
  --remote-branch main --revision 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'

The dry-run boundary is valuable even when the server does not provide a full preview. It confirms the selected local commits and exposes command-level assumptions before an external side effect. The server decides whether the ref is refs/for/main, which commit messages are accepted, and how reviewers, topics, labels, WIP/ready, notifications, and validation options are interpreted. jj's local responsibility is selecting and exporting the commit set.

Review changes an early change

before review: main--B--C--D(@)
                         B, C, D uploaded

review says:   B needs a stronger invariant
local edit:    main--B'--C'--D'(@)
               same jj changes, new commit IDs,
               same Gerrit footers if preserved

Edit the logical change by change ID, not by an old commit prefix:

jj edit 'change_id(API_CHANGE)'
# edit implementation and tests relevant to B
jj status
jj diff
jj describe -m 'API: reject negative quota

Change-Id: I0000000000000000000000000000000000000001'
jj evolog -r 'change_id(API_CHANGE)'
jj log -G -r 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'

Because C and D have B as an ancestor, automatic descendant rebasing uses B' as their new parent. Their diffs are replayed in the new context. If the replay is clean, C' and D' have new commit IDs but keep their jj change IDs; if context no longer applies, one or more descendants become conflicted commits. The correct next action is not a Git-style rebase continuation. Inspect the stored conflict set, work on the affected change, resolve it, and then inspect the whole stack.

jj log -r '::@ & conflicts()'
jj diff -r 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'
jj resolve
jj log -G -r 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'

After the local stack is coherent, re-upload the same commit set. Gerrit should associate each commit with its footer when the server's rules permit it, generating new patch sets rather than unrelated reviews. That association is a Gerrit server fact; local validation can only prove that the footer survived and that the exported commit message contains the expected bytes.

A lower change lands while the upper stack remains

Suppose B lands first, perhaps after review and submit, while C and D remain under review:

server main:  main--B
local before: main@gerrit--B--C--D(@)
after fetch:  main@gerrit--B'   # server's landed object may differ
local work:   C--D still based on old imported boundary

Fetch to import the server's new main and determine whether the landed change is identical, an amended equivalent, or a different object:

jj git fetch --remote gerrit
jj log -G -r 'main@gerrit | roots(main@gerrit..@)::'
jj diff --from main@gerrit --to 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'

Rebase only the remaining mutable changes onto the new remote boundary. Do not rebase the remote bookmark itself and do not assume a commit ID equality is required for semantic equivalence:

jj rebase -b 'roots(main@gerrit..@)' -o main@gerrit
jj log -r '::@ & conflicts()'
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main \
  --revision 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'

The remaining commits may receive new IDs again. Their Gerrit footers should remain constant if descriptions are preserved, so the server can update the existing reviews. If the server's submit strategy created a merge or changed the effective base, inspect the resulting ancestry and choose the new remote bookmark as the authoritative base.

Topics, reviewers, and upload options

Gerrit upload options are a second channel of review metadata. A topic is not a bookmark name. A reviewer flag is not a commit author. A WIP/ready flag is not a jj mutability predicate. Keep these channels explicit:

ChannelLocal jj meaningGerrit meaning
jj change IDEvolution identity used to find a mutable change.No direct server interpretation.
Commit message footerText in the commit description.Review association when server policy recognises Change-Id.
BookmarkOptional local publication name.Git ref/name used to transfer a commit set.
--topicUpload option.Requests server-side topic grouping; Gerrit permissions and server policy determine whether the request is accepted.
--reviewer/--ccUpload option.Server review metadata, permissions permitting.
--label/--hashtagUpload option.Server label/hashtag request, subject to validation.

Pass explicit remote and branch arguments in portable scripts. The jj 0.45.1 configuration surface documents Gerrit defaults such as gerrit.default-remote, gerrit.default-remote-branch, and gerrit.review-url. A default reduces typing but increases the importance of inspecting effective configuration before a public upload.

Conflict, abandonment, and replacement

If a conflict appears after trunk movement, resolve the local graph first and re-upload only after the stack's diffs are understood. If a review is abandoned on the server, that does not abandon the local jj change. The local change may be retained, renamed, duplicated into a new review with a new footer, or abandoned locally after an operation checkpoint. Choosing among these is a review-lifecycle decision.

# Preserve evidence before replacing a review
jj op log -n 10
jj evolog -r 'change_id(API_CHANGE)'
jj bookmark create rescue-gerrit -r 'change_id(API_CHANGE)'
# either amend the same footer and re-upload, or intentionally create a
# new change/message and new publication identity
jj duplicate -r 'change_id(API_CHANGE)' -o main@gerrit

Do not use jj undo to claim that an already uploaded patch set disappeared. Undo changes local repository state; it cannot retract a Gerrit review. Use Gerrit's abandon/delete/restore controls according to server policy and then fetch to observe the resulting refs. Local and server cleanup are separate operations.

Evidence boundary for Gerrit

ClaimAuthority
jj change ID and commit ID have distinct roles.jj's local change and commit model.
Automatic descendant rebasing changes descendant commit IDs.jj's rewrite semantics.
Commit message footer survives if the user preserves it.Local commit-message content.
Git refs and fetch/push mechanics.jj's Git backend and the Git server.
refs/for/main review creation and patch-set association.Gerrit's upload protocol and server documentation.
Reviewer/label/topic permissions and submit strategy.The target Gerrit installation and project policy.

Part X — Conflicts and merges

A jj conflict is a first-class, serialisable value in a commit. A rewrite can produce a conflicted successor; descendants can carry that conflict forward. The conflict may be materialised as marker files in the working copy, but the markers are a rendering of stored sides, not the authoritative state.

base -- A -- C
  \       \
   \- B -- merge/rebase result with sides A and B

jj log -r 'conflicts()'
jj resolve --tool meld
jj diff
jj describe -m 'resolved: quota conflict'

Use jj resolve with the configured merge editor/tool, or edit the materialised markers and let the next snapshot record the result. Multi-sided conflicts can have more than two input terms; do not assume a two-column Git index. Configure marker style and merge tools explicitly, and check the result with jj diff plus jj log -r 'conflicts()'.

Because the conflict is stored in the commit, you can continue unrelated work, resolve later, rebase a conflicted stack, split a conflict, or restore selected paths. A merge commit is an intentional multiple-parent commit; it is not the same as a conflict value. Use repeated rebase destinations or jj new A B where the command's syntax creates a merge, then resolve its content.

Conflict lifecycle laboratory

A conflict is a structured value in a commit tree. It has a base and one or more sides for a path; the working copy renders that value as conflict markers so a human or tool can produce a resolved file. The marker file is not the complete representation: a multi-sided conflict can encode more alternatives than a two-way marker layout suggests.

Creation by rebase

base -- A: change line 10 to "red"
  \
   B: change line 10 to "blue"

before moving B onto A:
base -- A
  \
   B

after jj rebase -r B -o A:
base -- A -- B′(conflict)
                  |
                  \- B's change is preserved as a stored conflict value

The command has completed: B′ exists and can be selected by its successor/evolution relationship. The conflict is visible to conflicts(), and a current workspace at B′ materialises markers. A descendant C is rebased onto B′ and may itself be conflicted or may carry the conflict value through untouched paths.

jj rebase -r B -o A
jj log -r '::@ & conflicts()'
jj resolve --list
jj diff
jj resolve --tool meld
jj log -r '::@ & conflicts()'

Resolution rewrites B′ into B″. C receives a successor C′ because its parent changed from B′ to B″, even if C's own file edits were not involved. The operation log contains both the conflict-producing rewrite and the resolving rewrite. If resolution was wrong, undoing the resolution returns to the stored conflict; restoring the earlier operation returns to the prior graph.

Manual markers versus a merge editor

There are two common resolution paths. jj resolve --tool NAME invokes the configured merge tool with the stored sides. Alternatively, edit the materialised file, remove markers, and let jj snapshot the working-copy commit. The latter is convenient for a simple file; the former is preferable when the conflict has binary files, directory/file changes, or a tool-specific merge policy.

# Discover paths before selecting a subset
jj resolve --list -r @
jj resolve --tool :ours -r @ -- 'root-file:"src/quota.rs"'
jj resolve --tool :theirs -r @ -- 'root-file:"docs/design.md"'

The built-in :ours and :theirs choices refer to applicable conflict sides, not universally to “my branch” and “their branch” in a Git branch sense. In a multi-sided conflict, inspect the materialisation and command help before choosing a side. A side choice is a semantic content decision, not a conflict acknowledgement.

Conflict propagation through a stack

A -- B -- C -- D
     ▲
     B′ conflicted after B is rebased

A -- B′(conflict) -- C′(conflict?) -- D′
                         ▲
                         descendants preserve/reapply diffs over B′

Propagation is path-sensitive. C′ may not be marked conflicted if its diff does not overlap the unresolved path, but its parent tree still contains a conflict value. A stack can therefore contain a conflicted ancestor even when a descendant's own conflict() is false. Query the ancestry as well as the individual commit:

jj log -r 'conflicts()'
jj log -r 'conflicts()::'
jj log -r '::@ & conflicts()'
jj diff -r 'roots(::@ & conflicts())..@'

Do not use the presence of a marker file as the repository-level conflict test. The filesystem may be incomplete, the current workspace may point elsewhere, or markers may have been edited without a snapshot. The stored commit and conflicts() are the authoritative query.

Merge commits and conflict values

A merge commit has multiple parents; a conflict value is a tree entry whose content has multiple terms. A merge can be conflict-free, and a single-parent rebase can produce a conflicted commit. Conversely, resolving a conflict does not remove a merge commit's multiple-parent topology. Use merges() and conflicts() as separate predicates.

jj new A B -m 'Merge API and documentation'
jj log -r 'merges()'
jj log -r 'merges() & conflicts()'

The merge's diff is calculated against the automatic merge of its parents. If the parents disagree, resolving the conflicting file contents does not make the graph linear. Preserve the merge when it expresses integration history; use rebase/parallelize when the graph should express a stack instead.

Rewriting while conflicted

Because the conflict is stored, ordinary graph operations remain available. You can rebase a conflicted stack onto a new trunk, split the conflicted commit, restore one path from a known-good commit, or continue unrelated work in another workspace. Each operation may create a new conflict state; inspect the path-level result.

jj edit 'conflicts() & heads(::@)'
jj restore --from main@origin --into @ -- 'root-file:"Cargo.toml"'
jj split --interactive -r @
jj rebase -s @ -o main@origin
jj log -r '::@ & conflicts()'

There is no mandatory conflict queue. The useful discipline is to make conflict state visible in the daily log, keep the operation that produced it, and resolve at a deliberate graph boundary rather than accidentally committing marker text as ordinary content.

Conflict checklist

  1. Identify the commit and paths with resolve --list and conflicts().
  2. Determine whether the conflict is in an ancestor and therefore affects the whole stack.
  3. Inspect the graph and the automatic merge base; do not infer sides from bookmark names.
  4. Choose tool, side, or manual edit; record the policy when a review is involved.
  5. Snapshot/resolve, then inspect diff, conflict predicate, descendants, and operation.
  6. Only publish after the selected publication bookmark points to the resolved successor.

Conflict lifecycle laboratory: from graph result to resolved tree

A jj conflict is a value in a commit, not a paused rebase session. That difference changes the work sequence. A rewrite can finish by producing a conflicted successor; descendants can be rebased over that value; unrelated changes can be inspected or even edited; and resolution can happen later. There is no hidden index state that must be cleared before the next jj command can make progress.

base--A--B--C(@)              clean stack
       \     B changes same line
rewrite: base--A'--B'--C'(@)  B' carries a conflict
                              C' may carry propagated conflict

The conflict has graph consequences and tree consequences. The graph stores the conflict as part of the commit's tree value. A working copy materialises conflict sides using the configured marker style so an editor can repair files. The materialised files are only the workspace view; the resolved content becomes a new snapshot and therefore a new successor commit. A conflict marker in a file is not, by itself, proof that the commit has a conflict object, and a conflicted commit need not currently be checked out.

Creation and propagation

Conflicts arise when a diff cannot be applied cleanly to its new parent or when multiple parent trees cannot be merged without choosing content. Common producers are rebase, squash, restore, split, and an explicit merge. The producer operation can complete even when the result is conflicted. Automatic descendant rebasing then attempts to apply each descendant diff to the changed context. A descendant that does not touch the affected region may remain clean; one that does may carry a conflict of its own.

jj log -G -r '::@'
jj log -r 'conflicts() & ::@'
jj log -r 'conflicts() & @:: & mutable()'
jj show -r 'conflicts() & ::@' --summary

Query the graph before opening an editor. If B' is conflicted and C' is clean, editing C' first can still be useful for reviewing its independent diff, but a later repair to B' may rebase C' again. If the conflict is at an ancestor, resolving it can change every descendant commit ID even when their content remains semantically identical. Use change IDs to follow the logical changes and operation/evolution logs to account for object churn.

Materialisation and sides

For a two-sided conflict, the workspace contains a marker representation with a base and the competing sides according to the configured conflict marker style. A multi-sided conflict can contain more than two alternatives because repeated rebases and merges preserve more than one side. Treat markers as an input format to a merge editor, not a syntax to resolve by deleting lines at random.

What the materialised file looks like

In jj 0.45.1 the default marker style is diff. The following is an illustrative two-sided file; the abbreviated IDs and descriptions are labels, not part of the conflict algebra:

before:
apple
grape
orange

after materialising the conflict:
<<<<<<< conflict 1 of 1
%%%%%%% diff from: BASE1234 "merge base"
\\\\\\\        to: SIDEA123 "change A"
 apple
-grape
+grapefruit
 orange
+++++++ SIDEB456 "change B"
APPLE
GRAPE
ORANGE
>>>>>>> conflict 1 of 1 ends

Read this as an instruction for constructing a result, not as two independent files separated by a line of equals signs. The +++++++ section is a complete snapshot of one side. The %%%%%%%/\\\\\\\ section describes a diff from the base to another side: context lines begin with a space, removed lines with -, and added lines with +. Applying that diff to the snapshot produces the other side. In this example the useful resolution is to combine the intent—APPLE, GRAPEFRUIT, ORANGE—and remove the markers before jj snapshots the result.

In that example, the one-space rule applies only to the diff section between %%%%%%% and the next side marker: the literal leading spaces on apple and orange are context prefixes. The uppercase APPLE, GRAPE, and ORANGE lines belong to the complete snapshot section and intentionally have no diff prefix.

A multi-sided conflict uses the same structure but has one snapshot section and more than one diff section. Conceptually, for a base B and sides S1, S2, and S3, the file has the shape:

<<<<<<< conflict 1 of 1
+++++++ S1 "one snapshot side"
...complete contents of S1...
%%%%%%% diff from: B "common base"
\\\\\\\        to: S2 "second side"
...diff B → S2...
%%%%%%% diff from: B "common base"
\\\\\\\        to: S3 "third side"
...diff B → S3...
>>>>>>> conflict 1 of 1 ends

The exact commit labels identify the stored terms; the marker count identifies the conflict region within the file. If a file contains two independent conflict regions, their headers are conflict 1 of 2 and conflict 2 of 2. A conflict can therefore have both multiple regions and multiple sides. Do not infer the number of parents from the number of visible marker blocks: the conflict value records the terms, while the file is only its textual projection.

The three stable marker styles and one experimental value
StyleFile representationMulti-sided behaviourUse it when
diff (default)One complete snapshot plus diffs from the base to the other sides.Supports arbitrarily many sides; additional sides appear as additional diff sections.You want a compact, reviewable representation that makes each side's change explicit.
snapshotA complete snapshot section for each side and the base.Supports multiple sides directly, at the cost of repeated unchanged content.You need to inspect the full contents of every term or use a tool that expects snapshot blocks.
gitGit diff3-style <<<<<<<, |||||||, =======, and >>>>>>> sections.Only supports two-sided conflicts; jj falls back to a snapshot-like representation for more than two sides.A tool requires Git-style diff3 markers and the conflict is genuinely two-sided.
diff-experimentalExperimental alternative to the default diff-based materialisation.Accepted by the jj 0.45.1 configuration schema and capable of materialising conflicts, but its textual layout is not treated as a stable book-level interface.Only when deliberately testing the target release and willing to track changes in later jj versions.

These are alternatives; set exactly one value in an effective [ui] configuration table:

[ui]
# Choose one. jj's default: one snapshot plus one or more diffs
conflict-marker-style = "diff"

# Or: complete snapshots for base and every side
conflict-marker-style = "snapshot"

# Or: Git diff3 compatibility; not a general multi-sided format
conflict-marker-style = "git"

The 0.45.1 schema also accepts conflict-marker-style = "diff-experimental". It is intentionally not given a fixed marker example here: the value is experimental, and its rendering is subject to change. The stable choices for a book, merge-tool configuration, or interchange script are the three styles described above. Inspect the target with jj util config-schema and run a disposable conflict fixture before relying on the experimental style.

For comparison, the two-sided part of snapshot style is represented as complete sections rather than a diff:

<<<<<<< conflict 1 of 1
+++++++ SIDEA123 "change A"
apple
grapefruit
orange
------- BASE1234 "merge base"
apple
grape
orange
+++++++ SIDEB456 "change B"
APPLE
GRAPE
ORANGE
>>>>>>> conflict 1 of 1 ends

A three-sided snapshot contains one +++++++ section for each side plus the ------- base section. It is easy to read but can repeat a large amount of unchanged text; the default diff style represents the same alternatives more compactly.

In Git style, the conceptual two-sided form is:

<<<<<<< SIDEA123 "change A"
apple
grapefruit
orange
||||||| BASE1234 "merge base"
apple
grape
orange
=======
APPLE
GRAPE
ORANGE
>>>>>>> SIDEB456 "change B"

Changing ui.conflict-marker-style changes only this materialised representation. It does not change the stored conflict value or make a conflict two-sided. Marker lines are normally seven characters long, but jj can lengthen them when file content could otherwise be mistaken for a marker. Files without a terminating newline receive special treatment so that every marker begins on its own line; the closing marker may consequently have no terminating newline. These details matter to scripts and parsers, so use jj's configured merge tooling rather than matching marker text with an ad-hoc regular expression. The layouts and fallback behaviour in this section follow the official jj conflict-marker documentation; the abbreviated examples are original and use illustrative labels.

jj log -r @ -T 'conflict ++ \" sides=\" ++ conflicted_files.map(|f| f.conflict_side_count()).join(\",\") ++ \"\\n\"'
jj resolve --list
jj resolve --tool :builtin

In jj 0.45.1, jj resolve --list lists the conflicts, jj resolve --tool NAME selects a resolver, and the builtin tools include :ours and :theirs. The stable invariant is that a resolver reads the stored conflict and writes a chosen tree. If the resolver leaves a conflict, the resulting commit remains conflicted. Check with jj log -r @ -T 'conflict' and inspect the files rather than assuming the tool's exit status means all conflict objects disappeared.

Manual resolution is a snapshot boundary

A safe manual repair has four checkpoints:

  1. Save the current operation ID and the conflicted change's change ID.
  2. Inspect the conflict sides and the intended semantic result.
  3. Edit files, run focused tests, and snapshot deliberately.
  4. Verify that the change is no longer in conflicts() and review every descendant.
jj op log -n 5
jj log -r '@' -T 'change_id ++ \" \" ++ commit_id ++ \" \" ++ conflict ++ \"\\n\"'
# edit files and test
jj status
jj log -r '@' -T 'change_id ++ \" \" ++ commit_id ++ \" \" ++ conflict ++ \"\\n\"'
jj log -r '::@ & conflicts()'
jj diff -r @

If a test or editor changes files after the initial snapshot, the next jj command may record them. If reproducibility matters, use an explicit snapshot command or run the command that owns the snapshot boundary, then record the operation. Avoid --ignore-working-copy for the verification that is supposed to observe the repair unless you first understand which recorded tree it will read.

Rewrite, squash, split, restore

When squashing into a conflicted or conflict-adjacent change, ask whether the incoming diff is meant to resolve the conflict or merely to add more content. A fileset can restrict the paths moved, but it cannot choose among conflict sides. When splitting a conflicted commit, the conflict may be divided between the resulting changes or remain in both if each diff depends on the unresolved context. Afterward inspect each commit's conflict predicate.

Restore can be used to replace a conflicted path with a known tree version, but it is not a conflict resolver in the semantic sense. It copies content from a source or reverses a selected change. A subsequent snapshot may clear the conflict if all conflict objects are represented by the edited tree; otherwise the conflict remains. Keep a temporary bookmark before a broad restore and use jj diff --from/--to to confirm the chosen side.

jj bookmark create before-resolve -r @
jj restore --from main@origin --into @ -- 'root-prefix-glob:"src"'
jj log -r '::@ & conflicts()'
jj diff --from before-resolve --to @ -- 'root-prefix-glob:"src"'

Merge commits versus conflict results

A merge commit has multiple parents. It can be clean or conflicted. A conflicted single-parent successor created by a rebase is not automatically a merge commit; it records an unresolved diff application against one new parent. Conversely, an explicit jj new P Q creates a merge shape even if the trees happen to agree. Use parent inspection, not conflict status, to distinguish these cases.

jj new A B -m 'Merge independent lines'
jj log -r @ -T 'parents.map(|p| p.commit_id()).join(\" \") ++ \"\\n\"'
jj log -r 'merges()'
jj log -r 'conflicts()'

A merge can be a deliberate review or integration boundary. Keep it only when the project wants that ancestry; otherwise rebase or simplify parents may produce a more linear diff story. A conflict may be resolved in a merge commit by editing the working copy, but the resulting tree must be reviewed as a merge result against both parents.

Validation matrix

StateGraph checkFilesystem checkNext safe action
Stored conflict, not checked outconflicts() & REV selects it.No marker is necessarily in current files.jj edit REV or inspect with show.
Stored conflict, checked outconflict template is true.Markers/materialised sides are present.Resolve or create a new child and leave it for later.
Clean descendant over conflicted ancestorDescendant absent from conflicts().Depends on current workspace.Review whether its diff is still semantically valid.
Resolution snapshotTarget removed from conflict set.Resolved file is materialised.Run focused tests and inspect descendants/evolution.
Unresolved multi-sided valueConflict side count remains greater than one.Marker style may show several blocks.Use a merge tool or resolve sides explicitly.

The most dangerous conflict mistake is treating a clean status as a semantic proof. A descendant can be syntactically clean while its assumptions were invalidated by the ancestor rewrite. Review the diff and tests, not just the marker predicate.

Part XI — Operation history, change evolution, undo, and recovery

Operation history: repository-wide transformations

jj has two graphs:

commit DAG:     root - A - B - C
                         \ rewrite
operation DAG:  op0 - op1 - op2 - op3
                           \ concurrent op

The commit DAG describes source history. The operation DAG describes repository transformations: snapshots, rewrites, imports, ref moves, and recovery. This is richer than a Git reflog, which is primarily a per-ref movement record.

jj op log
jj op show OPERATION
jj op diff --from OP1 --to OP2
jj op restore OPERATION
jj op abandon OPERATION
jj op revert OPERATION
jj undo
jj redo

jj undo reverses the latest operation; redo reapplies the most recently undone operation when available. op restore loads a repository state from the operation DAG. --at-operation OP inspects an old state without snapshotting the current filesystem. Operations created with --no-integrate-operation are not merged into the current operation head until explicitly integrated.

Views and IDs

An operation ID identifies a repository transformation in this clone. Loading jj --at-operation OP log asks jj to evaluate the commit graph and refs as they were at that operation, while ignoring today's working-copy snapshot. It does not roll back the filesystem. A historical view is therefore an observation tool, not a checkout command.

jj op log -n 20
jj op show OP
jj op diff --from OP1 --to OP2
jj --at-operation OP log -r 'all()'
jj --at-operation OP status

Record operation IDs before a risky rewrite, not only after it. The ID printed by op log may be a short unique prefix; retain the full ID in an incident note when the repository is important. A later operation does not necessarily erase the earlier record, but garbage collection or operation abandonment can reduce recoverability.

Undo, restore, revert, and abandon are different

OperationTargetResultUse
jj undoMost recent integrated operation.Creates a reverse operation.Immediate, unambiguous mistake.
jj redoAvailable undone operation.Reapplies it when redo state exists.Recover from an over-hasty undo.
jj op restore OPNamed historical repository state.Creates a new state matching selected operation data.Return to a known graph/ref state.
jj op revert OPEffect of a selected operation.Creates a reversing operation while remaining in operation history.Reverse a named operation after later history exists.
jj op abandon OPOperation record.Removes/abandons an operation according to local semantics.Maintenance after recovery, not commit deletion.
jj abandon REVSelected commit.Hides/abandons a change and rebases or updates dependants.Declare graph work no longer wanted.

In particular, jj op revert is not jj revert. The former reverses repository-state effects; the latter creates an inverse content change. Likewise, jj op restore does not promise to restore an external push or today's files. If the mistake crossed a network boundary, repair that server separately and then fetch to make the local observation agree.

Evolution log: following one change through time

jj evolog is the command to use when the question is “what happened to this logical change?” It follows one jj change ID through the successive commit objects that represented it. That is a different question from “what did the repository-wide operation do?” (jj op show) and from “where did a bookmark point?” (jj bookmark list). A Git commit ID identifies one object; an evolution entry connects that object to its predecessor versions of the same logical change.

logical change X

X0  --describe/rewrite-->  X1  --ancestor rebase-->  X2  --resolve-->  X3
|                          |                           |
commit c0                  commit c1                   commit c2
operation o0               operation o1                operation o2

The arrows are not ordinary parent edges in the commit DAG. A successor may have the same parent, a new parent, a different tree, or different metadata; its change ID normally remains the logical identity. Descendants can receive their own successors because their parent commit IDs changed. A bookmark normally follows the rewritten local graph target, while an already fetched remote bookmark remains the local observation of the server until the next import.

Evolution is therefore not a second commit DAG and not a ref log. It is a change-centric history layered over commit objects. The operation DAG supplies the wider causal context: it can show that one operation rewrote X, its descendants, a bookmark, and a workspace together. Evolution tells you which of those commit objects belong to X.

A reusable fixture: record identities before reasoning

Use a disposable repository with a named logical change, several amendments, and a descendant. The important discipline is to record full IDs, not the short graph labels used in diagrams:

mkdir -p /tmp/jj-evolog-lab
cd /tmp/jj-evolog-lab
jj git init --colocate
printf 'one\n' > api.txt
jj describe -m 'API: initial contract'
change=$(jj log -r @ --no-graph -T 'change_id ++ "\n"')
c0=$(jj log -r @ --no-graph -T 'commit_id ++ "\n"')

printf 'two\n' > api.txt
jj describe -m 'API: two contract'
c1=$(jj log -r @ --no-graph -T 'commit_id ++ "\n"')

printf 'three\n' > api.txt
jj describe -m 'API: three contract'
c2=$(jj log -r @ --no-graph -T 'commit_id ++ "\n"')

jj new -m 'Tests: cover API'
printf 'test\n' > test.txt
jj status
child=$(jj log -r @ --no-graph -T 'change_id ++ "\n"')

printf 'logical change: %s\n' "$change"
printf 'initial/current/descendant: %s %s %s\n' "$c0" "$c2" "$child"
jj evolog -r "$change" -G -T \
  'commit.commit_id() ++ "\t" ++
   commit.change_id() ++ "\t" ++
   operation.id() ++ "\t" ++
   commit.description().first_line() ++ "\n"'

The last command is deliberately a tabular evidence export. Its template runs in the CommitEvolutionEntry context, so the commit and operation are accessed as commit.commit_id() and operation.id(), not as the ordinary log keywords commit_id and change_id. Store the output when correlating a review or incident. Short IDs are useful for a screen; the full commit ID, change ID, and operation ID are the durable local evidence.

StageCommit-DAG stateEvolution evidenceRef/operation consequence
Initialroot -> X0c0 and change are recorded before the first rewrite.The working-copy commit points at X0; no publication bookmark is required.
Amendmentsroot -> X1, then root -> X2c1 and c2 differ, while change is normally unchanged.Each describe creates an operation and hides the preceding commit from ordinary visible output.
Descendantroot -> X2 -> TT has its own change ID and can be followed independently.A bookmark at T names a publication boundary; it does not replace X's evolution history.
Ancestor rewriteroot -> X3 -> T'evolog -r "$change" finds X0...X3; evolog -r "$child" can find T and T'.T' may have a new commit ID even when its own intended diff is unchanged, because its parent changed.

This table separates four identifiers that are often collapsed in review conversations:

  • change ID: the logical identity followed by evolog;
  • commit ID: one exact tree/parent/metadata object, suitable for matching a CI result or exported Git object;
  • bookmark: a local publication/navigation name that may move to a successor;
  • operation ID: the repository-wide transformation that created or rewrote the commit.

Reading order, selection, and output modes

The basic command follows the change selected by the revision set. With no -r, the default is @; in scripts, select the logical change explicitly and save the full value first:

change=$(jj log -r @ --no-graph -T 'change_id ++ "\n"')
jj evolog -r "$change"
jj evolog -r "$change" --reversed
jj evolog -r "$change" -n 4
jj evolog -r "$change" -G

Normal output presents the current version first and walks backwards through predecessors. --reversed presents the oldest entry first and the current version last, which is usually better for a narrative of a review. -n/--limit limits the entries after jj has selected and topologically ordered the evolution; with --reversed, the limit therefore describes the beginning of the reversed display, not necessarily the newest versions. -G/--no-graph removes graph decoration but does not change which entries are selected.

Use a template when the question is identity or correlation rather than prose:

jj evolog -G -r "$change" -T \
  'commit.commit_id().short(12) ++ " " ++
   commit.change_id().short(12) ++ " " ++
   operation.id().short(12) ++ " " ++
   commit.description().first_line() ++ "\n"'

The template context is an evolution entry. The important methods are commit(), operation(), predecessors(), and inter_diff(). Use the corresponding commit methods when the report needs signatures and timestamps. Keep an unlabelled, newline-delimited form for scripts; terminal labels and graph glyphs are presentation, not evidence.

Comparing successive versions with -p

jj evolog -p adds the inter-diff between an evolution entry and its previous version. It answers “what changed in this logical change between these two versions?”, which is usually the question a reviewer means by “what changed in patch set 4?”:

jj evolog -r "$change" -p
jj evolog -r "$change" -p --stat
jj evolog -r "$change" -p --name-only
jj evolog -r "$change" --reversed -p

The first entry has no earlier version of the same change, so it has no meaningful predecessor diff. Later entries show the change between successive versions, not the complete diff from the repository root and not necessarily the diff between two arbitrary branch tips. Use jj diff --from OLD --to NEW when the endpoints are arbitrary commits rather than adjacent versions of one change.

Parent-rebase caveat. If the previous version has different parents, jj temporarily rebases that previous version to the new version's parents before computing the inter-diff. This prevents an unrelated ancestor change from appearing as though it were part of the logical change's revision. The displayed patch is therefore an evolution comparison, not necessarily the raw tree diff between the two stored commit objects. Do not reconstruct it by blindly running jj diff --from OLD --to NEW when their parent contexts differ.

For a machine-readable review record, combine the identity template with a separate patch command. Save the current and predecessor full IDs from the evolution output, then run the explicit diff only when you intentionally want object-to-object comparison:

jj evolog -G -r "$change" -T \
  'commit.commit_id() ++ " " ++ operation.id() ++
   " " ++ commit.description().first_line() ++ "\n"'
# After choosing adjacent entries OLD and NEW deliberately:
jj diff --from OLD --to NEW --git

Ancestor rewrites: one operation, several evolutions

Rewrite the named change after creating a descendant, then inspect both evolutions:

jj edit "$change"
printf 'four\n' > api.txt
jj describe -m 'API: four contract'
jj evolog -r "$change" --reversed -G
jj evolog -r "$child" --reversed -G
jj op log -n 10
jj op show

The change-centric result shows X's versions. The child-centric result shows that T received a successor when its parent changed. The operation-centric result shows the one command that caused the related graph rewrites. This is why a review stack can report several new Git commit IDs after the author changed one early patch: each descendant's parent field contains a different commit ID, so jj creates a successor even when the descendant's own intended content is unchanged.

QuestionUse firstWhat it provesWhat it does not prove
How did logical change X evolve?jj evolog -r XSuccessive commit versions and their operation links.Why unrelated bookmarks or descendants also moved.
What did the rewrite operation affect?jj op show OP or jj op diffRepository-wide graph/ref/workspace effects.That every affected commit belongs to one logical change.
What changed between two X versions?jj evolog -p -r XSuccessive-version inter-diff with parent-context handling.A comparison between arbitrary non-successor commits.
Where was X published?jj bookmark list, remote bookmarks, Git refsNames and locally observed publication targets.The complete local evolution history or server review history.

Divergence: two successors of one logical change

Two independent operations can start from one operation head and rewrite the same change differently. After both operations are integrated, the visible graph can contain two successors with one change ID:

              X1  (successor one, change qqq...)
             /
X0  --------<
             \
              X2  (successor two, change qqq...)

This is not two ordinary commits that happen to have similar text. It is one logical change with multiple visible evolutions. A bare change-ID symbol is consequently ambiguous; inspect the evolution and select a specific offset or full commit ID only after comparing the alternatives:

jj log -r 'divergent()'
jj evolog -r 'divergent()'
jj log -r 'change_id("PREFIX")' --no-graph -T \
  'commit_id ++ " " ++ change_id ++
   " " ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'
jj op log -n 20

Possible decisions are different operations, not spelling variants: keep one successor and abandon the other; duplicate one as a new independent change; edit one and converge the visible evolutions with jj converge; or preserve both if they represent genuinely different work. Compare descriptions, parents, diffs, conflicts, bookmarks, and review identifiers before choosing. A convergence operation combines the selected divergent evolutions into one successor for that logical change; it is not a squash merely because several commits are involved.

When a change has diverged, change_id("PREFIX") selects all matching visible successors. To select one successor, append the offset to the bare full change ID or unique change-ID prefix; the offset is not appended to the change_id() function call:

jj show -r 'FULL_CHANGE_ID/0'
jj show -r 'FULL_CHANGE_ID/1'
jj diff --from 'FULL_CHANGE_ID/0' --to 'FULL_CHANGE_ID/1'
jj converge -r 'divergent()'
jj evolog -r 'change_id("PREFIX")'
jj op show

The offset is a selection of an evolution, not a permanent name. After another rewrite or convergence, use the full commit ID, bookmark, or current change-ID resolution shown by the latest evolog. If a command requires one commit, verify cardinality before passing a divergent query to it.

Recovery: evolog beside operation history

For a Git expert, the safest replacement for the single-word question “reflog?” is to choose the evidence layer:

Questionjj evidenceGit evidenceGerrit evidence
How did this logical change evolve locally?jj evologNo direct equivalent; a reflog follows refs, not jj change identity.Not a server-side Gerrit question.
Which repository-wide operation caused it?jj op log/show/diffRef/reflog and command-specific logs, with less jj graph context.Server audit where available.
Which exported object was reviewed?Commit ID plus publication bookmark and fetched remote bookmark.Commit ID and ref history.Patch set number plus Gerrit Change-Id.
What changed between two versions?jj evolog -p for successors, or explicit jj diff.Commit/range diff.Patch-set comparison.

A practical recovery sequence is:

# First preserve both kinds of evidence.
jj op log -n 20
jj evolog -r "$change" --reversed -G

# Inspect, without changing the live repository.
jj op show OP
jj op diff --from OP_BEFORE --to OP_AFTER
jj --at-operation OP_BEFORE log -r 'all()'

# Choose the repair only after comparing the evidence.
jj undo                         # only for the latest integrated operation
jj op restore OP_BEFORE        # restore a named repository state
jj op revert OP                 # reverse one operation while retaining later history

evolog cannot restore a repository state. op restore cannot tell you which successor is the intended version of a review change. undo is appropriate only when the unwanted operation is the latest integrated operation; otherwise use a named operation or perform a deliberate graph repair. Neither local tool can undo a GitHub/Gerrit push: fetch the server state, identify the exported commit/ref, and repair the remote publication separately.

Publication, Git transfer, and review-system identity

A local evolution entry becomes externally meaningful only when a particular commit object is exported. Git transport transfers commit objects and refs; it does not transfer jj's local operation DAG or the complete evolution ledger. A remote bookmark such as review@origin tells this clone which remote ref was observed at a fetch. It is not a server-side copy of evolog. If a later push replaces the publication bookmark, the server sees a new Git commit ID or ref target; the local change ID is not part of the Git protocol.

GitHub normally treats the pushed bookmark as the PR branch. Gerrit normally treats each commit pushed to refs/for/<branch> as a review change, matching later patch sets by the Gerrit Change-Id trailer. These are three different identity layers:

LayerStable across a local rewrite?Where it is observed
jj change IDNormally yes, while the logical change evolvesjj evolog, log output, local jj metadata
Git commit IDNo: a changed tree, parent, or metadata creates another objectGit refs, CI records, GitHub commits, Gerrit patch-set commit
Gerrit Change-IdUsually yes when the trailer is preservedCommit message and Gerrit review page
GitHub PR / bookmarkThe PR name may remain while its branch target movesPublication ref and hosting service

For an upload incident, record all four where available. “The change is still the same” may be true in jj's evolution model and in Gerrit's review model while false for the Git commit ID used by CI. Conversely, a commit with a familiar Git message is not enough evidence that it is the intended successor: compare its full ID, parent, diff, bookmark, and operation.

# Export one exact evolution entry, then correlate it with transport state.
jj evolog -G -r "$change" -T \
  'commit.commit_id() ++ " " ++ commit.change_id() ++
   " " ++ operation.id() ++ " " ++
   commit.description().first_line() ++ "\n"'
jj bookmark list --all-remotes
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj log -r 'review | review@origin' -T 'commit_id ++ " " ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'
jj op log -n 20

The exact inspection command depends on the publication path. Do not infer a remote's current state from a stale remote bookmark: fetch first. Do not infer an operation from a Gerrit patch-set number: use the local evolution and operation records, then match the exported commit ID and message trailer. The operation ID is local evidence and may have no counterpart on another machine.

Incident exercise: CI commit 2, Gerrit patch set 4, local commit 5

Use the following exercise to practise a realistic review investigation. The numbers are deliberately from different namespaces:

  • CI commit 2 is the Git commit ID recorded by an earlier CI run.
  • Gerrit patch set 4 is the fourth uploaded patch set for one Gerrit review, identified by its Change-Id.
  • local commit 5 is the current jj commit object for the same logical change, after a later local rewrite.
jj evolution:    X2 --> X3 --> X4 --> X5
                 |       |       |       |
CI:              c2      c3      c4      c5
Gerrit:          ps2     ps3     ps4     (not uploaded)
operations:      o2      o3      o4      o5

Do not answer “patch set 4 is commit 5” merely because both are described as the latest review. Perform the correlation:

  1. Fetch the Gerrit remote and record the commit ID currently attached to the review ref or fetched bookmark.
  2. Run jj evolog -r CHANGE --reversed -G and export full commit IDs, change IDs, operation IDs, and descriptions.
  3. Find the entry whose full commit ID matches the commit Gerrit used for patch set 4. Verify its Change-Id trailer and parent(s).
  4. Use jj evolog -p -r CHANGE to inspect what changed from the preceding local version; use an explicit jj diff only when comparing deliberately chosen stored objects.
  5. Use jj op show o5 and jj op diff to establish why local commit 5 exists. If an ancestor was rewritten, inspect the descendant's evolution as well.
  6. Decide whether commit 5 is a new patch set to upload, an unintentional local successor, or a divergent alternative. Do not push until the bookmark and review identity have been checked.
EvidenceQuestion answeredQuestion not answered
Gerrit patch set 4 and its commit IDWhich Git object the server reviewedWhich local operation produced it
jj evolog entry for that commitWhich logical change version it was locallyWhether the server accepted a later push
jj evolog -pWhat changed between adjacent local versionsWhat an arbitrary server-side comparison displayed
jj op show/op diffWhat local rewrite or publication operation affected the graphWhether a remote review was merged or abandoned
Fetched remote bookmark and server UIWhich object is currently published and reviewedWhat was present only in an unfetched local clone

This is the practical purpose of evolog: it lets a GitHub or Gerrit user follow the logical change while separately accounting for the exact Git objects and the local operations that produced them. It complements, rather than replaces, the operation log, remote bookmarks, server review history, and Git commit inspection.

Correlating operation history with change evolution

The two histories answer different questions and become most useful together. jj evolog identifies the successive commit objects that represent one logical change; jj op show identifies the repository-wide transformation that created or rewrote it. Correlate them when an ancestor rewrite produces several successors, when a review upload must be matched to a local version, or when recovery needs both the intended change and the surrounding ref/workspace effects.

# Select one logical change and record both evidence layers.
change=$(jj log -r @ --no-graph -T 'change_id ++ "\n"')
jj evolog -r "$change" -G
jj op log -n 10
jj op show OPERATION
jj op diff --from OP_BEFORE --to OP_AFTER

An evolution entry is not an operation and an operation is not a commit. The compact rule is: use evolution history to choose which version of the change you mean, then use operation history to explain what else changed at the same time. The recovery laboratory below applies that distinction to named exercises; the later concurrency section covers operation branches, retention, and the limits of local history across clones.

Recovery laboratory: named states, undo, and repair

Recovery has two different targets. If the mistake is “the logical change is no longer where I intended”, use the commit graph, bookmarks, and evolution log. If the mistake is “the repository as a whole was transformed incorrectly”, use the operation DAG. A commit ID remembered from before a rewrite can locate a predecessor, but it does not by itself tell you which operation should be restored.

QuestionFirst toolWhy
What did the last command do?jj op showShows repository changes made by one operation.
Where did my change go?jj evolog -r CHANGEFollows one change's predecessors/successors.
What did the repository look like earlier?jj --at-op OP log -r all()Loads a historical repository view without snapshotting current files.
Undo the immediate mistake?jj undoCreates a reverse operation for the latest integrated operation.
Restore a named state?jj op restore OPMoves local repository state to an operation, with selectable portions.
Compare two candidate states?jj op diff --from A --to BShows repository changes without guessing from current IDs.
Recover after a server push?Server/ref inspection plus local operation toolsLocal undo cannot undo an external remote mutation.

Exercise 1: rewrite the wrong change

jj log -r '@:: & mutable()'
jj op log -n 3
# mistakenly select an ancestor:
jj edit A
jj describe -m 'WRONG: temporary experiment'
jj op log -n 3

Do not immediately perform another edit to “put things back”. Record the newest operation ID and inspect it:

jj op show
jj evolog -r A
jj --at-op OP_BEFORE log -r '::@'
jj undo

undo reverses the operation that integrated the mistaken description/edit state. The working-copy filesystem may need a deliberate update, and any external files changed by an editor are outside the operation's protection. Verify the current @, the target change's description, and descendants before continuing.

Exercise 2: abandon useful work, then recover it

jj bookmark create rescue -r @
jj abandon -r 'change_id(important...)'
jj log -r 'visible()'
jj op log
jj evolog -r 'change_id(important...)'

The temporary bookmark is a publication/name safety net, but evolution and operation state are still useful. If the bookmark was deleted by the command, the commit may remain as a predecessor/hidden commit. Inspect the operation immediately and restore or undo before GC. A recovery bookmark can be created at a predecessor only after the exact commit has been selected.

Exercise 3: a bookmark moved to the wrong tip

jj bookmark list --all-remotes
jj bookmark set review -r wrong-tip
jj op show
jj log -r 'review | review@origin'
jj undo

Undoing the local bookmark operation does not undo a push that already happened. If the wrong tip was pushed, inspect the server's current ref and use an explicit, policy-approved update. If the remote changed independently, tracking state may make the expected old target visible; do not force simply because a local undo makes the local name look right.

Exercise 4: several operations happened before discovery

Undo is intentionally convenient but may be the wrong granularity after later work. Use the operation graph:

jj op log
jj op show OP_BAD
jj op diff --from OP_BEFORE --to OP_BAD
jj --at-op OP_BEFORE log -r 'all()'
jj op restore --what repo OP_BEFORE
jj op log

The restore creates a new operation; it does not delete the old operation node. This gives the repository an auditable “restored to earlier view” event. If remote-tracking state is restored along with repository state, later pushes may compare against old observations; the experimental --what repo form can be preferable when the goal is to repair local graph/bookmarks while retaining current remote observations.

Exercise 5: evolution divergence

jj evolog -r 'change_id(abc...)'
jj log -r 'divergent() & change_id(abc...)'
jj show -r 'FULL_CHANGE_ID/0'
jj show -r 'FULL_CHANGE_ID/1'

Choose the successor by content and graph context, not by offset number. One successor may contain the reviewed change and another a local experiment. You can edit one, rebase it, duplicate it to a new change, or abandon the unwanted successor. Then inspect descendants and bookmarks: a publication name can keep a commit visible even when the logical change has divergent forms.

Exercise 6: operation views are local

Clone A and clone B share commits only after fetch/push. Their operation IDs may both begin with a root operation but are not a shared timeline. A commit recovered through jj op restore on A does not become a recoverable operation on B. To transfer a useful state, create a temporary bookmark, push it, fetch it, and create a new local working-copy commit on B.

# A
jj bookmark create handoff -r @
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark handoff

# B
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj log -r 'handoff@origin'
jj new 'handoff@origin'
jj bookmark forget 'handoff'

Delete the temporary remote bookmark only after verifying the receiving clone. The filesystem's uncommitted edits and local operation history are not transferred by this procedure; commit them deliberately or copy the files through a separate channel.

Recovery stopping rules

  1. Stop mutating the repository when the mistake is noticed.
  2. Record operation ID, current workspace, bookmarks, and relevant commit/change IDs.
  3. Use --at-op for inspection and avoid snapshotting into historical views.
  4. Choose undo for the latest operation; choose restore/diff for a named state.
  5. Do not run GC, abandon recovery evidence, or push until the local graph is understood.
  6. Separate local repair from server repair and record both.

Conflict laboratory: a conflict is stored in the graph

Construct two changes from the same base that edit the same lines, then merge or rebase them. jj can represent the unresolved result as a commit with a conflict value. The commit is still a graph node: it has an ID, a change ID, parents, descendants, and an operation that created it. “Unresolved” describes one value in its tree, not an interrupted global transaction.

        B: timeout = 30
       /
A-----+
       \ C: timeout = 60

merge M has parents B and C:
A--B----+
   \    |--M[conflict]
    C---+

When a conflict is materialised in a working copy, jj writes conflict markers or the configured marker representation into files. Materialisation is a projection of the stored conflict into the filesystem; editing the markers and running jj resolve records a resolved tree in the relevant commit. The conflict value itself can have multiple sides, including nested or repeated conflict terms after successive rewrites. Do not assume every conflict is a two-way “ours/theirs” merge.

jj status
jj log -r 'conflicts() & ::@'
jj resolve --list
jj resolve --tool=:ours
jj resolve --tool=:theirs
jj resolve --tool=meld

:ours and :theirs are convenient only where their interpretation is unambiguous. With a merge commit, “ours” is associated with the destination/first side and “theirs” with the other side according to the command’s merge model; in a multi-sided conflict, choosing one side may discard content from more than one parent. A real merge tool should expose every side, and the result must be tested rather than judged by marker absence alone.

Conflict propagation through descendants

before rewrite:
A--B--C--D
   B changes config key
   C changes same key as a dependent test
   D changes docs about C

rewrite B → B′:
A--B′--C′[conflict]--D′[conflict or adjusted]

Conflict propagation is why jj can let work continue on a stack while a lower change is unresolved. C′ is a valid commit to inspect, describe, or even further rewrite. Its descendant D′ is likewise present, though its diff may be represented relative to a conflicted parent. Resolve from the lowest semantically understood conflict upward. After resolving C′, inspect D′ because the stored conflict value may have changed even if D′’s own files were untouched.

There are two useful strategies. Resolve immediately when the conflict is small and the intended invariant is clear. Or carry the conflict while investigating the stack, then resolve after related changes reveal the intended final interface. The second strategy is safe only if your tests and publication tooling accept conflicted commits; a push or review upload may reject them, and a build workspace may not be able to materialise a useful tree.

Conflict-aware commands

OperationWhat conflict meansPractical check
RebaseThe diff could not be replayed cleanly onto a new parent.Find the earliest conflicted commit, then inspect its descendants.
SquashCombining trees or diffs yields a conflict value.Verify source remainder and destination state before resolving.
SplitA selected portion may carry one side while the residual commit carries another.Inspect both resulting changes and their conflict predicates.
RestoreCopying content from a conflicted source can preserve conflict structure.Use show/diff on the source before materialising.
ResolveReplaces the conflict value with a concrete tree.Run tests and verify conflicts() no longer selects it.
Push/uploadServer transport may reject conflicted commits or represent them poorly.Resolve before publication unless the server workflow explicitly supports them.

Concurrency, retention, and cross-machine limits

Once the operation model has been established above, these are its boundary conditions. Concurrent operations can branch the operation history, retention and garbage collection affect recovery, and Git transport does not transfer operation IDs to another clone.

commit DAG:       A--B--C(@)
                      \
                       D

operation DAG:   O0--O1--O2--O3
                         \   \
                          O4  O5

O2 may have rewritten B→B', C→C' while O4 is an
independent operation started from O2. Commit identity and
operation ancestry are related but not interchangeable.

Concurrency and operation integration

Two processes can start at one operation and produce independent operations. --no-integrate-operation deliberately leaves a successful operation outside the current integrated head and prints an operation ID. It does not make external side effects transactional and does not protect the filesystem from another writer. jj op integrate OP brings that operation into the current operation history; integration may expose divergent repository state or conflicts that were not visible from either isolated view.

jj status --no-integrate-operation
# save the printed operation ID
jj op log
jj op integrate OP
jj op diff --operation OP
jj log -G -r 'all()'

Use this mode when a supervisor wants to control integration or when testing concurrency. It is not a replacement for a filesystem lock. Editors, build tools, Git, jj, and workspaces can still race over files and refs. Serialise mutation of one worktree and use separate workspaces or clones for concurrent tasks.

Retention and garbage collection

Recovery depends on data that has not been pruned. Abandoning a commit hides it from ordinary views but may leave it addressable; abandoning an operation removes recovery metadata according to the command's semantics; repository GC can reclaim objects no longer considered reachable. Before maintenance, inspect the operation and evolution history, confirm that published refs and temporary rescue bookmarks are no longer needed, and make an independent backup if policy requires one.

jj op log
jj evolog -r 'all()'
jj bookmark list --all-remotes
jj util gc

The command's successful exit status is not a guarantee that every recovery path remains available. The operation log is local to a clone and is not transferred by Git push/fetch. A clone on another machine can recover commits that were published or fetched there, but it cannot use this clone's operation ID unless the repository state and operation store are shared through an explicitly supported mechanism.

Recovery decision record

RecordReason
Current operation ID and relevant earlier ID.Defines the repository views being compared.
Current commit/change IDs and bookmark targets.Separates exact objects from logical changes and names.
Whether a remote push/fetch occurred.Local operation tools cannot reverse server side effects.
Whether the filesystem has unrecorded edits.Historical operation views ignore today's working-copy snapshot.
Chosen recovery operation and why.Prevents a second recovery action from erasing the first intention.
Post-recovery log/evolution/ref evidence.Confirms the graph, not only the command's success message.

Part XII — Workspaces and multiple machines

Workspace model in detail

A workspace is jj's persistent association between one directory on disk and one working-copy commit in a repository. It is the unit that answers two questions which Git often answers through a worktree and HEAD: “which files are materialised here?” and “which commit does this directory currently represent?” Every jj repository has a default workspace, and it may have additional named workspaces. The name is a repository-level identity; the directory is its filesystem location; its working-copy commit is the mutable commit that @ resolves to when a command runs from that directory.

A workspace is not a bookmark: it is not a publication name and it does not have to be visible to a remote. It is not a clone: workspaces share the same repository commit store, bookmarks, tags, and operation history. It is also not merely another spelling for a Git branch or detached HEAD. The closest Git comparison is a Git worktree with an explicitly recorded, independently mutable checkout commit, but the comparison breaks because jj workspaces participate in the same mutable DAG and operation system rather than being separate ref-oriented checkouts.

one jj repository

shared commit store, refs, and operation DAG
        |
        +-- workspace "default"  /home/me/project
        |       default@ -> C        files for C
        |
        +-- workspace "review"   /home/me/project-review
                review@  -> R        files for R

@ means the workspace-local working-copy commit;
C and R may be unrelated commits.

Workspace state is therefore local in one sense and shared in another. The directory, its filesystem contents, its current working-copy commit, and its sparse patterns belong to that workspace. The commit objects those commits point to, the repository's bookmarks and tags, and the operation log are shared. A rewrite performed from review can change a commit that default is based on; jj may then need to rebase or mark default's working-copy commit stale. Conversely, moving review's @ does not move default's @.

Additional workspaces are created with jj workspace add DESTINATION. By default the new working-copy commit is created on the same parent set as the current workspace's working-copy commit. --revision R instead makes it a child of the supplied parent commits, with the same graph effect as jj new R; --name NAME controls the workspace symbol. The command creates another materialisation of the shared graph, not another repository. The remaining workspace lifecycle and sparse-pattern options are covered below after the basic state transition is visible.

before: one workspace

        A---B---C
                \
                 default@

jj workspace add --name review ../project-review -r B

after: two workspace-local tips in one graph

        A---B---C
            |   \
            |    default@
            \
             review@

The two directories can now be edited and snapshotted independently. A workspace is not a promise that its filesystem is current at every instant: an editor, build tool, or another jj process can change the directory after the last snapshot. Normal jj commands reconcile the live directory with that workspace's recorded working-copy commit; --ignore-working-copy deliberately reads the recorded state without doing so. Keep the shared graph, workspace record, last recorded tree, and live filesystem distinct.

The 0.45.1 workspace subcommands are add, forget, list, rename, root, and update-stale. A build workspace can edit a stack while a review workspace remains at a stable commit:

jj workspace add ../project-build -r @
jj workspace add ../project-review -r main@origin
jj workspace list
jj -R ../project-build status
cd ../project-build
jj workspace rename ci
jj workspace update-stale
jj workspace forget review

Each workspace has its own @; commit edits and graph rewrites are shared, so a rewrite can move the commit a second workspace points at. Update stale workspaces deliberately and inspect filesystem state before deleting one. Sparse patterns are workspace working-copy materialisation rules, configured with jj sparse list, set, edit, and reset; they do not change the commit tree.

Machines

Clones have independent operation DAGs and workspace pointers. Fetch/push commits and bookmarks through Git remotes; do not expect @ or jj undo on machine A to exist on machine B. To move unfinished work, publish a temporary bookmark, fetch it on the other clone, edit it there, and delete/forget the temporary publication after the handoff. This is safer and more observable than inventing operation-log synchronisation.

Workspace laboratory: one store, several materialisations

A workspace is a named view over a shared repository, with its own working-copy commit and filesystem. It is not a lightweight branch and it is not an independent clone. The commit store and operation history are shared; the workspace pointer, sparse patterns, and files on disk are local to that workspace. This division makes build/review separation powerful and makes concurrent filesystem writes dangerous.

shared commit store:  main--A--B--C
workspace dev:                  dev@ = C, full tree
workspace build:                build@ = B, sparse src/
workspace review:               review@ = A, full tree

A rewrite of A or B is visible to all workspaces because it changes the shared graph. Each workspace then needs its own update policy. A workspace whose recorded working-copy commit is rewritten may need its checkout record updated; a workspace with ordinary unrecorded filesystem edits is not thereby stale. Ask which workspace owns a file before running a formatter, test generator, or jj command.

Development, build, and review scenario

jj workspace add ../project-build -r @
jj workspace add ../project-review -r main@origin
jj workspace list
cd ../project-build
jj workspace rename ci
jj status
cd ../project-review
jj workspace root
jj log -r @

The rename command takes one new name for the current workspace in 0.45.1. It does not take an old and new name pair. Use the workspace's own directory or jj -R to select the operating location, then verify the new workspace symbol with jj workspace list. Workspace symbols can be used in revsets, but the filesystem directory remains the authority for which process is writing files.

The build workspace can edit or test a particular change without moving the development workspace's @. It still shares commits, so a rewrite performed from the build workspace can change what the development workspace sees. A review workspace can remain at an immutable remote boundary while the development workspace advances. This is a graph coordination tool, not a promise that test results remain valid after a later rewrite.

Build and review workspace invariants

A build workspace should normally be boring: pin it to an explicit bookmark or immutable commit, use sparse materialisation only when the build system supports it, and avoid making source edits there. If a build tool generates files, decide whether they are tracked inputs, ignored outputs, or disposable files before allowing a snapshot. A review workspace can remain at an imported remote bookmark while development continues elsewhere; its value is a stable observation point, not a publication name.

cd ../project-build
jj edit main@origin
jj status
# run the build; inspect generated files before any snapshot
cd ../project-review
jj log -r '@ | @-'

Do not assume that a workspace at main@origin follows later fetches. The remote bookmark may advance while the workspace's working-copy commit remains the previously selected commit. Update it explicitly, and verify the resulting commit ID before trusting a build result.

Stale workspaces and repair

In jj 0.45.1, a workspace is stale when its recorded working-copy commit is no longer the current commit for that workspace because another repository operation changed the recorded checkout state. Ordinary edits made by an editor, build tool, or native filesystem command are unrecorded working-copy changes; they do not by themselves make the workspace record stale. A moved directory, missing metadata, or a native Git ref change is a separate location/backend diagnosis, not a synonym for stale state.

Inspect all workspaces before attempting repair:

jj workspace list
jj workspace root
jj -R ../project-build status
jj -R ../project-review status
jj -R ../project-build workspace update-stale

update-stale repairs the stale workspace record/checkout relationship; it is not a general graph repair and it is not a command for incorporating arbitrary filesystem edits. If it reports that the workspace is not stale, leave the files alone and diagnose the live-versus-recorded snapshot instead. If files contain valuable unrecorded edits, snapshot them with an appropriate jj command or copy them aside before an operation that will replace the checkout. If the graph target is wrong, choose an explicit commit with jj edit or jj new in that workspace. If the directory was moved or damaged, repair the filesystem/location problem separately.

Sparse build workspace

Sparse state is per workspace. Use sparse set to specify patterns; sparse edit opens the external editor for the pattern configuration and takes no fileset argument in 0.45.1.

cd ../project-build
jj sparse set --clear --add src --add Cargo.toml
jj sparse list
test -f src/main.rs
test ! -e docs/guide.md
jj file list -- 'root-prefix-glob:docs'
jj sparse reset

The commit tree still contains docs and tests while the sparse filesystem does not materialise them. A build that runs successfully in a sparse workspace may therefore omit an input. Make the sparse policy part of the build command's evidence and run a full-tree validation before publication. Changing sparse patterns may add/remove files in the filesystem but does not create a content commit in the same sense as editing a tracked file.

Forget and cleanup

Forgetting a workspace removes its workspace metadata; it does not abandon the commits that workspace's @ pointed at. Check for unrecorded files and useful working-copy changes first. A forgotten workspace's commit may still be reachable from bookmarks or the graph, and its operation history remains part of the shared repository until retention removes it.

jj -R ../project-build status
jj -R ../project-build diff
jj workspace forget ci
jj workspace list
jj log -r 'working_copies()'

Clean the filesystem directory only according to the repository's workspace management rules. Do not confuse removing a directory with workspace forget; one is a filesystem action and the other changes repository metadata. If a stale directory is later reused, inspect its workspace identity and root before assuming it represents a fresh checkout.

Two machines and unfinished work

Independent clones have independent operation DAGs and independent workspace pointers. Git transport moves commit objects and refs; it does not move @, sparse patterns, workspace names, or operation IDs. The portable handoff for unfinished work is an explicit temporary bookmark:

# machine A
jj bookmark set handoff/alice -r @
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark handoff/alice

# machine B
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj log -r 'handoff/alice@origin'
jj new 'handoff/alice@origin'
# continue work, then publish the next handoff explicitly

Creating a child on machine B gives that machine its own working-copy commit. The original machine can continue to inspect the remote bookmark, but it must not assume the remote target follows B's new child. After handoff, delete or forget the temporary publication according to whether the server ref should remain available. If both machines edit the same logical change independently, fetching can expose divergent successors; compare evolutions before choosing a winner or converging.

Concurrency rules

SharedWorkspace-localConcurrency implication
Commit store and graph.Working-copy commit pointer.A graph rewrite can affect every workspace's target.
Operation history.Filesystem and sparse patterns.Operation inspection is shared; file writes still need serialisation.
Bookmarks/tags.Current directory and local tools.Ref moves are repository mutations visible to all workspaces.
Remote observations.Editor/build process state.Fetch/import and builds should not race a writer.

A robust multi-workspace routine gives each process one directory, one workspace, and one writer role. Use --ignore-working-copy only for a deliberate repository-view read. It prevents the command from reconciling the directory's files, but it does not make a concurrent filesystem process safe.

Part XIII — Configuration

Configuration is TOML and is layered.
