Built-in defaults are overridden by user config, repository config, workspace config, command-line --config-file, then command-line --config NAME=VALUE according to the installed precedence rules. On Linux, use XDG locations such as ~/.config/jj/config.toml and supported conf.d directories. Confirm actual paths with jj config path; do not assume a distribution's packaging layout.

jj config list
jj config get user.name
jj config set --user user.name 'A. Engineer'
jj config set --repo ui.diff-formatter ':git'
jj config set --workspace ui.pager 'less -FRX'
jj config unset --user ui.pager
jj config edit --user
jj config gc

The available 0.45.1 config commands are edit, gc, get, list, path, set, and unset. The exact scope flags should be taken from local help. In jj 0.45.1, JJ_CONFIG selects the user/system TOML file or directory set; it is not an inline TOML string. Use --config for a one-command reproducible override and --config-file to load an additional file.

A maintainable Linux layout

~/.config/jj/
|-- config.toml
\-- conf.d/
    |-- 10-ui.toml
    |-- 20-revsets.toml
    |-- 30-templates.toml
    |-- 40-git.toml
    |-- 50-gerrit.toml
    \-- 60-aliases.toml

Organise by intent, not alphabetically. Important namespaces include user.*; ui.* (editor, pager, colour, timestamps, diff and merge presentation); git.* (backend, remotes, push/fetch, private commits); gerrit.* (including the 0.45.1 keys default-remote and default-remote-branch); revsets.*; templates.*; merge-tools.*; fix.tools.*; signing.*; immutable-head settings; aliases; and snapshot/workspace behaviour.

[ui]
default-command = ["log", "-r", "@:: & mutable()"]
paginate = "auto"
diff-editor = "meld"

[revsets]
log = "@:: & mutable() | bookmarks() | remote_bookmarks()"

[revset-aliases]
stack(x) = "x:: & mutable()"

[templates]
log = 'builtin_log_compact'

[gerrit]
default-remote = "gerrit"
default-remote-branch = "main"

Use jj util config-schema and the generated config inventory for the exhaustive target-release key surface. Some configuration is security-sensitive: repo/workspace config can be untrusted input in a checked-out repository, so 0.38+ layouts moved it outside the repository. Review effective config before using aliases or external tools.

jj 0.45.1 supports conditional configuration with --when variables and scoped configuration, as well as ordered files in ~/.config/jj/conf.d/. Use those mechanisms for host-specific policy when they make the distinction auditable. A robust alternative is explicit command aliases: jj git push --remote github --bookmark gh/topic and jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit. Never let a convenient default choose a publication remote silently.

Configuration design: build policy in layers

Configuration is executable policy. A useful configuration says what the repository should do when a human invokes a command, what a script may assume, and which decisions must remain explicit at a publication boundary. Keep the user layer ergonomic, the repository layer reproducible, the workspace layer local, and the command line layer temporary.

LayerPut hereDo not put here
Built-in defaultsFallback revsets, templates, pager, formatter behaviour.Organisation policy; defaults vary by release.
UserName/email, editor, pager, preferred display, personal aliases.Repository-specific remote or review policy.
RepositoryProject revsets, template aliases, fixer/merge-tool definitions, immutable heads.Secrets; assumptions that should apply to every checkout.
WorkspaceLocal default command, sparse/workspace-specific display or tool choice.Policy other contributors must discover implicitly.
Command lineOne-run overrides, CI pinning, explicit remote and output controls.Long-lived aliases; shell secrets embedded in process listings.

On Linux, verify the actual files with jj config path --user, --repo, and --workspace. XDG conventions are useful defaults but packaging can alter paths. JJ_CONFIG selects the user/system TOML file or directory set in the target release; it is not an inline TOML string. --config-file loads additional input, while --config NAME=VALUE applies an inline override.

Progressive setup

# identity first
jj config set --user user.name 'A. Engineer'
jj config set --user user.email 'a@example.test'

# safe display and explicit daily scope
jj config set --user ui.pager 'less -FRX'
jj config set --user revsets.log '(@:: & mutable()) | bookmarks() | remote_bookmarks()'

# personal aliases
jj config set --user 'revset-aliases.unpublished()' 'mutable() ~ ::remote_bookmarks()'
jj config set --user 'command-aliases.stack' 'log -r "@:: & mutable()"'

Use config edit for nested TOML and multi-line values; command-line setting must satisfy both the shell and the TOML parser. The last line is illustrative of a command alias and should be checked against the exact alias syntax in the installed schema/help before adoption. A config test should inspect the effective value rather than assuming the write landed in the desired layer.

UI and output policy

ui.* settings govern editor, pager, colour, timestamps, diff formatter/editor, merge editor, default command, movement policy, and related presentation. Separate human output from machine output: a human default may use a pager, graph, colour, relative dates, and compact descriptions; a script should specify --no-pager --color=never, a bounded revset, and an explicit template.

[ui]
pager = "less -FRX"
paginate = "auto"
color = "auto"
default-command = ["log", "-r", "@:: & mutable()"]
movement.edit = true
diff-editor = "meld"
merge-editor = "meld"

Do not put a default command that mutates state behind a shell prompt. A default log that snapshots is still a mutation in the operation log; if prompt latency and side effects matter, use a prompt-specific command with --ignore-working-copy.

Revset and template policy

[revsets]
log = '@:: & mutable() | bookmarks() | remote_bookmarks()'
status = 'mutable() & ::@'
fix = 'reachable(@, mutable())'
sign = 'bookmarks()'

[revset-aliases]
stack(x) = 'x:: & mutable()'
unpublished() = 'mutable() ~ ::remote_bookmarks()'
review-candidates() = 'heads(unpublished() ~ empty() ~ conflicts())'

[templates]
log = 'builtin_log_compact'

[template-aliases]
short-id = 'change_id.shortest(10)'
subject = 'description.first_line()'
state = 'separate(" ", if(conflict, "CONFLICT", ""), if(empty, "EMPTY", ""), bookmarks)'

Aliases are language code and should be reviewed as such. A revset alias affects selection; a template alias affects rendering. Keep names semantically precise. Document whether an alias includes hidden commits, remote refs, empty changes, or conflicts, because those choices determine whether a publication script is safe.

GitHub and Gerrit policy

[git]
push = "github"

[gerrit]
default-remote = "gerrit"
default-remote-branch = "main"
review-url = "https://gerrit.example/review"

[command-aliases]
publish-gh = ["git", "push", "--remote", "github", "--bookmark"]
publish-gerrit = ["gerrit", "upload", "--remote", "gerrit", "--remote-branch", "main"]

Use explicit remote arguments in publication aliases. A default push remote is convenient but dangerous in a repository used for both GitHub and Gerrit. jj 0.45.1 documents the dedicated Gerrit keys shown above. Confirm exact command-alias value shape against jj help config and the target schema.

Immutable heads and repository policy

The immutable-head configuration defines the commits jj protects from rewrite. A sensible project policy commonly includes imported trunk and tags/release boundaries, but the right set depends on whether the repository permits local rebasing over remote bookmarks. Explain the policy as a revset, test it against a fixture graph, and keep an emergency --ignore-immutable procedure separate from normal aliases.

[revset-aliases]
"immutable_heads()" = "main@origin | tags() | root()"

In 0.45.1 this is the alias that jj itself evaluates when it checks rewrite protection. It is deliberately under [revset-aliases], not a made-up [revsets] key. Verify the effective policy before relying on it:

jj log -r 'immutable_heads()'
jj config get 'revset-aliases."immutable_heads()"'
jj rebase -s @ -d main@origin

The exact key/value syntax is release-sensitive, but the policy has an observable contract: protected commits appear in the query and an ordinary rewrite that would alter them is rejected. An immutable head is not automatically every server ref, and changing the config does not retroactively make a rewrite safe. Always inspect which commits are protected before using --ignore-immutable.

External tools and security

Merge tools, diff editors, fixers, signers, pagers, and command aliases can execute programs. Repository/workspace configuration can therefore alter what a command runs. Review config list and the file paths before operating in an unfamiliar repository. Prefer absolute executable paths or trusted PATH policy in CI, and do not let a checked-out repository silently replace a user's merge tool.

FamilyQuestions before enabling
merge/diff toolsWhat files are passed? Does the tool modify them? What exit status means success?
fix toolsDoes it support modified-line ranges? Is it deterministic? Can it rewrite every selected commit?
signingWhich key/agent is used? Does signing rewrite descendants? Is verification available on CI?
aliasesDoes the alias mutate, publish, or choose a remote implicitly?
pager/editorCan a non-interactive environment hang? Are colour and terminal escapes safe?

Configuration diagnosis

jj config path --user
jj config path --repo
jj config path --workspace
jj config list ui
jj config list git
jj config list gerrit
jj config get revsets.log
jj util config-schema

When behaviour differs between two shells, compare effective config, environment variables, current workspace root, and jj version. When behaviour differs between two repositories, compare repository/workspace config and remote URLs. When behaviour differs between the installed release and future releases, diff the captured schemas and command help rather than guessing from a release note.

Configuration reference conventions

Appendix F groups significant keys by user-facing purpose. Each reference row records the key, TOML type, usual scope, effect, default/absence behaviour, security or performance concern, and version note. The machine-generated schema remains useful for detecting newly added keys, but a schema cannot explain that git.push chooses a remote while bookmark tracking chooses a relationship, or that a template alias can shadow a builtin. Those interactions belong in the book.

Configuration laboratory: build a safe Linux configuration

Configuration is executable policy. Build it in layers so that a change in one layer has a visible reason and scope. Start with identity and UI, then add revset/template aliases, then repository transport, then hosting-specific policy.

[user]
name = "Ada Example"
email = "ada@example.org"

[ui]
pager = ["less", "-FRX"]
diff-editor = ":builtin"
merge-editor = "diffconflicts"
default-command = ["log"]

[revsets]
log = "builtin_log()"

[templates]
log = "builtin_log_compact"

Check the actual accepted value shapes with jj util config-schema for the target release; configuration keys and types are version-sensitive. The example illustrates design intent, not a universal drop-in file. Keep the base file free of credentials and repository-specific bookmarks.

Layered files and precedence

On Linux, user configuration normally lives under the XDG configuration directory, with jj’s own directory and the ordered conf.d/*.toml fragments supported by jj 0.45.1. Repository and workspace configuration can narrow policy. Command-line --config values are useful for one invocation and for tests; --config-file loads a file without pretending it is the user’s permanent configuration. In jj 0.45.1, configuration commands also expose a direct --file target for editing a particular file.

LayerGood useRisk
Built-in defaultsPortable baseline.Defaults can change between releases.
User configIdentity, editor, pager, personal aliases.Hidden policy affects every repository.
Repository configTrunk, remotes, fixers, project aliases.Trust boundary for cloned repositories.
Workspace configSparse/build/review-specific behaviour.Only one workspace sees the setting.
Command lineTests, temporary overrides, automation.Harder to audit if embedded in aliases.

When debugging a surprising value, use jj config list, jj config get NAME, and jj config path. Record the invocation’s explicit config and environment in automation logs. Avoid aliases that silently add --ignore-immutable, select a remote, or permit an unsafe push.

GitHub and Gerrit conditional intent

Hosting-specific settings should be opt-in. A repository that has both remotes should not infer its publication target from whichever remote happens to be listed first. Use explicit --remote and --bookmark in scripts, and reserve defaults for a repository where the policy is unambiguous.

# GitHub publication
jj git push --remote github --bookmark pr/parser

# Gerrit review upload
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main -r '@:: & mutable()'

For 0.45.1, Gerrit-specific defaults such as gerrit.default-remote, gerrit.default-remote-branch, and gerrit.review-url can reduce repetition. In a shared config, document that those keys are not a guarantee that a GitHub push will use the same remote. Separate command aliases by transport and require a bookmark argument for destructive or public operations.

Aliases as an interface

An alias is a small program in configuration. Name it for its invariant, not its keystrokes. A good read alias prints stable IDs and uses a bounded revset. A risky alias should be explicit about its source, destination, remote, and safety behaviour. Version aliases that use a target-release-specific command or predicate, or gate them with a documented release check.

[aliases]
st = ["log", "-r", "@:: & mutable()", "-T", "builtin_log_compact"]
pub = ["git", "push", "--remote", "github", "--bookmark"]
review = ["gerrit", "upload", "--remote", "gerrit", "--remote-branch", "main"]

Test aliases in a disposable repository. Configuration parsing errors, command aliases that recursively invoke themselves, and aliases whose revsets return multiple commits are all ordinary failure modes. A useful alias is shorter than the reasoning it makes visible; it should not hide the reasoning.

Configuration reference: the keys that shape daily behaviour

The schema is the authoritative machine-readable inventory, but a human reference must describe which decisions each family controls and what it does not control. The target 0.45.1 schema groups settings as follows; some keys are tables whose contents are repository-specific.

NamespaceImportant keysDecision controlledDoes not control
username, emailAuthor identity defaults.Gerrit Change-Id or cryptographic identity.
operationhostname, usernameOperation-log attribution.Commit author/committer.
uidefault-command, color, paginate, pager, editor, diff-editor, merge-editor, conflict-marker-stylePresentation and interactive tools.Graph semantics and remote ref movement.
fsmonitorbackend, watchmanFilesystem change detection performance.Which files are logically committed.
colorslabel-to-style mappingsTerminal style for semantic labels.Machine-readable output semantics.
diffcolor-words, git, statDiff presentation defaults.Diff ownership.
gitfetch, push, private-commits, sign-on-push, colocate, object-hashBackend/transport and publication defaults.Server branch protection and credentials.
remotesremote tablesRemote URL/name configuration.Which remote a human intended without an explicit flag.
gerritdefault-remote, default-remote-branch, review-urlGerrit upload defaults in 0.45.1.Gerrit server permissions and review identity.
mergehunk-level, same-changeMerge/conflict heuristics, including individual diff-hunk handling.Whether a conflict is conceptually acceptable.
revsetslog, fix, run, sign, short-prefixesDefault selections and display policies.What a command means when an explicit selector is supplied.
snapshotauto-track, auto-update-stale, max-new-file-sizeFilesystem snapshot behaviour.Files already in a commit’s tree.
working-copyeol-conversion, exec-bit-changeWorking-copy representation details.POSIX file permissions outside jj’s snapshot rules.
fixtoolsConfigured fixer programs and file patterns.Whether a fixer is semantically safe for every commit.
merge-toolsnamed tool tablesExternal conflict/diff merge commands.Correctness of the selected merge result.
templateslog, show, op, bookmark, tag, config, file templatesHuman output templates.Underlying graph/ref state.
aliases, revset-aliases, fileset-aliases, template-aliasesnamed commands/expressionsReusable interfaces.Version compatibility unless explicitly managed.

UI, editors, and pagers

ui.editor is used for descriptions and metadata editors; ui.diff-editor handles editing at individual diff-hunk granularity; ui.merge-editor handles conflict resolution. They are different contracts. A program that can edit a unified diff is not automatically a three-way merge tool. Configure builtin tools first, then add external tools by name in merge-tools and test them with a disposable conflict.

[ui]
editor = ["nvim", "-f"]
diff-editor = ":builtin"
merge-editor = ":builtin"
pager = ["less", "-FRX"]
paginate = "auto"
color = "auto"
conflict-marker-style = "git"

The 0.45.1 documented pager default changes to include K in the non-Windows less flags. If a printed book or CI log must not contain terminal controls, use --no-pager and --color never in the command rather than relying on user config.

Git policy and private commits

git.private-commits is a revset policy for commits that should not be exported/pushed by default. It is not encryption and does not prevent a user from explicitly selecting a private commit. A private commit can still be part of a local descendant chain and can still be rewritten. Use it to express publication policy, then verify the selected push set.

[git]
private-commits = 'description(regex:"(?i)wip|do not publish")'
sign-on-push = true
track-default-bookmark-on-clone = true

Do not combine broad private predicates with a script that later uses --all and assumes the result is public. Print the push preview. Signing on push can produce a new successor or alter exported metadata according to backend behaviour; test it against the server’s verification policy.

Revset defaults

The revsets namespace chooses default commit sets for commands such as log, arrange, fix, run, sign, and simplify-parents. Defaults should be readable and bounded. builtin_log() is usually a better base than copying a release-specific expansion. A default that uses a private alias or a target-release-specific function must be version-gated.

[revsets]
log = '@:: & mutable()'
fix = 'mutable() & ::@'
run = 'mutable() & ::@'
sign = 'mutable() & ::@'

Always remember that a default is used only when the user omits the relevant option. It does not override an explicit -r. For an operationally important command, include the explicit revset in the script even if the interactive default is convenient.

Fixers and merge tools

Fixer configuration is a table of named tools with command, root, patterns, environment, and working-copy behaviour. A fixer should be deterministic, bounded by a fileset, and tested on conflicted, generated, binary, and sparse trees. Formatters that rewrite every file can accidentally produce enormous successor chains or change line endings.

[fix.tools.rustfmt]
command = ["rustfmt", "--edition", "2024", "--emit", "files"]
patterns = ["glob:**/*.rs"]

[merge-tools.meld]
program = "meld"
edit-args = ["$left", "$right", "-o", "$output"]
merge-args = ["$base", "$left", "$right", "-o", "$output"]

Use the schema to confirm exact key names and shapes for the installed release. The book’s policy is to show the design and test contract, not pretend that every external program uses the same argument protocol.

Conditional configuration

The --when conditional configuration table can select repositories, hostnames, workspaces, commands, platforms, and environments. Use it to separate GitHub and Gerrit defaults only when the condition is more reliable than a human’s memory:

[[--when]]
repositories = ["~/src/github/**"]
[--when.git]
# repository-specific keys in the supported conditional shape

[[--when]]
repositories = ["~/src/gerrit/**"]
[--when.gerrit]
default-remote = "gerrit"
default-remote-branch = "main"

Check the exact TOML shape in local help/schema; conditional configuration has changed across versions and the illustrative table is not a substitute for that check. Explicit command flags remain the clearest safety boundary for publication.

Configuration debugging and migration

jj config path
jj config list --include-defaults
jj config get revsets.log
jj util config-schema > schema.json
jj config gc

When upgrading between installed and future releases, compare schema keys, default templates, default immutable heads, pager defaults, Gerrit keys, and revset functions. Do not run config gc as a migration tool without inspecting what it will remove. Keep a copy of the old config and apply changes in one namespace at a time.

Configuration laboratory: construct policy without losing the layers

Configuration is executable policy. A useful jj configuration says what an interactive command should do by default, what a script must state explicitly, and which repository boundaries must remain protected. It also has a trust boundary: user configuration is personal, repository configuration may be shared, workspace configuration is local, and command-line configuration is ephemeral. The same key can have a different operational consequence at each layer.

Find the effective value before changing it

jj config path
jj config list
jj config get user.name
jj config list --include-defaults
jj config list --include-overridden

Use config get when a script needs the effective scalar value without the formatting used by config list. Use config list when precedence and overridden values matter. The exact scope options belong to the installed command surface; in jj 0.45.1, the durable scope is chosen by the command's scope flags and an additional file is loaded with --config-file. The config commands also add --file PATH targeting for relevant subcommands.

LayerBest usesReview question
Built-inFallback templates, revsets, pager, safety policy.Could a release change this default?
UserName/email, editor, pager, personal aliases.Would another checkout want this?
RepositoryProject aliases, tools, immutable policy, review conventions.Could a checked-out repository influence an unsafe tool?
WorkspaceLocal default command, sparse/build preferences.Does this affect only one working directory?
Command lineCI pinning, explicit remote/output, experiments.Will the value be visible in process arguments?

Do not store credentials or tokens in aliases or command-line values. A process listing, operation description, shell history, or repository config can expose them. Prefer Git's credential/SSH facilities and the host's agent. jj's role is to select the commit/ref operation and invoke the configured transport.

Progressive Linux layout

~/.config/jj/config.toml
~/.config/jj/conf.d/10-identity.toml
~/.config/jj/conf.d/20-ui.toml
~/.config/jj/conf.d/30-revsets.toml
~/.config/jj/conf.d/40-templates.toml
~/.config/jj/conf.d/50-remotes.toml
~/.config/jj/conf.d/60-tools.toml

Use jj config path to confirm what the build actually reads. XDG paths are a useful Linux convention, not a substitute for checking the installed binary and distribution patches. jj 0.45.1 supports a configuration directory, so keep its fragments ordered and independently parseable. Do not invent a second loader around that mechanism.

[user]
name = "A. Engineer"
email = "a@example.org"

[ui]
editor = ["nvim", "-f"]
pager = ["less", "-FRX"]
paginate = "auto"
color = "auto"
default-command = ["log", "-r", "(@:: & mutable()) | bookmarks() | remote_bookmarks()"]

Start with identity and output, then add selection aliases, then add transport policy. A broken template or alias in the user file can make every repository unusable; add one family at a time and run a disposable command after each change.

Revset and template defaults

[revsets]
log = '(@:: & mutable()) | bookmarks() | remote_bookmarks()'
status = 'mutable() & ::@'
fix = 'mutable() & ::@'
run = 'mutable() & ::@'
sign = 'mutable() & ::@'

[revset-aliases]
'stack(tip)' = 'roots(trunk()..tip)::'
'unpublished(tip)' = 'tip ~ ::remote_bookmarks()'
'reviewable(tip)' = 'heads(unpublished(tip) ~ empty() ~ conflicts())'

[template-aliases]
identity = 'change_id.shortest(10) ++ " " ++ commit_id.short(10)'
state = 'separate(" ", if(conflict, "C", ""), if(empty, "E", ""), if(immutable, "I", ""))'

A default revset is invoked only when the command's explicit selector is absent. It is not a security boundary: a user can pass another revset. Keep defaults bounded and name aliases after the set they denote. A template alias changes rendering, not selection. If a default includes remote bookmarks, remember that a fetch changes the result without changing local mutable work.

Immutable heads: the safety setting that must actually work

In 0.45.1 the rewrite-protection policy is the revset alias immutable_heads(). The correct TOML location is [revset-aliases], with a key whose literal name includes parentheses:

[revset-aliases]
"immutable_heads()" = "main@origin | tags() | root()"

Verify both the value and an attempted protected rewrite in a disposable repository:

jj config get 'revset-aliases."immutable_heads()"'
jj log -r 'immutable_heads()'
jj rebase -s @ -d main@origin

The alias controls the set jj checks; it is not a label and does not make every remote ref immutable. --ignore-immutable disables the check for one operation but does not change the query's value. A repository can therefore be configured with a public boundary that a normal command protects while an emergency command deliberately crosses it. Record why before using that override.

GitHub and Gerrit remote policy

[git]
private-commits = 'description(regex:"(?i)wip|do not publish")'

[gerrit]
# jj 0.45.1 documented defaults; pass flags explicitly in mixed-remote repositories.
default-remote = "gerrit"
default-remote-branch = "main"
review-url = "https://gerrit.example.invalid/c/project/+/"

[command-aliases]
push-gh = ["git", "push", "--remote", "github", "--bookmark"]
upload-gerrit = ["gerrit", "upload", "--remote", "gerrit", "--remote-branch", "main"]

Use separate aliases for separate publication protocols. A default remote is a convenience, not a permission boundary. In jj 0.45.1, a portable Gerrit script should pass --remote and --remote-branch explicitly. The named defaults can reduce repetition, but explicit arguments remain clearer in a repository with multiple publication protocols.

Conditional configuration is useful when a single clone talks to both hosts. jj 0.45.1 provides the conditional-configuration mechanism described above; use it only when the repository predicate and resulting policy are easy to audit. A conservative design keeps the host choice in the command alias and requires a bookmark argument. Do not infer “Gerrit repository” solely from the presence of a remote named origin, and do not let a GitHub default send a Gerrit review ref.

Editors, merge tools, fixers, and trust

ui.editor, ui.diff-editor, and ui.merge-editor are separate contracts. A diff editor selects changes between two trees; a merge editor resolves conflict sides; a normal editor writes a description or metadata. Configure a builtin tool first, then add an external executable only after testing it in an untrusted/reproducible environment.

[ui]
diff-editor = ":builtin"
merge-editor = ":builtin"

[merge-tools.meld]
program = "meld"
edit-args = ["$left", "$right", "-o", "$output"]
merge-args = ["$base", "$left", "$right", "-o", "$output"]

[fix.tools.rustfmt]
command = ["rustfmt", "--edition", "2024", "--emit", "files"]
patterns = ["glob:**/*.rs"]

External commands can read repository content, environment variables, credentials available to the process, and files outside the repository. Do not accept a repository's tool definition without review. A fixer also has graph scope: a broad default can rewrite many mutable commits. Bound both commits and files, capture operation output, and test no-op, changed, conflicted, generated, binary, and sparse cases.

Snapshot and workspace policy

Snapshot-related keys control when filesystem state is noticed, which files are tracked, and how large or ignored files are handled. Workspace settings control movement and defaults; sparse patterns control materialisation. These are not interchangeable. A snapshot setting can change the working-copy commit; a sparse setting can make a file absent without removing it from the commit tree; a movement setting can choose whether a navigation command edits a child or creates another working-copy commit.

jj config get snapshot.max-new-file-size
jj config get snapshot.auto-track
jj config get ui.movement.edit
jj sparse list
jj workspace list

Before changing snapshot policy in a repository with generated files, establish which files are currently tracked and which are ignored. Before changing workspace movement policy, make a two-workspace test and record each workspace's @. Defaults that feel convenient interact with editor and build processes; document the ownership boundary in the repository's developer notes.

Schema validation and migration

jj util config-schema is the machine-readable authority for types and available keys in the installed release. It does not replace a human reference: a schema can say that a value is an array without explaining why a list of command arguments is safer than a shell string. Use the schema to detect removed/added keys, then test the semantic contract.

jj util config-schema > schema.json
jj config list --include-defaults --include-overridden
jj util config-schema > schema-0.45.1.json

Migrate one family at a time. Preserve the old config, run the binary's config parser, inspect effective values, and run a fixture. In particular compare immutable heads, pager flags, remote/tag predicates, Gerrit defaults, aliases, and command defaults between the installed release and future releases. A successful parse is not proof that a key still has the intended meaning; an unknown key can be accepted as data and simply never be read.

Configuration review checklist

  1. Identify the layer and trust level.
  2. Read the effective value and overridden values.
  3. Check whether the key is a default, a language alias, or a command setting.
  4. Check the jj 0.45.1 schema for the key's spelling and type; when preparing a later-release configuration, repeat that check against the later schema.
  5. Keep remote, bookmark, and force decisions explicit at publication boundaries.
  6. Test editors/tools in a disposable repository.
  7. Run a semantic fixture after changing immutable, snapshot, revset, or template policy.

Part XIV — Template language

Jujutsu templates are a small, typed, functional rendering language. They are not format strings with a bag of magic substitutions. A template is parsed, evaluated against a context object, and rendered as labelled output. In jj log the context is a Commit; in jj op log it is an Operation. A keyword such as description is shorthand for a zero-argument method on that context object.

Target surface. This chapter describes the template help captured from jj 0.45.1. Template details are release-sensitive: when building scripts, run jj help -k templates for the installed binary and treat a parse error as a compatibility signal. The examples below use only the target-release surface.

1. The evaluation model

There are three stages:

  1. Parsing: jj parses the expression and checks syntax and many type constraints before walking commits.
  2. Evaluation: the expression is evaluated once for each selected object. A method can return another typed object, a list, an optional value, or a renderable template.
  3. Rendering: the result is converted to terminal output. Colour labels and hyperlinks are metadata around output, not ordinary characters; stringify() deliberately removes those labels.

This explains why a template can fail before printing any commits, why a missing optional value can be tested but not blindly dereferenced, and why parsing JSON with a shell tool is safer when the template emits explicit separators and disables colour.

jj log -r '::@' -T 'change_id.short() ++ " " ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'
jj log -r '::@' --color=never -T 'commit_id ++ "\t" ++ change_id ++ "\t" ++ description.first_line().escape_json() ++ "\n"'

In the first command the log command supplies one Commit object per selected commit. In the second, full IDs and a JSON-safe description are emitted with tabs. The graph display is independent of -T; add -G when you explicitly want graph characters in a custom log.

2. Literals, shell quoting, and grammar

Use single- or double-quoted string literals. Double quotes support \\", \\\\, \t, \r, \n, \0, \e, and \xHH. Single-quoted literals have no escape syntax, which makes them convenient for a template containing double quotes and inconvenient for an embedded apostrophe. The shell adds another quoting layer: the outer shell quotes must preserve the inner template exactly.

# Shell single quotes; template double-quoted literals
jj log -T 'change_id.short(12) ++ "\t" ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'

# Shell double quotes; template single-quoted literals
jj log -T "change_id.short(12) ++ ' ' ++ description.first_line() ++ '\\n'"

Templates use method calls (x.f()), function calls (f(x)), unary operators, arithmetic and comparisons on integers, logical operators, and concatenation. Parenthesise mixed expressions even when the precedence is known; it makes a durable configuration reviewable.

BindingFormsMeaning and consequence
strongestx.f(), f(x)Method/function call. description.first_line() is evaluated before concatenation.
-x, !xInteger negation and Boolean negation.
p:xString-pattern or pattern-alias syntax where a pattern argument is required.
* / %Integer multiplication, division, remainder.
+ -Integer addition/subtraction; do not confuse with template concatenation.
>= > <= <Integer comparison.
== !=Equality for Boolean, byte string, integer, and string-compatible values.
&&Short-circuiting Boolean and.
||Short-circuiting Boolean or.
weakestx ++ yConcatenates template output. It is not integer addition.

For example, if(parents.len() > 1, "merge", "linear") compares an integer and chooses a string. The equivalent-looking parents.len() ++ 1 is not integer addition. Write (parents.len() + 1) for arithmetic, or stringify the result intentionally.

3. Values, conversions, and optional values

The type system matters at boundaries. A String, ByteString, List, and Option can be tested as Boolean. A non-empty string/list and a set option are true; an empty value or unset option is false. A Commit cannot itself be printed, but its methods can produce templates, strings, lists, or other objects.

Type familyCan becomeUse in practice
Boolean, IntegerTemplate/SerializeConditions, arithmetic, counts, JSON.
String, ByteStringTemplate, Stringify, SerializeDescriptions, paths, IDs, JSON-safe output.
List/AnyListBoolean and often TemplateMap/filter/join; empty lists can suppress separators.
Option<T>Boolean; methods of T when setTest optional signatures, remotes, keys, roots before use.
Commit, OperationSerialize but not directly TemplateCall methods; use json() where serialisation is intended.
jj log -r @ -T 'coalesce(description.first_line(), "(no description)") ++ "\n"'
jj log -r @ -T 'if(signature, signature.status(), "unsigned") ++ "\n"'

try() catches runtime failures in its alternatives but not parse/type errors. coalesce() chooses the first non-empty rendered value, useful for a missing description or absent bookmark. Use if(option, option.method(), "fallback") when the branch itself should be explicit.

4. Global functions

The following functions are the compositional toolkit. A function's argument type is part of its contract; a value that merely prints as text may not be accepted where a parse-time string literal is required.

Function and signatureSemanticsApplication and edge case
fill(width, content)Wraps lines to a display width.Descriptions in show; control sequences require care.
indent(prefix, content)Prefixes non-empty lines.Indent a multi-line description without prefixing blank lines.
pad_start(width, content, [fill])Left-pads a one-line value.Align counts/IDs; newlines are invalid.
pad_end(width, content, [fill])Right-pads a one-line value.Align subjects; use one display-width fill character.
pad_centered(width, content, [fill])Pads both sides; odd remainder goes right.Terminal report headers.
truncate_start(width, content, [ellipsis])Removes leading characters to fit.Keep a path suffix; ellipsis appears only after truncation.
truncate_end(width, content, [ellipsis])Removes trailing characters to fit.Keep subject prefix; do not use on multi-line content.
hash(content: Stringify)Returns a hexadecimal digest.Fingerprint generated output; not a commit identity.
label(label, content)Applies a space-separated colour/style label.Mark conflicts or refs; custom labels need configured style.
hyperlink(url, text, [fallback])Uses OSC 8 when colour is enabled, otherwise fallback/text.Link commit IDs; terminals and PDFs may discard OSC 8.
raw_escape_sequence(content)Preserves escape sequences and strips labels.Terminal control only; visible output breaks wrapping.
replace(pattern, content, lambda)Replaces matches while preserving untouched formatting.Lambda receives RegexCaptures.
stringify(content)Converts to string and removes labels.Useful before hashing or embedding output.
json(value)Serialises a supported value as JSON.Object output; serialised fields are not an eternal API.
if(condition, then, [else])Conditionally evaluates a branch.Guard optional values and suppress empty punctuation.
try(expr, fallback...)Returns the first successful expression.Catches runtime errors, not static type errors.
coalesce(content...)Returns first non-empty rendered content.Defaults for descriptions and refs.
concat(content...)Equivalent to repeated ++.Readable aliases with many fragments.
join(separator, content...)Separates every argument.Use when empty arguments are meaningful.
separate(separator, content...)Separates non-empty arguments only.Optional bookmark/tag/signature fields.
surround(prefix, suffix, content)Wraps non-empty content.Render parentheses only when content exists.
config(name)Looks up config as an option.Extract with as_boolean(), as_integer(), as_string(), or as_string_list().
git_web_url([remote])Best-effort remote-to-HTTPS URL.Defaults to origin; empty on failure; SSH aliases unsupported.
jj log -T 'separate(" ",
  if(conflict, label("conflict", "CONFLICT"), ""),
  if(empty, label("empty", "EMPTY"), ""),
  bookmarks, tags, change_id.shortest(8)
) ++ "\n"'

separate is preferable to concatenating spaces inside each branch. The rendered value of bookmarks or tags can be empty, so output remains stable when a commit has no names.

5. Strings, bytes, and patterns

String is UTF-8 text; ByteString preserves arbitrary bytes and is used for some repository paths or raw content. Both provide len, contains, match, prefix/suffix tests and removal, trimming, substring, first-line, line splitting, splitting by a string pattern, replacement, upper/lower conversion. String indices are UTF-8 byte offsets, not Unicode scalar indexes. Do not use byte slicing as a human-character counter.

jj log -T 'description.first_line().substr(0, 48) ++ "\n"'
jj log -T 'description.lines().filter(|line| line.contains("TODO")).join("\n") ++ "\n"'
jj log -T 'description.replace("API", "Interface") ++ "\n"'

A bare string pattern literal is case-sensitive substring matching. Explicit pattern kinds make intent clearer. A pattern argument is normally written directly at the call site rather than stored as a dynamic value. String.escape_json() is useful for a field; json(value) is useful for a serialisable object.

6. Lists and lambdas

Lists are where templates become a language rather than a pretty-printer. The target surface provides len(), join(), filter(), map(), any(), all(), first(), last(), get(), reverse(), skip(), and take(). Lambda parameters are typed by the list being traversed.

jj log -r 'merges()' -T 'parents.map(|p| p.commit_id().short()).join(", ") ++ "\n"'
jj log -T 'trailers.filter(|t| t.key() == "Change-Id").map(|t| t.value()).join(",") ++ "\n"'
jj log -T 'bookmarks.take(3).join(", ") ++ "\n"'

first(), last(), and get() fail on an empty/out-of-range list. Wrap them in try when emptiness is normal. map returns an AnyList; it can usually be joined, but is not a typed list with every original method.

7. Commit context and identity

In a commit template, all zero-argument methods of Commit are available as keywords. The following table is the core of a useful daily log.

Keyword/methodResultMeaning and trap
commit_id, change_idID objectsUse .short(), .shortest(), or full rendering. Rewrites change the former, normally not the latter.
description()StringUsually has a trailing newline when non-blank; use first_line() for one-line output.
trailers()List<Trailer>Preserves order and duplicate keys; do not assume one Change-Id.
parents()List<Commit>More than one parent means a merge; parent order can matter in display.
author(), committer()SignatureAuthor and committer can differ; each has name, email, timestamp.
signature()Option<CryptographicSignature>Presence is cheap; status/key/display can verify cryptography.
mine()BooleanMatches author's email against current user.
working_copies(), current_working_copy()List/ref and BooleanDistinguishes any workspace at this commit from this workspace's @.
bookmarks(), local_bookmarks(), remote_bookmarks()List<CommitRef>Use the specific method when tracked-remote presentation matters.
tags(), local_tags(), remote_tags()List<CommitRef>Tags have the analogous tracked-remote display rule.
divergent(), hidden(), immutable(), conflict(), empty(), root()BooleanState predicates. The template method is conflict(); the revset function is conflicts().
change_offset()Option<Integer>Useful for divergent evolution display; may be absent.
contained_in(revset)BooleanArgument must be a parse-time literal such as "mutable()".
diff([files]), files([files])TreeDiff/List<TreeEntry>TreeDiff itself is not printable; call summary(), stat(), or git().
conflicted_files()List<TreeEntry>Useful for conflict path/count reports.

CommitId and ChangeId both offer short([len]) and shortest([min_len]). The shortest form returns a ShortestIdPrefix with prefix() and rest(). Change IDs have normal_hex() for conventional hexadecimal rather than jj's canonical reversed alphabet.

jj log -T 'change_id.shortest(8).prefix() ++
  label("dim", change_id.shortest(8).rest()) ++ " " ++
  commit_id.short(10) ++ "\n"'

Short IDs are a display convenience, not an interchange format. A short prefix can become ambiguous after another object enters the repository.

8. References, tracking, and publication state

CommitRef provides name(), an optional remote(), presence/conflict tests, normal/added/removed targets, tracking tests and ahead/behind hints, and synced(). This lets a log distinguish a local publication bookmark from the remote state it tracks:

jj log -T 'bookmarks.map(|b|
  separate("",
    if(b.remote(), "@" ++ b.remote(), ""),
    b.name(),
    if(b.conflict(), "!", ""),
    if(b.tracked() && !b.synced(), "*", "")
  )
).join(" ") ++ "\n"'

The ! and * are presentation choices; they do not alter refs. A conflicted ref has multiple target sets, so normal_target() may be unset and added_targets()/removed_targets() are safer forensic fields.

9. Signatures, timestamps, paths, and diffs

A Signature has name(), email(), and timestamp(). Email values support local() and domain(). A timestamp supports ago(), format(strftime), utc(), local(), after(date), before(date), and since(timestamp). A timestamp range has start(), end(), and duration().

jj log -T 'author.name() ++ " <" ++ author.email() ++ "> " ++
  author.timestamp().local().format("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M %Z") ++ "\n"'
jj log -T 'committer.timestamp().ago() ++ " " ++
  author.timestamp().since(committer.timestamp()).duration() ++ "\n"'

For reproducible machine output prefer UTC and an explicit format. Signature verification is separate: testing signature() for presence is cheap, but status(), key(), and display() can invoke GPG or SSH tooling.

RepoPath offers absolute(), display(), and optional parent(). FsPath offers absolute() and relative(). Preserve repository-relative paths when output is consumed by another jj command; display paths are for humans and can depend on the current directory.

A TreeDiff can render summary(), a Git-style diff with git([context]), a colour-word diff with color_words([context]), or statistics with stat([width], [max_bar_width]). Its files() entries have path, status, status character, source, target, and display path. A DiffStats has per-file entries and total added/removed counts.

jj show -r @ -T 'description ++
  "\nFiles:\n" ++ diff().summary() ++
  "\nStat:\n" ++ diff().stat(72, 24) ++ "\n"'

A template is evaluated for each commit. A large inline diff is consequently expensive. Keep daily logs to summaries and reserve diff().git() for show or a tightly bounded revset.

10. Operation and workspace templates

In jj op log, the context is an Operation. Its methods are current_operation(), description(), id(), attributes(), time(), user(), snapshot(), workspace_name(), root(), and parents(). Operation IDs support short([len]). Compose scalar methods; the operation object cannot be printed directly.

jj op log -T 'id.short(12) ++ " " ++
  if(current_operation, "* ", "  ") ++
  if(snapshot, "snapshot ", "") ++
  workspace_name ++ " " ++ description ++ "\n"'

Keep operation ID, user, workspace, and description visible during recovery. An operation template describes local repository history; it does not synchronise operation IDs to another clone.

WorkspaceRef has name(), target(), and optional root(). The root can be absent for old records or stale/moved paths:

jj log -r 'working_copies()' -T 'working_copies.map(|w| w.name() ++ ":" ++ w.root()).join(" ") ++ "\n"'

11. Colour labels, styles, and hyperlinks

jj automatically attaches labels based on command, context, and method names. Discover exact generated labels with --color=debug rather than assuming a stable taxonomy. Use label("name", content) for an explicit semantic label, then configure its style in UI colour configuration.

jj log -T 'label("bookmarked", bookmarks) ++
  if(conflict, label("conflict", "✖"), "") ++ "\n"' --color=debug

For scripts use --color=never. stringify() strips labels; raw_escape_sequence() bypasses sanitisation and should be limited to terminal control sequences. hyperlink() emits OSC 8 only when colour output is enabled. Keep a visible ID fallback:

jj log -T 'if(git_web_url(),
  hyperlink(git_web_url() ++ "/commit/" ++ commit_id, commit_id.short(10)),
  commit_id.short(10)
) ++ "\n"'

git_web_url() is best-effort and returns an empty string if conversion fails. It defaults to origin and does not resolve SSH host aliases. Terminals, pagers, PDF output, and machine readers may discard OSC 8 metadata.

12. JSON and machine-readable output

Templates can emit JSON, but JSON validity is the author's responsibility when fields are concatenated manually. Use json() for serialisable objects and escape_json() for scalar strings. Emit one record per commit with a newline delimiter and disable colour/pager:

jj log --color=never --no-pager -r '::@' -T \
  '"{\"commit_id\": " ++ json(commit_id) ++
   ", \"change_id\": " ++ json(change_id) ++
   ", \"description\": " ++ json(description) ++
   ", \"empty\": " ++ json(empty) ++
   ", \"conflict\": " ++ json(conflict) ++ "}\n"'

Use a real JSON parser to consume this output. The serialised representation of underlying jj objects can change across releases even when ordinary human fields remain available. Pin jj and test fixture output if it feeds a build or publication gate.

13. Template aliases

Aliases are configuration-defined expressions in [template-aliases]. They can define keywords, functions, and pattern aliases. Functions can be overloaded by parameter count, but an alias with a builtin name shadows the builtin; avoid such names in shared configuration.

[template-aliases]
short-id = 'change_id.short()'
'format-field(key, value)' = 'key ++ ": " ++ value ++ "\n"'
'json-line' = 'json(commit_id) ++ "\n"'
'pat:x' = 'x ++ "\n'

Alias names may be exposed to completion with documentation:

[template-aliases]
compact-id = { definition = 'change_id.shortest(10)', doc = 'Short unique change ID' }

Keep aliases small and composable. A repository's template policy is easier to review when ID, ref-state, subject, and JSON aliases each have one responsibility. If an alias embeds a revset through contained_in() or a value through config(), document the required scope and release assumptions beside it.

14. Building a daily advanced log

Build a template from stable fields rather than trying to clone every glyph of the builtin log. First create an unambiguous record:

jj log -G -r '@:: & mutable()' -T \
  'change_id.shortest(10) ++ " " ++
   commit_id.short(10) ++ " " ++
   description.first_line() ++ "\n"'

Then add graph-relevant state and publication names:

jj log -G -r '(@:: & mutable()) | bookmarks() | remote_bookmarks()' -T \
  'change_id.shortest(10) ++ " " ++ commit_id.short(10) ++
   " " ++ if(conflict, label("conflict", "CONFLICT "), "") ++
   if(empty, label("empty", "EMPTY "), "") ++
   description.first_line() ++ separate(" ", bookmarks, tags) ++ "\n"'

Finally add author/date only when the output is being used for review:

jj log -G -r '(@:: & mutable()) | bookmarks() | remote_bookmarks()' -T \
  'change_id.shortest(10) ++ " " ++
   if(current_working_copy, "@", " ") ++ " " ++
   commit_id.short(10) ++ " " ++ author.timestamp().ago() ++
   " " ++ description.first_line() ++
   separate(" ", bookmarks, tags) ++ "\n"'

This is a display template, not a new revset alias. Keep the revset and template independently configurable so a log can change its search domain without changing its fields.

15. Debugging, failure modes, and performance

SymptomLikely causeRepair
Parse error before outputUnbalanced quote/parenthesis, unsupported method, or invalid operator.Reduce to a literal, add one method at a time, and run installed keyword help.
Type errorArithmetic used where concatenation was intended, or non-printable object emitted.Use + for integers, ++ for templates, and call a scalar method.
Inline runtime errorfirst()/get() on empty list or method on an unset option.Test with if or use try; do not hide parse errors with try.
Columns misalignNewlines, wide Unicode, colour control, or raw escape sequence in padding.Use one-line values with pad_*; keep raw escapes invisible.
Pipeline contains escape codesColour or OSC 8 enabled.Pass --color=never --no-pager and explicit delimiters.
Template is slowLarge diffs, signature verification, URL work, or broad revset.Narrow -r, render summaries, and avoid verification in routine logs.
Works on one machine onlyAlias/config absent or release surface differs.Version-control aliases and run fixture template tests after upgrades.

Debug in layers: jj log -r @ -T 'commit_id', then one method at a time. Test empty descriptions, merge commits, conflicts, unsigned commits, no bookmarks, divergent refs, non-UTF-8 paths, and a commit with multiple workspaces. A large inline diff, cryptographic verification, remote URL conversion, and a broad commit set can each make a template expensive.

16. Design rules

  1. Keep graph selection (-r) separate from rendering (-T).
  2. Use full IDs for interchange and short IDs for human scanning.
  3. Use first_line() for one-line fields; descriptions normally carry a trailing newline.
  4. Use separate and surround for optional punctuation.
  5. Guard optional values and empty lists before calling methods that require an element.
  6. Prefer summaries to full diffs in a multi-commit log.
  7. Disable colour and the pager in automation.
  8. Treat template aliases as code: review, test, document, and version them.
  9. Do not treat a template hash, short ID, or rendered label as repository identity.

Appendix E repeats the type/method inventory as a lookup reference. The language is documented for jj 0.45.1 and corroborated by the official template documentation. The book paraphrases the rules and uses original examples.

Template laboratory: from a field to a review dashboard

Templates become manageable when developed as typed expressions. Begin with one value, add a separator, then introduce a conditional or list operation. Do not begin with a full replacement for the builtin log: a syntax error in a large template hides which value or method was wrong.

jj log -r @ -T 'commit_id ++ "\n"'
jj log -r @ -T 'commit_id.short() ++ " " ++ change_id.short() ++ "\n"'
jj log -r @ -T 'description.first_line() ++ "\n"'
jj log -r @ -T 'if(conflict, "CONFLICT ", "") ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'

Keywords in a commit template are typed properties. The form commit_id yields an ID object; commit_id.short() invokes its method and yields a shorter rendering. description is a description value with methods such as first_line(). A method call is not interchangeable with a global function call: signature() is not the right spelling in a commit context when the language exposes signature as a keyword. When in doubt, consult the type-specific help and test the smallest expression.

Formatting a record

jj log --no-graph -r '@:: & mutable()' -T '
commit_id.short() ++ "\t" ++
change_id.short() ++ "\t" ++
if(empty, "E", "") ++
if(conflict, "C", "") ++
if(mutable, "M", "I") ++ "\t" ++
author.email() ++ "\t" ++
description.first_line() ++ "\n"
'

This is useful for a terminal report because the output has an explicit delimiter and a stable field order. It is not automatically safe as a TSV format: descriptions and emails can contain tabs or newlines, and labels can introduce escape sequences. For machine consumption, use JSON helpers or an unambiguous encoding policy and test descriptions containing control characters.

Conditional output and optional values

Use if for presence and state, not for string concatenation that can be achieved by a list separator. A conditional should make the empty case intentional:

if(bookmarks, " [" ++ bookmarks ++ "]", "")
if(remote_bookmarks, " <" ++ remote_bookmarks ++ ">", "")
if(conflict, "\n  conflict: " ++ conflict, "")

Some values are optional or collection-valued. Rendering an optional value directly may yield an empty string, while calling a method that requires a concrete object can fail. The try, coalesce, and collection functions are useful for controlling this boundary. Test a template on root, merge, conflicted, empty, signed, unsigned, bookmarked, unbookmarked, and working-copy commits; the ordinary linear non-empty case exercises almost none of the interesting type surface.

Lists, lambdas, and separators

Parents, bookmarks, remote bookmarks, and tags are collections. Use list methods and lambda expressions to transform elements, then use join, separate, or surround to render punctuation once:

parents.map(|p| p.commit_id().short()).join(", ")
bookmarks.map(|b| b.name()).join(", ")
separate(" ", change_id.short(), author.email(), description.first_line())
surround(" [", "]", bookmarks)

The precise element methods depend on the object type. A list of commit objects is not a list of strings; call the ID or name method before joining. This is the same discipline as a typed programming language: if a method is missing, inspect the element type rather than adding arbitrary string conversion until the output happens to look right.

Commit, operation, and workspace contexts

Log templates run with a commit as the current object. Operation templates run with an operation object, whose fields include operation ID, description, timestamp, snapshot and workspace information as documented in the installed template help. Workspace-oriented commands may expose workspace records. A template written for one context cannot assume that commit keywords exist in another.

# Commit context
jj log -r 'all()' -T 'commit_id.short() ++ " " ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'

# Operation context
jj op log -T 'id.short() ++ " " ++ description ++ "\n"'

# Workspace-aware commit output
jj log -r 'working_copies()' -T 'working_copies.map(|w| w.name()).join(",") ++ "\n"'

When designing a monitoring report, choose the context first. A repository health report may need two commands—one for operation history and one for commit state—because forcing both concepts into one template makes the output ambiguous.

Labels, colours, styles, and hyperlinks

Labels are semantic annotations that the UI can style. They are better than embedding raw terminal escape sequences because output policy can then decide whether colour is enabled. Functions such as label, raw_escape_sequence, and hyperlink should be used with awareness of output destinations. A terminal can interpret OSC hyperlinks; a PDF or log file may display the escape bytes or remove them inconsistently.

label("change_id", change_id.short())
label("conflict", if(conflict, "CONFLICT", ""))
hyperlink(git_web_url(), commit_id.short())

Keep machine output unlabelled and use --color never where the command supports it. Use a separate human template for colour and hyperlinks. Labels are also useful in the default log template because the graph renderer and pager can apply consistent styling to bookmarks, remote bookmarks, change IDs, and conflict indicators.

JSON and safe extraction

JSON is a boundary protocol, not a decoration. Quote and escape values with the template’s JSON function rather than hand-building a JSON string. Emit one complete object per record only if the consuming tool expects newline-delimited JSON; otherwise emit an array with deliberate separators. Test quotes, backslashes, Unicode, empty descriptions, and multiline descriptions.

jj log --no-graph -r '@:: & mutable()' -T '
"{\"commit\":\"" ++ json(commit_id) ++
"\",\"change\":\"" ++ json(change_id) ++
"\",\"subject\":\"" ++ json(description.first_line()) ++ "\"}\n"
'

The exact JSON helper’s return type and escaping behaviour are versioned; test it against the binary that will run the automation. Do not parse the ordinary jj log graph output in scripts. The graph contains visual layout decisions and can change with labels, topology, and terminal width.

Aliases and composition

Template aliases let a repository define a named rendering function or reusable fragment. Use aliases to give stable names to concepts such as “review marker”, “compact identity”, or “publication refs”. Keep aliases small enough that an error points to one concept. A large alias that embeds a complete log, revset, and colour policy becomes difficult to override.

[template-aliases]
'book-id' = 'change_id.short() ++ " " ++ commit_id.short()'
'review-mark' = 'if(conflict, "C", "") ++ if(empty, "E", "")'
'publication' = 'separate(" ", bookmarks, remote_bookmarks, tags)'

When an alias accepts parameters, document the parameter types and call syntax in the repository’s configuration comments. A parameterised alias is a small function, not a textual macro: quoting and type checking still apply. Test aliases with a direct -T invocation before making them the default template.

Reconstructing and replacing the default log

The default log is a composition of graph rendering, change identity, description, author/date metadata, ref labels, working-copy state, and conflict/empty markers. Reconstructing it is an educational exercise: first print the commit ID and description, then add change ID, author, refs, parents, state flags, and labels. Compare against builtin_log() or the documented builtin template in the target release. Do not copy an internal builtin into a long-lived config without recording the version it came from.

jj log -r '@:: & mutable()' -T '
change_id.short() ++ " " ++
commit_id.short() ++ " " ++
if(conflict, "[conflict] ", "") ++
if(empty, "[empty] ", "") ++
description.first_line() ++
if(bookmarks, " " ++ bookmarks, "") ++
"\n"
'

A compact daily template should privilege decisions: which logical change is this, what immutable object is checked out, is it conflicted or empty, and what publication names refer to it? A forensic template should add parents, timestamps, signatures, and remote refs. One template cannot optimise simultaneously for a one-line prompt, code review, and audit export.

Template debugging checklist

  1. Confirm the command’s template context: commit, operation, or workspace.
  2. Test the field without methods.
  3. Test the method on a commit known to provide the value.
  4. Test an empty, merge, conflict, root, and unsigned commit.
  5. Add one operator or function at a time.
  6. Run with --no-pager and colour disabled when comparing output.
  7. Use explicit separators and inspect trailing whitespace.
  8. Pin aliases and rerun validation after upgrading jj.

A failed template is often valuable evidence about the type model. Treat “unknown keyword”, “method not found”, and “expected one value” as distinct errors. The repair is usually to change context, call a method on the correct object, or map a collection—not to add more quoting blindly.

Template language laboratory: types, evaluation, and stable output

The template language deserves the same discipline as a small typed programming language. A keyword has a type, a method returns another type, operators have domains, and evaluation can fail at runtime for an empty option or list. The fact that a template is written inside a shell command adds another language boundary. Develop it incrementally and keep the output contract visible.

Contexts and values

In a commit template, zero-argument methods on the current Commit object are available as keywords. Thus commit_id is shorthand for self.commit_id(). In an operation template the current object is an Operation, so commit keywords such as author do not become available merely because the operation caused a commit. This explains many “unknown keyword” errors: the expression is valid in a different context.

ContextUseful valuesTypical consumer
Commitcommit_id, change_id, description, parents, signatures, refs, state predicates, diff/tree methods.jj log, jj show, jj diff.
Commit evolutionCurrent commit, predecessor list, operation that created it, inter-diff.jj evolog.
OperationOperation ID, description, timestamp, user, snapshot flag, workspace, parents.jj op log, jj op show.
Tree/diffPaths, status, conflict sides, line/file statistics, formatted diff.file, diff, annotation.

Start with a context probe:

jj log -r @ -T 'self ++ "\n"'
jj log -r @ -T 'commit_id ++ " " ++ change_id ++ "\n"'
jj op log -n 3 -T 'id ++ " " ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'

If a value is not printable directly, call the method that converts it to a display value. An ID object has short() and shortest(); a signature has name(), email(), and timestamp(); a list has map, filter, and join. A template that happens to print through implicit conversion is less explicit than one that states the desired representation.

Operators and evaluation order

Method and function calls bind most tightly. Negation and logical not apply to the next expression. Pattern syntax is used in places that expect a string pattern. Integer arithmetic uses *, /, %, +, and -; comparisons use integer or scalar values; && and || short-circuit; ++ concatenates template values. The difference between + and ++ is not stylistic: the former requires integers while the latter builds rendered output.

1 + 2 * 3
(1 + 2) * 3
if(conflict, "C", "")
commit_id.short() ++ " " ++ description.first_line()
parents.len() == 2 && parents.first().empty()

Use parentheses when mixing arithmetic, Boolean tests, and concatenation. Short-circuiting is useful for guards, but it is not a substitute for understanding optional values. A method called on the right side of && is not evaluated when the left side is false; the same expression may fail when the guard is removed.

Strings, bytes, and escaping

The language distinguishes String, ByteString, and Template. A string is textual and has methods such as trim, first_line, lines, split, replace, upper, and lower. A byte string has byte-oriented length and slicing, which matters for commit descriptions or paths that are not guaranteed to be valid UTF-8. A template is rendered output and can carry labels. stringify() turns a stringifiable value into a string and strips colour labels; ++ preserves template composition.

description.first_line().trim()
description.lines().take(3).join(" | ")
description.replace(regex:"\\s+", " ")
description.substr(0, 40)
if(description.contains("WIP"), "[wip] ", "")

String literals recognise escaped quote, backslash, tab, carriage return, newline, NUL, escape, and hexadecimal byte forms. The shell parses its own quotes first. For a template containing double quotes, either use a single-quoted shell argument or escape both layers. A command that works interactively can fail in a shell script when the script changes quoting context.

# shell single quotes protect the template's double quotes
jj log --no-pager -T 'description.replace(regex:"\\s+", " ") ++ "\n"'
# a literal newline is a template escape, not a shell line break
jj log -T 'commit_id ++ "\n"'

Lists, mapping, and empty collections

Collections are not strings. parents, bookmarks, remote_bookmarks, tags, files, and trailers contain typed elements. join can render elements, while map first transforms each element. filter retains elements satisfying a Boolean lambda; any and all reduce a list to a Boolean. first, last, and get require a valid element and can fail on an empty list or bad index.

parents.map(|p| p.commit_id().short()).join(", ")
bookmarks.map(|b| b.name()).join(", ")
files.filter(|f| f.conflict()).map(|f| f.path().display()).join(", ")
if(parents.len() > 1, "merge", "linear")
if(bookmarks.any(|b| b.remote()), "remote-ref", "local-only")

To render optional punctuation, prefer separate or surround:

separate(" ", change_id.short(), author.email(), description.first_line())
surround(" [", "]", bookmarks)
surround(" <", ">", remote_bookmarks)
coalesce(description.first_line(), "(no description)")

These functions differ in a way that matters for empty values. join puts separators between all supplied content; separate omits empty content; surround emits both delimiters only for non-empty content; coalesce chooses the first non-empty value. Use them to prevent dangling brackets and spaces in root, empty, or unbookmarked commits.

Commit identity, refs, and review state

commit_id and change_id are different objects. A commit ID's short form is an exact-object display convenience; a change ID's short form represents the logical change. shortest(n) asks for a unique prefix with at least a requested length, while short(n) truncates to a requested display length. Use full IDs in machine output and shortest or short IDs only in human output.

commit_id
commit_id.short(12)
commit_id.shortest(10)
change_id
change_id.normal_hex()
change_id.shortest(10)

Reference collections contain CommitRef values. A ref exposes its name, optional remote, presence, conflict status, normal target, added/removed targets, tracking state, ahead/behind counts, and synced state. Rendering the ref object directly is not the same as rendering its name. The following separates local names, remote names, and tracking status:

bookmarks.map(|b| b.name()).join(", ")
remote_bookmarks.map(|b| b.remote() ++ "/" ++ b.name()).join(", ")
if(bookmarks.any(|b| b.synced()), "synced", "not-synced")
if(bookmarks.any(|b| b.conflict()), "REF-CONFLICT", "")

A conflicted bookmark can have more than one target. Do not call normal_target() without guarding or checking conflict(). A remote bookmark's presence is not proof that the server is current; it is the local observation produced by fetch/import. Templates can display that distinction, but they cannot fetch.

Signatures, timestamps, and diffs

A signature has a name, email, and timestamp. The email object can expose local and domain portions. Timestamps can be rendered as relative age, UTC, local time, or a format string, and can be compared with date-pattern methods. Use UTC for logs that cross machines and relative time for interactive scanning:

author.name() ++ " <" ++ author.email() ++ ">"
author.email().domain()
author.timestamp().utc().format("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
committer.timestamp().ago()

Diff values are structured as well as formatted. A tree diff can produce a summary, Git or colour-word output, statistics, or changed entries. A diff-stat entry carries path, status, status character, bytes, added/removed lines, and display path. Prefer structured statistics in dashboards and formatted diffs only in human review output:

diff.stat().files().map(|f|
  f.status_char() ++ " " ++ f.path().display()).join("\n")
diff.stat().total_added() ++ " +" ++ diff.stat().total_removed()
diff.summary()

Diff methods may be relatively expensive, especially over a broad commit set. A daily prompt should not compute complete diffs for every visible commit. Build separate “scan”, “review”, and “forensic” templates and use the narrowest one for the task.

Conflicts, signatures, and operations

State methods such as conflict(), empty(), immutable(), hidden(), divergent(), mine(), and root() are Booleans. They are excellent for labels but should not be confused with a server's review state. A cryptographic signature is an option; inspect its status, key, and display string rather than merely printing whether an object exists.

separate(" ",
  if(conflict, "CONFLICT", ""),
  if(empty, "EMPTY", ""),
  if(immutable, "IMMUTABLE", ""),
  if(divergent, "DIVERGENT", ""),
  if(signature, "SIGNED", "UNSIGNED"))
if(signature, signature.status() ++ " " ++ signature.key(), "")

Operation templates have a different identity. An operation ID identifies a repository transformation in this clone. Its description, user, time, snapshot flag, workspace name, and parent operations answer questions that cannot be answered by a commit template:

jj op log -T '
id.short(12) ++ " " ++
if(snapshot, "snapshot ", "") ++
workspace_name ++ " " ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"

Keep the plus signs out of the actual command when copying this example; they are line-continuation markers in the printed template source only. A production template should be written as one valid expression, for example:

jj op log -T 'id.short(12) ++ " " ++ if(snapshot, "snapshot ", "") ++ workspace_name ++ " " ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'

Formatting, labels, and terminal boundaries

fill wraps lines, indent prefixes non-empty lines, padding functions align single-line values, and truncation functions control width with an optional ellipsis. Padding counts display width rather than merely source bytes where the formatter can determine it; colour labels and raw escape sequences must not be treated as visible text by a custom terminal sequence.

pad_start(12, change_id.short())
pad_end(14, author.name())
truncate_end(60, description.first_line(), "…")
indent("  ", diff.summary())
fill(72, description)

Labels are semantic styling. label("conflict", "CONFLICT") allows the colour configuration to decide presentation, while raw escape sequences bypass sanitisation and can corrupt a file or PDF. Hyperlinks use OSC 8 when colour output is enabled, but a pager, terminal, log file, or PDF may not support them. Use a plain fallback for automation:

label("change_id", change_id.short())
hyperlink(git_web_url(), commit_id.short(), commit_id.short())

Do not put raw escape sequences in JSON or TSV output. Use --color=never and --no-pager for machine consumers. A template can be syntactically correct yet unsafe for a downstream parser because a label or hyperlink introduced control bytes.

JSON and aliases

json(value) serialises a serialisable value; String.escape_json() escapes a scalar string. Use one complete JSON object per output record and test quotes, backslashes, Unicode, empty values, and newlines. Do not parse ordinary graph output as JSON-like text.

jj log --no-graph --color=never -r '@:: & mutable()' -T '
"{\"commit\":" ++ json(commit_id) ++
",\"change\":" ++ json(change_id) ++
",\"subject\":" ++ json(description.first_line()) ++
"}\n"

The printed example is JSONL: each commit emits one object and one newline. If the consuming interface expects a JSON array, the template must deliberately emit brackets and separators; JSONL is usually simpler for streams. Pin the jj release when this is an API, because serialisation of object values is a versioned language surface.

Template aliases belong under [template-aliases]. Keep them small and typed by convention:

[template-aliases]
identity = 'change_id.shortest(10) ++ " " ++ commit_id.short(10)'
state = 'separate(" ", if(conflict, "C", ""), if(empty, "E", ""), if(immutable, "I", ""))'
refs = 'separate(" ", bookmarks, remote_bookmarks, tags)'
'field(name, value)' = 'name ++ "=" ++ value ++ "\n"'

An alias name can shadow a builtin, so use a project prefix for shared configuration when necessary. A parameterised alias is not textual shell interpolation; its arguments are parsed as template expressions. Test it directly with -T before making it a default. The reference appendix lists the target-version methods; the laboratory approach explains how to combine them without losing type or output discipline.

Part XV — Exhaustive CLI reference for jj 0.45.1

The jj 0.45.1 command tree contains 47 top-level commands and 121 public command paths including subcommands. This section is the reader-facing reference: it presents the important syntax, options, cardinality, state effects, and traps. The entries are deliberately interpreted rather than presented as a raw help dump.

Top-level commands

FamilyCommandsMutation/notes
Historyabandon absorb arrange bisect commit describe diffedit duplicate edit interdiff metaedit new parallelize prev next rebase restore revert run show simplify-parents split squashMost snapshot first; rewrite effects propagate to descendants.
Inspectiondiff evolog log status root versionRead commands still snapshot unless --ignore-working-copy.
Refsbookmark tagNames and publication relationships, not local branch-centric development.
Gitgit, gerritTransport, ref import/export, colocation, and review upload.
Repository stateoperation undo redoOperation DAG recovery and concurrent-operation control.
Workspace/contentworkspace sparse file fix resolve sign unsignFilesystem views, conflict tools, fixers, signing, and file metadata.
Configuration/toolsconfig help utilConfiguration layers, help keywords, completion, schema, GC, snapshot.

Command entries and traps

Command pathPurposeKey arguments/options and trap
abandonAbandon commits.Accepts a set; abandoning @ creates a new empty working copy.
absorbDistribute changes into mutable ancestors.Review the chosen stack and fileset; content may move farther than one parent.
arrangeTUI reorder/abandon.Interactive graph surgery; inspect operation log after leaving.
bisect, bisect runAutomated bisection.Script exit status and commit range are the contract; keep tests deterministic.
bookmark and subcommandsManage names and tracking.advance create delete forget list move rename set track untrack; tracking is not auto-follow.
commitDescribe current change and create child.Snapshot occurs first; unlike Git, @ already is a commit.
config and subcommandsRead/edit layered TOML.edit gc get list path set unset; inspect scope and precedence.
describeChange description/metadata.Exactly one commit; no new child unless combined with workflow.
diff, interdiffTree or diff comparison.Commit range and fileset are independent; interdiff compares diffs.
diffeditTouch up content.External diff editor and fileset options are config-sensitive.
duplicateCopy content to new changes.New change identity; it is not a successor.
editMove @ to one commit.Exactly one; updates filesystem and may snapshot old @ first.
evologShow change evolution.Use for predecessors, successors, and divergence.
file annotate/chmod/list/search/show/track/untrackFile operations.Search pattern defaults/options changed historically; quote filesets and patterns.
fixRun configured fixers.May rewrite many changes; line-range support is release-sensitive.
gerrit uploadUpload changes/stacks.Verify 0.45.1 server/protocol options; jj change ID is not Gerrit Change-Id.
git clone/initCreate Git-backed repositories.Choose --colocate deliberately.
git colocation enable/disable/statusChange backend layout.Native Git tools may stop seeing a worktree after disable.
git fetch/import/export/pushSynchronise Git objects/refs.Fetch imports; push publishes refs. Remote names and bookmark safety matter.
git remote add/list/remove/rename/set-urlManage remotes.Qualify same-name bookmarks by remote.
git rootShow Git root.Useful for colocated scripts; jj root shows workspace root.
log, show, statusInspect graph/diff/state.Default revsets/templates are config; stable scripts specify -r, -T, and colour.
metaeditRewrite metadata only.Commit ID changes; content does not.
newCreate child/merge.Multiple parents create a merge; @ normally moves.
operation diff/integrate/log/show/restore/abandon/revertInspect/manage operation DAG.Operation IDs are local; restore affects repository state, not remote servers.
parallelizeMake commits siblings.Graph-changing rewrite; descendants may rebase.
rebaseMove selected commits.-r -s -b -o -A -B; selection and destination are separate dimensions.
resolveInvoke external merge tool.Stored conflicts may be multi-sided.
restore, revertCopy content; apply inverse.Neither is a ref reset; distinguish tree copy from inverse diff.
runRun a command across commits.Each selected change gets a private working copy; effects may be one operation.
sign/unsignManage cryptographic signatures.Signing metadata and Git server verification are separate policies.
sparse edit/list/reset/setManage present paths.Changes materialisation only; commit trees remain complete.
splitDivide a change.Interactive/fileset selection; successors and descendants are rewritten.
squashMove selected content into destination.Destination and fileset determine what remains in source.
tag delete/list/set/track/untrackManage tag names.Tags are not moving review bookmarks.
undo/redoReverse/reapply operations.Not a Git reset; inspect operation log when state is surprising.
util backend/config-schema/completion/exec/gc/install-man-pages/markdown-help/snapshotLow-level utilities.Some are machine/admin oriented; debug snapshot history is release-sensitive.
workspace add/forget/list/rename/root/update-staleMultiple working directories.@ is workspace-local; commit graph is shared.

How to read the command entries
