Each entry below is organised around semantics rather than a transcription of help output. “Snapshot” means the normal command boundary at which jj records the current filesystem in the workspace commit. “Rewrite” means new successor commits may be created and descendants may be rebased. “One commit” means a command requires a single resolved commit; a revset can still be syntactically valid and operationally invalid if it returns zero or several commits.

Short options are retained because they are useful at a terminal, but durable aliases and documentation should prefer the long option when it makes the dimension explicit. Global options apply to every entry: -R/--repository, --ignore-working-copy, --no-integrate-operation, --ignore-immutable, --at-operation/--at-op, --debug, --color, --quiet, --no-pager, repeatable --config and --config-file, and help/version options. Their interaction is explained after the command entries.

Revision arguments: positional aliases versus real options

The spelling -r does not identify a special kind of revset. It has two different command-line roles in the 0.45.1 CLI, and the command's help tells you which role applies.

For some commands, a revision is the command's primary subject and the positional argument has -r as an alias. These forms are equivalent:

jj show C
jj show -r C

jj describe C
jj describe -r C

jj edit C
jj edit -r C

jj abandon C
jj abandon -r C

In this case -r is not adding another selection dimension. It is simply an alternate spelling of the positional REVSET. The help expresses this with wording such as [aliases: -r] beside the positional argument.

Other commands have a genuine revision-selection option because their positional arguments are filesets, or because they need several independently named revision roles:

jj log -r 'mutable() & ::@' -- 'glob:src/**'
jj diff -r 'C::D' -- 'root-glob:src/**'
jj rebase -r C --onto B
jj rebase --source C --onto B
jj squash -r C
jj squash --from C --into B

These are not all interchangeable. In jj log and jj diff, -r selects the commits to display or compare while the positional arguments select paths. In jj rebase, -r/--revisions means “rebase exactly this selected set”; -s/--source includes the selected commits' descendants, and -b/--branch selects the branch-shaped set defined by the command. In jj squash, -r selects the change whose content is moved into its parent, whereas --from and --into name the source and destination independently.

The practical rule is to read the argument heading and the option description together. A positional REVSET is the command's primary subject; an option-valued REVSET occupies a named role such as displayed revisions, source, destination, or parent. Both values are parsed by the same revset language, but the command determines their cardinality, default, and effect on the graph.

Alphabetical command reference entries

These reader-facing entries are ordered by canonical command path. The order is deliberately independent of the conceptual grouping used in the teaching chapters; use the browser's find function or the printed contents to reach a command, then follow the related-command links for semantics and workflows.

jj abandon

Purpose and model. Hides the selected commits from the ordinary visible graph and reconnects their children to the abandoned commits' parents. It is a graph operation, not deletion of immutable Git objects. The default commit is @; the argument is a revset and may select several commits.

Syntax/options. jj abandon [REVSETS...]; --retain-bookmarks keeps bookmarks by moving them to parent commits, and --restore-descendants preserves children’s content rather than preserving their diff relative to the changed parents. The latter can prevent a surprising descendant rewrite when the purpose is to discard an ancestor's content.

State effects. jj snapshots first, creates an operation, and may create a new empty working-copy commit if the current @ is abandoned. Descendants normally change because their parent edge and diff context change; conflicts can be produced. Bookmarks pointing at abandoned commits are normally deleted or handled according to the command's policy unless retained. Native Git refs are not the unit of selection, but exported bookmark movement can later affect Git.

jj log -r '@:: & mutable()'
jj abandon 'change_id(abc...)'
jj op log
jj evolog -r 'change_id(abc...)'

Trap and recovery. Do not use abandon as a private equivalent of “reset branch”: it changes visible graph topology and can rewrite descendants. Inspect the operation immediately; jj undo, jj op restore, or jj evolog can recover the intended change. Immutable commits require --ignore-immutable, which should be treated as an exceptional audit event.

jj absorb

Purpose and model. Distributes the current change's file-level modifications into suitable mutable ancestors. It is an inference-driven stack operation: jj compares the source diff with ancestor changes and moves an individual diff hunk to the nearest compatible destination, rather than blindly squashing all content into the parent.

Syntax/options. jj absorb [FILESETS...]; -f/--from REVSET selects the source (default @), -t/--into REVSETS bounds candidate destinations (default mutable(), only ancestors of the source), -i/--interactive chooses parts, and --tool NAME selects the diff editor and implies interactive mode.

State effects. The source and one or more mutable ancestors can be rewritten; descendants of every changed ancestor are rebased. The source may become empty or retain changes that could not be attributed. Change IDs normally follow their logical evolutions; commit IDs change for every rewritten node. A fileset restricts candidate content, not the commit domain.

jj absorb --from @ --into '@:: & mutable()'
jj absorb --interactive -- 'glob:src/**'
jj log -r '@:: & mutable() & conflicts()'

Trap. “Earliest compatible” is a semantic choice, not a promise that every individual diff hunk goes to the immediate parent. Review the diff and evolution log. Use jj squash when the intended destination is explicit, and jj undo if attribution was wrong.

jj arrange

Purpose and model. Opens the interactive graph arrangement interface for the selected commits. It is intended for visual reordering and abandoning of a graph region; it is not a text editor for commit messages and not a replacement for understanding the resulting parent edges.

Syntax/options. jj arrange [REVSETS...]; the default selection comes from revsets.arrange if no commit is supplied, and -r is the commit alias. There are no command-specific rewrite switches in 0.45.1. Global repository, immutability, colour, and operation-view options still apply.

State effects. The TUI can create several graph transformations in one operation. Mutable commits and descendants may receive new commit IDs; bookmarks can move or become conflicted according to the resulting graph. Snapshotting occurs at the normal command boundary. Review jj op show after leaving the interface because the visual action is otherwise hard to audit.

jj arrange -r '@:: & mutable()'
jj op show
jj log -r 'visible_heads() | bookmarks()'

Trap. Use a narrow revset. A broad arrangement selection can expose immutable boundaries or make the intended graph difficult to recognise. For repeatable automation use rebase, parallelize, new --insert-after, or explicit bookmark operations.

jj bisect and jj bisect run

Purpose and model. The parent command is a namespace for commit bisection and requires a subcommand in 0.45.1. Bisection searches a commit range using a user-defined test rather than moving a Git branch pointer. Candidate checkouts are temporary working copies; the result is a graph commit selected by bisection state and test outcomes.

Syntax/options. jj bisect run --range REVSET [COMMAND] [ARGS...]. The range is required; arguments beginning with a dash should follow --. The run subcommand accepts normal global repository/view options.

State effects. A zero/non-zero test status has the meaning defined by the local bisection help and script contract. Make the predicate deterministic and independent of the developer's primary filesystem. Do not assume a candidate checkout is the current @ or that a discovered commit should automatically become a bookmark.

jj bisect run --range 'good..bad' -- ./test-regression.sh
jj log -r 'bisect(@)'

Trap. A test that mutates files, depends on network state, or returns a status for an unrelated failure invalidates the search. Record the range and command; inspect the result with jj show and jj diff before applying a fix.

jj bisect run

Runs a test command over candidate commits in the required --range REVSET. Put command arguments after -- when they begin with a dash. The command's exit status is the test result; keep it deterministic and independent of the primary workspace.

Selection and lifecycle. The range is a revset describing the known-good/known-bad corridor; it is not a bookmark movement and does not mean “all commits between two Git branches” unless the revset says so. Each candidate is materialised for the test, then the bisection state records the result. Make the script distinguish a product failure from an unavailable dependency or infrastructure failure; otherwise the search can label a candidate incorrectly.

jj bisect run --range 'good..bad' -- ./test-regression.sh

Candidate working copies are temporary and are not publication bookmarks. The result does not change the meaning of @ in the primary workspace. Inspect the discovered commit with jj show, verify its full ID and diff, then create a bookmark or new change only if that is the intended next operation. If the predicate was wrong, rerun with a corrected range rather than trying to repair the graph with restore.

jj bookmark

Purpose and model. Names a commit for local navigation or publication and manages relationships with remote bookmarks. The parent command requires a subcommand; its aliases include b. A bookmark is a ref-like name over the commit DAG, not the unit of ordinary local work.

Subcommands. 0.45.1 provides advance, create, delete, forget, list, move, rename, set, track, and untrack. Each is described below. Names usually accept glob-like string patterns; commit options accept revsets with the cardinality required by the operation.

State effects. Bookmark operations change local ref state and create operations, but do not rewrite commit content. A later Git push exports the selected local bookmark; tracking is a relationship and does not make a bookmark follow @.

jj bookmark list --all-remotes
jj bookmark create review -r @
jj bookmark set review -r @ --allow-backwards
jj bookmark track review --remote origin

Trap. Always qualify same-name remote refs in review scripts and specify the remote on publication. “Bookmark changed” and “commit changed” are different facts.

jj bookmark advance

Moves matching bookmarks forward to a target selected by -t/--to REVSET, defaulting to revsets.bookmark-advance-to. Names are patterns and can match several bookmarks. It is intended for advancing bookmarks along descendant history, not for arbitrary sideways replacement.

jj bookmark advance --to @ review
jj bookmark advance --to 'main@origin::@' 'pr/*'

It changes ref state only; selected commits are not rewritten. If the target or bookmark set is ambiguous, narrow the name/revset. Use bookmark set when an intentional backwards or sideways move is required and review its safety option.

jj bookmark create

Creates one or more local bookmarks. -r/--revision REVSET (alias --to) supplies the target and defaults to @. The target must resolve as required by the command; creating several names at one target is useful when a server policy needs aliases.

jj bookmark create github/pr-42 -r @
jj bookmark create base feature -r A

Creation does not move @, rewrite commits, or create tracking by itself. A later push may automatically establish tracking for an untracked bookmark. Avoid creating a publication name before the graph boundary is intentional.

jj bookmark delete

Deletes local bookmarks matching the supplied name patterns. It changes local ref state; it does not erase the target commits. A tracked deletion can be exported as a remote deletion by an appropriate push.

jj bookmark delete 'github/pr-*'
jj bookmark delete review

Use forget when the goal is to discard local knowledge rather than express a deletion to the remote. Check tracking and server state before deleting a publication bookmark. If descendants or another bookmark still identify the commits, deleting this name changes neither their content nor reachability through those other names.

jj bookmark forget

Forgets local bookmark and, optionally, remote-bookmark knowledge. --include-remotes also forgets corresponding remote bookmarks; a future fetch recreates still-existing remote refs. Forgetting is local bookkeeping and is not a remote deletion request.

jj bookmark forget review
jj bookmark forget --include-remotes 'old/*'

Use this after a merged or closed review when the remote state should remain untouched. If the server ref must be deleted, use bookmark delete and push the deletion. Forgetting a remote observation also removes local comparison evidence until the next fetch; it is not a privacy or server-cleanup operation.

jj bookmark list

Displays local and selected remote bookmark state. Names are optional patterns. -a/--all-remotes includes synchronized remote bookmarks; --remote REMOTE limits a remote; --tracked, --conflicted, -r/--revision REVSETS, -T/--template, and output filters provide the important inspection dimensions in 0.45.1.

jj bookmark list
jj bookmark list --all-remotes
jj bookmark list --remote origin --tracked
jj bookmark list -T 'name ++ " " ++ if(synced, "synced", "changed") ++ "\n"'

Listing does not move refs but normally snapshots unless ignored. The default view can omit synchronized remote targets; use --all-remotes when auditing all server knowledge. A conflicted bookmark needs its target sets inspected before push.

jj bookmark move

Moves existing bookmarks to a target. Names are patterns, or -f/--from REVSETS selects bookmarks whose targets are in a commit set; -t/--to REVSET supplies the destination and defaults to @. It is a ref move, not a commit rewrite.

jj bookmark move review --to @
jj bookmark move --from 'heads(mutable())' --to @
jj bookmark move 'pr/*' --to 'main@origin::@'

Moving sideways or backwards may require the command's safety confirmation. Review local/remote divergence after a move; a tracked remote bookmark is not changed until push. The --from form selects bookmarks by their current targets, so print the matched names before using a broad pattern.

jj bookmark rename

Renames one local bookmark from OLD to NEW. --overwrite-existing permits replacing an existing name where the command's safety policy allows it. Target commit and content are unchanged; remote publication may need a new push/delete sequence.

jj bookmark rename review github/pr-42
jj bookmark rename --overwrite-existing old current

Renaming is not the same as creating a second name: tracking relationships and remote names need explicit review. Use list before and after.

jj bookmark set

Creates or updates bookmarks to a target. -r/--revision REVSET (alias --to) defaults to @; -B/--allow-backwards permits backwards or sideways movement that is otherwise protected.

jj bookmark set review -r @
jj bookmark set --allow-backwards review -r 'main@origin'

Set is convenient for a publication boundary but can hide whether a name was new or already existed. For an auditable existing-name move use bookmark move. Neither operation changes the commit DAG. In jj 0.45.1, --allow-backwards is a ref-safety override for the bookmark operation: it does not make the resulting commit immutable or force a remote update.

jj bookmark track

Creates a relationship between a local bookmark and a remote bookmark. Arguments can be bookmark patterns with --remote REMOTE or exact BOOKMARK@REMOTE symbols. Tracking does not move either target and does not make the local bookmark follow @.

jj bookmark track review --remote origin
jj bookmark track main@origin
jj bookmark list --remote origin --tracked

Tracking supplies comparison and push safety information: ahead, behind, synced, and expected remote target. It is especially important when a repository has GitHub and Gerrit remotes with the same branch names. The local name and remote name need not have been created by the same command, and tracking does not cause automatic movement when a rewrite changes the commit at the local tip.

jj bookmark untrack

Removes tracking relationships from local bookmark/remote bookmark pairs. It accepts the same pattern/remote forms as track, including BOOKMARK@REMOTE.

jj bookmark untrack review --remote origin
jj bookmark untrack main@github

Untracking is local metadata; it neither deletes the remote bookmark nor moves the local one. After untracking, a push may treat the name as a new publication, so inspect the push preview and specify the remote. Re-track only after confirming that the local and remote names refer to the intended pair; same-name bookmarks on another remote are independent.

jj commit

Purpose and model. Describes the current working-copy change and creates a new empty child on top of it. In jj, the current filesystem is already associated with @; commit is a boundary in the local patch stack, not the act of transferring files into a hidden index.

Syntax/options. jj commit [FILESETS...]; a fileset commits only selected paths, -i/--interactive selects diff hunks, --tool NAME chooses the diff editor and implies interactive mode, -m/--message supplies a description, and --editor opens the editor even after a message was supplied. Global snapshot controls apply.

State effects. jj snapshots first, updates @ with selected content and metadata, then creates a new empty child working-copy commit. Unselected filesystem changes remain in the new child. The old commit's change identity is preserved by the description operation; the new child receives a new change ID. A bookmark at the old @ does not automatically follow.

jj commit -m 'API: validate quota'
jj commit --interactive -- 'glob:src/**'
jj describe -m 'API: split validation'
jj status

Trap. Do not use jj commit to save an arbitrary ancestor: use jj edit, jj describe, or jj squash according to intent. An accidental child is recoverable with jj undo.

jj config

Purpose and model. Reads and writes layered TOML configuration. The parent namespace provides edit, gc, get, list, path, set, and unset. Scope is part of the command contract: user, repository, and workspace files are different state locations.

Safety. Config can invoke editors, external tools, aliases, fixers, merge tools, and transport behaviour. Treat repository/workspace config as input, not trusted code. Inspect effective values with config list before running a command from an unfamiliar checkout.

jj config list
jj config get ui.pager
jj config set --user user.name 'A. Engineer'
jj config path --repo

Configuration changes create operations only when they affect repository state according to the command; they do not rewrite commits by themselves. The full Linux design and grouped key reference appear in Part XIII and Appendix F.

jj config edit

Opens a selected configuration file in the configured editor. Exactly one of --user, --repo, or --workspace selects the scope in 0.45.1. The editor is an external side effect; --config-file can add input but is not the same as choosing the file to edit.

jj config edit --user
jj config edit --repo
jj config edit --workspace

Use this for multi-line templates, aliases, and tool definitions where shell/TOML quoting is risky. In 0.45.1, --file PATH is available for selecting a specific file; mark that as target-release-specific in shared instructions.

jj config gc

Garbage-collects obsolete configuration files or fragments according to the target release's config storage policy. It is maintenance, not a commit operation, and should be run only after understanding which generated/config files are no longer referenced.

jj config gc

Do not confuse config GC with repository object GC. Version-control important config and take a backup before maintenance on a non-standard layout.

jj config get

Reads one named configuration value. jj config get NAME reports the effective value after layers are applied; use scope options from local help when you need a particular layer. It is useful in shell guards because it tests the configuration jj itself will use.

jj config get revsets.log
jj config get git.push
jj config get gerrit.default-remote

Absent values and typed TOML values are different from empty strings. Use config list or config path to explain surprising results.

jj config list

Lists effective configuration, optionally restricted to a name/prefix. It is the best first diagnostic for precedence, aliases, templates, remotes, and tool definitions.

jj config list
jj config list ui
jj config list revset-aliases

Inspect before executing repo-provided aliases or external tools. Values can come from several files; use path/edit commands to locate and change the intended layer.

jj config path

Prints the path of a selected config scope. Exactly one scope flag is required in the 0.45.1 surface: --user, --repo, or --workspace.

jj config path --user
jj config path --repo
jj config path --workspace

Use it in diagnostics and backup scripts rather than assuming an XDG path. Repository and workspace config are intentionally separated from the repository in newer layouts to reduce accidental execution of untrusted checked-in configuration.

jj config set

Sets one TOML value in a selected scope. Syntax is jj config set --user|--repo|--workspace NAME VALUE. The value is a TOML expression; strings, arrays, booleans, integers, and multi-line strings therefore need both TOML and shell quoting.

jj config set --user ui.pager 'less -FRX'
jj config set --repo revsets.log '(@:: & mutable()) | bookmarks()'
jj config set --workspace ui.default-command '["log", "-r", "@:: & mutable()"]'

Use config edit for complex values. In 0.45.1, --file PATH can target a specific config file. Do not assume a string without quotes has the desired TOML type.

jj config unset

Removes a named value from a selected user/repository/workspace layer. It exposes lower-precedence values again; it does not necessarily mean the effective value becomes absent.

jj config unset --user ui.pager
jj config unset --repo revsets.log

Check config get before and after. In 0.45.1, --file PATH can target a specific config file; mark scripts using it as version-specific.

jj converge 0.45.1

Purpose and model. Groups visible commits by change ID in a selected search space and reconciles the multiple visible revisions of one logical change into one replacement revision. Divergence usually means that the same change was rewritten independently in two operation histories, so jj can see, for example, X1 and X2 with the same change ID but different commit IDs. Convergence is therefore not a lateral squash: it does not move the diff owned by one independent change into another change. It resolves competing evolutions of the same change, normally preserving that change's identity while choosing or combining their content, descriptions, parents, and other metadata.

Syntax/options. Use jj converge -r REVSET; the default search space is controlled by the jj 0.45.1 revset configuration. --no-interactive suppresses prompts and asks the heuristic convergence to proceed without interactive decisions. Check the target local help for the complete option surface.

State effects. The selected divergent revisions are replaced by one new revision for that change; if other visible revisions for the same change lie outside the revset, those remain divergent. The solution may have file conflicts even when the inputs were conflict-free. Descendants of every replaced revision are rebased onto the solution, and local bookmarks pointing at those revisions are moved to it. This is not a remote merge and does not merge Gerrit Change-Ids or GitHub pull requests. Review jj op show -p, jj evolog, the resulting diff, and conflicts(); use jj undo if the selected convergence was not intended.

jj converge -r 'divergent()'
jj converge --no-interactive -r 'mutable()'
jj op show
jj evolog
before:                 after:
P--X1--D1               P--X*--D1'
 \-X2--D2                    \-D2'

X1 and X2 share a change ID but are different visible revisions.
X* is the replacement; its parent shape and content depend on the
heuristic or interactive choices. It is not a squash from X2 into X1.

Version note. This command is part of the jj 0.45.1 target surface. Keep the search revset explicit in automation and inspect the resulting operation and evolution.

jj describe

Purpose and model. Rewrites the description and selected metadata of one or more commits, defaulting to @. It preserves logical change identity unless metadata is explicitly changed by another command; the commit ID changes because the commit object changes.

Syntax/options. jj describe [REVSETS...]; -m/--message avoids the editor, --stdin reads the description, and --editor forces editing after either. Multiple commits receive the same supplied description. The -r alias selects the commit set.

State effects. This is a metadata rewrite, but descendants can still be rewritten because their parent commit IDs change. The filesystem normally remains the same tree. Bookmarks follow successor graph locations; Git export sees a new Git commit when the changed commit is exported.

jj describe -m 'API: introduce quota limits'
jj describe --stdin -r 'mutable()'
jj log -r '@:: & mutable()' -T 'change_id ++ " " ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'

Trap. Supplying one message to a set is intentional but often wrong for a stack. Use one commit or a per-commit workflow. Use jj metaedit for author/timestamp/signature metadata.

jj diff

Purpose and model. Compares trees and renders a diff. Commit selection and path selection are independent: -r, --from/--to, and positional filesets describe separate domains.

Syntax/options. jj diff [FILESETS...]; -r/--revisions REVSETS shows the total change across a set, -f/--from REVSET and -t/--to REVSET compare endpoints, and no selector defaults to @. Important presentation options include --summary, --stat, --types, --name-only, --git, --color-words, -T/--template, context controls, and external diff controls.

Semantics. A multi-commit set must be connected: a gap such as A|C in a linear chain is not a diff range. A merge commit compares its tree with the automatic merge of its parents. A range expression such as B::D is not the same as selecting two unrelated trees.

jj diff -r @
jj diff --from 'main@origin' --to @ -- 'glob:src/**'
jj diff -r 'B::D' --stat
jj diff -r @ --name-only

Trap. A diff is not proof that a commit is single-parent; merges and conflicts have special tree semantics. For scripts prefer --name-only or controlled templates with colour disabled. Use jj interdiff for successive diff versions.

jj diffedit

Purpose and model. Touches up the content delta of an existing commit through a configured diff editor. It changes the diff while preserving the selected change's logical identity; unlike restore, it is expressed as editing a diff rather than copying an entire tree.

Syntax/options. jj diffedit [FILESETS...]; -r/--revision REVSET edits one commit (default @), --from/--to choose comparison endpoints, --tool NAME chooses the diff editor, and --restore-descendants controls descendant content. Positional filesets leave unmatched paths unchanged.

State effects. The target and descendants can receive successor commit IDs. The filesystem is updated to the resulting working-copy tree when the target is current; conflicts may be stored if the edited diff no longer applies cleanly.

jj diffedit -r A -- 'glob:src/**'
jj diffedit --tool meld -r @
jj log -r '::@ & conflicts()'

Trap. --from/--to here define the diff shown to the editor, not rebase source/destination. Use jj describe for metadata and jj squash for selected-content movement.

jj duplicate

Purpose and model. Creates a new change whose content is equivalent to a selected commit, placed at chosen parents. It is a copy, not a successor: the new change has a new change ID even if its tree and description match.

Syntax/options. jj duplicate [REVSETS...]; source defaults to @ and accepts -r. Use repeated -o/--onto REVSETS (alias -d/--destination), -A/--insert-after, or -B/--insert-before. Repeated destinations can create a merge.

State effects. The original remains. The duplicate and descendants at the insertion site can be rewritten; move publication bookmarks explicitly. A workspace generally stays at the resulting current location according to normal movement policy.

jj duplicate -r A -o 'main@origin'
jj duplicate -r A -o X -o Y
jj log -r 'A | descendants(A) | mutable()'

Trap. Continue an existing logical change with jj rebase or jj edit; publish an inverse with jj revert. Use duplicate when starting a new evolution is intentional.

jj edit

Purpose and model. Moves the current workspace's working-copy commit to exactly one existing commit. It is how an advanced user resumes or amends an earlier change; it does not create a bookmark or move another workspace's @.

Syntax/options. jj edit REVSET or -r REVSET; exactly one commit is required. --ignore-working-copy is usually inappropriate because edit is intended to update the filesystem. --at-op is for historical inspection, not continuation.

State effects. jj snapshots the old workspace first, then checks out the selected tree as the new @. The old working-copy commit remains unless abandoned. Filesystem edits made while another change was current become part of the pre-move snapshot.

jj edit 'change_id(abc...)'
jj edit 'bookmarks(exact:"review")'
jj status
jj new

Trap. “Edit A” is not Git checkout of a branch: A remains mutable and unnamed. Use jj new A to leave A unchanged and create a fresh child.

jj evolog

Purpose and model. Shows the evolution of a logical change: successive commit versions and their predecessor relationships. It answers what happened to one change, not what every repository operation did.

Syntax/options. jj evolog [OPTIONS]; -r/--revisions REVSETS follows changes (default @), -n/--limit bounds entries, --reversed reverses order, -G/--no-graph flattens output, -T/--template renders an evolution entry, and -p/--patch shows an inter-diff.

State effects. Observational, but normal snapshot rules apply unless disabled. It does not restore a commit or move a bookmark. Evolution entries link to operations, allowing a rewrite to be correlated with jj op log.

jj evolog -r 'change_id(abc...)'
jj evolog -p -r @
jj evolog --reversed -n 10

Trap. Evolution is not a ref reflog and does not record every unrelated abandoned change. Use operation history for repository-wide recovery.

jj file

Provides file-oriented inspection and metadata commands: annotate, chmod, list, search, show, track, and untrack. These operate on filesets and often a single commit; they are not Git's index commands.

A fileset selects repository paths, while a commit option selects the tree/commit. File tracking changes whether ignored/large paths participate in snapshotting; it does not create a commit by itself until a snapshot records the filesystem.

jj file annotate

Shows line attribution for one path. Syntax is jj file annotate PATH; -r/--revision REVSET selects the starting commit and -T/--template renders AnnotationLine values, including commit, content, line numbers, original line numbers, and diff-hunk boundaries.

jj file annotate src/quota.rs
jj file annotate -r main@origin -T 'line_number() ++ " " ++ commit().change_id() ++ " " ++ content()'

It is observational and can snapshot. The path is a single path argument, not a general fileset. Attribution follows jj's graph/evolution data and may differ from Git blame after rewrites.

jj file chmod

Changes executable metadata for filesets in a selected commit. Syntax is jj file chmod MODE FILESETS...; mode n/normal clears executable and x/executable sets it, while -r/--revision REVSET defaults to @.

jj file chmod x scripts/release.sh
jj file chmod n --revision A -- 'glob:bin/**'

This rewrites the target's tree metadata and can rebase descendants. It is not a filesystem chmod of every checkout; inspect the resulting tree and working copy. Use template TreeEntry.executable() to verify.

jj file list

Lists paths in the selected tree. Positional filesets filter output, -r/--revision REVSET selects the tree (default @), and -T/--template renders tree-entry metadata in jj 0.45.1.

jj file list --revision @
jj file list -r main@origin -- 'glob:src/**'
jj file list -- 'root-glob:docs/**/*.md'

Use it to validate a fileset before passing that fileset to restore, split, squash, or fix. It is observational but may snapshot.

jj file search

Searches file contents in a selected commit. Syntax requires --pattern PATTERN; -r/--revision REVSET defaults to @, positional filesets restrict file prefixes, and --name-only prints paths rather than matching lines. The pattern defaults to regex when no string-pattern kind is supplied.

jj file search --pattern 'quota' -- 'glob:src/**'
jj file search --pattern 'glob:*TODO*' --name-only
jj file search -r main@origin --pattern 'regex:^use ' -- 'glob:*.rs'

A glob pattern applies to the whole line, so glob:*foo* is different from glob:foo. This command searches a tree; it does not search the working filesystem independently.

jj file show

Prints file contents from a selected tree. Filesets are required; -r/--revision REVSET defaults to @, and -T/--template renders TreeEntry metadata.

jj file show -r main@origin -- src/quota.rs
jj file show -- 'glob:docs/**/*.md'

It is read-only repository inspection but normal snapshot policy still applies. A conflicted entry is not ordinary file content; inspect conflict metadata and resolve or select a side explicitly.

jj file track

Marks filesets for tracking even when ignored or too large only when requested. --include-ignored overrides ignore and maximum-file-size restrictions.

jj file track --include-ignored generated/schema.json
jj file track -- 'glob:vendor/**'

Tracking affects snapshot eligibility and can change a later working-copy commit; it does not itself publish or commit. Use sparingly because large/ignored content has performance and policy implications.

jj file untrack

Stops tracking selected paths. It affects future snapshots and working-copy materialisation, not historical trees already committed.

jj file untrack 'glob:generated/**'
jj status

Check status and sparse configuration afterward. Do not confuse untracking with deleting a file from a commit; use restore or filesystem deletion for content changes.

jj fix

Purpose and model. Runs configured fixer programs against files in selected commits. It is a history rewrite operation whose input is a commit domain and whose file scope is a fileset/configured fixer policy.

Syntax/options. jj fix [FILESETS...]; -s/--source REVSETS selects commits and descendants, defaulting to revsets.fix or reachable(@, mutable()). --include-unchanged-files fixes files even when not changed in the target; -a/--all-lines asks for all lines rather than modified lines when the fixer supports ranges.

State effects. Fixers can rewrite many commits and trigger descendant rebasing/conflicts. A failing fixer may leave a useful operation to inspect, but do not assume partial output is a valid stack. Fix configuration supplies commands, environment, file patterns, and range protocol; the working-copy commit is not special except as a selected commit.

jj fix -s '@:: & mutable()' -- 'glob:src/**'
jj fix --all-lines -s 'mutable()'
jj log -r 'mutable() & conflicts()'

Trap. Run first on a small revset and inspect the diff. A formatter that does not understand modified-line ranges can rewrite entire files. For reproducible automation, pin the fixer executable/version and use run --ignore-changes for checks that should not rewrite history.

jj gerrit and jj gerrit upload

Purpose and model. Provides Gerrit-aware upload on top of jj's mutable change graph. It is not a replacement for Gerrit's server identity: jj change IDs identify local evolution, while Gerrit uses a message Change-Id: I... footer or server/plugin policy to associate patch sets.

Syntax/options. The parent requires upload. In 0.45.1, jj gerrit upload accepts -r/--revision REVSET, -b/--remote-branch BRANCH, --remote REMOTE, -n/--dry-run, reviewer/CC/label/topic/hashtag/message options, edit/WIP/ready/private/remove-private, comment publication, notification, merged, validation, attention-set, deadline, custom and repeated -o/--option push options. Run local help for the exact spelling of server options.

State effects. Upload exports commits and review metadata; it can update remote-tracking state but does not make Gerrit a local bookmark manager. Rewriting an earlier jj change produces new commit IDs while a preserved Gerrit footer associates the new commit with its existing review. Descendants are automatically rebased locally before re-upload.

jj gerrit upload --dry-run --remote gerrit --remote-branch main
jj gerrit upload --revision 'roots(main@origin..@)' --remote gerrit --remote-branch main
git push gerrit 'HEAD:refs/for/main%topic=quota'

Boundary. Local jj transport and footer handling are testable with fixtures; Gerrit server review, patch-set, topic, permission, and submit behaviour is server-dependent. Never claim that a jj change ID is a Gerrit Change-Id.

jj gerrit upload

Uploads the selected commit stack to a Gerrit remote and branch. The principal selectors are -r/--revision REVSET, -b/--remote-branch BRANCH, --remote REMOTE, and -n/--dry-run. Reviewer, CC, label, topic, hashtag, WIP/ready/private, notification, validation, attention-set, deadline, custom, and repeated --option flags alter server-facing review metadata.

Cardinality and publication contract. The revision revset may describe a stack, but the upload must be bounded to the commits intended for one Gerrit target. Before uploading, render the exact set and its parents, check conflicts(), and inspect each commit's trailers. An existing Change-Id requests an update to that Gerrit review; a missing one is generated from the jj change ID for the uploaded object in 0.45.1. --dry-run validates local selection and command construction; it cannot prove server permissions, review association, or submit policy.

Rewrite and ref effects. Upload does not create or move a local bookmark unless the selected workflow does so separately. A rewritten ancestor gives descendants new commit IDs. Re-uploading an existing footer requests a new patch set; a missing footer causes jj to add a derived footer only to the uploaded commit, so the uploaded commit ID can differ from the local one and later fetch can expose divergence. Configure templates.commit_trailers when the footer should be present locally before upload. A rejected push leaves the local jj graph intact, so inspect the remote state before choosing a force or replacement action.

jj gerrit upload --dry-run --remote gerrit --remote-branch main --revision 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main --revision 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'

Local jj change IDs do not equal Gerrit Change-Id footers, although jj 0.45.1 can derive a missing upload footer from the local jj change ID. Server acceptance, patch-set association, and permissions remain Gerrit-dependent.

jj git

Purpose and model. Operates the Git backend, remotes, Git-compatible refs, and colocation. The parent is a namespace for clone, colocation, export, fetch, import, init, push, remote, and root.

jj metadata and the Git object database are related but not identical. A commit can have a jj change ID and operation history that Git does not know. A bookmark can be exported as a Git ref; an operation ID and workspace pointer cannot.

jj git root
jj git remote list
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj git import
jj git export

Native Git commands are useful in a colocated checkout, but after Git-side ref changes explicitly import them and avoid two writers changing the worktree concurrently. The detailed backend model appears in Part VII.

jj git clone

Clones a Git repository into a jj repository. Syntax is jj git clone SOURCE [DESTINATION]. In 0.45.1 the result is colocated by default unless git.colocate=false; --no-colocate selects the hidden backing layout and --colocate makes the default an explicit script precondition. Important options include --remote REMOTE_NAME, fetch branch/tag filters, and checkout/workspace options in the installed help.

jj git clone --colocate ssh://git@example.test/project.git project
jj git clone --remote upstream https://example.test/project.git project

A local source path is resolved to an absolute path. Colocation makes the directory usable by native Git and jj; non-colocation keeps jj metadata separate. The clone's operation DAG is new and independent of the source clone.

jj git colocation

Controls whether jj and Git share the repository/worktree layout. Subcommands are enable, disable, and status. Colocation is a backend layout property, not a branch or workspace mode.

jj git colocation status
jj git colocation enable
jj git colocation disable

Enable for Git-native tooling; disable only after checking scripts, Git roots, hooks, and worktree state. Existing Git objects/refs and jj metadata are not interchangeable merely because they reside nearby.

jj git colocation disable

Disables colocation. Git-native tools may no longer see the expected top-level Git repository, and scripts using git -C need revisiting. Do this only with a backup and an explicit transport plan.

jj git colocation disable
jj root
jj git root

jj git colocation enable

Enables Git colocation for a compatible repository. Native Git commands can then use the same worktree, but an export/import boundary still exists.

jj git colocation enable
jj git colocation status

jj git colocation status

Reports whether the current repository is colocated. It is a useful preflight for git, gh, hooks, and CI scripts.

jj git colocation status

jj git export

Exports jj bookmarks/tags and compatible commit information to Git refs. It is useful after local ref changes when a native Git consumer or hosting tool needs the Git view updated.

jj bookmark create review -r @
jj git export
git -C "$(jj root)" show-ref

Export does not publish to a remote; git push or jj git push is the network operation. Operation history, change IDs, conflict structure, and workspace pointers are not made into ordinary Git concepts.

jj git fetch

Fetches Git objects and remote refs, then imports them as remote bookmarks/tags. --remote REMOTE selects a named remote; -b/--branch repeats branch patterns, -t/--tag repeats tag patterns, and the command has options for remotes, pruning, depth, and parallelism according to local help.

jj git fetch --remote origin
jj git fetch --remote upstream --branch 'main'
jj git fetch --remote origin --tag 'v*'

Fetch does not rebase your mutable stack automatically. It moves remote bookmarks; rebase explicitly onto the imported commit. Branch filters use the fetch command's documented pattern rules, which are not necessarily identical to revset string patterns.

jj git import

Imports Git-side ref changes into jj's view without fetching from a network remote. It is the explicit bridge after native Git creates, moves, or deletes refs in a colocated repository.

git -C "$(jj root)" branch temp
jj git import
jj bookmark list --all-remotes

Import can alter remote bookmark/tag state and create an operation, but it does not turn a Git branch into a local jj working-copy commit or move @. Inspect the imported ref and rebase/publish deliberately.

jj git init

Initialises a Git-backed jj repository in the destination, defaulting to the current directory. In 0.45.1, --colocate creates/uses a top-level .git and is the default unless git.colocate=false; --no-colocate explicitly puts the backing Git repository under the jj metadata layout. --git-repo PATH selects an existing backing Git repository and is mutually exclusive with --colocate. There is one important same-path rule: if PATH is the same working directory as the jj destination, so that both .jj and .git are in that directory, the result is a colocated workspace and both native Git and jj commands work there. If PATH names a different directory, the jj destination is non-colocated and native Git commands must be run against the separate backing repository. jj git root reports the underlying Git directory, commonly the .git directory; it is not necessarily the workspace root. The destination is created if necessary.

jj git init --colocate
jj git init project                 # colocated in 0.45.1 by default
jj git init --no-colocate hidden-project
mkdir -p same-path backing
git -C same-path init
jj git init --git-repo "$PWD/same-path" "$PWD/same-path"  # same-path, colocated
git -C backing init
jj git init --git-repo "$PWD/backing" "$PWD/project"      # different path, non-colocated
git --git-dir="$PWD/backing/.git" show-ref

Choose colocation when GitHub/Gerrit tools and Git transport must share a worktree, but establish a single-writer rule for filesystem operations. Check jj root and jj git root after initialisation.

jj git push

Purpose and model. Publishes Git refs selected from local bookmarks/tags. It is the boundary where unnamed local work must acquire a publication name unless a release-specific change push mode is used.

Syntax/options. --remote REMOTE selects a named remote; -b/--bookmark PATTERN repeats bookmark patterns, -t/--tag PATTERN repeats tags, --all pushes all bookmarks/tags including new ones, --tracked pushes tracked refs, and --deleted pushes deletions. -r/--revision REVSETS selects bookmarks/tags pointing to revisions, --named NAME=REVISION creates or updates a named bookmark for publication, and -c/--change REVSETS creates a bookmark whose default name is based on the change ID. --allow-empty-description, --allow-private, and --allow-conflicts relax eligibility checks; --dry-run previews the operation. These are the jj 0.45.1 options; new-bookmark publication uses --named or --change, not an additional permission flag.

Safety. An untracked selected bookmark can become tracked automatically. A new bookmark is requested with --named or --change, not with a force or “allow new” switch. A backwards update is subject to jj's lease-like safety check: the remote must still match the state jj last fetched before the update is accepted. Review local and remote targets, specify the remote, and use jj 0.45.1's --dry-run before publishing.

jj git push --remote origin --bookmark review
jj git push --remote github --bookmark 'gh/*' --dry-run
jj git push --remote gerrit --named review=@
jj git push --remote origin --change 'change_id(abc...)' --dry-run

State effects. Push changes the remote server, not the commit DAG. It can update local remote-tracking state and operations. A later fetch observes server-side merge/rewrite. --no-integrate-operation only changes operation integration; it does not prevent the network push.

jj git remote

Manages named Git remotes. Subcommands are add, list, remove, rename, and set-url. Remote names qualify remote bookmarks and select push/fetch destinations; they do not identify a workspace.

jj git remote add github git@github.com:me/project.git
jj git remote add gerrit ssh://gerrit.example/project
jj git remote list
jj git remote set-url github git@github.com:me/project.git
jj git remote rename origin upstream

Inspect full URLs before pushing. A two-remote repository should use explicit --remote in scripts and qualify main@github versus main@gerrit in revsets.

jj git remote add

Adds a named remote with a URL. It changes Git remote configuration; no commits are fetched until jj git fetch.

jj git remote add origin ssh://git@example.test/project
jj git git remote add github git@github.com:me/project.git

The second line is intentionally wrong: the command is jj git remote add, not jj git git remote add. Shell aliases should not obscure the remote name.

jj git remote list

Lists configured remote names and URLs. It is read-only repository configuration inspection and is the first command to run before a dual-host push.

jj git remote list

jj git remote remove

Removes a configured remote. Existing imported remote bookmarks can remain as local knowledge until forgotten or pruned according to the command's policy. Removing a remote does not delete the server repository.

jj git remote remove old-origin
jj bookmark forget --include-remotes 'main@old-origin'

jj git remote rename

Renames a configured remote and therefore changes the qualifier of its remote bookmarks. Review tracking relationships and scripts after renaming.

jj git remote rename origin github
jj log -r 'main@github'

jj git remote set-url

Changes the URL for an existing remote. It does not fetch or push and does not rewrite commits. Use it when moving from HTTPS to SSH or changing a fork URL, then verify with remote list.

jj git remote set-url origin git@github.com:me/project.git
jj git remote list

jj git root

Prints the Git repository root used by the backend. It can differ in meaning from jj root, which prints the current workspace root. Use the result instead of assuming the current directory is a Git root.

git -C "$(jj git root)" show-ref
GIT_DIR="$(jj git root)/.git" git status

In a non-colocated repository, native Git use may be invalid or point at another repository. In scripts, first inspect colocation status.

jj help

Prints help for the root or a command path. jj help --help documents the help command itself; jj help command and jj help command subcommand select paths. Keyword search exposes language and conceptual material in the installed documentation.

jj help rebase
jj help bookmark track
jj help -k revsets
jj help -k templates

Help is the normative installed-CLI authority for syntax/defaults. It may link to a current documentation site; use the local version for behaviour. In a release audit capture root help recursively rather than relying on memory.

jj interdiff

Compares the diff changes between two commit versions. Use --from REVSET and --to REVSET as required by the 0.45.1 syntax, plus positional filesets and diff-formatting options. It is the right comparison for successive versions of one logical change whose parent context changed.

jj interdiff --from A --to B
jj interdiff --from A --to B --stat -- 'glob:src/**'

It does not rewrite commits or move refs, but normal snapshot policy still applies. Use diff for endpoint tree comparison and evolog -p when the commits are known successors of one change.

jj log

Purpose and model. Displays a graph projection of a commit set. It does not show “branches” by default; it shows the selected visible commits, their topology, and a template rendering for each. The default revset and template are configuration, so a stable script supplies both.

Syntax/options. jj log [FILESETS...]; -r/--revision REVSETS selects commits, -n/--limit N limits after filtering and topological ordering, --reversed shows older first, -G/--no-graph produces a flat list, -T/--template renders commits, -p/--patch includes patches, and --count prints a count. A fileset restricts commits that modify those paths.

jj log -r '@:: & mutable()'
jj log -r 'mutable() & conflicts()' -p
jj log -G --color=never -T 'commit_id ++ "\n"'
jj log -n 20 --reversed -r 'main@origin..@'

State effects. Normal log snapshots the working copy first; use --ignore-working-copy for a prompt or monitoring read. It never moves bookmarks or rewrites commits. The graph can contain hidden/divergent information only when the selected revset includes it.

Trap. Do not parse graph glyphs or assume the default revset is a complete repository view. For automation use explicit revsets, templates, colour, and pager options. A fileset is applied to changed-path history, not merely to the displayed tree.

jj metaedit

Purpose and model. Rewrites commit metadata without changing file content. It is the precise tool for author, timestamp, description, change ID, and related metadata edits.

Syntax/options. The commit set defaults to @. Important 0.45.1 options include --update-change-id, -m/--message, --update-author-timestamp, --update-author, --author, --author-timestamp, and committer controls shown by local help. The -r alias selects commits.

State effects. The tree is unchanged, but metadata changes the commit ID. Descendants may be rewritten because their parent ID changes; bookmarks follow successors. --update-change-id intentionally breaks local evolution continuity and should not be used merely because a commit ID changed.

jj metaedit --author 'A. Engineer <a@example.test>' -r @
jj metaedit --update-author-timestamp
jj metaedit --update-change-id -r 'mutable()'

Trap. Author/committer identity, jj change ID, and Gerrit Change-Id are separate. Use jj describe for editor-driven descriptions and jj sign for cryptographic signing.

jj new

Purpose and model. Creates an empty working-copy change with supplied parents. One parent creates a child; multiple parents create a merge. It is the ordinary boundary between patch-stack changes.

Syntax/options. jj new [REVSETS...] defaults to @; -m/--message describes it, --no-edit leaves the workspace where it is, -A/--insert-after inserts after selected commits and rebases their children, and -B/--insert-before inserts before selected commits. -o/--onto is an alias for parent selection in 0.45.1.

State effects. The old @ becomes a parent and remains intact. Insert modes are graph surgery and can rewrite descendants. Bookmarks at the old commit do not automatically move to the new child.

jj new main@origin -m 'API: introduce quota'
jj new @- @--
jj new --no-edit A
jj new --insert-after A

Trap. Multiple commits are explicit merge parents, not alternatives. Use jj edit when continuing an existing change.

jj next

Purpose and model. Moves from the current working-copy commit toward a child, optionally jumping to the next conflicted descendant. It can create a new child or edit the target directly according to movement policy.

Syntax/options. jj next [OFFSET] defaults to one step. -e/--edit edits the target; -n/--no-edit creates a new working-copy commit on the target; --conflict searches for the next conflicted descendant. These override ui.movement.edit.

State effects. Normal snapshotting records current edits before movement. Forks may not have a unique next child. No bookmark is moved merely by navigation.

jj next
jj next --edit
jj next --conflict
jj next 2 --no-edit

Trap. “Next” is graph navigation, not next commit on a branch. Use an explicit revset with jj edit or jj new when precision matters.

jj operation / jj op

Purpose and model. Manages the operation DAG, the local history of repository views. Subcommands are abandon, diff, integrate, log, restore, revert, and show. Operation IDs identify repository transformations in this clone; they are not commit IDs, change IDs, or remote refs, and they do not transfer through Git.

Cardinality and recovery contract. Operation selectors identify one operation unless a command explicitly accepts endpoints or a set. Inspect the operation graph before choosing a recovery action: undo moves to the previous integrated view, op restore creates a new view copied from a selected operation, and op revert constructs an operation-level inverse. None of them retracts a push, editor side effect, or test result outside the repository.

jj op log
jj op show
jj op diff --from OP1 --to OP2
jj undo

Use operation commands when repository state surprises you, especially after a rewrite, concurrent operation, or ref movement. The command family is explained in the recovery chapter and laboratory.

jj operation abandon alias: jj op abandon

Abandons an operation from the operation DAG. It is a history-maintenance action on local operation records, not the same as abandoning a commit. Do not use it until recovery is complete and retention policy is understood.

jj op abandon OP
jj op log

Once operation evidence is abandoned, recovery may become harder. Keep an external record of important operation IDs before pruning.

jj operation diff alias: jj op diff

Compares repository state between operations. --operation OP compares an operation with its parent; -f/--from and -t/--to compare endpoints; -G/--no-graph flattens changes and -p/--patch includes rebased diff detail. The endpoints are operation IDs, not commit revsets: use jj diff when the question is about two trees in the current repository view.

jj op diff --operation OP
jj op diff --from OP1 --to OP2 --patch

It is especially useful when later operations have changed commit IDs: compare repository views, not only remembered IDs. It is observational and does not restore either state.

jj operation integrate alias: jj op integrate

Integrates an operation created with --no-integrate-operation into the current operation head. It is the explicit convergence point for concurrent/unintegrated local operations; it does not mean converge the commit revisions of one change, which is the separate jj converge command.

jj status --no-integrate-operation
# record the printed operation ID
jj op integrate OP

Integration can expose conflicts or divergent operation history. It does not suppress or reverse external side effects performed by the original command.

jj operation log alias: jj op log

Displays operation history as a graph. Options include operation selection, -n/--limit, --reversed, -G/--no-graph, -T/--template, and diff/detail output according to local help. The rendered operation graph is not a reflog of one bookmark: it records repository-wide views, including rewrites, imported refs, and workspace metadata.

jj op log
jj op log -n 20
jj op log -T 'id.short(12) ++ " " ++ description ++ "\n"'

Operation log is the first recovery command. Record the current head before attempting repair; a later operation can make an earlier state harder to recognise but does not necessarily remove it. Use --at-operation to inspect a historical repository view without changing the live one, then use op show or op diff before restoring it.

jj operation restore alias: jj op restore

Restores repository state to an operation. The operation must be selected explicitly; inspect it with jj --at-op OP log first.

--what can repeat and, in the experimental 0.45.1 surface, selects repo and/or remote-tracking. Omitting remote-tracking state can preserve the ability to push after undo; restoring it can make the local view match the old state exactly.

jj --at-op OP log -r 'all()'
jj op restore OP
jj op restore --what repo OP

Restore creates a new operation representing the restoration; it does not move a server and does not make the filesystem historical unless the workspace is updated. Treat it as a deliberate state change, then inspect the new operation.

jj operation revert alias: jj op revert

Creates a repository operation that reverses the effect of a selected operation while retaining later state as appropriate. It is not commit jj revert: the former operates on repository metadata/graph state, the latter creates an inverse commit.

jj op revert OP

Use operation diff first. Operation revert is a recovery tool for an operation-level mistake, not a way to undo a public remote push.

jj operation show alias: jj op show

Shows one operation's metadata and repository changes. Select an operation ID from jj op log; options include diff and graph formatting.

jj op show OP
jj op show -p OP

Use it to answer what a rewrite actually changed. It does not change state. For the state itself, use jj --at-op OP log; for a controlled restore, use jj op restore OP.

jj parallelize

Purpose and model. Makes selected commits siblings by removing the edge that serialises them. It is useful when changes were accidentally stacked but should be independent.

Syntax/options. jj parallelize [REVSETS...]; -r is the commit alias and there are no additional 0.45.1 command-specific options.

State effects. New parent edges cause selected commits and descendants to receive successors. A child that depended on removed content may conflict or change diff. Bookmarks follow affected successors; remote publication does not happen automatically.

jj parallelize -r 'B|C'
jj log -r '::@'
jj log -r 'conflicts()'

Trap. Parallelisation is not reverting a dependency's files. Check every descendant; use jj rebase when an explicit destination describes the intention better.

jj prev

Purpose and model. Moves backward from the current working-copy commit. It can create a new child on the selected parent or edit the parent directly, mirroring next.

Syntax/options. jj prev [OFFSET] defaults to one parent. -e/--edit edits the parent; -n/--no-edit creates a new working-copy change; --conflict jumps to the previous conflicted ancestor.

State effects. Current edits are snapshotted first. A merge may have no unique parent, and an offset is graph navigation rather than a first-parent promise. Existing commits are not rewritten unless subsequently edited.

jj prev
jj prev --edit
jj prev --conflict
jj prev 2 --no-edit

Trap. Use jj edit for a non-linear review target. A new child protects the parent; edit mode makes later edits part of it.

jj rebase

Purpose and model. Rewrites parent edges for a selected set while preserving each selected commit's diff as far as possible. Source selection and destination placement are independent dimensions.

Syntax. jj rebase <destination option> [source option]. Source options are -r/--revisions REVSETS for explicit commits, -s/--source REVSET for a commit and descendants, and -b/--branch REVSET for the branch relative to the destination (default @). Exactly one destination mode is required: -o/--onto (aliases -d/--destination), -A/--insert-after (alias --after), or -B/--insert-before (alias --before).

ModeTransformationTypical intent
-r X -o YRewrite exactly X onto Y.Surgical move; useful with holes in a stack.
-s X -o YX and descendants onto Y.Move a whole stack.
-b X -o YBranch of X relative to Y onto Y.Update a current line without naming every node.
-A YInsert selected changes after Y and rebase Y's descendants.Insert between Y and its children.
-B YInsert before Y and rebase Y and descendants.Place a change before a known commit.
repeat -oMultiple destination parents.Create an intentional merge.

State effects. Rebased commits get successor commit IDs; change IDs normally persist. Descendants automatically rebase. Conflicts are stored in the resulting commits. Bookmarks follow rewritten graph targets, but remote publication requires an explicit push.

jj rebase -b 'roots(main@origin..@)' -o main@origin
jj rebase -r 'A|C' -o B
jj rebase -s A -A X
jj rebase -r D -o K -o M

Trap. Several source roots can produce several direct children, and a destination must satisfy its own cardinality. Inspect log, evolution, and operation state after a non-trivial rebase. There is no Git-style continuation session: resolve the stored conflict or perform another rewrite.

jj redo

Reapplies the most recently undone operation when redo state is available. It is repository-operation recovery, not replay of a Git reflog entry.

jj undo
jj redo

Any unrelated mutating operation can affect the redo chain. Inspect operation log before assuming redo is available or safe.

jj resolve

Purpose and model. Resolves stored file conflicts with a merge tool. It changes the conflict value in a selected commit; it is not a Git index continuation phase.

Syntax/options. jj resolve [FILESETS...]; -r/--revision REVSET defaults to @, -l/--list lists paths instead of resolving, and --tool NAME selects a configured three-way merge tool. Built-in :ours and :theirs choose sides one and two for applicable conflicts.

State effects. The selected commit is rewritten with resolved file content; descendants that depend on its tree may be rebased and conflicts can disappear or move. The filesystem is materialised for the current workspace, but the stored conflict value is authoritative. A fileset limits conflicted paths.

jj resolve --list -r @
jj resolve --tool meld -r @ -- 'glob:src/**'
jj resolve --tool :ours
jj log -r '::@ & conflicts()'

Trap. Multi-sided conflicts are not necessarily two-way, and marker files are a rendering. Inspect the resulting diff and conflict predicate. Resolving a child does not necessarily resolve an independent conflict in its descendant.

jj restore

Purpose and model. Restores selected file contents from one commit into another, or undoes the diff represented by a commit. It is a content operation, not a ref reset and not the same as revert. Ask whether the source tree, destination tree, or a commit's visible changes define the operation.

Syntax/options. jj restore [FILESETS...]; -f/--from REVSET is the source, -t/--into REVSET the destination, and -c/--changes-in REVSET undoes changes visible in a commit compared with the merge of its parents. Without options the default is effectively --changes-in @. -i/--interactive and --tool NAME select individual diff hunks; --restore-descendants preserves descendant content during rebasing.

State effects. The destination is rewritten with selected paths copied from the source or parent-derived inverse. Descendants may be rebased and conflicts may be stored. A fileset narrows paths, not commit selection. Restoring into @ changes the working-copy tree at the next snapshot.

jj restore --from main@origin --into @ -- 'glob:src/**'
jj restore --changes-in A
jj restore --from @- --into @ --interactive

Trap. Use revert for a review-visible inverse; use restore from a parent for local cleanup. Verify with jj diff before publishing.

jj revert

Purpose and model. Creates a new change that applies the reverse of selected commits. It preserves original history and expresses the reversal as a reviewable diff.

Syntax/options. jj revert --revision REVSETS --onto REVSETS, or use -A/--insert-after/-B/--insert-before. -r/--revision is required; -o/--onto (alias -d/--destination) supplies the destination. Multiple destinations can create a merge.

State effects. Original commits are not rewritten. A new change with a new change ID is created; conflicts can occur when the inverse no longer applies. Bookmarks move only if they point at the result or are advanced explicitly.

jj revert -r A -o @
jj revert --revision 'A::C' --onto main@origin
jj log -r '::@'

Trap. Revert is not abandon and does not erase a public change. For unpublished cleanup, restore/squash may communicate intent better.

jj root

Prints the current workspace root and is a shortcut for jj workspace root. It is useful for scripts that need to locate the repository from a subdirectory.

cd src/lib
git -C "$(jj root)" status

It reports the workspace root, not necessarily the Git backend root; use jj git root for the latter. The command is observational but follows global snapshot policy unless ignored.

jj run

Runs a command over selected commits. -r/--revision REVSETS selects the set, -j/--jobs N controls parallelism, --root changes the working directory, --clean discards reusable private workspaces, --passthrough connects output and requires one job, and --ignore-changes prevents rewriting commits.

Execution contract. Each selected commit is tested in a private materialisation; the selected revset is not a shell loop over the current workspace. A non-zero command status stops or reports the run according to the command mode, while files written without --ignore-changes become candidate tree rewrites. Parallel jobs require isolated caches and temporary directories. Use a bounded revset, a deterministic command, and a template or log record containing the tested commit ID.

Graph effects. With changes enabled, a formatter or generator can create successors and automatically rebase descendants. With --ignore-changes, output is evidence only and should not be mistaken for a clean working-copy or a committed fix. The operation log records the repository effects, but it cannot make an external test side effect reproducible.

jj run --ignore-changes --clean -r 'main@origin..@' -- ./check.sh
jj run -r '@:: & mutable()' -- ./format-and-test.sh

Without --ignore-changes, files written by the command can become commit rewrites and rebase descendants. The full execution model is in Part XVI.

jj show

Shows metadata and the diff of selected commits compared with their parent(s), defaulting to @. --reversed changes ordering, -T/--template renders metadata, and diff formatting includes --summary, --stat, --types, --name-only, --git, and context/diff options from local help.

jj show -r A
jj show -r @ --stat
jj show -r @ -T 'change_id ++ "\n" ++ description'

For a merge, the displayed change is relative to the automatic merge of parents. Show is observational but can snapshot; it does not create a new commit. Use diff to compare arbitrary endpoints and evolog to compare versions of one logical change.

jj sign

Purpose and model. Adds or replaces a cryptographic signature on selected commits. Signing rewrites commits because the signature is metadata; it is separate from a Git hosting server's verification policy.

Syntax/options. jj sign selects commits with -r/--revision REVSETS, defaulting to revsets.sign, and accepts --key KEY. Commits are re-signed even if they appear already signed; hardware-key workflows should account for that.

State effects. Signed commits receive new commit IDs and may cause descendant successors. Change IDs normally persist. Bookmarks follow successors locally; pushing signed commits still requires the relevant bookmark/ref and server policy.

jj sign -r 'bookmarks(exact:"release")'
jj sign --key KEYID -r @
jj log -r @ -T 'if(signature, signature.status(), "unsigned") ++ "\n"'

Trap. Presence does not prove a good signature. Template status/key/display can be expensive because verification may invoke GPG or SSH tooling.

jj simplify-parents

Purpose and model. Removes redundant parent edges while preserving the selected commits' tree meaning. It is graph normalisation: it does not turn a merge into an arbitrary squash and should be used when parent reachability makes an edge unnecessary.

Syntax/options. jj simplify-parents; -s/--source REVSETS simplifies commits together with their descendant trees, while -r/--revision REVSETS limits the operation to specified commits. If neither is supplied, 0.45.1 uses revsets.simplify-parents or reachable(@, mutable()).

State effects. Parent edges and therefore commit IDs can change; descendants may be rewritten. Filesystem content should remain semantically equivalent, but conflicts and merges must be inspected. Bookmarks follow target successors.

jj simplify-parents -r @
jj simplify-parents --source 'mutable()'
jj log -r 'merges()'

Trap. Use rebase when you want a particular destination, and do not treat parent simplification as a content cleanup. Compare before/after graph and diff.

jj sparse

Manages which repository paths are materialised in the current workspace. Subcommands are edit, list, reset, and set. Sparse state changes the filesystem view, not the complete commit tree.

A sparse workspace can therefore run a build or review focused on one subtree while commits still contain paths outside the materialised set. A rewrite can update absent paths in the commit without writing them into the sparse filesystem.

jj sparse edit

Opens the editor for the current workspace's sparse patterns. The editor is external and operates on configuration-like path patterns.

jj sparse edit
jj sparse list

Use it for complex patterns; use sparse set for repeatable commands. Sparse editing can update the filesystem and therefore should not run concurrently with another process writing the workspace.

jj sparse list

Lists sparse patterns for the current workspace. It is the first diagnostic when files appear absent from a checkout.

jj sparse list

An absent file may be sparse rather than deleted. Compare jj file list against filesystem listing before restoring or committing.

jj sparse reset

Resets sparse patterns to the default/full materialisation policy. It changes workspace files, not commit trees.

jj sparse reset
jj sparse list

Use before a full test when a sparse workspace could hide inputs. It may be expensive in a large repository and can overwrite local filesystem materialisation; snapshot or inspect status first.

jj sparse set

Sets sparse patterns directly. The fileset expressions describe paths to materialise; all other paths remain absent from the filesystem view.

jj sparse set --clear --add src --add tests
jj sparse set --clear --add Cargo.toml --add Cargo.lock

Patterns are workspace state, not history filters. A command such as jj diff can still see complete commit trees; use filesets separately when the diff itself should be narrowed.

jj split

Purpose and model. Divides one commit into two changes. The first result contains selected content and the second contains the remainder; this is a graph replacement, not merely a file move. By default the target is @.

Syntax/options. jj split [FILESETS...]; -r/--revision REVSET chooses the commit, -i/--interactive and --tool NAME select diff hunks, -o/--onto/-d/--destination and -A/-B place the resulting changes, -m/--message supplies a description, --editor opens the editor, and -p/--parallel controls parallel handling in the installed surface. A fileset selects paths for the first side when non-interactive.

State effects. The original commit receives successors representing the split. Descendants are rebased onto the second resulting change and can conflict. The split changes have distinct change IDs; neither should be assumed to be the original change's sole continuation without checking evolution. Bookmarks at the original target follow the command's successor policy, but publication bookmarks may need to be moved.

jj split -r @ -- 'glob:tests/**'
jj split --interactive -r A
jj split -r @ -m 'API: implementation'
jj log -r '::@'

Trap. A fileset is a path selection, not a semantic diff-hunk classifier. Check both diffs and descriptions. If the operation is wrong, undo before further edits; later, use evolution to identify the split successors.

jj squash

Purpose and model. Moves content from one or more source commits into a destination, normally the parent of the current change. It can fold all or selected paths and can perform experimental insertion-style rewrites in 0.45.1.

Syntax/options. jj squash [FILESETS...]; ordinary mode uses -r/--revision REVSET to squash a commit into its parent, or -f/--from REVSETS and -t/--into REVSET to name source and destination. -i/--interactive/--tool NAME select content. -m/--message sets the destination description, -u/--use-destination-message discards source descriptions, and --editor opens the editor. Experimental -o/--onto, -A, and -B insert the new commit.

State effects. Source and destination are rewritten; source may become empty and descendants receive new commit IDs. Change IDs of the surviving logical changes can persist, but moving content between changes changes which change owns the diff. Bookmarks at source/destination follow the resulting graph; remote bookmarks are not updated until push.

jj squash                         # current diff into parent
jj squash --from @ --into @- -- 'glob:src/**'
jj squash --use-destination-message
jj squash --interactive --tool meld

Trap. --revision mode is incompatible with experimental insertion options. Distinguish “copy these paths into a tree” (restore) from “move this diff ownership” (squash). Review descriptions and empty changes after a partial squash.

jj status

Reports high-level workspace status: current @, parent relationship, working-copy modifications, conflicts, and ignored/untracked information according to the workspace. Positional filesets restrict the status display.

jj status
jj status --ignore-working-copy
jj status -- 'glob:src/**'

By default status snapshots, so it can turn filesystem edits into a new working-copy commit. This is a major difference from a passive Git status check. Use the global ignore option when a prompt or monitor must not mutate repository state. Status does not move bookmarks or rewrite ancestors, except for the snapshot of @.

jj tag

Manages tag names, which are release/reference names rather than moving review bookmarks. Subcommands are delete, list, set, track, and untrack.

Tags can be local or remote and may be tracked, but their expected immutability and publication policy differ from a review bookmark. Use tags for release identity and bookmarks for moving work.

jj tag delete

Deletes local tags matching names/patterns. It changes local tag state; a tracked deletion can be pushed according to Git/tag policy. It does not erase the tagged commit.

jj tag delete 'v0.45.1-*'

jj tag list

Lists tags, optionally filtered by names, remote, tracking, or commit and rendered with a template according to local help. Use it to audit release names and remote tag state before a force-sensitive operation.

jj tag list
jj tag list --all-remotes

jj tag set

Creates or updates tags to a target commit. -r/--revision REVSET (alias --to) defaults to @; --allow-move permits moving an existing tag. Moving a release tag is a policy event, not ordinary diff editing.

jj tag set v1.2.0 -r @
jj tag set --allow-move v1.2.0 -r release-candidate

jj tag track

Associates local tag state with a remote tag. It changes tracking metadata, not the tag target or server.

jj tag track v1.2.0@origin

jj tag untrack

Removes a local/remote tag tracking relationship without deleting either tag. Review push behaviour after untracking because a later tag publication may be interpreted as new.

jj tag untrack v1.2.0@origin

jj undo

Undoes the most recent integrated operation by creating a reverse repository operation. It is the fast recovery path for a mistake noticed immediately.

jj undo
jj op log
jj redo

Undo does not automatically undo an already-pushed remote change, and it may not be the desired repair when several operations have happened. Use operation restore/diff for a named historical state and evolution for one change's identity.

jj unsign

Purpose and model. Removes cryptographic signatures from selected commits. It is metadata rewriting, not a content or ref operation.

Syntax/options. jj unsign accepts -r/--revision REVSETS; selection follows the command's default when omitted. Global immutability and repository-view options apply.

State effects. The affected commits and dependent descendants can receive new IDs while their trees remain unchanged. Change identities normally persist; bookmarks move with local successors and remotes remain unchanged until publication.

jj unsign -r 'mutable() & signed()'
jj log -r @ -T 'if(signature, "signed", "unsigned") ++ "\n"'

Trap. Do not unsign imported/public immutable history casually. Treat it like any other metadata rewrite and inspect the operation log.

jj util

Contains infrequently used administrative and generation commands: backend, completion, config-schema, exec, gc, install-man-pages, markdown-help, and snapshot. Treat this namespace as an implementation/tooling surface; commands can be version-sensitive and some can affect repository maintenance or external files.
