jj util completion bash
jj util config-schema
jj util backend name

jj util backend and jj util backend name

Inspects backend information. The name subcommand prints the active backend name. These are diagnostics, not commands for changing commit content.

jj util backend name

Use this in bug reports and environment audits. A backend name does not describe colocation; check jj git colocation status separately.

jj util backend name

Prints the active backend name for diagnostics. It does not report colocation, Git remote configuration, or the current workspace. Pair it with jj git colocation status and jj version in an environment report.

jj util backend name

jj util completion

Generates shell completion for the requested shell. It is output generation, not repository mutation.

jj util completion bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/jj
jj util completion zsh > ~/.zfunc/_jj
jj util completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/jj.fish

Install the generated file according to the shell's search path, then start a new shell or source it. Regenerate after a jj upgrade because command and option surfaces change.

jj util config-schema

Prints the machine-readable configuration schema for the installed version. It is the validation authority for key types and structure, not a human explanation of how keys interact.

jj util config-schema > config-schema.json
jj util config-schema | jq '.properties | keys'

The book's Appendix F interprets significant keys for humans; keep this schema in the research artefacts as the jj 0.45.1 machine-readable baseline. Do not treat every schema implementation detail as a stable public user-facing contract.

jj util exec

Executes a command in the repository/tooling context used by jj utilities. It is intended for internal or advanced integration use; ordinary shell commands should be run directly or through jj run when commits are the intended domain.

jj util exec -- command --arg

Read the installed help before scripting because argument forwarding and environment details are implementation-sensitive. It may have external side effects but does not by itself define a commit rewrite.

jj util gc

Runs repository object/storage garbage collection. It can remove unreachable data that would otherwise help recovery, so it is a maintenance boundary rather than a routine cleanup after every abandon.

jj op log
jj util gc

Run only after operation/recovery retention and remote publication state are understood. Garbage collection is distinct from commit abandonment, config GC, and Git remote pruning.

jj util install-man-pages

Installs generated manual pages for the current jj binary. It changes files outside the repository and should be run with an explicit destination/permission policy as shown by local help.

jj util install-man-pages --help

Regenerate after upgrading jj. Man pages are convenience documentation; local jj help remains the exact installed command authority.

jj util markdown-help

Generates Markdown help documentation from the installed command tree. This is useful for release audits and offline documentation, but generated output is not itself the authored book.

jj util markdown-help > jj-help.md

Keep it separate from the first-class HTML source. Compare generated help across binaries rather than silently mixing versions.

jj util snapshot

Forces or inspects a working-copy snapshot according to the installed utility help. It is useful in automation that deliberately owns snapshot timing, but it bypasses the convenient assumption that any ordinary jj command will establish the desired boundary.

jj util snapshot
jj status --ignore-working-copy

Coordinate with editors, build tools, and other jj processes. Snapshotting can create an operation and rewrite the working-copy commit; use the operation log when diagnosing unexpected changes.

jj version

Prints jj version/build information. Use it as the first line of a bug report, validation log, and version-sensitive script.

jj version
jj --version

The book's normative baseline is jj 0.45.1, which is separately inventoried from the installed binary. Never infer feature availability from current online documentation alone.

jj workspace

Purpose and model. Manages multiple working directories over one repository commit/operation store. Subcommands are add, forget, list, rename, root, and update-stale. Each workspace has a local @; a graph rewrite is shared. A workspace is therefore a filesystem view plus a pointer, not a second repository or a Git branch.

Safety contract. A graph rewrite can make another workspace's working-copy commit stale even though its files are untouched. Inspect workspace list after rewriting shared ancestors, update or repair the affected workspace deliberately, and do not let two processes snapshot the same directory concurrently. Sparse patterns belong to the workspace's materialisation policy; they do not remove paths from commit trees.

jj workspace list
jj workspace add ../build -r @
jj workspace root
jj workspace update-stale

Use workspaces for build/review separation, not as lightweight bookmarks. Filesystem state and workspace metadata need a single-writer discipline.

jj workspace add

Creates a workspace directory. The destination is required. --name NAME chooses the workspace symbol; -r/--revision REVSETS supplies zero or more parents for its working-copy commit; -m/--message describes it; --sparse-patterns copy|full|empty controls sparse state and defaults to copy.

jj workspace add ../project-build --name build -r @ --sparse-patterns full
jj workspace add ../project-review --name review -r main@origin
jj workspace add ../project-ci -r @ --sparse-patterns empty

With no commits, the new working-copy commit shares the current workspace's parents; with explicit commits, it is like jj new r1 r2 .... The new workspace has a distinct @ and can be independently edited.

jj workspace forget

Forgets a workspace's metadata. It does not necessarily remove the directory or erase commits; inspect the filesystem and repository state separately before cleanup.

jj workspace list
jj workspace forget review

Do not forget a workspace whose unrecorded filesystem changes matter. A temporary bookmark or operation record can preserve graph recovery, but neither preserves uncommitted external files automatically. Forgetting the record also removes the convenient name used to select that workspace; it does not publish a deletion and does not alter a bookmark.

jj workspace list

Lists workspaces and their working-copy commits. -T/--template renders WorkspaceRef fields such as name, target, and optional root.

jj workspace list
jj workspace list -T 'name ++ " " ++ target.commit_id() ++ "\n"'

Use it to find which workspace owns a commit before rewriting or updating stale state. A root path can be absent or stale. Listing is also the quickest check that @ in a command refers to the workspace you think it does; qualify a revision with workspace@ when comparing workspaces.

jj workspace rename

Renames a workspace symbol. The directory path and commit graph are separate concerns; a renamed workspace changes symbols such as review@, not commits.

cd ../project-build
jj workspace rename ci
jj workspace list

Update scripts and templates that refer to the old workspace name. The operation remains in local operation history.

jj workspace root

Prints the root directory of the current workspace, equivalent to top-level jj root. It is useful from a nested subdirectory and differs from jj git root in a non-trivial backend layout.

jj workspace root
cd src && jj workspace root

jj workspace update-stale

Updates workspaces whose working-copy state is stale after shared graph changes. It is a repair/materialisation command, not a rebase selection command.

jj workspace update-stale
jj workspace list
jj -R ../project-build status

Inspect filesystem edits before updating. A stale workspace may contain useful unrecorded files, and update policy may materialise a new tree or conflict. Use a temporary copy/bookmark when the state is valuable. Updating the workspace pointer does not rewrite unrelated commits, move publication bookmarks, or synchronise another clone.

Global option semantics

OptionOperational meaningUse/caution
-R/--repository PATHSelects a repository from any directory.Useful for workspaces/scripts; it does not select a Git remote.
--ignore-working-copyDoes not snapshot or update the filesystem.Reads a possibly stale commit; implied by --at-op.
--no-integrate-operationCreates an operation without integrating it into the current op head.Prints an ID for later integration; external side effects still occur.
--ignore-immutableDisables immutable rewrite protection.Use only with explicit audit/recovery intent.
--at-operation OPLoads a historical repository view.Read-only investigation; cannot snapshot today's filesystem into that view.
--color MODEControls colour/debug output.Use never in scripts; debug reveals labels.
--no-pagerDisables pager.Use for automation and captured fixture output.
--config NAME=VALUEApplies an inline TOML override.Repeatable; shell and TOML quoting both apply.
--config-file PATHLoads an additional config file.It is input, not necessarily the scope file selected by config edit.
--debugEnables diagnostic output/behaviour.Useful for bug reports, not stable machine output.

Global options are parsed before/alongside command options according to jj's CLI parser. Repeatable options such as --config accumulate. When combining a historical view, --ignore-working-copy is implied and filesystem state is deliberately not reconciled. When using --no-integrate-operation, the command's repository operation exists but another process may still advance the integrated operation head before you integrate it.

Global options

The 0.45.1 global surface includes -R/--repository, --ignore-working-copy, --no-integrate-operation, --ignore-immutable, --at-operation/--at-op, --debug, --color, --quiet, --no-pager, repeatable --config, and repeatable --config-file, plus -h/--help and -V/--version. The installed help is the option authority because defaults and accepted values are version-sensitive.

Version-specific notes

Verified against jj 0.45.1. This edition documents the command, configuration, revset, fileset, template, and default surfaces of jj 0.45.1. In particular, the target release provides jj converge, direct --file PATH targeting for relevant configuration commands, tracked and untracked remote-tag predicates, the documented Gerrit defaults, and the non-Windows pager default less -FRXK. Re-run the local inventory after a future upgrade because these are versioned interfaces.

Command contracts: how to predict side effects

The command reference is easiest to use when every invocation is classified along four axes: snapshot, selection, rewrite, and publication. Before running a command, ask four questions:

  1. Will jj read the filesystem and possibly create/update the workspace commit?
  2. What is the commit cardinality: zero-or-one default, exactly one, or arbitrary set?
  3. Does the command rewrite selected commits, their descendants, or only metadata?
  4. Can it move a bookmark, import/export a Git ref, or perform network I/O?

The answer predicts most side effects. For example, jj log -r 'all()' is a set-valued observation and normally does not rewrite commits. jj edit A is singleton-valued, snapshots before moving the workspace, and changes filesystem state. jj rebase -s 'B::D' -d main@origin is set-valued source selection, graph-rewriting, descendant-affecting, and non-networked. jj git push --bookmark review --remote origin is ref-publication and networked; it does not rewrite the local commit graph merely because the server accepts it.

DimensionInspection exampleMutation exampleQuestion to record in a script
Filesystem snapshotstatus, diffnew, describe, commitAre unsaved edits part of the intended operation?
Commit graphlog, showrebase, split, abandonWhich source set and destination set?
Content ownershipdiff, interdiffsquash, restore, absorbWhich tree contributes which paths?
Local refsbookmark listbookmark move/set/deleteWhich name should point where after the operation?
Remote stategit fetch, remote bookmarksgit push, gerrit uploadWhich remote and publication ref are explicit?
Operation stateop log/show/diffundo, op restore/revertCan this be reversed and how will it be identified?

Rewriting commands: source, destination, and ownership

rebase, new, duplicate, parallelize, and simplify-parents change parent relationships. squash, absorb, restore, diffedit, and split change tree/diff ownership. describe, metaedit, and signing commands change metadata. The categories overlap in descendant effects, but keeping them separate prevents the wrong mental shortcut.

For a parent-edge operation, write the old and desired edge before selecting flags:

old:  A--B--C--D
want: A--C--B--D       (reorder)
want: A--B----D        (remove C contribution)
want: A--B--C
           \--D       (fork/parallelise)

Then choose the operation that expresses that edge change. Do not start with “which Git command resembles this?” Git’s interactive rebase todo is a user interface for several transformations; jj exposes those transformations separately and applies them to commit sets.

Rebase destination modes

In 0.45.1, -o/--onto and its destination spelling place source commits on a new parent. -A/--insert-after and -B/--insert-before express relative placement. The aliases in the local help are important because examples copied from different jj releases can use different long names. Use the long form in the book’s prose and include the short form only where it improves terminal ergonomics.

jj rebase --revisions 'C::D' --onto main@origin
jj rebase --source C --insert-after B
jj rebase --branch C --insert-before D
jj rebase -r 'C::D' -d main@origin

A source set and a destination set can each contain multiple commits. Multiple destinations can create a merge-shaped graph; multiple sources can move a disconnected set only when the command’s topology rules permit it. Inspect the result with jj log -r 'all()' and a parent template. The visual graph alone can hide that a node gained two parents.

jj log -r 'C::D' -T '
commit_id.short() ++ " parents=" ++
parents.map(|p| p.commit_id().short()).join(",") ++ "\n"
'

Content commands: tree endpoints versus diff endpoints

restore copies selected file contents; squash moves a diff into another change; diffedit changes a selected diff through an editor. The commands may produce similar final files but differ in which logical change owns the content and which description/evolution receives the successor.

B tree: implementation
C tree: implementation + tests

restore from C into B:
  B′ tree = implementation + tests
  C may be unchanged

squash C into B:
  B′ owns implementation + tests
  C becomes empty/removed according to operation

diffedit C:
  C′ diff is edited; B is not destination

When a user says “bring these changes into B”, ask whether the source should remain, whether its logical review should survive, and whether the selected paths are a diff or a complete tree. Those answers determine the command.

Inspection and stable output

log is a graph-oriented view; show is a commit-oriented view; diff is a tree/diff view; status is a workspace/filesystem view. They answer different questions even when they display overlapping information.

NeedCommandWhy not the nearest alternative?
Find a topology or refjj log -r REVSETshow focuses on one commit and may hide the surrounding graph.
Inspect one commit’s metadata/treejj show REVlog may omit the full diff and file state.
Understand diff ownershipjj diff --from X --to Ystatus only sees workspace differences.
Understand disk versus @jj statuslog can snapshot or omit the filesystem dimension.
Understand a rewritejj op diff and jj evologCommit IDs alone do not explain successor relationships.

For machine output, use a template with explicit field delimiters and a controlled revset. Include full IDs when the output is evidence; use short IDs only for human reports. Never parse graph characters, colour labels, or the default description wrapping. The default template is a user interface and can change between releases.

Global options and their combinations

--ignore-working-copy is appropriate for a monitoring process that must not snapshot a half-written build tree. It can also make a human answer stale if unrecorded filesystem edits matter. --at-operation provides a historical repository view; combining it with the live filesystem is usually misleading because the files on disk belong to the current workspace, not the historical operation.

jj --ignore-working-copy log -r 'all()'
jj --at-operation OP log -r 'all()'
jj --at-operation OP --ignore-working-copy show @

--ignore-immutable changes the permitted rewrite boundary and should be visible in logs. --no-integrate-operation changes operation-head integration and should be used only by tooling that records the resulting operation. --repository changes the repository/workspace context; it does not turn a path into a revset. --config and --config-file alter interpretation and are therefore part of the command’s reproducibility record.

Command failure taxonomy

Most jj errors fall into a small set of categories:

  • Resolution: a symbol is unknown or a prefix is ambiguous. Inspect refs, IDs, and aliases.
  • Cardinality: a command expected one commit but got zero or several. Narrow the revset and print IDs.
  • Policy: a rewrite reaches an immutable commit or a push violates ref safety. Do not bypass until intent is established.
  • Tree/fileset: a path is absent, sparse, conflicted, or outside the selected tree. Inspect with file list and diff.
  • Editor/tool: an external program failed or returned an invalid result. Re-run with a builtin or explicit tool.
  • Transport: credentials, remote URLs, server permissions, or non-fast-forward state failed. Fetch and inspect before retrying.
  • Operation concurrency: an operation was created outside the integrated head or another writer changed state. Inspect operation history and integrate deliberately.

A failed command may have performed an automatic snapshot before reporting its main error. Check jj op log rather than assuming failure means no repository state changed. The operation record is the authoritative place to determine what was committed locally.

Version-aware CLI use

Scripts should probe the binary before depending on a release-sensitive feature. Do not test for a feature by running a destructive command and interpreting its error as a capability probe. The safe pattern is to compare jj version, inspect help in installation tests, and select a command alias or argument set accordingly.

case "$("$JJ" version | sed -n 's/^jj \\([0-9][^ ]*\\).*/\1/p')" in
  0.45.1.*) # this book's target release
           ;;
  *)       printf 'unsupported jj version\n' >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac

For this edition, jj 0.45.1 is normative. After upgrading, compare the installed help and schema because command options, builtin templates, and schemas are not frozen interfaces.

Command contracts: how to read an advanced jj command

A command reference is useful only when it describes the state transition, not just the spelling. For each command, ask four questions: what repository value is selected, what is rewritten or observed, which workspace is affected, and which refs or remote state remain unchanged. The same global option can alter several commands: normal snapshotting may turn an apparently read-only invocation into an operation, --ignore-working-copy reads a stale recorded tree, --at-operation selects a historical repository view, and --ignore-immutable changes only rewrite protection.

Contract fieldQuestion to answerEvidence to show
SelectionDoes the command accept one commit, a set, a range, or a fileset?Syntax and a cardinality/error example.
MutationDoes it create, rewrite, hide, or merely render?Before/after commit IDs and operation entry.
DescendantsWill parent identity changes rebase children?Graph showing successor IDs or conflicts.
WorkspaceDoes it move/edit @, materialise files, or leave the filesystem?Workspace-local log and filesystem check.
RefsDoes it move bookmarks/tags or only alter commits?Local/remote ref listing before and after.
NetworkDoes it contact Git/Gerrit or change only local observations?Remote bookmark/ref state and explicit remote option.
RecoveryWhat operation ID and evolution entry does it create?op show and evolog evidence.

Rewrite commands

jj describe changes the description of one mutable commit, usually @. It preserves the tree but changes commit metadata and therefore the commit ID; descendants can receive successors. jj metaedit performs metadata surgery such as author/timestamp and can intentionally update the change ID. jj edit moves one workspace pointer to one existing commit; it does not create a successor until a snapshot or rewrite occurs. jj diffedit edits a diff through a diff editor. These commands look similar from a Git perspective but have different state targets.

jj describe -r 'change_id(API_CHANGE)' -m 'API: reject negative quota'
jj metaedit -r 'change_id(API_CHANGE)' --update-author-timestamp
jj edit 'change_id(API_CHANGE)'
jj diffedit -r 'change_id(API_CHANGE)' -- 'root-prefix-glob:"src"'

jj squash moves the current or selected diff into a destination change. A partial fileset makes it a content-ownership operation; an unselected diff hunk stays at the source boundary. The destination's description and change identity are not the source's by default. Descendants of the destination can be rebased, and the source may become empty. If the source should remain as a separate logical change, use duplicate or restore instead of squash.

jj split turns one change into multiple changes. It is a boundary operation: the first resulting change receives selected content and the second receives the remainder according to the mode. Existing descendants are rebased over the new sequence. Treat the interactive editor as a content selector, then verify with two diffs and a parent-edge query. A split is not “make a branch”; it changes the diff stack's granularity.

jj absorb routes working-copy changes into suitable mutable ancestors. It is powerful precisely because it is a policy-driven multi-target rewrite. Before using it, inspect which ancestors are mutable, which files each owns, and whether the current change contains unrelated work. Use a narrow revset/fileset and an operation checkpoint. If an individual diff hunk matches several ancestors or no ancestor, the command's behaviour follows its configured applicability rules; do not promise ownership without inspecting the result.

jj duplicate creates a new logical change with copied content. It intentionally breaks evolution continuity. jj abandon removes a commit from ordinary visible work and reconnects or updates dependants according to graph rules. jj restore restores selected file contents or reverses a selected change. jj revert creates a new inverse change. The last two are both content operations but differ in whether the inverse is applied to an existing destination or represented as a new commit.

Rebase as a two-dimensional contract

jj rebase has a source dimension and a destination dimension. Source -r/--revisions X selects explicit commits; -s/--source X selects X and descendants; -b/--branch X selects the branch of X relative to the destination. Destination -o/--onto Y places the selected source on Y; repeating -o in jj 0.45.1 creates multiple parents; -A/--insert-after Y inserts selected changes after Y; -B/--insert-before Y inserts them before Y. The names are not cosmetic: changing -r to -s can turn a one-commit repair into a whole-stack rewrite.

before: base--A--B--C
                  \
                   X--Y

-r B -o X:     base--A--B'--C'     and X--B' if destination is X
-s B -o X:     base--A--B'--C'     all descendants selected/rebased
-r B -A X:     base--A--X--B'--C'  insert the selected diff after X
-r B -B X:     base--A--B'--X'--Y' rebase X and descendants after B'

The diagrams show the shape, not a promise that every shorthand combination is accepted by every release. Check local help and inspect the selected set before execution. A source with holes may preserve an edge to an unselected parent, may be rejected, or may cause a split of the selected roots according to the rebase algorithm. This is why jj log -r SOURCE, jj log -G -r SOURCE, and a temporary bookmark are useful preconditions.

After a rebase, compare four things: each selected change ID, each new commit ID, each descendant's diff, and every affected bookmark. Then query conflicts and operation detail:

jj log -G -r 'SOURCE | descendants(SOURCE)'
jj evolog -r 'SOURCE'
jj log -r 'conflicts() & descendants(SOURCE)'
jj bookmark list --all-remotes
jj op show -p

Inspection and diff commands

jj log accepts a many-valued revset and renders a graph or a template. It normally snapshots first, so “inspection” is not synonymous with “no operation”. Use --ignore-working-copy for a stable recorded view and --no-pager --color=never for automation. jj show focuses on one commit's metadata, tree, and diff; it is a good cardinality check before editing. jj diff compares a commit's diff, endpoints, or selected set and accepts a fileset independently.

jj log -G -r 'roots(main@origin..@)::'
jj show -r 'exactly(change_id(API_CHANGE), 1)'
jj diff --from main@origin --to @ -- 'root-prefix-glob:"src"'
jj diff -r @ --summary --no-pager

jj interdiff compares two versions of a logical change, not two arbitrary branch tips. Use it after a rewrite when the commit IDs differ but the review question is “what changed between patch set 1 and patch set 2”. jj evolog -p answers a related question by following a change's evolution and showing predecessor/inter-diff information.

Bookmarks and tags

bookmark create creates a local name at a commit; set creates or moves a name; move moves an existing name; advance moves it to a descendant under the command's safety rules; rename changes the local name; delete expresses local deletion suitable for publication; forget removes local knowledge without being the same as a remote delete; track/untrack manage a relationship with a remote bookmark; and list renders current state. None of these commands makes a bookmark follow @ automatically.

jj bookmark create pr/cache -r @
jj bookmark set pr/cache -r 'change_id(CACHE_CHANGE)'
jj bookmark move pr/cache --to @
jj bookmark track pr/cache --remote origin
jj bookmark list --all-remotes
jj bookmark forget pr/cache

Tags are release-oriented names with their own command family. A tag's presence in an immutable-head policy can protect an older commit even when no local bookmark reaches it. Fetch and tag tracking affect local observations; moving a tag is an intentional release/ref change. Display local and remote target states separately before any deletion or force publication.

Git transport commands

jj git clone creates a jj repository from a Git remote; git init initialises the backend and can colocate with an existing Git repository; git fetch imports remote objects and updates remote bookmarks; git push exports selected bookmarks/commits; git import notices Git-side ref changes; and git export writes jj refs/objects to the Git view where required. git root identifies the Git root and git remote manages the transport configuration. Colocation makes native Git visible but creates a second writer boundary.

jj git remote list
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj git import
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark pr/cache
GIT_DIR=$(jj git root) git show-ref

A fetch changes local remote observations, not the server and not the local mutable graph. A push is external side effect and may be rejected; inspect tracking and commit ancestry first. Explicit remote and bookmark selectors are safer than broad defaults, especially when GitHub and Gerrit coexist.

Operation, configuration, and workspace contracts

Operation commands act on the operation DAG. op log lists transformations; op show explains one; op diff compares views; op restore restores selected repository state; op revert reverses a selected operation; op abandon prunes an operation record; and op integrate joins an unintegrated operation. The op spelling is an alias, but the canonical family is operation in the 0.45.1 command tree.

config get/list/path are read operations with different output contracts; set/unset/edit mutate configuration; gc removes obsolete config entries according to its rules. A config command can target a scope or load an additional file. In jj 0.45.1, --file provides direct file targeting for relevant subcommands.

workspace add creates a second working directory over the shared store; list displays records; root reports the current directory's workspace root; rename changes the current workspace name and takes one new name in 0.45.1; update-stale repairs stale workspace state; and forget removes metadata without abandoning its commits. Treat workspace filesystem updates as a separate side effect from graph rewrites.

Content, conflict, and maintenance commands

file list/show/search/annotate inspect trees and content; file track/untrack change snapshot tracking; file chmod changes executable metadata. sparse set/list/edit/reset controls materialisation, with set accepting patterns and edit opening an editor without positional patterns. resolve operates on stored conflicts; fix applies configured fixers; sign/unsign rewrite cryptographic metadata; bisect and bisect run perform graph search using script exit status; and run executes a command over selected commits, potentially rewriting them unless changes are ignored.

Administrative commands have external or destructive boundaries. util gc can remove recovery data; util completion writes shell output; util install-man-pages writes files outside the repository; util config-schema produces a machine-readable schema; util snapshot controls snapshotting; and util exec forwards commands according to its own contract. Always read the installed help for a utility before placing it in automation.

A reader's command validation protocol

  1. Run the exact command with --help under the target jj binary.
  2. Identify revset and fileset positions and quote them as one shell argument.
  3. Build the smallest graph that exposes source, destination, descendants, refs, or conflicts.
  4. Record filesystem state and the working-copy commit before invocation.
  5. Run the command and capture the operation ID.
  6. Compare graph edges, commit IDs, change IDs, bookmarks, remote bookmarks, and conflicts.
  7. Inspect op show and evolog when the command rewrites.
  8. Repeat the experiment after an upgrade whenever the release notes or help show a changed surface.

This protocol is deliberately more demanding than a successful exit status. Use it whenever a command selects or rewrites more than one graph component, especially in automation.

Part XVI — Advanced mechanics

Immutability and safety boundaries

Configure immutable heads to protect imported/public history. The check applies to rewrites; the revset/template notions of immutable state remain observable even with --ignore-immutable. Hidden commits and divergent change IDs are useful forensic states, not garbage to delete reflexively.

Evolution, concurrency, and operation merging

Run concurrent read commands with a clear snapshot policy. --no-integrate-operation lets automation create an operation without changing the integrated operation head; it does not suppress side effects such as a network push. Inspect and integrate deliberately.

jj fix and jj run

Fix tools are configured programs that transform files. jj fix can operate over a commit set and may rewrite a stack. In jj 0.45.1, jj run uses private working copies for selected commits, allowing checks or formatters to update changes and propagate conflicts. Treat command exit status and operation boundaries as part of your automation contract.

jj run -r '@:: & mutable()' -- cargo test
jj run -r 'mutable() & description(substring:"API")' -- cargo fix
jj fix -s 'mutable()'

Bisect, tags, signing, completion, and maintenance

jj bisect run automates commit bisection; tags provide stable release names; jj sign/unsign manage supported cryptographic metadata; jj util completion generates shell completion. Use jj util gc and backend maintenance only after understanding operation/recovery retention. In large repositories, narrow revsets, use immutable remote boundaries, avoid rendering enormous diffs, and use --ignore-working-copy for stable monitoring reads.

Machine-readable output

Templates plus --color never, explicit separators, and a controlled revset are the most portable interface. Do not parse the human graph glyphs. Pin aliases and templates in a versioned config, and run the inventory/fixture checks after upgrading.

Advanced mechanics in practice

Immutable heads are a policy boundary

Immutability is rewrite protection expressed as a revset. It is not the same thing as committed, pushed, on a branch, or old. A mutable commit can be published, and an immutable commit can be local. The useful policy question is which graph boundary must not be rewritten by an ordinary command.

jj log -r 'immutable_heads()'
jj log -r 'mutable() & ::@'
jj rebase -b 'roots(main@origin..@)' -o main@origin

If a source set reaches an immutable commit, jj protects it unless --ignore-immutable is supplied. That flag is an explicit override, not a repair to the graph. Save the operation ID, explain which boundary is being crossed, and verify the result with operation and evolution logs.

StateOrdinary rewritePublication meaning
Mutable, unpublishedUsually permitted.No remote ref necessarily exists.
Mutable, publishedLocally permitted; push may need a safe non-fast-forward update.Server sees a Git ref, not jj mutability.
Immutable imported trunkRejected without explicit override.Remote bookmark is an observation and likely safety boundary.
Hidden predecessorNot in ordinary visible selection.May remain recovery evidence.

Hidden commits, divergent changes, and evolution

Abandoning a commit hides it from ordinary visible history but does not immediately erase its objects. Rewriting a change creates successors, and independent successors can be divergent. These states let jj preserve evidence instead of forcing every rewrite to destroy it.

jj log -r 'hidden()'
jj log -r 'divergent()'
jj evolog -r 'change_id(abc...)'
jj log -r 'all() & present(commit_id("prefix"))'

A hidden predecessor may be reachable from an operation view or evolution entry. A divergent change ID can have several visible versions. Use an explicit offset or full commit ID when a command requires one commit. Do not select an ambiguous change ID merely because a log can display the set.

Concurrency and operation integration

jj operations support concurrent processes, but that is not permission for multiple processes to mutate one working directory without coordination. --no-integrate-operation creates an operation and prints its ID without advancing the integrated operation head.

jj status --no-integrate-operation
# record OP_PRINTED
jj --at-op OP_PRINTED log -r 'all()'
jj op integrate OP_PRINTED

The operation can still have external side effects: a Git push reaches a server, an editor writes files, and a fixer modifies a private working copy. Integrating later does not roll those effects back. A concurrent operation can advance the current head before integration; inspect jj op log and jj op diff first.

For concurrent read-only automation, use --ignore-working-copy with explicit templates. For concurrent filesystem writers, assign one process to one workspace. A build workspace and a development workspace can run simultaneously because their filesystems differ; two processes snapshotting the same workspace remain a race.

Fixers and modified-line protocols

A fixer is a configured program invoked over commits, often with a protocol describing changed lines. This can update a stack without rewriting unrelated historical lines, but only when the program supports the protocol correctly.

[fix.tools.rustfmt]
command = ["rustfmt", "--emit", "stdout"]
patterns = ["glob:*.rs"]

jj fix -s 'roots(main@origin..@)::' -- 'root-prefix-glob:"src/**"'

Validate the exact fixer keys and protocol against the target schema and help. Use --all-lines when the tool cannot safely act on modified ranges. Use --include-unchanged-files only when a repository-wide invariant is intentional: it can rewrite substantially more history.

Fix can affect many mutable commits and descendants. Run it on a small stack, inspect changed paths and descriptions, record the operation ID, and undo before another fix if the result is too broad.

jj run as a graph-aware test harness

jj run has two distinct modes. With --ignore-changes it tests commit states. Without it, files written by the command are recorded back into selected commits, so it is a transformation tool. Reused private working copies preserve build artefacts; --clean removes that state.

GoalControlsReason
Check commits--ignore-changes --clean --passthroughNo rewrite; clean state; interactive output.
Apply formatterNarrow -r, intentional rewrite, explicit tool.Scope and graph effects are visible.
Parallel tests-j N, captured output.Avoid interleaved logs.
Interactive tool--passthrough, one job.TTY-like output; stdin is not inherited.
jj run --ignore-changes --clean -r 'main@origin..@' -- ./ci/check.sh
jj run -j 4 --ignore-changes -r 'heads(mutable())' -- ./ci/check.sh
jj run -r '@:: & mutable()' -- ./format-current-tree.sh

The current directory is the invocation directory unless --root is supplied. Use -- before command arguments beginning with a dash. Capture exit status and inspect the operation when changes are permitted.

Bisect, signing, and release boundaries

Bisection assumes a monotonic predicate over the selected graph range. Merge-heavy graphs, non-deterministic tests, and environment-dependent failures violate that assumption. Define the range, make the script exit status unambiguous, and preserve the discovered commit before leaving the investigation.

jj bisect run --range 'good..bad' -- ./test-regression.sh
jj show -r 'bisect(@)'

jj sign and jj unsign rewrite metadata. Signing an ancestor changes descendant commit IDs even when tree content is unchanged. Presence of a signature is cheaper to query than status/key/display, which can invoke GPG or SSH verification.

jj sign -r 'heads(bookmarks())'
jj log -r 'signed()' -T 'commit_id ++ " " ++ if(signature, signature.status(), "unknown") ++ "\n"'
jj unsign -r 'mutable() & signed()'

Tags name release points. Treat them as immutable policy even when --allow-move exists. Remote tag tracking is separate from bookmark tracking; jj 0.45.1 provides tracked/untracked remote-tag predicates, and target-release scripts can use the supported forms from local help.

jj tag set v2.4.0 -r @
jj tag list --all-remotes
jj git push --remote origin --tag 'v2.4.0'

Performance and machine-readable output

Cost is driven by selected graph size, tree/diff materialisation, external tools, signature verification, remote URL work, and rendering. Narrow the revset before optimising the template. A template that calls diff().git() for every commit can be much slower than one that renders IDs and subjects.

ConcernTechnique
Prompt latency--ignore-working-copy -r @, no diff, cached output.
Large log-n, heads(), explicit template, no full diff.
Slow signaturesQuery signed(); verify selected commits only.
Large fix/runNarrow commits/fileset; control jobs and clean/reuse.
Recovery retentionDo not GC until operation/evolution evidence is no longer needed.

For automation use explicit revsets, templates, --color=never, --no-pager, a pinned jj binary, and a fixture test. Human graph glyphs and default templates are presentation, not a stable API.

Fixers as controlled graph transformations

jj fix is not merely a formatter command. It can run configured tools over selected commits and turn their filesystem changes into successor commits. Its safe use therefore combines a revset, a fileset/pattern policy, a tool protocol, and a review of descendant effects.

selected stack:
A--B--C--@       each has Rust files

fix over 'mutable() & ::@':
A′--B′--C′--@′    if each fixer result is clean
       or
A′--B′[conflict]--C′[conflict]--@′

Fixers should be idempotent: running them twice should produce no new content after the first successful run. They should preserve files outside their patterns, return a meaningful exit status, and not depend on the user’s editor or network. A tool that rewrites generated files or line endings must be explicitly scoped. Run it on one commit in a fixture before applying it to mutable().

jj fix -s @
jj diff -r @
jj op show
jj fix -s 'mutable() & ::@' -- 'root-glob:src/**/*.rs'
jj log -r '::@ & conflicts()'

The exact fixer table belongs in configuration and the command’s accepted fileset form is version-sensitive. The invariant is independent: select commits first, select paths second, run a deterministic tool, then inspect the full evolved stack.

jj run: commit-scoped automation

jj run provides a controlled way to execute a shell command in private working copies for a commit set. This is useful for tests, formatters, and checks that need each commit’s tree rather than the current workspace. The private workspaces are an implementation mechanism; the important contract is whether filesystem changes are imported back as commit rewrites.

ModeUseGraph risk
--ignore-changesRun a read-only check or discard tool writes.Low graph mutation; tool can still affect external state.
defaultAllow command changes to update selected commits.Successors and descendant rebases are possible.
--cleanDo not reuse prior private workspaces.More predictable, slower, avoids stale generated files.
-j NRun independent commits concurrently.Output interleaves; tools must not share mutable external files.
--passthroughExpose one job’s live output.Incompatible with multi-job presentation.
--root PATHRun command at a chosen root.Relative paths and generated artefacts can differ.
jj run --ignore-changes --clean -j 4 -r 'main@origin..@' -- ./ci/check.sh
jj run --clean -r '@:: & mutable()' -- ./format.sh

Do not use an ordinary workspace path as a lock-free coordination directory for parallel jobs. A test that writes to /tmp/result, a shared compiler cache with unsafe locking, or a generated file outside the private root can make independent commits interfere. Capture each job’s status and map it back to the full commit ID. A successful command may still leave a failed graph rewrite if the tool’s exit status was misreported.

Bisect as a predicate search

Bisection is a search over a commit set given a monotonic predicate: there is a boundary where commits are good on one side and bad on the other. The graph need not be linear, but the selected range and the meaning of “between” must be clear. A test that is flaky or depends on an unrelated descendant invalidates the result.

jj bisect run --range 'good..bad' -- ./regression-test
# inspect the candidate
jj log -r 'bisect(@)'
jj show 'bisect(@)'

For a merge-heavy history, choose a first-parent or release corridor if the bug is associated with integration order. A query over all ancestors can find a commit that introduced the file change but not the first integration that made the system fail. Document the test environment, dependency versions, and whether the command mutates the candidate tree.

Signing and cryptographic evidence

Signing operates on a specific commit object. Rewriting description, metadata, parent, or tree produces a different object that needs independent verification/signing. A signature does not make a change immutable and does not make a bookmark safe to force-update. In a review workflow, sign immediately before publication or sign every successor as policy requires.

jj sign -r @ --key KEY
jj log -r @ -T 'commit_id ++ " " ++ if(signature, signature.status(), "unsigned") ++ "\n"'
jj unsign -r @

Separate cryptographic evidence into three questions: does the object have a valid signature, does the key belong to the expected identity, and does the hosting server trust that identity? jj can answer the first and expose metadata for the second; GitHub/Gerrit policy answers the third. Hardware tokens and agents are external dependencies; test them in the target environment and verify the resulting signature with the policy used by the host.

Tags and release boundaries

Tags name release graph positions and are deliberately less fluid than review bookmarks. Treat a tag as an immutable publication boundary in policy even if the underlying ref can technically be moved. Fetch tags explicitly when a release query depends on them, and distinguish local tags, remote tags, tracked remote tags, and untracked remote tags in jj 0.45.1.

jj tag list
jj log -r 'tags()'
jj log -r 'remote_tags()'
# 0.45.1:
jj log -r 'tracked_remote_tags()'
jj log -r 'untracked_remote_tags()'

In jj 0.45.1 the default immutable-head definition includes untracked remote tags, and the corresponding tracked/untracked tag predicates are available. This affects rewrite protection, not just display. A release script should use an explicit release tag and record the binary version rather than assuming that a future release has the same default immutable set.

Large repositories and performance

Performance problems often come from asking for a broad graph, rendering a large diff, or repeatedly snapshotting a large working tree. Narrow the revset, use bounded limits, separate graph selection from diff display, and use --ignore-working-copy for repository-only monitoring. Do not solve a slow query by making its result semantically broader.

jj log -r 'heads(mutable() & ::@)' -n 30 --no-pager
jj log -r 'main@origin..@' --no-graph -T 'commit_id.short() ++ "\n"'
jj diff --stat --from main@origin --to @
jj status --ignore-working-copy

Filesystem monitoring, sparse working copies, and private run workspaces can improve latency, but they introduce state that must be inspected when results are surprising. Measure with representative repositories. A prompt that runs an all-history template on every shell command is a design problem even if jj itself is fast.

Debugging and bug reports

A reproducible jj bug report should include version, backend, repository layout (colocated or not), workspace name/root, operation ID, exact command with redacted paths, revset/fileset, configuration layers, and whether the filesystem contained unrecorded changes. Include jj op show and a minimal graph rendered with full IDs if the issue is a rewrite.

jj version
jj root
jj util backend name
jj git colocation status
jj workspace list
jj op log -n 10
jj config list --include-defaults
jj log -r 'all()' --no-graph -T 'commit_id ++ " " ++ change_id ++ "\n"'

Use --debug when requested by jj’s diagnostics, but redact credentials, remote URLs containing tokens, private descriptions, and filesystem paths. The operation log may contain descriptions and usernames; it is repository data, not automatically safe to attach publicly.

Advanced mechanics laboratory: automation, signing, and maintenance

Running commands over commits

jj run provides temporary working environments for running a command against a commit set. It is useful for testing a stack, applying a deterministic fixer, or collecting a result at several graph points. It is not merely a loop around jj edit: the command can use private workspaces and, unless changes are ignored, files written by the process may become commit rewrites.

jj run --ignore-changes --clean -r 'main@origin..@' -- ./check.sh
jj run --ignore-changes -j 4 -r 'heads(mutable() & ::@)' -- ./test.sh
jj run --passthrough -r @ -- ./interactive-check.sh
Option/policyEffectUse when
--ignore-changesDo not record files written by the command as commit changes.Read-only tests or tools whose outputs are disposable.
--cleanDo not reuse existing private workspaces.Reproducible runs that must not inherit files.
-j NRun selected commits concurrently in jj 0.45.1.Independent deterministic tests; not a shared mutable worktree.
--passthroughConnect command output and constrain execution mode.Interactive diagnostics, not machine aggregation.
--rootChoose the command's working root.Scripts that must not depend on the caller's cwd.

Parallel execution requires test isolation. A test that writes to a shared cache, local database, or fixed temporary filename can make a graph query appear nondeterministic. Pin environment variables, use per-commit temporary directories, and record the selected commit in output. If the command is intended to rewrite commits, run one small fixture first and inspect its operation/evolution results.

Fixers are graph rewriters

jj fix applies configured fixer tools to selected commits and paths. A formatter is not automatically a safe no-op: line-ending changes, generated output, executable bits, and tool version changes alter commit trees and therefore commit IDs. A fixer that runs over an ancestor can trigger automatic descendant rebasing. Treat fixer configuration as both a tool policy and a graph-selection policy.

jj fix -s 'mutable() & ::@ & ~conflicts()' -- 'root-glob:src/**/*.rs'
jj log -r '::@' -T 'change_id.short() ++ " " ++ commit_id.short() ++ "\n"'
jj op show -p

Test a fixer in four states: unchanged input should produce no successor or a clearly explained no-op; changed input should have the expected paths; a conflict should be skipped or handled according to policy; and a sparse workspace should not silently imply that absent paths were checked. Keep generated files out of a source formatter unless the generator is part of the intended operation.

Bisect as graph search

Bisect narrows a commit set using a predicate supplied by the user or a script. The script's exit status is the test contract, so distinguish “known good”, “known bad”, and “infrastructure failure” in the script. A flaky or environment-dependent test can produce a plausible but wrong boundary. Keep the bisection range explicit and save the discovered commit before leaving the temporary checkout.

jj bisect run --range 'main@origin..@' -- ./test-regression.sh
jj show REVISION

There is no separate jj bisect log or jj bisect reset command in jj 0.45.1. Inspect the candidate with ordinary jj log -r 'bisect(@)' or jj show -r 'bisect(@)', and use jj op log/jj undo when you need to inspect or recover the operation sequence. A bisect result is not a diff to publish: it is evidence about graph history. If it identifies an ancestor that has since been rewritten, use change/evolution information to locate the current successor and verify the test at that object.

Signing and verification

Signing rewrites commit metadata and can therefore create successor commit IDs. It does not make a change immutable, publish it, or establish a Gerrit review identity. Verification status is a property of a cryptographic signature and key environment; a template can display it, but a successful local signing command does not prove that a remote host will trust the key.

jj sign -r 'bookmarks() & mutable()'
jj log -r 'signed()'
jj show -r @
jj unsign -r 'change_id(CHANGE)'

Define whether signing applies before or after review publication. Signing an already pushed commit may require a force update because the exported commit object changes. In a stack, signing an ancestor changes descendant commit IDs as well. Test with a disposable key or a controlled agent, keep private material out of repository config, and record the host's verification policy separately.

Tags as release boundaries

A tag names a release point rather than serving as a daily work pointer. Treat tag movement as an exceptional publication change, even when the local command permits it. A release query should name the tag explicitly and record the target commit ID, version, and binary used to compute the set.

jj tag set v2.4.0 -r @
jj log -r 'v2.4.0:: & ::main@origin'
jj tag list
jj tag track v2.4.0 --remote origin

Remote tags are local observations after fetch. jj 0.45.1 provides tracked/untracked remote-tag predicates and includes untracked remote tags in the documented default immutable-head expression. A tag can be a policy boundary without being a bookmark and without making every descendant immutable.

Maintenance and debugging

Repository maintenance has a recoverability cost. Before jj util gc, inspect operation history, evolution records, local rescue bookmarks, and remote state. Config GC is a different operation: it removes obsolete configuration entries, not unreachable commit objects. Git maintenance and jj maintenance can operate on related object stores in a colocated repository; use the backend's documented tooling and avoid concurrent writers.

jj op log
jj evolog -r 'hidden()'
jj bookmark list --all-remotes
jj util gc
jj util backend name
jj version

For a bug report, capture jj version, backend/colocation status, effective relevant configuration, command line, operation IDs, and a minimal graph that reproduces the result. Do not include credentials or private repository content. A machine-readable template should disable pager and colour and use full IDs. A human log can use labels, relative times, and short IDs, but it is not stable interchange.

Completion and Linux integration

Generate completion from the same binary whose commands are being documented:

jj util completion bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/jj
jj util completion zsh > ~/.zfunc/_jj
jj util completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/jj.fish

Static completion becomes stale after a release upgrade. Keep it under the shell's supported directory, start a new shell or source it as appropriate, and regenerate when the 0.45.1 command tree differs. A prompt should use a bounded, no-pager query and should not run a broad diff on every redraw:

jj --ignore-working-copy --no-pager --color=never log -r @ -T \
  'change_id.shortest(10) ++ " " ++ if(conflict, "C", "") ++ " " ++ bookmarks'

Shell functions should preserve exit status. If a prompt suppresses errors, it should do so outside publication and recovery commands; never wrap a push, rewrite, or restore in a fallback that hides failure.

Part XVII — Workflow map and complete real workflows

The eleven entries below are a map of the complete narratives that follow, not substitutes for them. Each map entry identifies the authoritative worked case; read that case for the starting graph, commands, resulting graph/ref state, identity consequences, conflicts, recovery, and cleanup. The detailed language and command explanations remain in Parts IV–XV; the cases apply them in sequence.

1. Branchless daily development — map

See Branchless day: from fetch to publication. Fetch; create a child of the imported trunk; work in @; use jj log -r '@:: & mutable()'; make changes with describe/squash/split/absorb; create a publication bookmark only at the boundary; push; then forget it when its server purpose ends.

2. GitHub feature and stacked PRs — map

See Case study: a branchless GitHub feature through review and stacked GitHub review. Use one bookmark per PR boundary, rebase the mutable stack onto main@origin, move bookmarks, push, and let GitHub merge. Treat server merge and local graph update as separate fetch steps.

3. Gerrit patch stack — map

See Gerrit patch stack over two review iterations. Keep Gerrit Change-Id footers in descriptions, use jj change IDs for local evolution, edit an early review, let descendants rebase, then upload the series again. Fetch landed changes and rebase the remaining stack.

4. Rewriting an early change after review — map

See Case 4: rewrite an early reviewed change.

jj edit A
jj describe -m 'API: corrected quota model'
jj squash --from @ --into @- -- 'glob:src/**'
jj log -r '::@'
jj git push --bookmark review --remote origin

Review the operation log before and after. The review bookmark must be moved to the successor tip; the change ID is the local continuity signal.

5. Upstream synchronisation — map

See Upstream movement with a conflict branch.

jj git fetch --remote origin
jj rebase -b 'roots(main@origin..@)' -o main@origin
jj log -r '@:: & mutable() & conflicts()'
jj resolve

Choose -b for a whole relative stack and -r for surgical selection. Do not substitute a Git branch mental model for the source/destination semantics.

6. Two remotes — map

See Case study: two remotes and one local DAG. Fetch GitHub and Gerrit independently, qualify symbols, name publication bookmarks explicitly, and make each push command specify its remote.

7. Moving unfinished work — map

See Two machines and a temporary publication. Create a temporary bookmark, push to a private remote, fetch on the second clone, edit or rebase there, and delete the temporary bookmark after verifying the receiving clone.

8. Build/review workspaces — map

See Case study: build, review, and development workspaces. Add separate workspaces at the build and review commits, use sparse patterns where appropriate, and remember that a shared rewrite can make either workspace stale.

9. Recovery — map

See Recovery and operations. Stop, record jj op log, inspect with --at-op, then undo or restore the operation. Do not attempt recovery by guessing commit IDs alone.

10. Git in a colocated repository — map

See Native Git in a colocated checkout. Use Git for inspection, hooks, and transport when useful; import ref changes before relying on them; never let independent worktree writers race.

11. Revset-driven daily work — map

See Revset-driven daily gate.

alias jj-stack='jj log -r "@:: & mutable()"'
jj log -r 'mutable() ~ ::remote_bookmarks()'
jj diff -r 'roots((@:: & mutable()))..@'
jj run -r '@:: & mutable() & conflicts()' -- test -f CONFLICTS

Revsets let policy be expressed once and reused across log, diff, run, rebase, and publication checks.

How to read a complete workflow

A workflow in this book is a state transition, not a list of commands. Read each narrative with two graphs in mind. The commit graph records the changes, parents, conflict values, and publication refs. The operation graph records how the repository view got there. A command can leave the commit graph looking familiar while still creating a new operation, changing the working-copy commit, or importing a remote ref. Conversely, a server-side merge or review action can change the remote graph without creating a local jj operation at all. The boundary matters whenever the next command depends on what is actually known locally.

The compact notation C1, C2, and C3 names commit IDs in a diagram; it does not name jj change IDs. A rewritten commit normally receives a new commit ID while its change ID can continue through the successor relationship. A bookmark is a name pointing at one commit, a remote bookmark is imported remote state, and a tracking relationship records which local and remote names correspond. None of those names makes @ follow automatically. The current workspace's working-copy commit is the only meaning of @, and another workspace can have a different @ in the same repository.

At each checkpoint, ask what was snapshotted, which commits were selected, where the destination is, and whether the command is a content operation, a graph rewrite, a ref operation, or an operation-log operation. That classification predicts most surprises. For example, jj restore changes recorded content; it is not an operation undo and it does not move a bookmark. jj undo changes the repository view to the prior operation; it does not mean “remove the diff from this commit”. jj git push publishes a Git ref and may update tracking state; it does not publish every mutable descendant merely because the commits are reachable.

CheckpointRecord before continuingWhy it is useful
Before editingworkspace, @, selected stack, bookmarks, remote bookmarks, conflicts, and jj op log -n 3Separates the local starting view from an already-imported remote change.
Before a rewritesource revset, destination revset, fileset, and whether the source is mutablePrevents a broad revset or an unintended fileset from changing an ancestor or a publication tip.
After a rewritenew commit IDs, preserved change IDs, successor/descendant graph, conflict values, and moved refsShows whether the operation preserved the intended logical change and which publication names now need movement.
Before publishingexact bookmark(s), remote, remote target, and the diff relative to the imported baseTurns “push my work” into an auditable ref update, especially when GitHub and Gerrit share a repository.
After publishinglocal bookmark, remote bookmark, tracking relation, server-side review state, and local operation IDDistinguishes a successful local ref export from a review that has actually been accepted or merged.

The narratives use this ledger selectively rather than printing the same five-row table every time. When a workflow says “the descendants rebase”, read that as a graph claim: jj creates successor commits whose parent edges and commit IDs may differ, then keeps the logical stack connected. When it says “the review bookmark must move”, read that as a ref claim: the bookmark remains a separate name and will not necessarily be carried to the successor by the rewrite. When it says “resolve and continue”, read that as a content claim: the conflict value is replaced in the affected commit and its descendants may then be rewritten again. These distinctions are the reason the workflows are not Git branch recipes with jj spelling.

Primary route and later lookup

The primary route through this Part is deliberately short at the map and long in the linked narratives immediately below. The authoritative workflow prose is here: the later Part XVIII casebook is a practice and lookup mode, not a prerequisite chapter. The route is therefore: read the map, choose a narrative, follow its links to the detailed operation or language explanation only when a command’s semantics need review, then use the appendices for spelling and option lookup. This keeps a reader who is solving a publication or recovery problem from having to infer the workflow from an alphabetical command list.

For review work, the GitHub narrative is the authoritative local-to-publication story and the Gerrit narrative is the authoritative patch-set story. For graph recovery, the operation laboratory is authoritative; for a file-level content rollback, the restore chapter is authoritative. The same subject can appear later because it serves a different purpose—practice, synthesis, or lookup—but the cross-reference should always point back to the teaching route rather than silently establishing a competing definition.

End-to-end workflow narratives

Branchless day: from fetch to publication

Start with an imported trunk and no local bookmark for the feature. This is not an unfinished branch; it is an intentional unnamed graph boundary.

main@origin -- T
                \
                 @_0  empty mutable working-copy commit
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj new main@origin -m 'Cache: bound memory use'
# implement the change
jj status
jj diff
jj describe -m 'Cache: bound memory use'
jj new -m 'Cache: expose metrics'
# implement dependent change
jj log -r 'roots(main@origin..@)::'
jj log -r 'mutable() ~ ::remote_bookmarks()'

At this stage the graph is useful without a bookmark. The first change can be revised by selecting it through a change ID or description; the dependent change automatically follows. The publication boundary appears only when a server review is ready:

jj bookmark create gh/cache -r 'roots(main@origin..@)'
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark gh/cache
gh pr create --head gh/cache --base main

If there are two changes intended as one PR, point the bookmark at the stack tip and use a server/UI description that explains the stack. If they are intended as two stacked PRs, create two bookmarks. The graph decides; the names are interfaces.

Review iteration and early rewrite

reviewed state:  main -- A -- B -- C
                              ▲    ▲
                            gh/base gh/tip

feedback on A:
main -- A′ -- B′ -- C′
         same logical A; all commit IDs after A may differ
jj edit A
# edit files
jj describe -m 'API: correct quota invariant'
jj log -r 'gh/base | gh/tip | ::@'
jj diff --from 'gh/base@origin' --to gh/base
jj bookmark set gh/base -r A
jj bookmark set gh/tip -r C
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark gh/base --bookmark gh/tip

Do not move only the tip if the base review has its own bookmark. Rewriting A can affect both server refs. If the push is rejected, fetch and compare expected remote targets before deciding whether the local rewrite should replace a remote update.

Upstream movement with a conflict branch

jj git fetch --remote origin
jj rebase -b 'roots(main@origin..@)' -o main@origin
jj log -r '::@ & conflicts()'
jj resolve --list
jj resolve --tool meld
jj log -r '::@ & conflicts()'
jj bookmark list --all-remotes

Resolve before moving the publication bookmark. If a conflict is in an ancestor, inspect descendants even if only the ancestor's file was changed. A review bookmark that remains at a conflicted predecessor can make the push appear to succeed while publishing the wrong graph boundary.

Gerrit stack over time

day 1: main -- A(I-A) -- B(I-B) -- C(I-C)
day 2: main′-- A_2(I-A) -- B_2(I-B) -- C_2(I-C)
day 3: main″-- A(landed) -- B_3(I-B) -- C_3(I-C)
jj new main@gerrit -m 'API: introduce quota

Change-Id: Iaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa'
jj new -m 'API: wire quota

Change-Id: Ibbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbb'
jj new -m 'API: expose metrics

Change-Id: Icccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccc'
jj gerrit upload --dry-run --remote gerrit --remote-branch main
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main
# later: edit the first change
jj edit 'subject(exact:"API: introduce quota")'
jj describe --editor
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main
# later: fetch landing
jj git fetch --remote gerrit
jj rebase -b 'roots(main@gerrit..@)' -o main@gerrit

At each review iteration, local jj change identity and Gerrit footer identity answer different questions. Record both in a review ledger if a team needs to audit patch sets. The local stack can be revised continuously; upload is a publication operation over the selected stack.

Two machines and a temporary publication

machine A: local unnamed @
              |
              \- temporary handoff bookmark → origin/handoff

machine B: fetch origin/handoff → new local @

# A
jj bookmark create handoff -r @
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark handoff

# B
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj new 'handoff@origin'
jj log -r '::@'
jj bookmark forget handoff@origin

The handoff transfers commits and a Git bookmark observation. It does not transfer A's operation DAG, workspace-local @, uncommitted filesystem edits, or editor state. If the work is unfinished, commit a deliberate WIP change rather than relying on files that another machine cannot see.

Multiple workspaces in one repository

shared DAG: root -- A -- B -- C
workspace dev:   dev@ = C (active edits)
workspace build: build@ = B (repeatable build)
workspace review: review@ = A (review baseline)
jj workspace add ../build --name build -r B --sparse-patterns full
jj workspace add ../review --name review -r A --sparse-patterns copy
jj workspace list
jj -R ../build run -- cargo test
jj -R ../review show -r @ --stat
jj workspace update-stale

The build command's private or workspace filesystem must not be confused with dev's current @. A rewrite of A changes the commit graph observed by all three workspaces. Update stale workspaces only after checking for unrecorded files and decide whether a stable build should instead use a temporary clone.

Native Git in a colocated checkout

jj bookmark create review -r @
jj git export
git -C "$(jj root)" show-ref
git -C "$(jj root)" log --oneline --all
git -C "$(jj root)" fetch origin
jj git import
jj bookmark list --all-remotes

Git is valuable for ecosystem tooling and transport, but it cannot show jj change IDs, operation history, or stored multi-sided conflict values. A Git-side ref change becomes visible to jj only at the import boundary. A Git-side worktree reset while jj is snapshotting can discard or misattribute filesystem changes; establish a single writer.

Revset-driven daily gate

[revset-aliases]
unpublished() = 'mutable() ~ ::remote_bookmarks()'
review-candidates() = 'heads(unpublished() ~ empty() ~ conflicts())'

# human inspection
jj log -r 'review-candidates()'

# machine gate
jj log --no-pager --color=never --count -r 'review-candidates()'

# inspect each candidate
jj show -r 'review-candidates()' --stat

The gate is intentionally a policy expression rather than a command alias that hides selection. Teams may choose to allow empty or conflicted WIP reviews; the important property is that the policy is explicit, testable, and reviewed as code.

Case study: a branchless GitHub feature through review

Start with a fetched trunk and no local feature bookmark. The developer creates a child of the imported remote tip and works in the workspace:

main@origin--A--B--@
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj new main@origin
jj describe -m "Parser: report malformed input"
# edit files and run tests
jj diff
jj status

The working-copy commit is already the reviewable logical change. If the tests reveal that documentation and implementation should be separate, split the change before publication:

jj split -r @ 'root-glob:src/**/*.rs'
jj log -r '@:: & mutable()'
main@origin--A--B--C(API)--D(docs)--@

Create a bookmark at the boundary GitHub should expose. If the two changes are one PR, use one bookmark at D. If they should be stacked PRs, create names at C and D and publish both explicitly. The bookmark is a ref for GitHub; it is not the local unit of editing.

jj bookmark create pr/parser-api -r C
jj bookmark create pr/parser-docs -r D
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark pr/parser-api
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark pr/parser-docs

Suppose review changes C. Edit C, amend its tree and description, and inspect the successors of D and @. Because C is an ancestor, the descendants receive updated commit IDs. Move only the publication bookmark that represents C and push it explicitly; the dependent PR bookmark must also be moved if its target changed.

jj edit C
# edit src/parser.rs
jj describe -m "Parser: report malformed input"
jj log -r 'C::@'
jj bookmark set pr/parser-api -r C
jj bookmark set pr/parser-docs -r D
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark pr/parser-api
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark pr/parser-docs

If GitHub rejects the update, fetch first and compare the remote bookmark. A rejection may indicate that another actor moved the ref, that the local tracking relationship is stale, or that server-side branch protection disallows the update. Do not respond with a blind force push. Determine whether the local graph is the intended successor of the remote commit and whether the GitHub branch policy allows replacement.

Case study: main moves under a stack

old: main@origin--A--B
                         \--C--D
new remote after fetch: main@origin--A--B--E--F

local stack before rebase:
                    C--D
                   /
main@origin(old)--B
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj log -r 'main@origin'
jj rebase -s 'roots(main@origin..D)' -d main@origin
jj log -r 'D:: & mutable()'
jj diff --from old-main --to main@origin

Choose the source set carefully. A broad source selection can include an unrelated fork; a narrow selection can leave a dependent child behind. Record the old trunk commit before the fetch if you need a precise comparison. After the rebase, inspect changed commit IDs and run tests at the stack head. Update publication bookmarks only after the graph is correct, then push them explicitly.

Case study: Gerrit’s patch-set lifecycle

Gerrit recognises a patch set by its commit message’s Gerrit Change-Id footer, while jj recognises an evolving logical change by its own change ID. They can coexist in one description. A rewrite normally changes the Git commit ID, may preserve the jj change ID, and should preserve the Gerrit footer if the intent is a new patch set for the same Gerrit review.

origin/main--A--B_1--C_1--D_1
                  |    |
                  review  review
                  Change-Id Iabc  Change-Id Idef
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main -r 'B_1::D_1'

Use the command’s supported commit and metadata options to set reviewers, topic, work-in-progress/private state, and push options. The local upload transport and the server’s review interpretation are separate layers: validate the former with jj’s dry-run/verbose facilities and treat the latter as Gerrit behaviour that requires server documentation or a real Gerrit instance.

Now a reviewer requests a fix to B_1:

jj edit B_1
# edit and test
jj describe -m 'API: validate parser limits

Change-Id: Iabc...'
jj log -r 'B_1::D_1'
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main -r 'B_1::D_1'

C_1 and D_1 are rebased descendants with new commit IDs. Their jj change IDs continue to identify their logical changes when the rewrite is an evolution; their Gerrit footers continue to identify their server reviews if descriptions were preserved. If a footer was absent at upload, jj 0.45.1 generated it on the uploaded object, not in the local description, so fetching can reveal a divergent uploaded successor. In that case either abandon the local duplicate and continue from the fetched review object, or rebase the local change onto the appropriate trunk with jj rebase --skip-emptied ..., as the target help describes. If a footer is missing or duplicated in the actual uploaded description, inspect the commit trailers and server response rather than assuming jj metadata supplies the server identity.

Case study: landed lower change, remaining upper stack

before server integration:
main@origin--A--B
                 \--C(review 1)--D(review 2)--E(review 3)

after review 1 lands:
main@origin--A--B--C′
local reviews:       D--E (still based on old C)

Fetch the new remote branch, identify whether the landed commit is equivalent to the local C by change ID, diff, or server metadata, then rebase the remaining stack onto the fetched trunk. Do not simply delete C and assume D/E will find the right parent: abandoning or rebasing the wrong node can produce duplicate changes or conflicts.

jj git fetch --remote gerrit
jj log -r 'main@origin | C::E'
# choose the remaining stack explicitly
jj rebase -s 'roots(D::E)' -d main@origin
jj log -r 'E:: & mutable()'

When a review is abandoned, a local change can be retained as a new change, moved to another publication bookmark, or abandoned after creating a safety bookmark. The correct action depends on whether the code is still wanted; server review state is not a command to delete local graph state.

Case study: two remotes and one local DAG

local graph:
upstream/main@origin--A--B--C--@--D

refs:
  origin/main       = B
  gerrit/main       = B
  github/pr-parser  = C

Qualify all remote symbols. Use origin/main or the exact jj remote-bookmark spelling shown by jj log, and pass --remote on push/upload. A local bookmark called main can obscure which publication channel is intended; avoid it unless the repository convention gives it one unambiguous meaning.

jj git fetch --remote origin
jj git fetch --remote gerrit
jj log -r 'main@origin | main@gerrit | github/pr-parser'
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark github/pr-parser
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main -r '@:: & mutable()'

One commit can be reachable from multiple publication systems, but server policy is not shared. A GitHub branch protection rule does not protect a Gerrit review ref, and a Gerrit upload option does not affect a GitHub push. Keep credentials, aliases, and remote names explicit.

Case study: moving unfinished work safely

Unfinished work has value but also a publication risk. Create a temporary bookmark with a name that says why it exists, push only to an access-controlled remote, and remove it after the receiving machine verifies the graph:

jj bookmark create transfer/2026-09-parser -r @
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark transfer/2026-09-parser
# machine B
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj log -r 'transfer/2026-09-parser@origin'
jj new transfer/2026-09-parser@origin
# after verification on both machines
jj bookmark delete transfer/2026-09-parser
jj git push --remote origin --deleted

Do not treat a temporary bookmark as a private stash unless the remote and access controls actually make it private. If the graph is sensitive, transfer via an encrypted private remote or another controlled mechanism. The operation log itself is not the transport protocol between independent clones.

Case study: build, review, and development workspaces

Use one repository with three workspaces when the tasks need different filesystem states but share object storage:

jj workspace add --name build -r main@origin ../repo-build
jj workspace add --name review -r 'bookmarks(exact:"pr/parser")' ../repo-review
jj workspace list

In the development workspace, rewrite the stack freely. In review, inspect the publication target and run review-specific tools. In build, run a clean build against the pinned commit. After a rewrite, check all three workspaces; a stale review or build workspace should be updated deliberately, not silently moved by a prompt hook.

Workflow casebook: maintain the graph across a working week

The following cases use the same operating rule: maintain a local graph that represents the work, and create or move a publication name only when an external system needs a ref. Each case records the graph, the publication boundary, and the recovery boundary. The commands are examples for jj 0.45.1; hosting behaviour is marked separately.

Case 1: branchless daily development

Monday after fetch:
  main@origin--A--B(@)
                 B = API change, unnamed

Tuesday review preparation:
  main@origin--A--B--C(@)
                      C = test/docs tail

Thursday upstream moves:
  main@origin--A--B--C
                     \
  new main@origin-----B'--C'(@)  after rebase
  1. Fetch and inspect the imported trunk.
  2. Create a child and do not name it while the change is private.
  3. Use jj new for a new logical boundary and jj describe for the current change.
  4. Use jj log, jj diff, and a bounded revset to inspect the stack.
  5. Create a bookmark only when a review or handoff needs a Git ref.
  6. After upstream movement, rebase mutable roots, resolve stored conflicts, and republish explicit bookmarks.
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj new main@origin -m 'API: enforce quota'
# edit and test
jj new -m 'API: add quota tests'
jj log -G -r 'roots(main@origin..@)::'
jj bookmark create review/quota -r @
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark review/quota

The local history never required a branch to move the working copy. The bookmark was an interface introduced at publication time. If the review is abandoned, keep or forget the bookmark according to server state; abandoning a local commit is a separate decision.

Case 2: stacked GitHub review

main@origin--A--B--C--D(@)
               ▲     ▲
             pr/api  pr/metrics
