Publish B and D as boundaries only after verifying that B is the intended base PR and D is the intended dependent PR. When review changes A, edit by change ID. Automatic descendant rebasing produces B', C', and D'. Compare each local bookmark with its remote counterpart, update all affected bookmarks, and push explicitly. When GitHub merges the base PR, fetch before rebasing the remaining stack. The server's PR base and merge strategy are not encoded by jj's operation log.

jj log -r 'pr/api | pr/metrics | pr/api@origin | pr/metrics@origin'
jj edit 'change_id(API_CHANGE)'
jj describe -m 'API: correct invariant'
jj log -r 'roots(main@origin..@)::'
jj diff --from pr/api@origin --to pr/api
jj bookmark set pr/api -r 'change_id(API_CHANGE)'
jj bookmark set pr/metrics -r 'change_id(METRICS_CHANGE)'
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark pr/api --bookmark pr/metrics

Case 3: Gerrit patch stack over two review iterations

iteration 1: main@gerrit--B--C--D
             Iapi         Itest       Imetrics

iteration 2: main@gerrit--B'--C'--D'
             same footers, new commit IDs,
             new Gerrit patch sets when server accepts

Use one jj change per reviewable change and preserve a Gerrit Change-Id footer in each description. Upload a selected stack to the review ref according to Gerrit policy. On an early review comment, edit the jj change by change ID; do not create a local fixup branch solely to obtain a new commit. Inspect descendants, resolve any stored conflict, and re-upload. jj can prove the footer and local IDs; only Gerrit can prove that the server associated the object with the intended review and patch set.

jj evolog -r 'change_id(API_CHANGE)'
jj log -r 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::' -T 'change_id ++ " " ++ commit_id ++ "\n"'
jj gerrit upload --dry-run --remote gerrit --remote-branch main \
  --revision 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main \
  --revision 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'

When B lands, fetch the new Gerrit main and rebase C/D, not the remote bookmark. If a submit strategy changes the effective ancestry, use the fetched remote bookmark as the new base after inspecting it. Abandoning a Gerrit review does not abandon the local change; clean the local graph only after preserving any needed footer and operation evidence.

Case 4: rewrite an early reviewed change

before: main--A--B--C--D(@)
              A reviewed and published

after:  main--A'--B'--C'--D'(@)
         A/B/C/D change IDs follow successors;
         all affected commit IDs change

Make a safety record with op log and a temporary bookmark. Edit A by change ID, make the smallest semantic repair, run focused tests, and inspect the entire descendant stack. The fact that B' is clean does not prove its tests still test the same contract. Compare old and new diffs with evolution/inter-diff output. Move every review bookmark and publish with an explicit safety decision.

jj bookmark create before-early-rewrite -r @
jj op log -n 3
jj edit 'change_id(A_CHANGE)'
# edit, test, and snapshot
jj evolog -r 'change_id(A_CHANGE)' -p
jj log -G -r 'roots(main@origin..@)::'
jj log -r 'conflicts() & ::@'

Case 5: GitHub and Gerrit from one clone

                 +-- github/pr-cache
main@github --A-+
                 \-- gerrit review stack
main@gerrit ----A--B--C(@)

One local commit can be exported to both systems, but the systems may have different trunk objects, review identities, ref namespaces, permissions, and merge policies. Keep two publication stories. Fetch each remote explicitly; qualify revsets such as main@github and main@gerrit; create a GitHub bookmark only for the GitHub ref; and invoke Gerrit upload with its explicit remote/branch. Do not assume a Gerrit footer controls GitHub review or that a GitHub branch name supplies a Gerrit topic.

jj git fetch --remote github
jj git fetch --remote gerrit
jj log -G -r 'main@github | main@gerrit | ::@'
jj bookmark create github/cache -r @
jj git push --remote github --bookmark github/cache
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main \
  --revision 'roots(main@gerrit..@)::'

Case 6: move unfinished work between machines

Operation IDs and @ do not transfer through Git. Publish a temporary bookmark, fetch it on the second clone, and create a new local child there. The first machine can continue to observe the handoff ref but must not assume it follows the second machine's new working-copy commit. If both machines edit the same logical change, fetching can expose divergent successors. Compare evolog and select a policy before force-updating the handoff ref.

# A
jj bookmark set handoff/alice -r @
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark handoff/alice

# B
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj new 'handoff/alice@origin' -m 'Continue cache work'
# after handoff:
jj bookmark set handoff/bob -r @
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark handoff/bob

Case 7: recovery after a wrong rewrite

Stop after noticing the mistake. Do not create several “repair” operations while guessing. Record the current operation, use op show and --at-op to identify the last good state, use undo only when it is the immediate last operation, and use named restore/revert when later operations must remain meaningful. If a remote push occurred, perform a separate server/ref repair and fetch afterward.

jj op log -n 20
jj op show OP -p
jj --at-operation OP log -G -r 'all()'
jj op diff --from GOOD --to CURRENT
jj op restore GOOD
jj op log -n 5
jj log -G -r 'all()'

After the repair, verify the commit graph, operation graph, bookmarks, remote bookmarks, working-copy files, and any published review identities. A command returning zero is not the recovery assertion; the assertion is that the repository is now in the intended state and that the choice is recorded.

Case 8: revset-driven automation

Use revsets to define a bounded domain and templates to emit stable records. Discovery should be read-only and cardinality-aware. Mutation should receive full IDs or explicit commit selectors, run with a known configuration, and leave an operation record. Never parse the graph glyphs of ordinary jj log in automation.

domain='mutable() & ::@ ~ ::remote_bookmarks() ~ conflicts()'
jj log --no-pager --color=never -r \"$domain\" \
  -T 'change_id ++ \"\\t\" ++ commit_id ++ \"\\t\" ++ description.first_line() ++ \"\\n\"'
jj diff --no-pager -r \"$domain\" --summary
# apply a selected, reviewed operation only after checking cardinality

Run this style of automation in CI with an explicit JJ_CONFIG or --config-file, a pinned binary, and no implicit remote. Make the script fail when the domain is empty or unexpectedly broad if either condition would be unsafe. Keep a fixture that exercises a fork, merge, conflict, remote bookmark, and duplicate subject so the query is tested against the cases that make shortcuts fail.

Part XVIII — Practice, reference, and fieldbooks

Part XVII closes the linear teaching route. Part XVIII is an intentional second mode of use: the advanced field manual applies the model to day-to-day decisions, the language and command sections are lookup references, the labbook and curriculum provide controlled practice, and the hosting/recovery sections supply incident and publication procedures. The headings below are grouped here so that the reader does not mistake a reference atlas for another competing introduction.

Read this part selectively. A first pass can stop after Part XVII. A reader investigating a difficult graph can enter the field manual; a reader writing automation can enter the language or command reference; a reader preparing a review can enter the hosting fieldbook; and a reader recovering from an error can enter the recovery recipes. The cross-links point back to the primary teaching chapters whenever a detail depends on an earlier invariant.

SubjectAuthoritative teachingPractice or workflowLookup reference
Graph and rewritingParts II–IIIRewrite and mechanics laboratoriesAppendices A, B, G
Revsets, filesets, templatesParts IV, V, XIVLanguage laboratories and revset-driven caseAppendices C, D, E
Bookmarks and Git transportParts VI–VIIGitHub/Gerrit workflowsAppendices H, I
Conflicts and recoveryParts IX–XConflict and recovery laboratoriesAppendix J
Workspaces and configurationParts XI–XIIWorkspace and Linux configuration laboratoriesAppendix F, K
CLIRelevant semantic chaptersPart XVII workflows and command laboratoriesPart XV and Appendices A–B

The rule is simple: the Parts named in the second column teach the subject; the later sections in the third column exercise it; the locations in the fourth column are lookup aids. A later fieldbook may combine subjects, but it is not a second canonical definition. When a fieldbook appears to disagree with a teaching chapter, follow the target-version command entry and the cited local validation before treating it as a new rule.

The advanced field manual — practice and decision procedures

Use this field manual when a jj operation crosses several state boundaries at once. A single operation can snapshot a filesystem, rewrite a set of commits, move local names, update a workspace, and leave an operation record. Looking at only one of those layers is how apparently impossible states are produced. The useful question is not “which command is the jj equivalent of my Git command?” but “which state transition do I want, and which of the other layers must remain invariant?”

Every investigation in this chapter uses the same notation. A capital letter is a symbolic commit label in a disposable fixture; cid(A) is its commit ID; chg(A) is its change ID; @ is the current workspace working-copy commit; and op_n is an operation-log node. A line such as bookmark review → C is a local name, while review@origin → C_0 is a remote bookmark observed after fetch. These are not interchangeable identifiers.

State accounting before action

Before a risky operation, write down a small state ledger. This is faster than recovering from a mistaken broad revset and it makes a code review of shell automation possible.

LayerQuestionEvidence commandWhat a mismatch means
FilesystemAre there edits not yet in the recorded working-copy tree?jj diff --summary, then jj statusThe next command may snapshot more than the operator thinks.
Working copyWhich workspace owns @ and which commit is it?jj log -r @, jj workspace listA second workspace may be the one that becomes stale.
GraphWhat are the exact parents, descendants, and heads?jj log -r 'all()' with a parent templateA visual linear stack may conceal a merge or fork.
IdentityIs this a commit ID, change ID, bookmark, tag, or operation ID?jj show, jj evolog, jj op logUsing a short ID from the wrong namespace can select nothing or the wrong object.
ImmutabilityWhich commits are protected by immutable_heads()?jj log -r 'immutable_heads()'A failed rewrite may be protection working correctly.
PublicationWhich local and remote names point into this graph?jj bookmark list --all-remotes, jj tag listA local rewrite may require an explicit force update or a new review ref.
OperationsWhat operation created the state, and is it integrated?jj op log, jj op showRecovery should start from the operation boundary, not guesswork.

Record the ledger before and after. In a real repository, use full IDs in the record but symbolic labels in discussion. A shell script should discover full IDs, validate its assumptions, perform one operation, and discover the resulting state again. It should not assume that a commit ID remains valid after a rewrite merely because the change ID is stable.

Read-only observation and snapshot policy

There are two different meanings of “read-only”. A command may not intentionally rewrite history, yet it may snapshot the working copy. For a human at a terminal that is normally a convenience: the graph catches up with the editor before the log is displayed. For a diagnostic script, it is an implicit write to repository state and can race another process editing the same workspace.

Use ordinary commands when the current filesystem is part of the question. Use --ignore-working-copy when the question is specifically about the last recorded commit, or when another process owns the workspace. Use --at-operation OP when the question is about a historical repository view; it implies that current filesystem state must not be inserted into that view.

# Human inspection: include edits in the snapshot boundary.
jj status
jj log -r '@:: & mutable()'

# Stable inspection of the recorded commit, without taking a snapshot.
jj --ignore-working-copy log -r @ -T 'commit_id ++ " " ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'

# Historical inspection: OP is an operation ID from jj op log.
jj --at-operation OP log -r 'all()'

Do not infer that --ignore-working-copy makes a mutating command safe. It prevents snapshotting; it does not turn rebase, abandon, bookmark movement, or operation restoration into observation. The four questions remain separate: what state is loaded, what set is selected, what mutation is requested, and which workspace or ref is updated.

Graph invariants as tests

A robust workflow states invariants in terms of relationships rather than display order. For example, after rewriting an early change in a three-change stack:

  • the edited change has the same change ID before and after;
  • its commit ID is different if its tree, parents, metadata, or conflict value changed;
  • the descendant changes still exist and are successors of their prior evolutions;
  • the local publication bookmark points to the intended new stack tip;
  • the remote bookmark has not moved until an explicit push;
  • the operation log contains one operation describing the rewrite and any automatic rebases.

These assertions survive changes to the default log template. Assertions based on “the third line begins with @” do not. In a fixture, print a tab-separated record with full commit ID, change ID, parent IDs, bookmark names, conflict state, and description. Compare the fields separately so an expected commit-ID change is not mistaken for a lost change.

Publication boundaries in practice

Local jj development can remain unnamed, but a Git server consumes refs. The publication boundary is therefore an interface, not a preference. The local graph may be:

main@origin -- A -- B -- C -- D -- @
                         ↑             ↑
                   review/base     review/tip (local only)

At publication, choose which node represents the server-facing boundary. If the review should contain C..D, create or move a bookmark to D and push that name. If it should contain the whole stack from A, the server's base and the pushed ref define that interpretation; a local bookmark is not a substitute for checking the server's base.

After a push, local and remote bookmarks are two observations. A tracking relationship lets jj report whether the local name is ahead, behind, synchronised, or conflicted with the corresponding remote name. It does not make a local bookmark follow the working-copy commit. Editing files after a push changes @, not a bookmark that happens to have pointed at the old @.

A safe publication protocol

  1. Fetch the target remote and inspect main@remote, the local bookmark, and the candidate stack.
  2. Choose a publication name that identifies the server-facing review, and set it to an exact commit only after inspecting that commit's parents.
  3. Run a dry-run or preview where the command provides one. Otherwise print the candidate ref and its remote counterpart with full IDs.
  4. Push one named bookmark to one explicitly named remote. Avoid an unqualified push in a repository with GitHub and Gerrit remotes.
  5. Fetch again if the server transforms or creates refs, then inspect the resulting remote bookmark.
  6. After review feedback, rewrite the local change, verify change and commit identity, and push the same publication name. The server-side interpretation of that update is host-specific.

The protocol is intentionally more explicit than “push @”. @ is a workspace symbol, and its value can change on every snapshot or jj new. A bookmark is a durable interface choice that can be reviewed, tracked, and published.

Same bookmark names on several remotes

Suppose a repository has github and gerrit remotes, each with a main bookmark. The unqualified symbol main denotes a local bookmark; main@github and main@gerrit denote different remote observations. They may have identical commit IDs today and diverge tomorrow. A local bookmark can track one corresponding remote relationship; it cannot mean “the main branch of the organisation” without naming which remote supplies that fact.

jj git fetch --remote github
jj git fetch --remote gerrit
jj log -r 'main@github | main@gerrit'
jj bookmark list --remote github
jj bookmark list --remote gerrit

# Publication remains explicit.
jj git push --remote github --bookmark github/pr-17
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main -r 'roots(gerrit-main..@)'

Do not use a config default to conceal this distinction in a shared script. A personal alias can choose a remote for interactive work, but the alias should print or encode the remote and should refuse to publish if the selected bookmark is absent, conflicted, or unexpectedly behind its tracking target.

Colocation and native Git boundaries

A colocated repository has a Git directory and jj metadata associated with the same working directory. This is valuable for an advanced Git user because Git-native tools can inspect exported commits and refs while jj provides mutable graph operations. It also means two tools can change related state. The safe model is “one filesystem owner at a time, explicit import after Git-side ref changes”.

ActionGit object/ref effectjj effectFollow-up
Edit a fileNone until Git writes a commitNext jj snapshot sees itDecide which command owns the next snapshot.
git commitCreates a Git commit and moves a Git refjj metadata is not automatically a matching logical changeUse the supported Git import path, then inspect the jj graph.
git update-refMoves a Git refjj's remote/local bookmark view may be staleRun jj git import and inspect remote bookmarks.
jj bookmark setMay export through backend policyMoves a jj bookmarkUse jj git export when the local Git view must be current.
jj rebaseCreates/exportable Git objects for successorsRewrites mutable jj commits and descendantsPush the intended bookmark, not an obsolete commit ID.
git reset --hardMoves a Git ref and overwrites filesCan leave workspace state stale or create surprising next snapshotsPrefer jj workspace commands; if used, stop other writers and reconcile.

Git object reachability and jj operation reachability are different graphs. Git garbage collection knows about Git refs and Git objects; it does not preserve an unexported jj operation history merely because that history is important. Conversely, jj operation recovery can restore a repository view whose commits have not yet been exported to Git. Do not run aggressive Git maintenance without knowing which objects and refs provide recovery.

Ref import/export experiment

In a disposable colocated fixture, create a bookmark in jj, export it, and compare the Git ref. Then move the Git ref directly and import:

jj bookmark create experiment -r @
jj git export
git show-ref --verify refs/heads/experiment

# This changes Git state without moving the jj bookmark first.
git update-ref refs/heads/experiment "$(jj log -r 'root()' -T commit_id)"
jj git import
jj bookmark list --all-remotes

The exact exported ref names and handling of imported Git refs are part of the Git backend contract, not an invitation to edit internal jj files. Always use supported import/export commands. The experiment establishes a habit: after a Git-side ref mutation, refresh jj's view before reasoning about a remote bookmark or immutability boundary.

Review identities: one local change, several server views

Review systems commonly associate successive Git commits with a review by a message footer, a ref, or server metadata. jj's change ID is a local identity for an evolving change. These identities can coexist without being equal. A rewrite may preserve the jj change ID while changing the commit ID; a Gerrit upload may preserve a Change-Id: footer while creating a new patch set; a GitHub pull request may continue to use the same branch ref while its tip commit changes.

jj change Q
  |- commit q_0, footer I123, pushed at patch set 1
  \- commit q_1, footer I123, pushed at patch set 2

server review identity             jj identity
review ref / Change-Id              change ID Q
particular object                   commit ID q_0 or q_1

When debugging a review update, record all three: old and new commit IDs, the jj change ID, and the host-side review identifier. If one is missing, the update may be correct but difficult to explain. A command that only prints a short commit ID is insufficient evidence for a review audit.

Rebase surgery: choosing the smallest transformation

Rebase is often described as moving commits, but in jj its source selection and destination selection are independent. Start by stating whether parent edges, tree deltas, or both should change.

IntentPrimary operationWhat remains invariantInspect afterwards
Move a stack to a new baserebase -s STACK -d BASESelected changes and order, subject to conflictsParents, successors, bookmark tip, conflicts
Move one independent changerebase -r CHANGE -d BASEUnselected graph edges as far as descendant rebasing permitsWhether descendants followed the rewritten parent
Put a change after anotherrebase -r CHANGE -A DESTChange diff, unless context creates a conflictExact parent list and merge shape
Make one change own selected filessquash, restore, or splitDepends on whether source remains and a new change is madeDiff of both source and destination
Apply a change elsewhereduplicateContent intent, not change identityNew change ID and parent edges
Remove a change from visible historyabandonUnselected commits and recovery recordsDescendants, operation log, bookmark targets

The source selection is not “the commit I clicked”. -r selects commits individually; -s selects a source commit and its descendants; -b selects a branch-like set according to the command's definition. A source set with a hole is not a contiguous stack: descendants that remain selected may be rebased around the hole, while the omitted commit stays in place. Use a parent template to verify the result.

jj log -r 'all()' -T '
commit_id.short() ++ " " ++ change_id.short() ++
" parents=[" ++ parents.map(|p| p.commit_id().short()).join(",") ++ "] " ++
description.first_line() ++ "\n"

Ancestor rewrite with a publication bookmark

Consider a published two-change stack:

main@origin -- A -- B -- C
                    ↑       ↑
                 review/base review/tip

If B is edited, the new B′ has a new commit ID. Descendant C cannot retain its old parent edge, so jj creates a successor C′ rebased onto B′. A local bookmark pointing at C is moved to its successor as part of the rewrite. The remote bookmark remains at its previously exported commit until a push. The review server therefore sees a ref update containing new objects, while the local user experiences one logical edit to B and automatic maintenance of the stack.

If the rebase cannot apply cleanly, C′ can contain a conflict. The correct response is not to abandon B′ merely because the descendant is conflicted. Inspect the conflict value, materialise it if needed, resolve it in the descendant, and rerun tests at the stack tip. The operation log records the rewrite and resolution as separate boundaries, making “before the rebase” and “after resolution” recoverable states.

Three languages, three failure classes

jj's commit language, fileset language, and template language often appear in the same command, but they are evaluated in different domains:

LanguageValueTypical failureDiagnostic
RevsetSet of commitsA range includes a merge ancestor or has the wrong cardinalityjj log -r 'EXPR' -T commit_id
FilesetSet of repository pathsShell expands a glob or a relative path uses the wrong basejj file list 'EXPR'
TemplateTyped rendering valueMethod is called on the wrong type or an optional value is unsetjj log -T '...' in a fixture

Do not fix a revset problem by changing the template, or a fileset problem by changing the commit selector. First render the selected commits with one full ID per line. Then render selected paths against one known tree. Only then combine both in a mutating command.

Fileset command boundaries

A fileset can limit a display without limiting a graph operation, or it can define exactly which diff paths move. jj diff -r R -- root-glob:src/** restricts output. jj restore --from R --into S -- root-file:src/config.toml copies one path from one tree to another. jj squash --from R --into S -- root-glob:tests/** changes diff ownership for selected paths. The same syntax describes a path set, but the command supplies the semantics of applying that set.

When a command accepts both a commit option and fileset arguments, prove both independently. If R is a source commit and paths selects tests, first run jj diff -r R -- paths. Next check that resulting source/destination diffs differ only under paths. A successful command is not proof that the intended fileset was parsed; an empty selection can be a valid no-op.

Operation recovery as forensic work

The operation log should be treated as a forensic record, not a magical undo button. First identify the bad operation, then decide whether recovery is a new operation that reverses it or a restoration of the repository view as it existed then. These differ: restoring a historical operation can discard later integrated changes from the current view, while a revert-like operation creates a new state that preserves later history.

QuestionPreferred inspectionLikely recovery
Was the immediately previous operation wrong?jj op show, then compare current and parentjj undo
What did the repository look like before a named operation?jj op show OP, jj op diff OPRead with --at-operation; restore only after review.
Was useful work abandoned?jj evolog, hidden/explicit commit lookupDuplicate or restore useful evolution into current work.
Did a bookmark move incorrectly?jj bookmark list --all-remotes, operation diffSet/move the bookmark to the intended commit.
Did another process advance the operation head?jj op log and operation parentsInspect competing operation before undoing.

Do not run repository garbage collection while an abandoned commit or old operation is your only recovery path. Preserve the operation ID, full commit IDs, and any untracked files outside the workspace before a large repair. An operation record cannot restore an editor buffer or a file that was never snapshotted.

Recovery exercise: wrong ancestor

  1. Make a disposable three-change stack and record jj op log, the current tip, and every change ID.
  2. Edit the middle change when the intention was to edit the tip. Do not immediately continue working.
  3. Use jj op show and jj op diff to identify the operation that rewrote the ancestor.
  4. Use jj undo once. Confirm that the middle and tip commit IDs, bookmark target, and filesystem are back at the recorded state.
  5. Repeat the mistake, then perform one unrelated description edit before noticing. Compare undo with inspecting the historical operation and using an explicit restore/revert strategy.

The exercise teaches an important limitation: “undo the thing I meant” is not a semantic operation. undo operates on the latest integrated operation. Once other operations have been integrated, choose the historical operation deliberately and account for their changes.

Workspace ownership and staleness

A workspace gives another directory its own working-copy commit, not another copy of the commit store. Two workspaces can therefore have different @ values while sharing ancestors, bookmarks, and operation history. A graph rewrite seen by one workspace can make another workspace stale. The stale workspace's filesystem is still real; updating it is a reconciliation action, not a harmless refresh.

shared store
    A -- B -- C′
          \
workspace dev:   dev@ = C′
workspace build: build@ = C (stale working-copy successor)

Use a development workspace for editing and a build workspace for long-running tests when the build workspace can tolerate being updated. Before rewriting an ancestor, check jj workspace list and quiesce other writers. After the rewrite, inspect each workspace's filesystem edits before jj workspace update-stale. If build output is valuable, keep it outside the workspace or make the build reproducible; do not expect an update to preserve arbitrary generated files.

Moving unfinished work between machines

Clones do not share an operation log. They share commits and refs only when those objects are transferred through the Git backend. The portable unit is therefore an explicitly published bookmark, even if that bookmark exists for only a few minutes.

# Machine A
jj status
jj diff --stat
jj bookmark set handoff -r @
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark handoff

# Machine B
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj log -r 'handoff@origin' -T 'commit_id.normal_hex() ++ "\n"'
jj new handoff@origin
jj status

# Machine A, after confirmation
jj bookmark delete handoff
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark handoff

Do not promise that jj undo on machine B recovers an operation performed on machine A. It cannot. If the unfinished work was not exported, the second clone cannot discover it from Git. If a publication bookmark was moved twice, fetch and inspect both the current remote target and the originating machine's operation/evolution history before deciding which state is authoritative.

Book-wide case study: one change through its entire life

The following narrative deliberately follows one logical change rather than one command. It is a useful model for review notes, incident reports, and CI tooling because it keeps the change ID, commit IDs, graph edges, workspace, operation log, and host ref visible at each stage.

Stage 0: imported base

root -- A -- B
             ↑
         main@origin
workspace dev: @ = B + empty working-copy commit

After fetch, main@origin is an observation of a remote bookmark. The local repository may have an ordinary local main as well, but that is a separate ref. The working-copy commit is a child of the selected base even if it is empty. It has a commit ID and change ID, and its workspace association is local metadata. A branch-oriented Git user may describe this as checking out a branch and then creating an index/worktree state; a detached-HEAD-oriented user may describe it as detached HEAD plus an index. The jj description is more exact for both habits because the working-copy commit is part of the commit DAG and is updated through snapshot operations.

At this stage, the safe audit is: render @, @-, main@origin, full IDs, and parents; run jj status; and record jj op log. Do not create a bookmark just to make the working copy feel named. The absence of a local publication name is intentional.

Stage 1: first edit and description

Edit src/quota.rs. The filesystem changes immediately; the commit tree does not change until a snapshot boundary. Running jj status ordinarily snapshots the edit and updates the working-copy commit. The new working-copy commit has a new commit ID because its tree changed, while its change ID identifies the same evolving working-copy change. Use jj describe -m to add a subject. That metadata change can create another successor, so a script should not cache the commit ID across both operations.

jj status
jj describe -m 'add quota API'
jj log -r @ -T '
change_id.normal_hex() ++ "\t" ++ commit_id.normal_hex() ++ "\t" ++
parents.map(|p| p.commit_id().normal_hex()).join(",") ++ "\n"

The working-copy commit is not a staging area. There is no need to ask which diff hunks are “staged” before creating a new change. If the edit belongs in a separate logical change, use jj new before editing or use split/diffedit after the fact. The choice is about graph and diff ownership, not the durability of the current files.

Stage 2: dependent change

Run jj new and add tests. The old API change remains a parent, and the new working-copy commit is an empty or partially edited child while you work. Once the tests are snapshotted, the graph is:

root -- A -- B -- Q -- R
             main@origin  API  tests
                              @ = R

Q and R are separate change identities. The fact that R is a child of Q is the dependency relationship. If a test change also needs a documentation file, that is diff ownership within R; it does not require a second bookmark. The query Q::R returns both commits, while Q..R excludes Q and expresses the diff range above Q. Using the wrong one in a review tool can change the displayed diff even though both look like “the changes between Q and R”.

Stage 3: publication

For GitHub, create github/quota at R. For Gerrit, the upload command can select the range without a local bookmark, although a local name can help human review. The publication choice is not a graph operation: Q and R keep their IDs. The push may export Git objects and create a remote bookmark, after which the local tracking relationship records the remote target.

jj bookmark create github/quota -r @
jj git push --remote github --bookmark github/quota
jj bookmark list --remote github --tracked
jj gerrit upload --dry-run --remote gerrit --remote-branch main -r 'Q::R'

The GitHub ref and the Gerrit upload are different interfaces to the same local graph. A GitHub PR normally names one head ref and one base ref. Gerrit commonly receives each commit in a selected range through a review ref and associates it using message metadata. The local fact that Q is the parent of R is shared; the host-side display and review identities are not.

Stage 4: review feedback on the ancestor

The reviewer finds an API problem in Q. Use jj edit Q, modify the file, and snapshot. jj rewrites Q to Q′ and automatically rebases R to R′. The graph now has successors:

old: root -- A -- B -- Q -- R
new: root -- A -- B -- Q′ -- R′
                         ↑       ↑
                   same change  same change
                   IDs normally IDs normally

Q′ and R′ have new commit IDs. Q and R retain their logical change IDs in the ordinary evolution. The local GitHub bookmark follows the local successor of R. The remote GitHub bookmark remains at R until pushed. The Gerrit footer in Q′ should remain the same if the intended result is a new patch set of the same server review. This is the exact point at which a Git user who thinks only in branch tips may miss the fact that the dependent review also changed.

Run an interdiff or a pair of diffs for Q/Q′ and R/R′. The first shows the review response; the second mostly shows the parent-context update but can contain conflict-resolution or test changes. Record both so reviewers can distinguish intended feedback from automatic descendant consequences.

Stage 5: trunk movement

While the review is open, upstream adds C and the remote main moves. Fetch it. Do not move the local publication bookmark to C; it is a review boundary, not trunk. Rebase the local stack onto the fetched trunk and inspect the new parent edges. If the server has merged Q in the meantime, fetch its actual landed result instead of assuming C is the new parent.

jj git fetch --remote github
jj log -r 'main@github'
jj rebase -s 'roots(main@github..@)::' -d main@github
jj log -r 'main@github..@' -T '
commit_id.short() ++ " " ++ change_id.short() ++ " " ++
description.first_line() ++ "\n"

A merge from upstream can cause conflicts in Q′ or R′. The conflict is part of the new commit value. Continue to inspect, materialise, resolve, snapshot, and test; there is no separate rebase continuation token to preserve. If a stack contains multiple publication boundaries, move and push them in a way that matches the host review dependency order.

Stage 6: closure and cleanup

When GitHub merges the PR, fetch main and compare the fetched commit with the reviewed tip. The server may have used squash, merge, or rebase; the new remote main is the authority for the next local base. The feature bookmark can be forgotten locally after its remote ref is no longer needed. If deleting the remote ref is desired, express and push that deletion separately. Closing a GitHub PR, deleting its ref, forgetting a local bookmark, and abandoning a jj change are four different actions.

When Gerrit submits Q but R remains, fetch Gerrit main, rebase R onto the landed server result, preserve R's Change-Id footer, and upload a new patch set. The local jj evolution of R is still useful, but it cannot predict the exact commit that Gerrit created when Q landed. This is why host integration always begins with fetch.

What to record in a lifecycle review note

FieldExampleReason
Target versionsjj 0.45.1, Git 2.53.0Syntax and default policies are versioned.
Base refmain@github at full IDExplains the diff range and host comparison.
jj change IDsQ and R full IDsTracks logical evolution through rewrites.
Commit IDsq_0/r_0 then q_1/r_1Identifies concrete uploaded objects.
Publication refsgithub/quota, remote targetExplains what a push changed.
Server identityGerrit Change-Id: I... or PR numberMaps local change to host review.
Conflict stateCommit, path, resolution operationDistinguishes a stored conflict from a clean rewrite.
Operation IDsrewrite, resolve, push-related operationsProvides local recovery and evidence.

A review note like “rebased branch and force-pushed” is too lossy for mutable history. The fuller record states which logical changes survived, which concrete objects were replaced, which server ref moved, and which host identity remained stable.

Edge-case catalogue

Empty commits

An empty commit has no tree delta relative to its parents, but it can carry a description, a bookmark, a signature, a workspace target, and descendants. It may be an intentional review boundary or an accidental result of a squash. Query empty() within the domain you care about. Do not remove every empty node from a stack without checking whether its message records a meaningful change or whether a publication workflow uses it as a boundary.

Merge commits

A merge has multiple parents, and many operations treat its parent list as a set rather than a single base. parents(G) returns both sides. roots, heads, ranges, first-parent traversal, and descendant selection all produce different results around a merge. Before a linear-only command, query merges() & domain. If it is non-empty, state whether the operation should preserve, flatten, or deliberately introduce the merge.

Hidden commits

Hidden does not mean unreachable from every mechanism. An explicit full commit ID can identify a hidden predecessor; an ordinary visible query may omit it. If a hidden ID is introduced into a traversal, its ancestors can enter the search space. This is useful for recovery and surprising in a broad query. When comparing two results, state whether the search was current-visible or explicitly seeded with a hidden commit.

Divergent changes

A divergent change has multiple visible successors for one logical change ID. A command requiring one commit may reject the bare change ID. Use offsets or an explicit query that chooses by topology, bookmark, description, or operation provenance. Do not pick the first displayed successor solely because it appears first; the display order is not an authorship or recency guarantee unless the template says so.

Bookmark conflicts

A bookmark conflict is ref state with competing target information, usually after incompatible local/remote updates. It is not a file conflict and is not resolved by editing a conflict marker. Fetch authoritative remote state, inspect target sets, decide whether to retain, move, or delete the name, and publish only after the result is explicit. Use bookmark list with remote and tracking filters rather than a commit log alone.

Private commits

Private is a publication policy defined by a revset, not a filesystem attribute or a second commit type. A private commit can be mutable, conflicted, bookmarked, or visible locally. Ordinary push excludes it according to configuration; an explicit allow option changes that safety policy for one invocation. Always render the private set and the candidate push domain before overriding it.

Working-copy edge cases

The working-copy commit can be empty, conflicted, bookmarked, immutable after a push, stale in another workspace, or based on multiple parents. A command that creates a new child can leave the old working copy as a useful change. A command that edits an ancestor can cause the current working copy to become a successor or a conflict. Query @, @-, working_copies(), and conflicts() when the prompt alone is ambiguous.

Shell edge cases

There are at least three parsers in a complicated invocation: the shell, jj's revset/fileset/template parser, and any external editor/tool. Quote the whole expression, use -- when the command's help documents it, and avoid command substitutions that turn an empty result into a missing argument. A path containing whitespace is not evidence that a fileset is wrong; an unquoted glob being expanded before jj sees it is.

Automation edge cases

Automation must decide whether it owns snapshotting, whether it can tolerate multiple commits, whether external tools may write files, and whether network publication is allowed. Use explicit binaries, config, commit sets, filesets, templates, remotes, and colour/pager modes. Capture operation IDs and exit statuses. Fail closed on unexpected cardinality, a conflicted publication target, an untracked remote, or a changed remote target.

Language fieldbook — practice: deriving selections and output

Revsets, filesets, and templates are all functional languages, but their values live in different universes. A revset value is a set of commit nodes. A fileset value is a set of repository-relative paths. A template expression evaluates against a typed object and emits formatted output. The three languages meet at command boundaries, not in one shared evaluator. That distinction explains why an expression can be syntactically valid in one position and meaningless in another.

Revset evaluation workbench

Use this graph for the evaluations in this section. The arrows point from parent to child. The merge has two parents; F is not a head of the set containing G because F is an ancestor of G.

                 E -----+
                /        \
root -- A -- B -- C ----- G -- H
                \        /
                 D -----+

bookmarks:
  main@origin → B
  topic       → H
  release     → G
ExpressionIntermediate reasoningResult
B::Start at B; follow every child path.{B,C,D,E,G,H}
::GStart at G; follow both parent paths, including their common ancestors.{root,A,B,C,D,E,G}
B..GAncestors of G minus ancestors of B.{C,D,E,G}
B::GDescendants of B intersect ancestors of G.{B,C,D,E,G}
heads(B::G)Remove every member that is an ancestor of another member.{G}
roots(B::G)Remove every member with a parent also in the set.{B}
(C|D)..Not ancestors of C and not ancestors of D; do not distribute .. over the union.{E,G,H} subject to the visible search domain.
C.. | D..Union two complements of ancestry sets.Usually larger than (C|D)..; calculate each side first.
topic ~ ::BStart at H and remove all ancestors of B.{H}\`

The exact set printer can be made independent of graph glyphs:

jj log --no-pager --color never -r 'B::G' \
  -T 'description.first_line() ++ "\t" ++ commit_id.normal_hex() ++ "\n"'
jj log --no-pager --color never -r 'heads(B::G)' \
  -T 'description.first_line() ++ "\n"'

When checking a worked example, do not use only the visible order in jj log. A merge is normally shown with graph indentation, but the indentation is a rendering. The semantic test is the parent list. Render each selected commit's parents and verify the closure or boundary by hand.

Set algebra and complement

x | y is union, x & y is intersection, and x ~ y is relative difference. Prefix ~x is the complement of x in the revset search domain. The domain matters: hidden commits are generally absent unless explicitly introduced, and all() is not an unrestricted database query. If a hidden ID is mentioned, its ancestors become available to the expression; this can change what a later traversal includes.

Relative difference is the usual way to express “my set, except the published part”:

mutable() ~ ::main@origin
mutable() & ::@
(::@ ~ ::main@origin) & ~conflicts()

These are not interchangeable in every graph. The first removes every ancestor of remote main from the mutable set. The second first narrows to ancestors of the current workspace and then removes remote ancestry. The third additionally excludes conflicted nodes. State the intended universe before choosing the algebra.

A complement is best used inside a bounded expression. ~bookmarks() means every visible commit that is not named by a bookmark, not “the commits in my current stack that have no bookmark”. The latter is (@:: & mutable()) ~ bookmarks() or another explicitly bounded set. This is one of the most common ways a correct operator produces an unsafe mutation.

Reachability and ranges

The double-colon operators are closures; the double-dot operators are ancestry differences. x::y is a bounded path-shaped intersection: descendants of x that are ancestors of y. x..y is ancestors of y excluding ancestors of x. The endpoints do not have to be related. In a fork, left..right can include the right branch and common descendants while excluding the common base; it is not a list of edges on one unique path.

QuestionDerivationWhy the obvious spelling can fail
What changed since base?base..tipIncludes all ancestors of tip not also ancestors of base, including side branches merged into tip.
What is on the ancestry path from base to tip?base::tip then remove the base if the diff should exclude itbase..tip has different endpoint and fork semantics.
What is the complete stack below the current change?@:: & mutable() or an explicitly configured alias@:: includes descendants of @, while the mutable filter excludes immutable descendants.
What is reachable from either publication ref?::(main@origin | release)::main@origin | release has the same result only if the grouping and parser precedence are understood.
What remains unpublished in a bounded topic?(topic:: & mutable()) ~ ::main@originmutable() ~ ::main@origin can include unrelated work.

For an expression with a range on the left, always parenthesise unions:

(A | B)..          # not ancestors of A and not ancestors of B
A.. | B..          # commits not ancestors of A OR not ancestors of B
(A | B).. = A.. & B..

This identity follows from De Morgan's law applied to ancestry complements. It is not a jj peculiarity; it becomes visible because .. is defined as a complement of reachability rather than as a path enumerator.

Symbol resolution in detail

Resolution is deliberately ordered. Tags take priority over bookmarks, which take priority over commit-ID or change-ID interpretation. This makes a short symbol convenient for humans but potentially unstable in automation. Use commit_id("..."), change_id("..."), bookmarks(exact:"..."), or tags(exact:"...") when the namespace matters.

A full commit ID identifies one object. A unique prefix identifies one object until a later object makes the prefix ambiguous. A full change ID identifies the visible evolution of a logical change; a divergent change ID requires an offset or an explicit query over the divergent commits. A short change ID copied from a review message is therefore not a safe immutable handle. Record the full commit ID for an exact object and the full change ID for the evolving change.

# Treat a string as a literal symbol when punctuation is meaningful.
jj log -r '"x-"'
jj log -r 'commit_id(exact:"a1b2...")'
jj log -r 'change_id(exact:"qwer...")'

# Qualify remote state.
jj log -r 'main@origin'
jj log -r 'main@github | main@gerrit'

Shell quoting is an additional parser. In jj log -r 'x-', the shell passes one string and jj interprets the suffix as the parents operator. In jj log -r '"x-"', jj receives a revset containing a quoted string symbol. A script should quote the complete expression, not merely the individual words that happen to be visible in an example.

Cardinality and command contracts

Revsets always produce sets, even when a command wants one commit. The command applies a cardinality contract after parsing. log, diff, and many reporting commands accept arbitrary sets. edit, describe, and other operations that need one current target generally reject zero or multiple results. Some commands accept several explicit commits but impose topology constraints. Read the command's help and test the exact invocation.

candidate='heads(mutable() & ::@)'
jj log -r "$candidate" -T 'commit_id.normal_hex() ++ "\n"'
count=$(jj log -r "$candidate" -T 'commit_id ++ "\n"' | wc -l)
test "$count" -eq 1
jj edit "$candidate"

The shell guard is valuable because a query that was singleton yesterday may become multi-valued after a fork or a new workspace. If the operation is safe over several heads, use a set-valued command intentionally. Do not force a singleton with first() merely to make an error disappear; that converts an explicit ambiguity into an arbitrary policy.

Function families and their contracts

The function inventory is easiest to learn by the fact it computes. Topology functions transform or inspect graph reachability. State predicates select stored properties. Reference functions select names and remote relationships. Content predicates inspect trees or diffs. Metadata predicates match typed fields. The following tables state the contract, not just the spelling.

FunctionSignature/argumentsSemantics and edge caseOperational use
parentsparents(x[, depth])Parents at exactly the requested depth; merges return multiple parents; root becomes empty.Find the base of a stack without assuming one parent.
childrenchildren(x[, depth])Direct or depth-limited children; a merge's parents can have several children.Find immediate successors after a rewrite.
ancestorsancestors(x[, depth])Inclusive parent closure; depth zero is the starting set according to the release contract.Bound a review or build dependency.
descendantsdescendants(x[, depth])Inclusive child closure; branch and merge paths are all followed.Estimate rewrite blast radius.
first_parentfirst_parent(x[, depth])Follows first-parent edges rather than all ancestry; important for merge-shaped history.Produce a release-line view without selecting side branches.
connectedconnected(x)Connected graph component containing the set under the documented visibility domain.Check whether a proposed range spans unrelated roots.
reachablereachable(sources, domain)Walk from source commits but include only nodes satisfying the domain; a domain is not merely an output filter in every graph shape.Find commits reachable from refs while excluding immutable or private regions.
rootsroots(x)Members with no parent in x; a merge-boundary set can have more than one root.Find patch-stack bases.
headsheads(x)Members with no descendant in x; an ancestor of a selected merge is not a head.Find publication tips and test endpoints.
mergesmerges()Members with more than one parent.Intersect with a domain, such as merges() & ::@, before a linear-only operation.
Function familyMembersInterpretation
Stateempty(), conflicts(), mutable(), immutable(), divergent()Predicates over stored commit state; an empty commit can still be published, and a conflicted commit can have descendants.
Visibilityall(), none(), visible_heads(), immutable_heads(), builtin_immutable_heads()Define the query domain and rewrite boundary; custom immutable heads are configuration, not a new commit type.
Identitycommit_id(pattern), change_id(pattern), present(x)Resolve object or logical-change identity explicitly; inspect successive versions with jj evolog, not a revset function.
Referencesbookmarks, remote_bookmarks, tracked_remote_bookmarks, untracked_remote_bookmarks, tags, remote_tagsReference state is not the same as reachability from a branch-like name; inspect native Git refs through the backend when needed.
Workspace/operationworking_copies(), at_operation(op,x)Working-copy commits and historical-operation views are queryable; workspace records themselves are managed by jj workspace.
Metadataauthor, committer, author_email, committer_email, author_date, committer_date, descriptionArguments are string/date patterns; there is no email: pattern kind.
Contentfiles, diff_lines, diff_lines_added, diff_lines_removedTree and diff predicates can be expensive and should be bounded before mutation.

For an unfamiliar function, establish four facts before using it in a destructive command: does it accept a set or a single commit argument; does it include its argument or only its closure; does it search visible commits or explicitly named hidden commits; and does it inspect metadata at one commit or compare two trees? The name alone does not answer these questions.

Fileset language workbench

Create a tree with deliberately similar names:

src/main.rs
src/lib.rs
src/generated/schema.rs
tests/api.rs
docs/api.md
Cargo.lock
README.md
build/output.bin
notes/old api.txt

By default, an unqualified path is a cwd-relative prefix glob. From the repository root, src selects src recursively. From a subdirectory, that same spelling is interpreted relative to the current working directory. Root-qualified forms make scripts independent of the caller's location:

ExpressionMatchesRecommended use
srccwd-relative prefix below srcInteractive command from a known directory.
root:srcworkspace-relative prefixExplicit subtree in a command where prefix form is intended.
root-file:src/lib.rsone exact pathScripts that must not include neighbours.
root-glob:src/*.rsRust files directly below srcNon-recursive glob selection.
root-prefix-glob:src/*.rsmatching files and matching prefixesRecursive path-oriented glob policy.
root-glob-i:docs/*.MDcase-insensitive glob matchesRepositories with inconsistent case; the -i suffix is supported by jj 0.45.1.

Operators have the same useful shape as revsets: function/pattern, complement, intersection or difference, then union. Thus 'src ~ root-glob:src/**/generated/**' selects the source subtree except generated files. Parenthesise a union before complementing it; '~a | b' is not the same as '~(a | b)'.

jj file list 'root:src ~ root-prefix-glob:src/**/generated/**'
jj diff -r @ -- 'root-file:README.md | root-glob:docs/**/*.md'
jj restore --from SOURCE --into @ -- 'root:src & ~root-glob:src/**/*.generated.rs'

Quoting has two layers. The shell expands unquoted *, ?, and brackets before jj can parse them. Then jj parses operators, function calls, and string literals. Quote the complete fileset. If a path contains whitespace or parentheses, quote at both layers as the target syntax requires:

jj diff -- 'root-file:notes/old api.txt'
jj diff -- '~"notes/old api.txt"'
jj diff -- 'root-file:"notes/old api.txt"'

Use the exact pattern spelling supported by the installed help for paths containing a colon or quote. When a command accepts multiple path arguments, do not assume they are unioned in exactly the same way as one fileset expression; test the command contract and prefer one explicit expression when the difference matters.

Template language workbench

Start with a scalar and keep the output contract visible:

# Typed object rendered through a method.
jj log -r @ -T 'commit_id.short() ++ "\n"'

# A list mapped to strings and joined at the output boundary.
jj log -r @ -T 'parents.map(|p| p.commit_id().short()).join(", ") ++ "\n"'

# A conditional over a Boolean.
jj log -r @ -T 'if(conflict(), "CONFLICT ", "") ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'

# Width and truncation for a human log.
jj log -r '@:: & mutable()' -T 'pad_end(12, commit_id.short()) ++ " " ++ truncate_end(72, description.first_line(), "…") ++ "\n"'

Methods are resolved from the value's type. commit_id.short() is a method on a commit-ID value. description.first_line() is a method on a string-like value. parents.map operates on a list and invokes a lambda once per element. Calling a commit method on commit_id.short(), or a string method on the commit itself, is a type error, not a formatting preference.

Optional values require a policy. A signature may be absent, a remote ref may not be tracked, and a workspace root may be stale. Use a Boolean predicate, if, try, or coalesce as appropriate. A fallback should identify absence rather than quietly render a misleading zero value.

jj log -r 'all()' -T '
if(signature, signature.name() ++ " <" ++ signature.email() ++ ">", "(unsigned)") ++
" " ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"

The output of json is a string, so escape and delimit it at the record boundary. A description can contain a newline, tab, or control character. In the 0.45.1 template language there is no general object-literal syntax; emit independently escaped JSON scalar fields or use an external filter to assemble records:

jj --no-pager --color never log -r 'all()' -T '
json(commit_id.normal_hex()) ++ "\t" ++
json(change_id.normal_hex()) ++ "\t" ++
json(description.first_line()) ++ "\n"

For display templates, labels are semantic style rather than content. A label can be mapped to a configured colour and can be stripped when colour is disabled. Machine output should avoid labels and use --color=never. Raw escape sequences are an escape hatch for terminal control; they should not be used in a file intended for a Kindle PDF or a parser.

Revset reference atlas — lookup

This is a reader-facing reference, not a transcription of help output. Each entry states the input kind, the set returned, and the question it answers. The examples use the query-lab graph; replace the symbolic labels with real commits only after rendering the set. A function that accepts a commit expression does not necessarily require a single commit, and a function that returns a set does not make every consuming command set-valued.

Topology and closure

FunctionInputResultExample and use
parents(x)Revset, optional depthParents of members of x; unioned as a set.parents(@) finds the immediate base; use a parent template for a merge.
children(x)Revset, optional depthDirect or depth-limited children of x.children(B) distinguishes a fork from a linear successor.
ancestors(x)Revset, optional depthInclusive transitive parent closure.ancestors(@, 2) bounds a local context without including all trunk.
descendants(x)Revset, optional depthInclusive transitive child closure.descendants(B, 1) estimates immediate rewrite blast radius.
first_parent(x)Revset, optional depthFirst-parent walk, useful for merge-oriented views.Use on a release line when side-parent changes should not appear as a linear series.
roots(x)RevsetMembers with no parent also in x.roots(main@origin..@) identifies the base of each unpublished component.
heads(x)RevsetMembers with no descendant also in x.heads(B::G) is G in the worked merge, not its parent-side ancestor.
merges()RevsetMembers with more than one parent.merges() & ::@ audits whether the current ancestry is actually linear.
connected(x)RevsetThe connected component or components containing the set under the documented graph domain.Use before a bulk rewrite to detect independent roots.
reachable(s, d)Source revset and domain revsetWalks from s while restricting the reachable result using d.reachable(bookmarks(), mutable()) asks which mutable nodes are reachable from named refs.

The closure functions are inclusive at depth one: ancestors(B, 0) and descendants(B, 0) are the useful boundary cases to test against the installed binary because an omitted depth and an explicit depth have different meaning. A merge makes set union visible: parents(G) contains both parent sides, and ancestors(G) contains their common ancestry only once. Do not interpret a returned set as an ordered path.

roots and heads are dual boundary operators within a selected set. They are not the repository root and the repository's all-time tips unless their input is the corresponding whole domain. On B::G, roots returns B and heads returns G. On ::G, roots returns the repository root and heads returns G. On a union containing unrelated stacks, both can return multiple commits.

State, visibility, and identity

FunctionContractEdge caseOperational pattern
all()All visible commits in the current repository view.Hidden commits are not silently included; explicitly naming one changes the available search space.Use for fixture inspection, not unbounded mutation.
none()Empty commit set.Useful in aliases and tests; commands may reject an empty selection even when parsing succeeds.Use as a safe default for an optional publication set.
visible_heads()Heads of the visible commit graph.Not the same as heads of an arbitrary selected set.Define the visible traversal boundary explicitly.
immutable_heads()Configured immutable-head boundary.The alias is configuration; an inert key with a similar name changes nothing.Inspect before --ignore-immutable or policy changes.
builtin_immutable_heads()Built-in immutable boundary before custom policy.Useful for comparing policy to release defaults.Audit a repository's safety policy after changing aliases.
mutable()Commits permitted to be rewritten under the current policy.A mutable commit may still have an immutable ancestor and a remote bookmark.Bound local surgery with mutable() & ::@.
immutable()Commits protected by the current policy.Protection is a command safety rule, not permanent object storage.Find the boundary before explaining a rejected rewrite.
conflicts()Commits containing conflict values.A clean working directory does not prove this set is empty elsewhere.Use after rebase, merge, squash, or restore.
empty()Commits whose tree delta is empty under the command's comparison semantics.An empty commit is still a graph node and can have descendants or a bookmark.Audit accidental empty review changes.
divergent()Commits belonging to divergent change evolutions.A divergent change ID may require an offset or a set query.Find local evolution forks before convergence or manual surgery.
present(x)Commits in x that are present/visible under the current view.Useful around optional names; it does not resurrect an arbitrary deleted object.Guard a publication query against a missing remote ref.
Evolution historyNot a revset function in jj 0.45.1.Use jj evolog -r X to inspect successive commit versions of a logical change.Investigate what an ancestor rewrite replaced without pretending the evolution log is a commit set.
root()The repository root commit.Its parent set is empty; it is not a normal mutable working change.Use root():: for a complete ancestry domain.

Visibility and immutability are independent dimensions. A hidden commit can remain immutable, and a visible commit can be mutable. A remote bookmark can point at a mutable commit if local policy permits it; publication does not automatically make every local descendant immutable unless the configured boundary says so. Use separate predicates in a query when both dimensions matter.

Bookmarks, tags, remotes, and workspaces

FunctionArgumentsMeaningExample
bookmarks()Optional name patternCommits targeted by local bookmarks matching the pattern.bookmarks("pr/*") finds local PR boundaries.
remote_bookmarks()Optional name and remote patternsCommits targeted by remote-tracking bookmarks.remote_bookmarks("main", remote="origin") selects fetched trunk.
tracked_remote_bookmarks()Optional patternsRemote bookmarks participating in tracking relationships.Audit only refs that supply ahead/behind information.
untracked_remote_bookmarks()Optional patternsRemote bookmarks without local tracking.Find fetched refs that a push script must qualify explicitly.
tags()Optional name patternCommits targeted by local tags.tags("v*") finds release points.
remote_tags()Optional name and remote patternsFetched remote tag targets.Compare release tags across remotes.
working_copies()No argumentsCommits serving as working copies across all workspaces.working_copies() detects a commit held by one or more workspaces; use jj workspace list to identify the workspace names.
at_operation(op, x)Required operation and revsetEvaluates x in the repository view at operation op.at_operation(OP, @-) or at_operation(@-, visible_heads()); both arguments are required.

Reference functions return targets, not the names themselves. To render names, use a commit template's bookmark or tag methods. This separation is useful: bookmarks() can select a set of commits, while a template can then show all names attached to each selected commit. If two local names point to the same commit, the selection still contains one commit.

Remote arguments are patterns and can be qualified by labels according to the installed syntax. An unqualified remote_bookmarks("main") can select same-named refs from several remotes. In a publication safety check, pass the remote pattern or use an explicitly qualified symbol. In jj 0.45.1, remote tag predicates distinguish tracked and untracked relationships.

Metadata and content predicates

FunctionArgumentMatching ruleExample
description(pattern)String patternMatches commit descriptions using explicit pattern kinds.description(substring:"quota").
author(pattern)String patternMatches author identity according to the installed pattern semantics.author(glob:"A.*").
committer(pattern)String patternMatches committer identity.Use when import/rewrite actor differs from author.
author_email(pattern)String patternMatches the author email field.author_email(exact:"dev@example.org").
committer_email(pattern)String patternMatches the committer email field.Distinguish automation from the original author.
author_date(pattern)Date patternMatches author timestamps.author_date(after:"2026-01-01").
committer_date(pattern)Date patternMatches committer timestamps.Find changes rewritten this week.
commit_id(pattern)String patternResolves commit IDs without bookmark/change-ID precedence surprises.commit_id(exact:"full-id").
change_id(pattern)String patternResolves visible change IDs and their matching evolutions.Use a full ID or offset for divergence.
files(fileset)Fileset expressionSelects commits whose changes match the fileset.files("root-file:src/api.rs").
files(fileset)Fileset expressionSelects commits changing/containing paths under the documented predicate.Bound to a stack before use in automation.
diff_lines(text, [files])String pattern and optional filesetMatches changed content line by line in a diff.diff_lines(substring:"diagnostic", "root:src").
diff_contains(pattern) deprecatedCompatibility string patternAccepted by jj 0.45.1 but emits a deprecation warning.Use diff_lines(pattern) in new queries.
diff_lines_added(pattern)String patternMatches added lines.Audit introduction of an API or marker.
diff_lines_removed(pattern)String patternMatches removed lines.Find the change that removed a compatibility path.

Pattern arguments are not a single universal string syntax. String patterns support explicit kinds such as exact:, substring:, glob:, and regex:. Date patterns have their own forms and ranges. The invalid form author(email:"...") fails because email is not a pattern kind in 0.45.1; use author_email(exact:"...") or the documented author pattern semantics.

Content predicates can be expensive. A file predicate compares trees and a diff predicate examines diff content. First narrow the graph with mutable() & ::@, a publication range, or a date window. If the query is used in a bulk rewrite, render the result and record how many commits matched before invoking the mutation.

Patterns, dates, and aliases

A pattern is a typed value passed to a matcher. It is not the same thing as a shell glob and not the same thing as a fileset. The shell must pass the pattern intact; jj then parses the pattern prefix. These examples show the intent:

description(exact:"fix quota boundary")
description(substring:"quota")
description(glob:"fix * boundary")
description(regex:"quota[0-9]+")
author_email(exact:"dev@example.org")
author_date(after:"2026-01-01" & before:"2026-02-01")

Use exact patterns for identity and release automation. Use substring for interactive search. Use glob when a conventional naming family is deliberate, and regex only when the additional syntax is worth the portability and escaping cost. A pattern alias can hide that policy; give aliases descriptive names and document whether they match case, punctuation, and whitespace.

Revset aliases are parsed in the context in which they are used. A parameterless alias names a reusable set; a parameterised alias behaves like a function. Keep aliases small enough that jj log -r ALIAS remains explainable. Avoid aliases that silently choose the first result or that combine publication and mutability policy without a name that reveals both. Test recursive aliases and aliases that shadow builtin functions in a disposable configuration.

[revset-aliases]
"unpublished_stack()" = "(@:: & mutable()) ~ ::remote_bookmarks()"
"owned_work()" = "author_email(exact:\"dev@example.org\") & mutable()"
"release_line()" = "first_parent(tags())"

The examples above show the conceptual shape; quote TOML strings and pattern arguments exactly as required by the installed parser. A parameterised alias's argument substitution is not shell interpolation. If an alias is used in a script, include one expansion test in the repository's validation suite.

Derivation exercises

Exercise: derive unpublished work

Start with a graph containing two local stacks and two remote bookmarks. The goal is “mutable commits in the current workspace's ancestry that are not reachable from any remote bookmark”. Begin with ::@. Intersect with mutable(). The publication exclusion is ~::remote_bookmarks(). The derived expression is mutable() & ::@ ~ ::remote_bookmarks(), with parentheses added around the positive domain if it is extended. Verify that a mutable commit on an unrelated branch is excluded, while a mutable unpublished ancestor remains. If the expression returns a merge, decide whether its heads or all changes are wanted.

Exercise: heads of a non-linear query

Using the workbench graph, calculate B::G first. It contains B, both side paths, and G. Test each member for whether it is an ancestor of another member. B, C, D, and E are ancestors of G; G is not an ancestor of another member in the set. Therefore heads(B::G) is {G}. Now calculate heads((B::G) ~ merges()). The merge is removed from the domain, so the heads can change; the answer must be derived from the resulting set, not copied from the earlier result. This is why a heads query should be evaluated after every filter.

Exercise: a range across a fork

Let L and R be sibling tips from a common base. Calculate L..R as ::R ~ ::L. The result contains R's ancestry that is not also in L's ancestry; it does not represent a unique sequence of edges from L to R. Now add a merge descendant that contains both sides and recalculate. The merge can enter the set even though L is not an ancestor of R. A Git user accustomed to a branch range should write the intended review base and server ref explicitly rather than relying on the visual branch names.

Exercise: precedence proof

Compare A | B & C, (A | B) & C, and A | (B & C). The first and third are equivalent because intersection binds more tightly than union; the second is different. Then compare A ~ B & C with A ~ (B & C). Difference and intersection have the same precedence and associate left-to-right in the installed grammar, so the unparenthesised form is (A ~ B) & C. Do not rely on a language remembered from another tool.

Exercise: cardinality as a changing property

Define candidate = heads(mutable() & ::@). It is singleton-valued in a linear stack. Create a second child or a fork; the same expression becomes multi-valued. A command such as jj edit "$candidate" now fails rather than choosing arbitrarily. This is a useful failure. A script may assert one result, or it may use a set-valued command and handle several tips. The query has not become wrong merely because its cardinality changed; the consumer's precondition has changed.

Configuration and template reference — lookup

Configuration is part of jj's execution model. It selects defaults, defines aliases, controls immutability, chooses external tools, and can change which commits an apparently unqualified command touches. A configuration file is therefore closer to a program's policy module than to a collection of cosmetic preferences. Keep the stable personal layer small, keep repository policy reviewable, and treat workspace overrides as local experiments.

The layer model

On Linux, jj loads built-in defaults and then the configured user, repository, workspace, and command-line inputs in the order documented by the target release. The exact paths are discovered with jj config path; do not hard-code an XDG path in an installer. --config NAME=VALUE is an invocation override. --config-file PATH adds a file as input; it is not the same as selecting the user/repository/workspace file that config edit modifies.

LayerTypical scopeGood contentsHazard
Built-inEvery invocationSafe defaults supplied by jjDefaults can change between releases.
UserOne Linux user across repositoriesIdentity, pager, editor, personal aliasesA remote or immutable policy can unexpectedly affect unrelated repositories.
RepositoryOne repositoryProject revsets, fileset aliases, tool policyOpening an unfamiliar repository can load policy you did not write.
WorkspaceOne working directoryTemporary log view, build/review defaultsAnother workspace in the same store does not necessarily share it.
Command lineOne processVersion gates, dry runs, explicit remote, diagnostic overrideQuoting and TOML typing errors are easy to hide in shell history.

For a scalar key, a higher layer normally replaces a lower value. For tables and aliases, merging and replacement rules make it unsafe to assume that “unset the top-level table” removes every child. Diagnose with config list, then inspect the scope files. Use a temporary alternative config file when testing a policy; never edit the production user config first.

A progressive Linux configuration

# ~/.config/jj/config.toml, discovered with jj config path --user
[user]
name = "A. Engineer"
email = "a.engineer@example.org"

[ui]
pager = "less -FRX"
paginate = "auto"
color = "auto"
default-command = ["log", "-r", "@:: & mutable()"]

[revset-aliases]
"mine()" = "author_email(exact:\"a.engineer@example.org\")"
"my_work()" = "mine() & mutable()"
"published()" = "::remote_bookmarks()"
"unpublished()" = "my_work() ~ published()"

[fileset-aliases]
"LOCKFILES" = "root-glob:**/Cargo.lock | root-glob:**/package-lock.json"

[template-aliases]
"brief_commit(commit)" = "commit.change_id().short() ++ \" \" ++ commit.description().first_line()"

Start with identity and output. Add revset aliases only after testing them against a non-linear fixture. Add fileset aliases when the same path policy appears in several commands. Add template aliases last, because a typo in a type-sensitive method can make all log output fail. A repository-specific config may redefine the log revset, but a publication alias should name its remote explicitly or accept the remote as a visible argument.

jj 0.45.1 supports splitting user configuration under conf.d, loaded in lexical order. Verify the effective result with config list and a harmless sentinel value in a disposable configuration. The maintainable principle is independent of the directory name: keep UI, aliases, templates, Git transport, and Gerrit policy reviewable as separate units and document their precedence.

UI, snapshot, and editor policy

FamilyKey examplesDesign choiceInteraction
Identityuser.name, user.emailDefault author/committer identityExplicit metadata options can override it; operation username/hostname is a separate record.
Outputui.color, ui.paginate, ui.pager, ui.graph, timestampsInteractive readability versus stable scriptsCommand-line --color=never and --no-pager should win in automation.
Editingui.editor, ui.diff-editor, ui.merge-editorHow descriptions, diffs, and conflicts are editedExternal tools have their own merge-tools.* configuration and exit-status contract.
Conflict renderingui.conflict-marker-styleHow stored conflicts are materialisedChanging style changes the working-copy representation, not the underlying conflict value.
Snapshotsnapshot.auto-track, size/EOL/exec-bit policyWhich filesystem paths enter the next treeIgnored/untracked files can make a command appear to have done nothing.
Movementworking-copy movement/update policyHow commands choose or update @Workspace-local state and stale-workspace repair must be considered.

The pager is a particularly common source of false failures. A program that pipes jj log to a parser may receive a pager process or terminal control sequences unless it explicitly disables both. Conversely, forcing --no-pager in every interactive alias can make a large history unusable. Keep human and machine aliases distinct.

Snapshot settings are policy, not a substitute for .gitignore-style project discipline. Test a maximum new-file size with a disposable large file, test executable-bit changes on a filesystem that supports them, and test a repository from a subdirectory. Record whether the policy prevents tracking, warns, or refuses an operation. A configuration that “looks right” in TOML can still be ineffective if the command's default snapshot path never considers the file.

Revsets, aliases, and rewrite safety

Defaults such as the log, status, fix, sign, run, and bookmark-advance revsets are executable policy. A default is evaluated in a graph that changes over time, so a command that was narrow when configured can become broad after a merge or workspace handoff. Before changing a default, run the old and new expressions side by side on the query fixture.

old=$(jj config get revsets.log)
jj log -r "$old" -T 'commit_id.short() ++ " " ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'
jj log -r '(@:: & mutable()) | main@origin' -T 'commit_id.short() ++ " " ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'

The immutable boundary is a special case. In 0.45.1, the configured function is revset-aliases."immutable_heads()", whose definition can refer to tags, remote bookmarks, and the root. A key called revsets.immutable_heads is merely unknown data and does not redefine the function. Demonstrate a safety setting by querying the function and attempting a protected rewrite in a disposable repository.

[revset-aliases]
"immutable_heads()" = "builtin_immutable_heads() | main@origin | tags()"

Keep parameterised aliases small. An alias that accepts a pattern and inserts it into a regex or fileset can be useful, but it also creates a second quoting boundary and can be a source of injection-like mistakes in shell automation. Prefer fixed aliases for publication and require an explicit commit argument for destructive operations.

GitHub and Gerrit configuration

Git transport configuration should identify credentials and remote URLs, not silently encode a publication decision that differs by repository. Use jj git remote list to inspect names and URLs, and use explicit --remote in pushes. A repository can have an origin GitHub remote and a gerrit remote without either being “the” remote in the abstract.

[git]
# Keep publication remote explicit in shared scripts.
private-commits = "mutable() ~ ::remote_bookmarks()"
