Remote management has its own namespace: remote add records a name and URL, remote list displays them, remote remove removes a configured remote, remote rename changes the local name, and remote set-url changes its URL. None of those operations fetches or pushes by itself. A remote URL can be valid while its credentials or server permissions are not.

jj git remote add github git@github.com:org/project.git
jj git remote add gerrit ssh://review.example.org/project
jj git remote list
jj git fetch --remote github
jj git fetch --remote gerrit

After a native Git fetch in a colocated repository, run jj git import before querying remote bookmarks. After a jj bookmark update, jj exports the Git ref; a Git-native tool can then inspect the new ref. Concurrently changing the worktree with Git and jj is unsafe even if the two commands target different refs; snapshot ownership is a filesystem concern.

Tag commands

jj tag set creates or moves a local tag at a selected commit; tag list inspects tags; tag delete changes local tag state; tag track and tag untrack manage relationships to remote tags. Tag names are publication labels, not mutable stack organisation. A release tag should be placed only after the exact commit and parents have been tested, and the release policy should make the tag part of the immutable-head boundary.

jj tag set v2.4.0 -r release-candidate
jj tag list
jj tag track v2.4.0 --remote origin
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark release-candidate

In jj 0.45.1, jj git push --tag NAME publishes a selected tag; a local tag operation alone does not publish it. jj 0.45.1 also provides tracked/untracked remote tag revset predicates. Use those predicates in a target-release shared alias only when their policy meaning is intentional.

Utilities and maintenance

CommandUseWhy it deserves a contract
jj versionPrint binary versionUse in every reproducibility report and version-gated script.
jj helpDiscover command tree and topicsHelp is the installed release's normative syntax surface.
jj util completionGenerate shell completionCompletion can expose aliases and descriptions but is not a substitute for help.
jj util config-schemaEmit machine-readable config schemaSchema validates types and keys but not human policy interactions.
jj util backend nameIdentify the backendUseful when a repository's storage assumptions are unclear.
jj util gcGarbage-collect jj storageCan reduce recovery options; run only after op/evolution retention review.
jj util snapshotExplicit snapshot utilityChanges the normal command-boundary assumption; coordinate workspace ownership.
jj util execUtility-level command executionArgument forwarding and environment are release-sensitive; do not use as an undocumented shell wrapper.
jj util markdown-helpGenerate installed help materialUseful for research; generated help is not the authored book.
jj util install-man-pagesInstall local man pagesWrites outside the repository and should be treated as an installation action.

Maintenance commands are deliberately absent from the everyday alias layer. A daily alias may call status, log, or a bounded diff; it should not call storage GC, config GC, or an operation-abandoning command as a side effect. Keep repository maintenance explicit and independent of ordinary inspection aliases.

Global options as an explicit contract

-R/--repository selects a repository. It does not select a Git remote, workspace, or operation. --ignore-working-copy prevents snapshot/update of the filesystem. --at-operation loads a historical repository view and therefore implies that current filesystem edits must not be inserted into it. --ignore-immutable bypasses rewrite protection and should be rare in a script. --no-integrate-operation changes operation integration and creates a concurrency/recovery responsibility.

--color, --no-pager, and --quiet affect output. Repeatable --config and --config-file affect input. -h/--help and -V/--version are discovery/version controls. The fact that a flag appears globally does not make its semantic effect identical in every subcommand; the command-specific help remains authoritative.

Mechanics synthesis: why the graph changes

The commands in jj are easier to predict if the underlying transformations are understood. This chapter describes the conceptual algorithms without pretending to expose an implementation API. The commit store, working-copy state, reference state, and operation store are separate pieces of repository state. A command can update more than one, but the updates have different invariants.

Rewrite as a successor function

Let a commit be a tuple containing parent IDs, tree ID, author/committer metadata, description, and conflict values. Its commit ID is a function of that tuple. A rewrite changes at least one component. The new tuple receives a new commit ID. jj also records that the new tuple is a successor of the old logical change. Descendants whose parent tuple contains the old commit ID cannot retain their old commit object unchanged, so jj derives successors for them too.

old B = (parent A, tree tb, metadata mb) → cid(B)
new B = (parent A, tree tb′, metadata mb) → cid(B′)
old C = (parent B, tree tc, metadata mc) → cid(C)
new C = (parent B′, rebased tree, metadata mc) → cid(C′)

The logical change ID is attached to the evolution rather than recomputed as the commit ID. This is why a commit message can refer to a change after several rewrites, while a CI system that stores only the commit ID must update its record. If two processes derive B′ and B″ independently from B, both successors can remain visible and the change becomes divergent.

The successor relationship is not a promise that the diff is textually identical. A descendant rebase may resolve cleanly, may alter context, may introduce a conflict value, or may require a new merge shape. The invariant is graph evolution: the descendant is the successor of the old descendant under the changed parent context. Review the diff to determine whether the logical change survived as intended.

Automatic descendant rebasing

Automatic descendant rebasing is the consequence of maintaining parent identity, not an optional convenience. If an ancestor changes, leaving descendants pointing at the old object would produce a stale branch of the graph. jj instead rewrites affected descendants so their parent edges point at the new successors. This can be surprising when editing a small early change changes many commit IDs, but it is what keeps a stack coherent.

Ancestor operationDescendant conditionTypical result
Description/meta editDescendant directly or transitively depends on changed commitNew descendant commit IDs with equivalent or rebased trees.
Diff editDescendant's diff applies to new ancestorClean successor with changed parent and often changed tree ID.
Diff editDescendant's diff cannot applySuccessor contains a stored conflict.
Ancestor abandonDescendant depends on abandoned nodeReparenting/rebase according to topology; possible conflict.
Ancestor splitDescendant points at old changeSuccessor points at the new split tip.
Ancestor duplicated elsewhereOriginal descendant does not depend on duplicateOriginal stack unchanged; duplicate has independent identity.

Bookmarks are updated as references to local successors where the operation can determine the corresponding evolution. A remote bookmark is not silently changed because it represents a fetched external state. A workspace working-copy pointer can also be updated or become stale depending on whether its commit was rewritten and whether its filesystem has unrecorded content.

To reason about a large rewrite, compute the descendant closure before the command:

jj log -r 'descendants(TARGET)' -T '
commit_id.normal_hex() ++ "\t" ++ change_id.normal_hex() ++ "\t" ++
description.first_line() ++ "\n"

Then run the operation and compute it again. The set of exact commit IDs will differ; the set of intended logical changes and their parent relationships is the useful comparison. If the new closure includes unrelated work, the source set or destination was too broad.

Trees, diffs, and context

A commit stores a tree, while a review usually discusses its diff relative to a parent. The same tree can represent different diffs under different parents. Rebase preserves a change's intended tree transformation as far as possible, but its diff can change when context changes. Restore copies selected file contents; squash changes which commit's parent-to-tree difference owns content; diffedit edits a diff; and split creates new boundaries through one tree delta.

parent P:  config = old, code = old
change Q:  config = new, code = new

restore Q → R:
  R receives selected tree values
  Q remains a separate change

squash Q into P:
  P′ owns the diff
  Q may become empty

split Q:
  P -- Q_1 -- Q_2
  Q_1 and Q_2 compose to Q's original tree delta

When a path is selected, ask whether its value is present in the source tree, whether it differs from the source parent, and whether the destination has a conflicting value. A fileset that selects an unchanged path can be a valid empty diff selection. A path missing from a sparse workspace can still be present in the stored tree and must be reasoned about with a commit/fileset command rather than a filesystem listing.

Diff context is also why automatic descendant rebase can produce a conflict without losing the descendant's logical change. The source side, destination side, and common ancestor are retained in the conflict value. The resolution must choose a tree that satisfies the domain invariant; “take ours” is only correct when the parent orientation and desired semantics make it correct.

Conflict values as algebra

A conflicted tree entry records sides and a base relationship. Materialising the working copy displays a representation of that value. Resolving it replaces the conflict value with a normal tree value. The commit can therefore move through these states without an interrupted transaction:

clean Q
  | rebase/merge
  ▼
conflicted Q′ -- edit/resolve/snapshot -->  clean Q″
  |                                      |
  \-- descendant R′ may also be conflicted +

Conflict propagation follows graph operations. A descendant created on top of a conflicted parent can remain meaningful, but a subsequent rewrite may materialise or propagate the conflict. Query conflicts() over the full review stack, not only the current workspace. If a merge editor resolves a path in one workspace, other workspaces may need stale update/materialisation before they see the resolved tree.

Conflict marker style controls presentation. The “diff” style can show base and sides differently from “git” style, and experimental styles can change between releases. Do not store marker text as the conflict identity. The stable evidence is the conflicted predicate and the resulting tree after resolution.

The operation DAG model

The commit DAG answers “what commits exist in this repository view?” The operation DAG answers “how did this repository view change?” One operation can update refs without changing commits. Another can rewrite commits and update workspace state. A third can recover a historical view. The commit graph and operation graph therefore have different nodes, edges, and recovery semantics.

commit DAG:       A -- B -- C′
                         \
                          D

operation DAG:       op_0 -- op_1(rewrite B)
                              |- op_2(snapshot)
                              \- op_3(move bookmark)

Operation descriptions are useful but should not be treated as a complete semantic diff. Use op show and op diff to inspect the repository-view changes. A snapshot operation may rewrite the working-copy commit; a bookmark operation may change only a ref; a push has external side effects that the local operation record cannot roll back at the server.

An operation created without integration can be inspected at its operation ID. Integrating it is a deliberate change to the current operation head. Concurrent operation nodes can be compared and possibly integrated. If two operations rewrite the same logical change differently, the operation graph may be easy to merge while the commit evolution becomes divergent. These are separate conflicts.

Recovery granularity

Recovery toolGranularityUse whenLimit
undoLatest integrated operationThe last operation was clearly wrong.Later operations change what “latest” means.
redoPreviously undone operationThe undo itself was a mistake and the operation remains redoable.Not a general commit reapplication mechanism.
op restoreRepository viewYou want the whole repository state at a known operation.Can remove later integrated state from the current view.
op revertRepository-view inverseYou want a new operation that reverses a selected operation.Not every external side effect is reversible.
evologLogical change evolutionYou need an old or divergent form of a change.Does not restore unrecorded files or remote server state.
Git remoteExported commits/refsYou need to move work to another clone.Does not transfer operation history or filesystem buffers.

Recovery should preserve evidence. Before a destructive-looking command, create a full-ID record and note the current operation. After a mistake, stop making changes until the wrong operation is identified. If a server push already happened, treat the server state as a separate incident; local undo cannot erase a remote review or ref update.

Git backend object boundary

The Git backend gives jj a way to exchange commit trees and refs with Git. It does not turn all jj metadata into Git metadata. Commit IDs can be represented as Git objects; bookmarks can be exported as refs; operation IDs, workspace symbols, change evolution, and conflict representation are jj concerns. A Git-native tool sees the exported object graph and refs, not the complete local jj state.

Colocation is therefore a coordination contract. After git update-ref, import. After jj changes a bookmark, export before a Git-native inspection. After a Git commit, import through supported mechanisms and inspect how it entered the jj graph. Do not edit .jj internal files or assume the Git index is a jj staging area.

Object reachability also affects recovery. An unexported jj commit may not be available in another clone. An abandoned local commit may be retained by jj operation/evolution storage but not by a Git remote. Git GC and jj GC have distinct roots. Preserve a temporary bookmark or an exported ref before maintenance if the object matters.

Synthesis: proof-driven jj practice

The most useful way to close the gap between knowing individual commands and operating a difficult repository is to treat every non-trivial jj action as a small proof. The proof is not formal verification in the theorem-prover sense; it is a disciplined record of the state that makes the intended transformation unambiguous. This matters more in jj than in a branch-centred workflow because a single command can rewrite an ancestor, rebase several descendants, move local bookmarks, update a workspace, and create a new operation while leaving remote observations untouched.

Begin by naming the question in graph terms. “Put the tests with the API change” is underspecified. It might mean move the test diff into the API change, copy the test tree into the API change, split one mixed change, or create a new dependent change. Those are different tree and identity transformations. A useful precondition record therefore contains the selected commit set, the destination commit set, the selected fileset, and the intended diff owner. It also records whether the operation is allowed to cross an immutable head and whether a publication bookmark currently names any affected commit.

Proof itemQuestionTypical observation
DomainWhich commits can the expression see?jj log -r 'visible() & ::@'
SelectionWhich exact commits will the command consume?jj log --no-graph -r 'roots(@:: & mutable())'
Tree deltaWhich paths and diff hunks are actually changing?jj diff -r R -- fileset
DestinationWhich parent edge or tree endpoint will change?jj log -r 'parents(R) | destination'
IdentityWhich commit IDs and change IDs may evolve?jj log -T 'commit_id ++ " " ++ change_id'
PublicationWhich local and remote names are involved?jj bookmark list --all-remotes
RecoveryWhich operation and temporary ref preserve the before-state?jj op log plus a temporary bookmark

After the command, repeat the observations rather than trusting the success message. For a rewrite, compare parent edges and the diff at every affected change. For a bookmark operation, compare the local target with the imported remote target. For a workspace operation, inspect both the workspace symbol and the filesystem. For a push, record the remote response separately: the local operation log can show what jj requested, but it cannot undo a server-side ref update or remove a review patch set.

proof loop:
  state description
       |
       v
  source/destination/fileset query
       |
       v
  operation O_n
       |
       +-- commit DAG and evolution
       +-- workspace materialisation
       +-- bookmarks and remote observations
       +-- operation DAG
       |
       v
  postcondition checks

This loop also explains why a command that merely “works” can still be wrong. A broad -r expression may be accepted and produce a coherent graph, but if it includes a sibling stack the operation has violated the intended precondition. A fileset may parse and select existing paths while selecting no changed diff hunks. A bookmark may be moved locally while the user believes a server ref has moved. A template may render a plausible empty field for an absent optional value. Proof-driven practice makes these errors visible at the boundary where they are cheapest to correct.

Rewrite proof: diff ownership, topology, and identity

Consider a stack with a public base and two private changes:

main@origin
    |
    A  public API change
    |
    B  tests and compatibility
    |
    C(@) documentation and examples

Suppose the intent is to move only the compatibility tests from B into A while keeping the documentation as a separate change. The operation is not “amend A”. First determine whether the tests are complete files, diff hunks within a file, or a diff that is already shared with C. A path-level squash can move a complete path; a diff editor is needed for diff-hunk-level ownership. The precondition is that A and B are mutable, that the selected paths are present in B's diff, and that C is a descendant whose diff can be reapplied over the new B.

jj log -r 'A|B|C' -T 'change_id.short() ++ " " ++ commit_id.short() ++ " " ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'
jj diff -r B -- root-glob:tests/**
jj diff -r A -- root-glob:tests/**
jj op log --limit 3
jj squash --from B --into A -- root-glob:tests/**

The postcondition is not simply that one file appears in A. A's successor must contain the intended test diff, B's successor must retain the unselected compatibility diff, and C's successor must have the same documentation diff relative to its new parent. If the test diff touched a file that A already changed, compare the combined tree rather than comparing file presence. A path can exist in both commits while contributing no delta. If C now conflicts, the conflict is evidence that its old diff depended on context changed by the ownership transfer; it is not evidence that squash failed to perform the transfer.

Identity gives a second independent postcondition. The rewritten A and B normally retain their respective jj change IDs while receiving new commit IDs. C also receives a new commit ID because its parent identity changed, even if its logical diff is unchanged. A bookmark at C may follow the local successor, while C@origin remains the fetched remote observation. A Gerrit footer in the commit message is a third identity channel and must be inspected independently. This is why a review note should record all three values when a published stack is rewritten.

The same proof pattern applies to split and rebase. For split, prove that the two new changes partition the original diff and that the descendant is rebased onto the second result. For rebase, prove the source set before the destination: -r, -s, and -b describe different source policies. Then prove every new parent edge. A visual log is useful, but a template printing full IDs and parents is stronger evidence when a graph has several forks or merges.

Publication proof: local graph, review ref, and remote observation

Publication is best modelled as a state machine with three layers. The local graph contains changes and their current commit successors. The local bookmark is a name chosen for a publication boundary. The remote bookmark is the last imported observation of a server ref. A tracking relationship connects the local and remote names but does not cause either to follow @. A GitHub pull request adds a server-side base/head view; Gerrit adds a review identity usually carried by a commit-message footer. None of those server objects is the jj change ID.

local graph:       A -- B -- C(@)
                                   |
local ref:                         review -> C
                                   |
tracking pair:                     review <-> review@origin -> B
                                   |
server request:                    update review@origin from B to C

In this state, the local bookmark is ahead of its imported remote target. The safe publication procedure is to fetch first when the observation may be old, verify the remote name and URL, compare B with the currently fetched target, and then push the explicit bookmark. The command is a request to update a Git ref; it is not a request to publish “the current change” in the abstract. If another contributor has moved the server ref, the expected old target no longer matches and the operator must decide whether to rebase, merge, or deliberately replace the ref through the hosting policy; jj 0.45.1's jj git push has no force flag.

jj git remote list
jj git fetch --remote origin
jj bookmark list review --all-remotes
jj log -r 'review | review@origin' -T 'commit_id.normal_hex() ++ " " ++ change_id.normal_hex() ++ "\n"'
jj diff --from review@origin --to review
jj git push --dry-run --remote origin --bookmark review
jj git push --remote origin --bookmark review

A rejected push has a small diagnostic decision tree. If the bookmark is absent remotely, determine whether creation is allowed and whether the chosen name is correct. If the remote target has advanced, fetch and inspect the new ancestor relation. If the local target is behind, a normal fast-forward push may be inappropriate; moving the local bookmark is a ref decision, not a rebase. If the server rejects the update because the branch is protected, the local graph is still valid but the publication protocol requires a pull request, a Gerrit review ref, or an authorised force update. If the commit cannot be exported, inspect private-commit policy and backend state before trying another ref.

GitHub and Gerrit can share one local graph without sharing publication semantics. A GitHub bookmark might name the head of a PR stack, while Gerrit upload selects a range and sends commits to refs/for/main. The same local commit can therefore be viewed as a GitHub branch tip and as one patch set in a Gerrit series. Keep remote names explicit, and use distinct local prefixes when that reduces operator ambiguity. Do not make a local bookmark track two server concepts merely because their visible names happen to be equal.

Cleanup is another state transition, not an aesthetic operation. After a GitHub PR merges, fetch and determine whether the merged commit is reachable from the imported base. Only then forget or delete the local publication bookmark according to whether the server ref should remain. After a Gerrit change lands, fetch the target branch and check whether the local change is now an ancestor of it; a server-side rebase or squash can mean that commit IDs differ while the diff is integrated. Preserve a temporary ref until that comparison is complete.

Conflict and recovery proof: preserve both graphs

A conflict drill should distinguish three events: conflict creation, conflict materialisation, and conflict resolution. Rebase or merge can create a conflicted successor in the commit DAG. A command can materialise that value as marker files in one workspace. Editing and snapshotting creates a successor with a resolved tree. These are not stages of an interrupted Git transaction; they are ordinary repository states connected by operations. A descendant may be created while an ancestor is conflicted, and a later rewrite may propagate or replace the conflict.

before:       A -- B -- C(@)
                       B changes shared API
rewrite B onto X:
              X -- B'! -- C'!
                   conflict value propagates
resolve B':   X -- B'' -- C''(@)
                   clean tree; new successors

When the conflict appears, record the current operation and identify the conflicted commits with a revset rather than assuming that the current workspace is the only location:

jj op log --limit 8
jj log -r 'conflicts() & ::@' -T 'change_id ++ " " ++ commit_id ++ "\n"'
jj log -r 'conflicts() & descendants(@-)' -G
jj status

Materialise only after deciding which workspace owns the resolution. If a build or review workspace is also present, record its workspace-local @ before updating it. Inspect the conflict sides and the parent list; “ours” and “theirs” are poor descriptions in a multi-parent graph. The domain invariant—such as preserving both API behaviours or retaining generated output policy—should decide the merged file. After editing, run a command that snapshots the result, then query conflicts() again and compare the tree and diff of every descendant.

Recovery has the same evidence requirement. jj undo is appropriate when the latest integrated operation is clearly the mistake. It is not a general reflog selector. If later operations occurred, inspect jj op log, use jj op show and jj op diff to identify the historical view, and decide between restoring that view, reverting its effects with a new operation, or recovering only a logical change from evolog. If work must move to another clone, create a temporary bookmark and push it; operation IDs and unrecorded filesystem contents do not travel through Git.

IncidentFirst safe actionEvidence before repair
Wrong ancestor editedStop ordinary commands; inspect the latest operation.Old/new commit IDs, change IDs, descendants, bookmark targets.
Useful change abandonedQuery evolution and operation history before creating replacements.Change ID, predecessor/successor chain, whether a remote copy exists.
Bookmark moved too farCompare local ref with fetched remote ref.Old target, new target, tracking state, server response if pushed.
Several mistakes accumulatedMake a recovery note and stop mutating the graph.Operation IDs and diffs for each candidate boundary.
Other machine needs unfinished workPublish an explicit temporary bookmark.Full commit ID, change ID, remote URL, and intended cleanup owner.

Do not use recovery to erase evidence prematurely. An operation restore changes the current repository view and can make later local work disappear from ordinary reachability. A remote push is outside the operation DAG. A workspace's unrecorded files are outside both graphs. The correct repair may therefore be a new graph operation, a filesystem backup, a server-side review action, or a combination of them.

Language and automation proof: revsets, filesets, templates

Revsets, filesets, and templates are three different languages that often appear in one command line. A revset selects commits; a fileset selects paths relative to the command's tree/filesystem context; a template renders typed values. Shell quoting happens before any of the three languages sees the expression. A reliable automation contract documents all four boundaries.

revset='heads(mutable() & ::@)'
fileset='glob:src/**/*.rs & ~glob:src/generated/**'
template='commit_id.normal_hex() ++ "\t" ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'
jj --no-pager --color never log -r "$revset" -T "$template"
jj diff -r @ -- "$fileset"

The two commands above do not necessarily consume the same kind of value. log -r accepts a commit set and can print many commits. diff -r accepts a commit expression whose tree comparison has its own endpoint semantics, then consumes a fileset after the -- boundary. A command such as edit generally requires one commit; a query that returns two heads should fail rather than silently choose one. Cardinality is therefore part of the script's precondition. Use an explicit assertion or a command designed for sets when the result can branch.

For revsets, calculate closures before reductions. For example, given two independent stacks:

root -- A -- B
               \
                C(@)
root -- X -- Y
               \
                Z(@2)

heads(mutable()) may return both C and Z. heads(mutable() & ::@) restricts the domain to the current workspace's ancestry before reducing it. heads(mutable()) & ::@ reduces globally and intersects afterward; these operations can differ when a global head is an ancestor of a current-workspace head or when a filter removes the descendant that made a node non-maximal. Parenthesise the policy and inspect the result in a template before handing it to a rewrite command.

For filesets, evaluate the path set against the actual tree. A glob that matches a generated file is not automatically the same as a glob that matches a changed generated file. A relative literal is interpreted from the relevant working-directory or repository-root coordinate, depending on the command and prefix. Quote metacharacters so that Bash does not expand them first. If a fileset is intended to move diff hunks, prove it with a diff editor or a before/after diff comparison; file list proves names, not diff ownership.

For templates, keep typed values typed until the output boundary. A commit ID's short() method is not interchangeable with a string method; an absent signature is not an empty signature string; a list must be mapped or joined before concatenation. Machine output should disable colour and use an unambiguous record separator. JSON escaping belongs at the field boundary, and a template regression should test control characters, absent optionals, merge parents, and conflicts rather than only checking that the command exits successfully.

Versioned automation should pin the target jj binary and test the effective syntax. A release-specific function, option, or command should be checked against that binary rather than assumed from online documentation. Keep a small fixture with a merge, a fork, a conflicted commit, a bookmark, a remote bookmark, a divergent change, and descriptions containing whitespace. Store expected symbolic results and assert full IDs only where the fixture is deterministic. This turns automation examples into executable contracts and makes release upgrades a deliberate review rather than a silent change of query meaning.

Workspace and concurrency proof: local materialisations are not branches

Workspaces complicate the word “current” in a productive way. The commit DAG and operation DAG are shared by the repository, but each workspace has its own working-copy commit and filesystem. A development workspace can be editing C while a review workspace is inspecting B and a build workspace is materialising a clean candidate. These are not three branches, and moving one workspace's @ does not move the others. The correct unit of coordination is a workspace symbol plus its working-copy commit, not a branch name inferred from the directory.

shared DAG:       A -- B -- C -- D
                       |         |
development:          dev@      |
review:                review@ --+
build:                 build@ at B

each @ is workspace-local; A, B, C, D are shared commits

Before a rewrite, list workspaces and record their working-copy commits. If a workspace has unrecorded filesystem edits, updating it after an ancestor rewrite can either snapshot those edits into a successor or require explicit stale-state repair. A build workspace should normally be treated as disposable: reproduce its commit from a full commit ID or bookmark, run the build, and avoid using its @ as a publication handle. A review workspace may intentionally remain at an old commit while the development workspace evolves; that can be valuable evidence during a code-review comparison.

jj workspace list
jj log -r 'working_copies()' -T 'change_id ++ " " ++ commit_id ++ "\n"'
jj -R ../project-review log -r @
jj -R ../project-build status
jj workspace update-stale

Concurrency adds a second distinction. Two processes can begin with the same repository operation head and create operations that have the same logical parent but different effects. Operation integration combines repository views according to jj's operation model; it does not guarantee that two independent rewrites of one change become one unambiguous diff. The commit evolution may still be divergent. Inspect operation parents and change evolution separately, and do not call a clean operation integration proof that the resulting review stack is semantically correct.

When an automated job runs against a shared repository, choose one of three contracts. It can use --ignore-working-copy and inspect a stable commit without owning snapshotting. It can own the workspace and allow normal snapshot boundaries, provided no editor or other jj process writes there. Or it can use an independent clone and exchange commits through an explicit remote bookmark. The third contract is usually easiest for CI because it separates filesystem ownership, operation history, and publication. A shell loop that happens to pass in a quiet checkout is not evidence that two writers are safe together.

Reference-reading protocol: from a question to a safe command

The command reference is most useful when read as a contract rather than a catalogue of flags. Start with the object being changed: a commit tree, a diff boundary, a bookmark, a remote observation, a workspace, a configuration layer, or an operation view. Then identify the selector language and its cardinality. Finally identify what jj will snapshot or rewrite at the command boundary. This order prevents a familiar option such as -r from hiding the fact that the selected values are commits while a nearby path expression is a fileset.

QuestionReference section to consultMinimum proof
Which changes should move?Rebase, squash, split, absorb, and revset sections.Print source roots/heads and affected descendants.
Which content should move?Fileset reference and tree-endpoint command contract.Show the selected diff, not only matching filenames.
Which review should update?Bookmark, GitHub, or Gerrit fieldbook.Print local target, fetched remote target, and review identity.
Why did a commit disappear?Evolution and operation reference.Compare operation views and the change's predecessor/successor chain.
Why did output change?Template and configuration references.Disable colour/pager and test the typed field or effective key.
Can another machine continue?Git backend, workspaces, and recovery recipes.Export a reachable commit/ref; do not rely on an operation ID or dirty files.

This protocol also supplies a stopping rule. If the command's source set is not printed, the remote destination is not explicit, the fileset has not been evaluated, or the current operation cannot be identified, the next action should be inspection rather than mutation. That is not excessive caution: jj makes broad rewrites cheap and recoverable, but external publication and unrecorded filesystem state remain expensive to reconstruct. A clear precondition is often faster than diagnosing a valid command applied to the wrong graph.

For readers moving from either conventional branch-based Git or a detached-HEAD Git practice, the resulting routine is intentionally light. Keep local work unnamed while it is private when that suits the task; retain or create a bookmark when a team convention or publication boundary needs a name. Use change IDs to follow mutable evolution, and use commit IDs plus the operation/evolution history where a detached-HEAD user would previously reach for the reflog. Use revsets to describe the graph region and filesets to describe the tree region. Use templates to make the evidence legible. Use the operation log before recovery, and use Git remotes when work must cross a clone or machine. The point is not to reproduce Git's branch choreography with new verbs; it is to make the graph, its identities, and its interfaces explicit enough that either Git habit can be replaced by deliberate jj state accounting.

Template debugging as typed observation

Templates deserve the same proof discipline as graph operations because a misleading display can cause a correct command to be applied to the wrong commit. Build a template in layers: first print one stable scalar, then add identity, then add topology, then add optional state, and only then add labels or formatting. Run with --no-pager --color never while debugging. This separates a template-language error from a pager, terminal-colour, or shell-quoting problem.

jj log -r @ -T 'commit_id.normal_hex() ++ "\n"'
jj log -r @ -T 'commit_id.short() ++ " " ++ change_id.short() ++ "\n"'
jj log -r @ -T 'parents.map(|p| p.commit_id().short()).join(", ") ++ "\n"'
jj log -r @ -T 'if(conflict(), "CONFLICT ", "clean ") ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'

If the second command fails, the problem is identity or method syntax; if the third fails, inspect the parent value's type and the lambda's receiver; if the fourth renders an unexpected state, query conflicts() independently. A template should not be used to infer a Boolean property from a pretty symbol when the corresponding predicate can be queried directly. Conversely, a human display can deliberately combine several fields, provided its labels make absence, divergence, and remote state visible.

Templates also define an interface for scripts. Stable machine output should use full hexadecimal IDs, explicit separators, disabled colour, and a documented treatment of empty descriptions and absent signatures. Do not parse graph indentation or the default log template. If a release changes the default display, that is a presentation change; if a method changes its type or disappears, it is a compatibility change that belongs in the version matrix. Keep one fixture for both cases so your templates remain executable observations rather than attractive but unverifiable output.

One final distinction is useful when auditing a result: an observation can be locally correct and still operationally incomplete. A template can show that @ has a particular commit ID without showing that a second workspace has another working-copy commit. A revset can show all visible mutable heads without showing hidden predecessors that explain divergence. A bookmark listing can show a local target without proving that the target was exported to Git. A clean conflict query can describe the current commit while a stale workspace still contains marker files from its previous materialisation. Compose observations across state components whenever the question crosses a boundary.

That compositional habit is the book's durable reference algorithm: identify the state component, choose the language that selects or renders it, make the version and scope explicit, perform the smallest operation, and inspect every coupled component that the operation could have changed. It is equally applicable to a one-line daily edit and to a Gerrit stack with several descendants, multiple review identities, a moving trunk, and a conflict. The command syntax is release-specific; the accounting discipline is the jj skill.

For publication notes, write the before and after in the same vocabulary as the repository: “local bookmark review moved from C to C′; fetched review@origin remained at C; change ID qqq continued; commit ID changed; descendants R and S were rebased; operation O_n recorded the rewrite.” This sentence is more useful than “the branch was force-pushed” because it states which facts are local, which are remote, which identities evolved, and which consequences require testing. It also gives a future maintainer enough information to reproduce the decision without reconstructing it from a terminal scrollback buffer.

Use the same record for negative results. “No bookmark moved” is different from “the remote bookmark was not fetched”; “no conflict is materialised here” is different from “no commit is conflicted”; “the command selected one commit” is different from “the selected commit is the intended change”. jj rewards this precision because its separate state machines let work continue in more situations, but that flexibility means an operator must state which absence was actually observed.

In practice, these records become lightweight review artefacts: a shell transcript with full IDs, a saved revset, a temporary bookmark name, and the operation ID. They are especially valuable around force publication, immutable-head overrides, Gerrit patch-set replacement, and cross-machine handoff. Delete the temporary bookmark only after the receiving ref or fetched trunk proves that the intended state is reachable elsewhere.

That final reachability check closes the loop: the work is no longer dependent on one workspace, one operation head, or one operator's memory. It is represented by a reachable commit and, where publication is intended, by an explicitly named ref whose remote observation has been fetched and recorded.

If publication was not intended, the same proof ends at a local bookmark or a documented reachable commit. This is the practical meaning of branchless work: no name is required for every intermediate state, but every state worth preserving must have a deliberate reachability story.

The discipline is deliberately symmetric: before an operation, prove selection; after it, prove reachability. Between those points, jj may change many commit IDs, but the operator can still account for every intended change, descendant, workspace, and publication boundary.

That is the shortest reliable description of advanced jj work: selection is a query, rewriting is a graph transformation, publication is an explicit ref transaction, and recovery is evidence-led state selection.

Keep that sentence beside the terminal until it becomes instinctive.

It is a compact operational model for every command and every difficult history.

It keeps local graph work, filesystem materialisation, publication, and recovery visible as separate but connected responsibilities.

That separation is the practical safeguard against confusing a valid local rewrite with a completed publication.

Every boundary should be named and independently inspected.

That is deliberate.

Advanced mechanics labbook — practice

The unusual features of jj become useful only when they are treated as mechanics rather than slogans. This labbook gives experiments for the features that most often alter an expert user's operating assumptions: immutable heads, hidden commits, divergent changes, concurrent operations, sparse working copies, fixers, signing, and machine-readable output.

Immutable heads: a policy boundary, not a property of a commit

The immutable set is computed from a revset alias. A commit is not born immutable because it has a particular author, description, or age. It is protected because it is reachable from the configured immutable heads under jj's rewrite rules. This makes the policy inspectable and changeable, but it also means that a configuration change can materially alter which commands are permitted.

[revset-aliases]
"immutable_heads()" = "builtin_immutable_heads() | main@origin | tags()"

In the target 0.45.1 configuration syntax, query the resulting set with jj log -r 'immutable_heads()', then compare it with builtin_immutable_heads(). Create a disposable child below a protected commit and try an edit or rebase. The expected failure is evidence that the alias is active. Change an unrelated key named revsets.immutable_heads and repeat: the function result should not change. This negative experiment is important because unknown TOML keys are not necessarily rejected.

Do not make every remote bookmark immutable by reflex. A repository that routinely rewrites review bookmarks may need a boundary at fetched trunk and release tags while leaving local topic commits mutable. Conversely, a release repository may intentionally include all remote tags. In jj 0.45.1, untracked remote tags participate in the default immutable-head policy; inspect the effective function before relying on it.

Hidden commits, evolution, and divergence

When a mutable commit is rewritten, its predecessor may become hidden from ordinary visible queries. The predecessor is not the same thing as a deleted Git commit: it remains addressable through its full commit ID, an evolution query, or a historical operation view while retention permits. The successor is the current visible form of the logical change. A divergent change occurs when two visible successors exist for one change identity, commonly because two independent operations rewrote the same predecessor and were later brought together.

          q_0 (predecessor, hidden)
         /  \
    q_1 (visible)  q_2 (visible)
      same jj change ID
      divergent evolution

Use jj evolog to see the evolution rather than relying on jj log -r 'all()'. A change ID alone can be ambiguous in the divergent state; use a change offset or an explicit set of successors. The commit IDs distinguish the two concrete trees and parent relationships. If one successor is the intended one, inspect its descendants and bookmarks before abandoning the other. jj 0.45.1 includes converge, which can assist with reconciling divergent evolutions, but it remains a rewrite whose result must be reviewed.

Evolution is a local explanatory history, not a publication protocol. A remote server sees exported Git objects and refs, not the full jj predecessor/successor relation. Preserve a mapping in review notes when a server-side review is being updated. The mapping is also useful when a test report or CI system still mentions the old commit ID.

Concurrent operations and integration

jj operations are serialised through an operation head, but concurrent processes can create operation nodes from a common parent. One process may use --no-integrate-operation or otherwise finish while another process has advanced the integrated head. The operation graph then records more than one line of activity. This is not the same as two commit branches: the competing nodes describe repository-view transitions, not necessarily different commit parents.

          op-A: rebase stack
         /
op_0 ----+
         \
          op-B: update bookmark

integrate or inspect both before choosing a current view

When diagnosing concurrency, identify the common operation parent, inspect each operation's diff, and determine whether their changes touch disjoint repository state. An operation that changed a bookmark and an operation that rewrote a commit may be integrable, but this is a property of their repository transformations. Do not infer it from process start order. The operation integration command and its conflict behaviour are documented by the installed help; test them in the recovery fixture.

A single-writer rule is still the simplest policy for a workspace filesystem. Operation integration does not make simultaneous editors safe. Two processes snapshotting the same files can race before the operation graph has a chance to record the difference. Separate workspaces for build/test processes reduce that risk; separate clones eliminate shared filesystem ownership but also create independent operation histories.

Sparse working copies

Sparse patterns define which files are materialised in a workspace. They do not change the commit tree, the revset result, or the publication ref. A file absent from the sparse working copy can still exist in the commit and can still be selected by a root-qualified fileset. This is the correct mental model for a large monorepo: sparse state is a materialisation choice, not a history filter.

# Inspect the current pattern set.
jj sparse list

# Replace it with an explicit root-relative selection.
jj sparse set --clear --add src --add tests

# Restore the full materialisation when needed.
jj sparse reset

sparse edit opens the sparse-pattern configuration editor; it does not accept a fileset argument in 0.45.1. Use sparse set for command-line patterns and sparse reset for the full default state. A successful sparse command should be verified by checking both sparse list and actual filesystem presence. Test with at least one selected file and one excluded file so a no-op or inverted pattern cannot pass on exit status alone.

Fileset matching and sparse materialisation interact in a predictable but easy-to-miss way. jj file list -r @ -- root-file:docs/api.md can report a path that is not materialised. A subsequent external tool may fail because the file is absent locally, while jj can still reason about it in the stored tree. Use a full workspace for a tool that needs the entire tree or materialise the required sparse paths first.

Fixers as controlled rewrites

A fixer is an external transformation associated with a fileset and a commit selection. The tool should be deterministic, preserve the intended file encoding, and return a meaningful exit status. The fix command can rewrite selected commits, which means an innocent-looking formatter run may create successors throughout a stack. Treat fixer configuration as executable code: review the command, arguments, environment, and selected paths.

[fix.tools.rustfmt]
command = ["rustfmt", "--edition", "2021"]
patterns = ["root-glob:**/*.rs"]

[revsets]
fix = "mutable() & ::@"

The exact schema fields and command capabilities must be taken from the target version's config schema. The example illustrates the design, not an assertion that every tool accepts every field. First run the fixer on one disposable commit and one fileset. Record the diff before and after, inspect its change ID and descendants, then expand the commit set. If the tool changes generated files, keep generated-file policy separate from source formatting policy.

Fixers and absorb solve different problems. A fixer computes a transformation from an external program; absorb assigns existing working-copy diff hunks to ancestor changes. Running a formatter and then absorb may produce a clean stack, but it can also distribute formatting changes across reviews in a way the reviewer did not expect. Choose one ownership policy and inspect the resulting diff boundaries.

Running commands over commits

jj run is a graph-oriented facility for invoking a command over selected commits. The crucial question is whether the command is a predicate, an inspection, or a mutation. A test command should leave no meaningful filesystem mutation; a generator or fixer can intentionally alter the commit context. The commit domain must be printed before running, and the command's exit status should be associated with the selected commit in an artefact.

domain='main@origin..@ & mutable()'
jj log -r "$domain" -T 'commit_id.normal_hex() ++ "\n"'

# The exact run options are target-version specific; inspect jj run --help.
jj run -r "$domain" -- ./ci/check-one-commit
jj op log

Do not build a shell loop around jj edit unless you explicitly need one. Such a loop changes workspace state, can snapshot files at each iteration, and is easy to interrupt in a state that the operation graph does not describe as one conceptual test. If the command is intended to run once per commit, use jj's commit-oriented interface and capture its documented environment. If it is intended to test the current stack as a whole, run it once at a deliberate workspace commit instead.

Signing lifecycle

Signing belongs to the commit metadata layer. It is not a property of the change ID, and it is not equivalent to a remote host's verified badge. A signing operation can rewrite a commit and its descendants. If a local publication bookmark points at the affected tip, the bookmark can move locally while the remote ref stays at the old object until push.

jj log -r 'mutable() & ::@' -T '
commit_id.short() ++ " " ++ change_id.short() ++ " " ++
if(signature, "signed", "unsigned") ++ "\n"
'
jj sign -r 'mutable() & ::@'
jj log -r 'mutable() & ::@' -T '
commit_id.normal_hex() ++ " " ++ change_id.normal_hex() ++ "\n"
'

Configure a signing backend and key only after testing verification outside jj. GPG and SSH agents, key trust, hardware tokens, and server acceptance are external dependencies. Do not include secret material in configuration snapshots or research output. When signing a published stack, record the old commit IDs and verify that the review system accepts the new exported objects before moving a release tag.

Lab: machine-readable output

Human output is a user interface. Machine output should define a schema. Use full IDs, JSON or a delimiter that cannot occur unescaped, explicit colour/pager settings, and a version field when output crosses process boundaries. A template that prints a short ID and description is suitable for a human log but not for a database key.

jj --no-pager --color never log -r 'all()' -T '
json("jj-0.45.1") ++ "\t" ++
json(commit_id.normal_hex()) ++ "\t" ++
json(change_id.normal_hex()) ++ "\t" ++
json(description.first_line()) ++ "\n"
'

Descriptions may contain newlines, tabs, quotes, and Unicode. JSON encoding handles these at the record boundary; a hand-rolled tab format must escape or reject them. Parent order is meaningful for a merge, so preserve the list rather than converting it to an unordered set. Remote and bookmark names can also contain characters that make naive whitespace parsing unsafe.

For a script that performs mutation, use a two-phase protocol. Phase one renders and validates the candidate set and all preconditions. Phase two repeats the selection in the actual command and records the operation ID and resulting state. The graph can change between phases, so a long-running automation process should either hold an appropriate repository lock through the command or fail if its preconditions no longer match.

Shell completion and debugging

Generate completion from the installed binary with jj util completion and install it according to the shell's conventions. Bash, Zsh, and Fish have different completion file locations and evaluation rules; test the generated file in a clean shell. Completion describes command and alias syntax, but it is not a compatibility promise across releases. Regenerate it after a jj upgrade.

For a bug report, include jj version, the command, the exact revset/fileset/template, whether the repository is colocated, the relevant operation ID, and a reduced graph. Use --debug when requested by the installed help or issue instructions, but do not treat debug output as a stable API. Redact remote URLs, credentials, private descriptions, and signing identifiers before sharing.

Practice curriculum — twenty graph-first labs

These labs are designed for an experienced Git user who wants to internalise jj's semantics. Each lab starts with a disposable repository and ends with an assertion. Run them with the target binary and a clean environment; use the symbolic descriptions in the expected state rather than hard-coded generated IDs. The point is to observe the graph and operation transitions, not to memorise a transcript whose IDs will differ on every run.

Lab 1: snapshot boundary

Initialise a repository, create a file, and inspect jj status. Then edit the file without running jj and execute jj log -r @. The ordinary command snapshots the edit before rendering the log. Repeat with jj --ignore-working-copy log -r @ before and after a deliberate snapshot. The recorded tree differs from the filesystem in the first observation and agrees after the snapshot. The experiment separates a filesystem edit from a commit-tree edit and proves why a read command can create an operation.

printf 'one\n' > value.txt
jj status
printf 'two\n' > value.txt
jj --ignore-working-copy diff
jj diff
jj --ignore-working-copy log -r @ -T 'commit_id.normal_hex() ++ "\n"'

Do not use git status as the only comparison in a colocated repository: Git's index/worktree view and jj's working-copy commit are different observations. Record the operation log before and after each command. A snapshot-only operation is still relevant when diagnosing a race.

Lab 2: identity through description changes

Create and describe a change, record its commit and change IDs, then run jj describe again. The commit ID changes because metadata is part of the commit identity. The change ID normally remains the same because the operation is an evolution of one logical change. A child of the commit receives a successor because its parent object changed. Render all three values before and after, and use evolog to connect them.

Repeat with a metadata change on an ancestor that has a local publication bookmark. Verify that the local bookmark follows the successor while the remote bookmark remains unchanged. This is the minimal experiment that prevents a Git expert from treating commit IDs as long-lived change identifiers in a mutable repository.

Lab 3: edit versus a bookmark

Create a bookmark at a child and then run jj edit on its parent. The bookmark remains at the child; only the current workspace's @ moves. Edit the parent, snapshot, and inspect the child successor. The bookmark's target may follow the rewritten local evolution, but its name and the workspace pointer remain separate state. Add a second workspace and repeat the edit there to see that each workspace has a local @.

The assertion is not “the prompt changed”. It is: the workspace symbol resolves to the expected commit, the bookmark resolves to its expected target, and the graph has the expected parent edge. Use a template rather than relying on the current default display.

Lab 4: rebase source shapes

Build a forked graph and apply the same destination with -r, -s, and -b in separate disposable copies. With -r, only the selected commits are explicitly sourced; with -s, the source's descendants are included; with -b, the branch-shaped selection follows the command's topology definition. Compare the parent arrays after each operation.

Then introduce a merge and repeat. The visual graph can make the three results look similar while their selected sets differ. A proper lab report contains the source expression, the expanded selected IDs, destination IDs, and resulting parent edges. This is the evidence needed to choose a rebase mode for a real stack.

Lab 5: insertion after and before

Start with A-B-C and a separate D. Use the insert-after mode to place D after B and the insert-before mode to place D before C. The final graph can be linear in both cases, but the operation has different destination semantics when the named commit has multiple children or when the destination is a merge. Add a second child to B and verify whether the command rewrites one path or creates a graph with multiple parents/children according to the documented selection.

Use a parent template in the assertion. “It appears between B and C” is not enough if D gained a second parent or if C was rebased to a new successor.

Lab 6: partial squash

Create one change touching src/api.rs, tests/api.rs, and docs/api.md. Squash only the tests into the parent. Use a path listing before and after, then compare the diff of the source and destination. The source tree may still include unchanged paths; what matters is the diff relative to its parent. Repeat using an unqualified src path from a subdirectory and then using root:src. The differing result demonstrates why portable scripts should use root-qualified paths.

Lab 7: split with a descendant

Split a mixed change that has a child. Record the original child commit ID and parent. After the split, locate the child's successor through its change ID and inspect the new two-edge path. Confirm that the first and second split changes contain disjoint diffs whose combination equals the original diff. Then modify the description of the first part and show that the second part's commit ID can change again because its parent changed.

This lab makes two consequences visible: a split is not only a file-selection operation, and descendant rebasing is not an optional follow-up step. The child is maintained as a graph successor even when the user never selected it directly.

Lab 8: absorb ownership

Make an API change and a later test change, then edit one line in the API and another line in the test while at the tip. Run absorb and inspect which diff hunks moved into which ancestors. Use a deliberately ambiguous diff hunk to see how the tool handles uncertainty under the target configuration. The expected assertion is about diff ownership, not merely that the working-copy diff became empty.

Keep the original diff in a file before absorb and compare the union of resulting diffs with it. If the union is not equivalent, investigate line-range handling, ignored files, or a tool/configuration problem before accepting the operation.

Lab 9: duplicate versus revert

Create a feature change and a later change that modifies the same area. Duplicate the feature onto a separate base, then in another copy revert it at the later base. The duplicate carries the positive diff and gets a new change identity. The revert carries the inverse and gets a new change identity. If later context conflicts, the revert can contain a stored conflict; resolve it without deleting the fact that the original feature occurred.

Use this lab when a reviewer says “bring that diff over” or “undo that diff”. Those sentences do not specify whether the desired operation is copy or inverse.

Lab 10: abandon and recovery

Make a stack with a bookmark at its tip and abandon its middle change. Inspect the resulting descendants, bookmark state, evolution log, and operation log. Do not run storage GC. Recover the old change by its explicit identity, then either duplicate it onto a new base or restore the prior repository view in a copy of the fixture.

Repeat after making an unrelated description edit. Compare immediate undo with historical operation inspection. The lab's conclusion is that recovery is easier when the operator records operation IDs and uses an explicit recovery policy before performing further work.

Lab 11: non-distributive ranges

Use a merge graph and compare (C|D).. with C.. | D... Render both sets as symbolic descriptions. Then compute C.. & D.. and demonstrate the equality with (C|D)... Add a hidden predecessor explicitly and repeat; observe how the search domain changes. This lab should be a permanent regression test because range intuition is one of the most persistent sources of Git-to-jj mistakes.

Lab 12: symbol collision

Create a bookmark whose name is also a unique prefix of a commit ID, then resolve the bare symbol, commit_id(), and bookmarks(exact:"name") forms. Add a tag with the same name and compare tags(exact:"name"); observe the documented priority of the bare symbol. Repeat with a non-unique prefix and with a divergent change ID. The expected results belong in the query-lab documentation so later aliases do not accidentally depend on resolution priority.

Lab 13: fileset and shell parsing

Create files whose names contain spaces, parentheses, wildcard characters, and a colon. Run a simple path without inner syntax, then a complement and a function expression. Capture the shell's arguments with a harmless wrapper if necessary. The wrapper shows whether the shell expanded a glob before jj received it. Quote the complete expression and use explicit root-file: or root-glob: forms in the corrected command.

Repeat from a nested directory. A fileset can be syntactically correct yet select the wrong directory because its base coordinate changed. Root-qualified expressions are the portable answer.

Lab 14: one fileset, four consumers

Define source_paths = root:src ~ root-prefix-glob:src/**/generated/**. Use it with file list, diff, restore, and squash in copies of the same fixture. The set of matched paths should be stable, but the command effect differs: list displays, diff filters output, restore copies selected file contents, and squash changes diff ownership. Record the source/destination commits for the two mutating commands.

Lab 15: template optional values

Render author and committer signatures for a commit with distinct identities. Render a root with no parents, an unsigned commit with no signature, and a commit with no bookmark. Build a template that handles all three without error using conditionals and fallbacks. Then deliberately remove the guard and keep the failing command in the lab notes as a type/error example.

The assertion is that the template has a defined output contract for absence. A blank field is not the same as the literal string (none); choose deliberately.

Lab 16: JSON output

Make a description containing quotes, a newline, a tab, and Unicode. Render a JSON object with full commit/change IDs and parent arrays, then parse it with a JSON parser. Compare with a hand-written tab-separated template. The JSON record survives the description content; the hand-written format needs escaping rules. This is the minimum experiment before using jj output as CI input.

Lab 17: conflict propagation

Create two branches that edit the same line, merge or rebase them, and inspect the resulting conflict value. Add a descendant without resolving the parent. Query conflicts() over the stack and materialise the conflict in the workspace. Resolve only the intended file, snapshot, and query again. Inspect the descendant successor and run the test at the tip.

Repeat with a multi-sided conflict and write down each parent. The purpose is to prevent “ours/theirs” from becoming an unexplained policy when the graph has more than two meaningful sides.

Lab 18: operation forensics

Perform a description edit, a bookmark move, an ancestor rewrite, and a snapshot. Use op log to identify them and op diff to distinguish their repository-view effects. Read the repository at an earlier operation with --at-operation. Verify that this historical read does not import current filesystem edits. Then use op restore only in a disposable copy and compare the current operation graph before and after.

Lab 19: workspace staleness

Add a build workspace at a stack tip. Rewrite the ancestor from the development workspace and list workspaces. Inspect the build workspace's filesystem before updating it. If it contains no valuable edits, update-stale and assert that its @ is current. If it contains an unrecorded build configuration, preserve that file first and repeat. This demonstrates why stale repair is a stateful operation rather than a screen refresh.

Lab 20: cross-clone handoff

Create a bare remote and two clones. Make an unfinished change in clone A, publish a temporary bookmark, fetch in clone B, and create a new working-copy child there. Check that the commit is available in B but the operation IDs from A are not. Rewrite in B and push a deliberately different bookmark. Fetch in A and inspect both remote observations. Clean the temporary name only after confirming which machine owns the work.

This is the final lab because it combines the book's layers: a bookmark is the transport interface, the commit graph is portable through Git, the working-copy symbol is local, and the operation graph is clone-local.

Hosting protocol fieldbook — workflows

jj does not know whether a Git ref will be shown as a GitHub branch, a pull request head, a Gerrit change, or an internal deployment ref. It exports Git-compatible objects and names; the host interprets the ref and commit message according to its own protocol. A disciplined workflow therefore has a local half and a server half. The local half can be validated with a bare Git remote. The server half must be labelled as documented or server-dependent.

GitHub pull requests as a ref state machine

PhaseLocal jj stateGit ref stateGitHub state
UnpublishedMutable unnamed stack below fetched trunkNo feature refNo PR or an old PR unrelated to current stack
Boundary chosenBookmark at intended review tipLocal branch/ref candidateNot yet changed
First pushBookmark tracked or explicitly related to remoteRemote feature ref createdPR can be opened against selected base
Review iterationOne or more changes rewritten; successors and IDs changeSame ref updated to a new tipNew commit set/iteration displayed by the host
Stack updateEarly change rewritten; descendants automatically rebasedSeveral publication refs may moveDependent PR bases and diffs may need UI updates
MergeFetch host result; rebase/clean remaining local workTrunk ref advances; feature ref may remainHost applies chosen merge strategy
CleanupForget/delete local publication names intentionallyDelete feature ref only when intendedPR remains an audit/UI object even if its head ref is deleted

GitHub's pull request is not a jj object. The local bookmark is the bridge because the host requires a Git ref. A PR can remain open while the local bookmark is deleted if the remote ref remains; conversely, deleting a local bookmark cannot close a PR. Decide explicitly whether cleanup is local, remote, or UI-level.

For a single-change PR, the local stack may be main@origin-A-B-@ with a bookmark at @. For a stack, create a bookmark at each review boundary and ensure each dependent ref has the intended base. When an early change is amended, the descendant ref must move as well. Push order matters for a human review experience, even if the Git transport can send all reachable objects in one negotiation.

Rejected updates and remote movement

A rejected push is an information event. Fetch the remote and render the local and remote targets. The remote may have moved because another machine pushed, because a reviewer or automation updated the branch, because the bookmark was renamed, or because the server refuses the selected update. Do not immediately rebase onto whatever appears first in the default log.

jj git fetch --remote origin
jj bookmark list --remote origin --tracked
jj log -r 'review | review@origin' -T '
commit_id.normal_hex() ++ " " ++ change_id.normal_hex() ++ " " ++
description.first_line() ++ "\n"

If the remote target contains work that must be preserved, rebase or merge onto it according to the review policy. If the remote target is an obsolete version of the same review and the server permits an intentional replacement, document the old target and perform that replacement through the hosting system or a deliberately verified native-Git operation; jj 0.45.1's jj git push has no backwards-update flag. Tracking helps compare the states; it does not make the decision for you.

Fieldbook: fork/upstream topology

Keep the fork remote and upstream remote distinct. Fetch upstream trunk under its own remote name, publish PR refs to the fork, and avoid aliases that treat origin/main as universally authoritative. The graph can contain both:

main@upstream -- A -- B
                  \
                   C -- D
                        ↑
                 pr/42@fork

For a contributor, main@upstream is the update base while pr/42@fork is the publication observation. A local bookmark named pr/42 can track the fork ref; it should not be confused with a local main that tracks upstream. If the fork ref is deleted after merge, forget or delete only the local state whose removal is intended.

Gerrit changes as commit-message identity

Gerrit commonly associates patch sets by a Change-Id: I... footer in the commit message. That footer is not jj's change ID. The local jj change ID may stay constant across a rewrite; the Gerrit footer may stay constant so the server associates a new commit with the same review; and the commit ID changes every time the relevant object content, metadata, parent, or footer changes.

Local eventjj change IDCommit IDGerrit interpretation
Initial description and uploadQq_0Change I123, patch set 1
Edit subject/body but preserve footerQq_1Usually another patch set of I123, subject changed
Rewrite parent through descendant rebaseQq_2New patch set if uploaded with same footer
Remove or replace footerQq_3May create a new change or be rejected by server policy
Duplicate the changeD, not Qd_0Footer determines whether it is associated with I123 or another review
Abandon locallyQ may remain in evolutionOld objects may remain locallyServer review is unaffected unless a protocol command changes it

Never use a jj change ID where a Gerrit footer is required. Conversely, do not replace a jj change ID with a Gerrit footer in local revsets. Keep both in the commit description/log record and explain which identity a review comment refers to.

Three-change upload sequence

main@origin -- T -- Q -- R -- S
                       Iq   Ir   Is
                       ↑         ↑
                    review Q   review S
  1. Fetch the target branch and create the stack in local jj without publication bookmarks.
  2. Verify each description has the intended Gerrit footer and that the changes are in dependency order.
  3. Render the stack with full commit IDs and jj change IDs; record this as upload iteration zero.
  4. Run the available jj 0.45.1 jj gerrit upload --dry-run with explicit remote, branch, and commit selection.
  5. Upload the stack and record the server URLs/identities returned by the Gerrit instance.

The upload command's review options can set reviewers, CCs, labels, topics, hashtags, WIP/ready state, privacy, notifications, and other server push options. Their spelling and server acceptance are version/instance-sensitive. In a shared script, pass the remote and branch explicitly and keep server options in a reviewed configuration file. Test the local selection and footer before relying on the server response.

Early review feedback

Suppose the reviewer comments on Q. Run jj edit Q, make the smallest change that addresses the comment, and snapshot. The local graph becomes Q′, R′, S′. The Q change ID normally remains Q; all three commit IDs can change because R and S inherit a new parent. The Gerrit footer should remain Iq. Before upload, compare the interdiff of Q and Q′, and separately compare R/R′ and S/S′ to identify changes caused only by rebasing.

jj evolog -r 'Q'
jj log -r 'Q::S' -T '
change_id.short() ++ " " ++ commit_id.short() ++ " " ++
parents.map(|p| p.commit_id().short()).join(",") ++ " " ++
description.first_line() ++ "\n"
'
jj gerrit upload --dry-run --remote gerrit --remote-branch main -r 'Q::S'

Upload the intended commits with the same footer. The server-side patch-set association and displayed diff are documented by Gerrit and can vary with submit rules. If a footer was accidentally changed, stop and decide whether to restore it or intentionally create a new review; do not guess from a short commit ID.

Partial landing and trunk movement

If Q lands but R and S remain under review, the remote main ref may point to a server-created commit rather than q′. Fetch it. The remaining local stack is no longer necessarily based on the object that was uploaded for Q. Rebase R/S onto the fetched trunk and inspect their diff ranges against the new base. Preserve their Gerrit footers and upload new patch sets.

jj git fetch --remote gerrit
jj log -r 'main@gerrit'
jj rebase -s 'roots(main@gerrit..S)::' -d main@gerrit
jj log -r 'main@gerrit..@' -T 'commit_id.short() ++ " " ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'
jj gerrit upload --remote gerrit --remote-branch main -r 'main@gerrit..@'

The exact source expression must be adjusted for the actual graph. The point is to avoid keeping an obsolete local Q as the base merely because it shares a description with the landed review. If a server performs a squash or merge, the fetched ref is the authority for the new base.

Topics, reviewers, and push options

Topics and reviewers are Gerrit metadata, not jj bookmarks. A topic can group several Gerrit changes while the local graph supplies their dependency edges. Reviewers and labels can be supplied at upload time or through server UI/API. Push options can request draft/WIP, ready, private, notifications, validation, attention-set changes, or topic updates where the server allows them. Treat these options as side effects and record them in the upload command log.

Do not make a local bookmark called topic carry the meaning of a Gerrit topic. A bookmark names a commit; a Gerrit topic groups server-side changes. They can share a string for human convenience, but they are different namespaces and can drift.

Conflict, abandonment, and replacement

If the stack conflicts while rebasing onto new Gerrit trunk, resolve the stored conflict locally, test, and upload. If a review is abandoned, decide whether the local change is also abandoned, duplicated for another target, or retained as a historical change. If a replacement review is created, use a new Gerrit footer when the server expects a distinct change and a new publication boundary. A jj operation restore can recover local graph state; it cannot resurrect a review the server has permanently deleted.

One repository, two publication protocols

A single local DAG can feed GitHub and Gerrit independently:

                 +- github/pr-42 --→ GitHub PR
main@upstream ---+
                 \- gerrit stack ---→ refs/for/main

The graph is shared; the names, remotes, review identities, and server policies are not. Put host-specific publication names in separate namespaces, such as github/pr-42 and gerrit/topic-42. Fetch both remotes but qualify their trunk symbols. After rewriting a shared ancestor, inspect both publication boundaries before pushing either. It may be correct to update one review and leave the other at the previous object.

Keep a local publication ledger with columns for local bookmark, remote, remote bookmark, host review ID, jj change IDs, commit IDs, base ref, and last fetch. This is especially valuable when the same code is under review on two hosts with different policies. The ledger is not jj state; it is a human review aid that explains why a local graph has multiple outward interfaces.

Appendix directory and quick lookups

Use this directory to choose the right appendix. The short entries below are deliberately labelled as directory cards where a fuller reference appears later in the same book. The links are the authoritative route: they prevent a reader from mistaking a one-page orientation card for the complete fileset, template, configuration, or hosting reference.

    remote [add list remove rename set-url] root]

    [abandon diff integrate log restore revert show]

      markdown-help snapshot]

Role: quick lookup. This is generated from jj 0.45.1 help. The command paths are expanded in the reader-facing entries in Part XV. Use the tree to find a family, then use the command entry for arguments, options, cardinality, mutation, and examples.

Appendix B — Option index

FlagWhere/meaning
-R, --repositoryOperate on a repository path.
--ignore-working-copyDo not snapshot/update filesystem.
--no-integrate-operationCreate but do not integrate operation.
--ignore-immutableBypass rewrite protection.
